# To the READER.

->READER,<-

<margin>His need to provide a preface for this present treatise.</margin>
1. If it were only to apologize for breaking that silence which I seemed to have imposed on myself—by publicly hinting at the likelihood of it—it would have been necessary for that reason alone to write a *preface* to excuse the unexpected publication of this new *treatise*. <note>More refers to a previous public statement where he suggested he might stop publishing new works.</note>

But I have chosen such a *subject* that its very *title* sounds so harsh and discordant to some ears that this alone would be enough to force me into the trouble of a *prefatory apology*: **The Idea of Antichristianism**. Both of those words are so heavily burdened with preconceived offense and prejudice that the book might be judged and condemned before it is even read, simply for the sake of the *title*, unless I prepare the way for a better reception through proper and timely information.

<margin>The nature of this *Idea of Antichristianism*, and why it is not subject to any rude interpretation.</margin>
2. Know then, *reader*, that this *Idea* which I present to you is not a vain, hollow, Platonist <note>More, a "Cambridge Platonist," uses "Platonical" here to address the common misconception that an "Idea" is just an abstract, imaginary concept rather than an essential reality.</note>, or imaginary invention <note>original: "Chimerical Figment"</note>, as some imagine every *Idea* to be. Nor is my treatment of *Antichristianism* a rude, uncivil, or uncharitable way of ranting <note>original: "phraseological Form of railing"</note> against things or people who are not only innocent, but sacred. On the contrary, the nature of *Antichristianism* is so accurately defined by...

<meta>catchword: by</meta>

<summary>In this preface, Henry More defends his decision to publish a work with such a controversial title, explaining that he is not using "Antichristianism" as a mindless insult, but rather defining it as a specific philosophical and theological "Idea." He aims to clear away reader prejudice before they engage with his deeper arguments.</summary>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues Henry More's preface to "A Modest Inquiry into the Mystery of Iniquity." He is defending his use of the term "Antichristianism" by arguing that a clear, abstract definition prevents the term from being used as a casual insult.</meta>

<language>English</language>
<page-type>preface</page-type>
<header>To the READER.</header>

through this *Idea* [concept], and so appropriately limited by it, that it is actually a bridle on the tongues and lips of those who—not knowing what is truly *Antichristian* and what is not—call anything they dislike in religion by that name whenever they are in a petty mood or it does not suit their own whims and fancies. Furthermore, since this treatise is written as an *Idea*—that is, an abstract description or outline of the nature of *Antichristianism* without applying it to any specific person—what rudeness, incivility, or lack of charity could this project possibly carry? Is it considered rude or uncivil to define *vices* in the abstract <note>original: "in abstracto"</note> and describe them in their components and targets, and in whatever circumstances lead to a clear and perfect knowledge of them, provided it is done faithfully and skillfully? And truly, I can confidently appeal to the judgment of any capable and unbiased reader to see that I have not falsified anything in my description of *Antichristianism*. What I have identified as *Antichristian* is so by its very nature, whether it is called that or not. If everyone imitated this accuracy, nothing would do more for the peace of *Christendom* and the steady, firm promotion of *Protestantism* in every nation.

<margin>The abuse of a term does not take away the right to use it correctly.</margin>
3. Well, some might reply: "Even if nothing is handled falsely or unfaithfully in this task <note>original: "Province"</note> you have undertaken, isn't the project itself—though just and useful—somewhat ignoble, inglorious, and ungentlemanly? Is it not beneath you to color your style and stain your pen with terms like *Antichrist* and *Antichristianism*? The breath of the unrefined and ignorant masses usually smells as strongly of these words as it does of *onions* and *garlic*; they have so defiled these words by shouting them rudely and aimlessly that they have made them unfit for any polite person to say." In response, I must honestly confess that the *title* of my *discourse* may seem less appealing for this very reason. However, it is the true and proper name for the subject I am discussing. If these unrefined people had only been taught to apply the *term* correctly, it would never have acquired such a sickening prejudice as it seems to have done. And I hope I am at least excusable, if not deserving of thanks, for taking the trouble to teach them its proper and appropriate use.

<summary>More argues that by defining "Antichristianism" as an abstract concept rather than a personal attack, he provides a necessary intellectual restraint against the term's common abuse as a vulgar insult. He asserts that a precise definition is essential for the peace of Christendom and the progress of Protestantism.</summary>

<margin>That opposing Antichristianism, in the sense used here, is not at all ungentlemanly, but rather heroic.</margin>

4. But if there is any further meaning in the *objection*—as if it were ignoble or ungentlemanly, and beneath a man of a generous spirit, to concern himself with detecting or opposing *Antichristianism* itself—I must take the liberty to declare that I think the *objector* does not understand what *Antichristianism* is, or at least not what I understand by it, or how I have described it in this *Idea* [concept]. For the *Antichristianism* which I oppose, and expose here to the view of the world, is nothing other than real *Impiety*, gross *Fraud* and *Deception* <note>original: "Couzenage"</note>, and the most barbarous and unparalleled *Cruelty* against the harmless *members of Christ*. All of this—which infinitely worsens the crimes—is done under the show and pretense of *Piety* and *Religion*; indeed, under the most sacred of all religions, *Christianity* itself. If these things, therefore, are not only uncivil and ungentlemanly, but *savage* <note>original: "ferine"</note>, brutish, or rather *Diabolical*, can it be ungentlemanly or uncivil to heartily and openly oppose them?

<margin>Made evident to the judgments of Believers.</margin>
<margin>John 5:44.</margin>
<margin>John 12:43.</margin>

5. Or, to appeal more distinctly and particularly to two types of men: first, to those who have a conscience and a belief in the *Christian Religion* as it is delivered in the *Holy Scripture*. I ask them: how ignoble or inglorious a thing do they deem it to oppose that which is plainly and palpably opposite to the *Word of God* and to the *Commandments of Jesus Christ*? Is it beneath them to endeavor to demolish that which supplants and frustrates the very *purpose of the Gospel of Christ*, and is so diametrically opposed to the *interests of his Kingdom*? Certainly, whoever can judge such a *design* as this to be dishonorable must be of the same spirit as that group whom our Saviour long ago most righteously reproved in these words: *How can you believe, who receive honor from one another, and do not seek the honor that comes from God only?* As it is also said in another place: *For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.*

<margin>But even to Infidels or Atheists themselves.</margin>

6. And now for those who think it is such a noble and glorious thing to be indifferent to all *religions*, or indeed to believe in none—those who are not even touched by a sense of our common *Christianity*, which all who call themselves *Christians* agree upon—yet if they have not...

...discarded the *feelings* of common *Humanity* (than which nothing can be more *barbarous* and *unrefined*), I ask them: what offense can it be against the *laws* of the highest *nobility* <note>original: "Generosity"</note> to express a man's disgust and enmity toward a system of things that runs directly against not only the *Law* of *Christ* and the plain *teachings* of the *Scriptures*, but also against the most indispensable and indelible *rules* of *Nature* and *Reason*, and against the common and universally acknowledged *rights* of *mankind*? Suppose you yourself scarcely believe there is a *God*, much less anything to come after this *life*, and therefore have a *conscience* open to any *religion*, no matter how wicked or foolish, and can laugh at the arrogant *deceptions* <note>original: "Impostures"</note> of the *priest* when you are finished. 

But can you be sure that your *children* will be like you, or that the *wife* of your bosom will remain so, even if she is for now? Can you promise the same for your most intimate *friend*, who is as dear to you as yourself? Indeed, can you promise for yourself that *God* might not powerfully strike your *conscience* at some point and convert you to the true knowledge of himself and of his son *Jesus*? Now I tell you briefly and all at once: the very *structure* <note>original: "Contexture"</note> of this *Antichristianism* which I oppose is a mere *trap* or *net* spread for your own *life*, and the lives of your *friend*, your *wife*, and your *children*. No one can be, in knowledge and judgment, the *openly faithful servants of God* and of his *Christ* without being, by that very fact <note>original: "ipso facto"</note>, made vulnerable <note>original: "obnoxious"</note> to the bloody *savagery* of this *Antichristian monster*.

But suppose your own *conscience* is not yet awakened; can you be so devoid of natural *affection* or—while you talk so loudly of *nobility*—degenerate so far below even the brute *creatures* as to not be affected, or even deeply and unbearably *distressed*, at the dragging of your *wife* from your *bosom*, and the tearing of your *friends* and *children* from your *arms*? ...children, but your *wife* herself—as if she were a *witch* or a *poisoner* of her *husband*—could be burned at the *stake*. This might happen even if she were pregnant, the birth being forced out by the merciless *midwifery* of the parching *flames*. All this cruelty is exercised upon them simply because they refuse to sin against God and their own conscience.

This holy *sensitivity* <note>original: "Sensibilitie"</note> of spirit and awe-filled *reverence* of the *Deity* might seem like a weakness to you, given the coarseness of your own *philosophy*. Yet, because it is a blemish that, even in your own judgment, carries no mark of dishonor—indeed, it is considered highly honorable in those who are successful, and is deeply pitied in those who are afflicted and suffering—it should not lessen your deep affection for your suffering *friends* in such a case. The *loveliness* of their character, their polite and *obliging* behavior, and their constant *faithfulness* and *helpfulness* in all *duties* and *affairs* have left such a deep impression of *love* and *esteem* in you that it cannot easily be erased.

Can therefore the opposing of such a barbarous system of things as this—which is so painful and intolerable to your own senses and judgment—be considered ignoble or inglorious under any pretext? Is it not instead highly *noble* <note>original: "Generous"</note> and *heroic*? To suggest otherwise would be like saying all the *acts* of *Hercules* <note>The legendary Greek hero known for his strength and his "labors" in killing monsters.</note>, and his famous victories over the destructive *monsters* of his age, were merely the petty exploits of some pitiful *schoolmaster* <note>original: "Pedant"</note> or *theatrical pretender* <note>original: "Histrionical Whiffler"</note>? 

On the contrary, we may safely declare that anyone who does not feel a hearty loathing and abhorrence for such an ugly and hateful *structure* <note>original: "Frame"</note> as I have described in this *concept* <note>original: "Idea"</note> is not only in a state of being *spiritually unrenewed* <note>original: "Unregeneratedness"</note> and utterly devoid of the *life of God* (and consequently incapable of eternal *salvation*), but has even sunk below the nature of a *man*. Such a person has become not only uncivilized, but either *stupid* and *dull*, or else possesses a temperament that is plainly *savage* and *inhumane*.

7. But even if the *Antichristianism* <note>The system of religious corruption and persecution the author is attacking.</note> described in your *concept*—

<meta>This page continues Henry More’s defense of his "Idea of Antichristianism." He transitions from describing the horrors of religious tyranny to addressing critics who might argue that his description is merely a theoretical abstraction rather than a historical or prophetic reality.</meta>

# To the READER.

<margin>
That this *concept* <note>original: "Idea"</note> of *Antichristianism* is not a mere abstraction, but a true record from *history*. * *Herodotus* book 1, chapter 172.
</margin>

...if it (*some will further urge*) is such an impious and tragic business, yet in the meantime we must remember that it is only a *concept* <note>original: "Idea"</note>. Therefore, to have our emotions so stirred up against mere shadows would be as foolish and furious as the *Caunii* <note>A people of ancient Caria (modern Turkey) described by Herodotus as arming themselves to drive out foreign gods.</note> beating the empty *air* with their clubs, shouting out *to drive out the foreign gods* <note>original: "ἐκβάλλειν τὸς ξενικὸς θεὸς" (ekballein tous xenikous theous)</note> when there was no physical *object* before their eyes to pursue. But I do not need to repeat that our *inquiry* into this *mystery* is intentionally humble in more ways than one. And yet, I cannot hide the fact that this *Antichristian* system has emerged so far above the condition of a mere abstraction that its main features are plainly prophesied in *Holy Scripture*. I believe I have proven this with evidence as certain as *mathematics* in a *treatise* regarding that matter. As you know, *divine* prophecy is a very reliable guarantee of future reality. Indeed, the *progression* of time is so prefigured, and its duration so precisely measured out, that I may safely add that it has been more than just a concept for several *centuries*. While remaining within the bounds of humility, I may further declare that it is so far from being a mere abstraction that it is a vivid *image*, or a faithful *record* from *history*, of what has been too often, too much, and for too long within *Christendom*. Therefore, to explicitly state who is most involved in this system would have been a needless imitation of the clumsy methods of ancient, ignorant *painters*. Because they were unable to paint their *pictures* realistically enough, they were forced to write underneath one, *This is a bear*, and under another, *This is a horse*, or a *lion*, or whatever other *animal* they intended to depict.

<margin>

# To the READER.

...that *Imperious Lady of Rome* <note>A common Protestant rhetorical reference to the Roman Catholic Church.</note>, whom I cannot deny is most concerned in this *description*. But for our own *Church* <note>The Church of England.</note>, I declare that I could not devise <note>original: "excogitate"</note> anything that I believed, in my own judgment, would serve her *interests* better than the framing of this *concept* <note>original: "Idea"</note>. 

For consider how she is attacked by the *Romanists* <note>Roman Catholics.</note> on one hand and the *Sectaries* <note>Radical Protestant dissenters who had broken away from the Church of England.</note> on the other—corroding, undermining, and wearing her away from both sides. The *Romanists* claim she is *schismatic* <note>original: "Schismatical"; meaning she has split away from the "true" Catholic church.</note>, while the *Sectaries* claim she is *Antichristian*. 

What could be more useful or reasonable than to draw such a true and authentic *concept* of *Antichristianism*? By doing so, that other Church [Rome], which appears to bear such a close resemblance to it by comparison, may in the future be ashamed to call us *schismatics* for not *communicating* <note>Participating in the Eucharist or remaining in formal fellowship.</note> with her. Furthermore, once we are fully cleared <note>original: "assoiled"</note> from any stain of whatever is really and truly *Antichristian*, we may shame the *Sectaries* for their own *schismatic nature* in refusing to *communicate* with a *Church* that is so clearly pure and *apostolic*.

9. The importance of this project will, I hope, excuse my unexpected reappearance in public. She is not being reached for by only one hand, but is being stabbed at from both sides—or rather, as the *Psalmist* complains, she is surrounded by her enemies like a swarm of bees. # A MODEST ENQUIRY INTO THE MYSTERY OF INIQUITY.

## BOOK I.

### CHAPTER I.

*1. That the Mystery of Iniquity or Antichristianism implies the secret undermining of the goals of Christianity by a power that pretends to be Christian. 2. The inconvenience of describing Antichrist by circumstantial traits while leaving out the essential parts of the description. 3. The two general principles of which Antichristianism consists. 4. The correct method of drawing a true concept of Antichristianism, with a division of the sketch into its two most general parts.*

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'T' intertwined with foliage and vine patterns.</image-desc>The wickedness of the *Mystery* <note>original: "Mystery of Iniquity," a biblical term from 2 Thessalonians 2:7 referring to a hidden or deceptive form of evil.</note> we are about to discuss is not blatant *profanity* or openly admitted *evil*. This is evident from the title itself, as it is described as *Mysterious*, hiding itself under the appearance of *justice* or *godliness*. While this kind of *mystery* might work to undermine any religion established for the true worship of God and as a defense against *atheism* and *profanity*, there is no doubt that the *Mystery of Iniquity*—a phrase Christians use frequently—refers to *a mystery intended to defeat the purpose, weaken the power and effectiveness, and secretly undermine the very foundations of the religion called Christian.* For this reason, they also call this Mystery of Iniquity *Antichristianism*, and name its chief author and supporter (whether it is

<header>The great necessity of defining what Antichristianism is. Book I.</header>

one single person or body of men) by the name of ***Antichrist***: whether you understand that to mean *one who opposes Christ, or one who puts himself in the place of Christ*, pretending to act for, but indeed acting against, the true interest of His Kingdom.

2. The sound of these words and phrases has filled Christendom with their echo for several centuries. But I do not remember that even the most passionate hunters of this "strange beast"—not even those who thought they had found and captured him—have left such a perfect and essential description of his nature (separated from external circumstances) that a person might have a proper and full understanding of what this ***Mystery of Antichristianity*** <note>original: "Mystery of Antichristianity," referring to the deceptive nature of religious corruption that appears godly but acts against Christ.</note> really consists. Therefore, they have left the world liable to think that certain things are essential to this Mystery when they are not, and to think others do not belong to it when they actually do. It is as if, in the description of a ***bear***, someone was careful not to omit his collar and the ring in his nose, yet left out the essential parts of his body.

Such imperfect and vague representations tend only to stir up men's passions against things that are innocent in themselves, while overlooking those things that are truly vicious and harmful. For example, if a man should declare in general terms that the ***Turk*** <note>original: "Turk," a common historical shorthand for the Ottoman Empire or the religion of Islam.</note> is Antichrist, or the ***Pope***, without explaining what it was that actually made them so, the only result would be this: we would congratulate ourselves that we are neither "Turks" nor "Papists" (even though we may actually have a large measure of the *Mystery of Iniquity* within ourselves) and we would take offense at the sight of a **turban**, a **crosier** <note>original: "Crosier," a staff topped with a crook, carried by bishops as a symbol of their office.</note>, or a **mitre** <note>original: "Miter," a traditional ceremonial hat worn by bishops.</note> (or other things that are as harmless, or even more so, than these) simply because they are found among the Turks or the Papists. And yet, I think the most furious Reformers should not have so little wit in their anger as to think the Reformation is incomplete until they have used pickaxes and spades to dig down the ***seven hills*** at ***Rome*** <note>original: "seven Hills at Rome," a reference to the hills on which Rome was built, often associated in Protestant interpretation with the "seven mountains" in Revelation 17:9.</note> and tossed the earth with shovels toward the four winds of heaven. For that seems to be the most obvious external characteristic of the ***Whore of Babylon*** <note>original: "Whore of Babylon," a figure from the Book of Revelation often used by Reformers to symbolize a corrupt church.</note> (whoever that Whore may be) that is to be found in the **Scripture**.

3. We see it, therefore, very necessary—so that we do not fight against shadows—to seek out and propose such a description of ***Antichristianism*** as ignores harmless circumstances and includes what is truly and essentially *Antichristian*. We must not make anything a part of the ***Mystery of Iniquity*** that has no iniquity in it; for we cannot well define any recognized wickedness except as the result of some pretended holiness. In these two things, generally, does this *Mystery of Iniquity* or *Antichristianism* consist:

First, *in the instituting of such laws, or authoritatively teaching such doctrines, and promoting or commanding such practices, as naturally defeat and frustrate the true purpose and goal of the Gospel of Christ.*

And then, secondly, *in doing this with such trickery and such fair pretenses that they lead the world to believe, in the meantime, that they are doing the work of God and promoting the interest of the Kingdom of His Son Jesus.*

This, I say, in general, is the very nature and essence of ***Antichristianism***. And where this poison is swallowed by public authority, so that either one

<page-num>3</page-num>
<header>Chap. II. Wherein Antichristianism consists in the general.</header>

Any person, or political body, or both of them together, if they are the first beginners or continuers of this *Mystery of Iniquity* <note>original: "Mystery of Iniquity," a biblical phrase from 2 Thessalonians 2:7 referring to the hidden workings of evil and lawlessness within the church.</note> in its full scope, are surely that *Antichrist* that causes such a stir in the Christian world. And as for others who do not possess it to such a high degree, yet so far as they are teachers, supporters, or enforcers of such practices or principles under the pretense of religion—things that naturally frustrate the purpose of the coming of Christ—they are to that extent also *Antichristian*.

4. Therefore, he who has duly considered and satisfied himself as to what the great goal of the Gospel of Christ is, and simply finds out (which he cannot easily miss) what things are contrary to it; if he only disguises them with plausible pretenses of promoting the interest of Christ, he has *by that very fact* <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> drawn the true *Image* or *Idea* of Antichrist, by which he may surely recognize him wherever he is. Now, that great scope and those main concerns that the Gospel of Christ aims at are plainly these: namely, *the uprooting of idolatry from the world*, as well as *a release of God's people from the unprofitable burden of Jewish ceremonies* (which we may call the *Negative Goal* <note>original: "Privative End"</note> of the Gospel); and *the exaltation of the Divine life*, whose root is *faith in God* and in a world to come, and whose branches are *humility*, *charity*, and *purity*, as I have discussed more at length in my *Explanation of the Mystery of Godliness*. And in this is comprised the *Positive Goal* of *Christ’s* coming into this world.

---

## CHAP. II.

1. *The rooting out of idolatry by the Messiah as prophesied by Jeremiah; That all the gods that did not make Heaven and Earth shall perish.*
2. *An explanation of that prophecy, and an assertion of our Saviour's right to be worshipped forever as the Eternal Word <note>original: "Logos"</note> who made Heaven and Earth.*
3. *Proofs from the Psalms that the Messiah was to root out idolatry.*
4. *Several places in the New Testament witnessing against idolatry and image-worship.*
5. *That the spirituality of the Christian religion indicated <note>original: "indigitated"</note> by our Saviour gives abundant evidence of the unlawfulness of image-worship or any other kind of idolatry.*

1. THAT God intended the rooting out of idolatry by sending Christ into the world appears both by those prophecies of the Old Testament that foretell that all idolatry shall be rooted out (for by whom should it be done but by the *Messiah*, in whom all the nations of the earth should be blessed?) as well as by several passages in the New.

Of the first sort is that in *Jeremiah* chapter 10, where the Prophet puts this prophecy in the mouths of the Jews who were carried captive into *Babylon*:
> *Thus shall you say unto them (he says): The gods that did not make the heavens and the earth, they shall perish from the earth and from under the heavens.*

But the preceding context is so lively and magnificent, and so relevant to our purpose, that it ought not to have been omitted. At the seventh verse

### That one Purpose of Christ's coming was to root out Idolatry. Book I.

...therefore, *Who would not fear you, O King of Nations? For to you does it belong. Because among all the wise men of the nations, and in all their kingdoms, there is none like you. But they are altogether dull and foolish; their wooden idol is a lesson in vanity. Silver beaten into plates is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphas, the work of the craftsman and of the hands of the goldsmith. Blue and purple is their clothing; they are all the work of skilled men. But the Lord is the true God; he is the living God and an everlasting King. At his wrath the earth shall tremble, and the nations shall not be able to endure his indignation.* And then follows this prophetic denunciation against every improper object of divine worship: *Thus shall you say to them: The Gods that did not make the heavens and the earth, they shall perish from the earth and from under these heavens.*

2. Things are extremely clear in this prophecy, except for that comparison of the *King of Nations* with the *wise men of the nations*. Between these two there is such an infinite disparity that the comparison seems very inappropriate if we assume the *pure Deity* is being compared here with any *wise men* whatsoever. Hugo Grotius <note>original: "Grotius" – a famous 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian known for his biblical commentaries.</note> therefore cleverly suggests that this refers to some of the *wise men of the nations* who had been elevated to the status of their *Gods*—such as *Taautes* <note>original: "Taautes" – an ancient Phoenician deity often identified with the Egyptian god Thoth or the Greek Hermes.</note>, for example. This slightly clarifies one part of the comparison, as these *wise men* are supposed to have been granted divine honors after their death and were numbered among the gods.

But I must confess that even the passage in the 86th *Psalm*—*Among the gods there is none like you, O Lord; there is none that can do as you do*—has often puzzled me. It seems strange that the prophet would deign to compare the gods of the nations (who were merely deified mortals, or at best specific angels or "daemons" <note>original: "Dæmons" – in this context, the author refers to the Platonic concept of "daimons," which were intermediate spirits between gods and humans, rather than evil "demons" in the modern sense.</note> in that higher sense) with the pure, infinite, and omnipotent Deity. This has often made me suspect that such passages as these should be understood as referring to the *Messiah*. He was to be incarnated and become the true God-man <note>original: "θεάνθρωπος" (theanthropos)</note>, and as a result of his sufferings, he would be <margin>Revelation 15:3–4</margin> declared *King of Nations and the object of worship for the whole Earth*. This aligns with what follows in that Psalm: *All nations whom you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and shall glorify your name.* As you know, he was the *Logos* <note>original: "Logos" – the Divine Word or Reason of God.</note> or *Word* which was in the beginning, without which nothing was made that was made. As the author of the Letter to the Hebrews <margin>Psalm 102:25</margin> also testifies: *You, Lord, in the beginning laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands.* This is spoken of the *Messiah*, as his era is clearly identified there, appearing in the 22nd verse: *When the people are gathered together, and the kingdoms to serve the Lord.* From this it is also clear that Christ shall always be <margin>Verse 27</margin> the *same*, and that his years shall have no end. Therefore, this prophetic denunciation—*The Gods that made not Heaven and Earth shall perish from the Earth and from under these Heavens*—cannot apply to him. However, the worship of anything else that is not the pure Deity must be discarded, according to the meaning of that prophecy.

3. That passage in the 97th *Psalm* also plainly shows that idolatry is to be abolished at the coming of Christ: *Shame on all those who serve carved images, who boast of idols; worship him, all you gods.* Which...

# Chapter II. That one Purpose of Christ's coming was to root out Idolatry.

...the author of the Epistle to the *Hebrews* expressly interprets as referring to *Christ*. By this, he proves Christ's divinity and thereby disapproves of giving any *religious worship* to anyone but the true Deity, as I have noted in its proper place.

4. As for the passages in the New Testament, they are more numerous and no less direct. <margin>Chapter 14, verses 14–15</margin> The first is in the *Acts of the Apostles*, where the priest of *Jupiter* attempted to offer sacrifices to Paul and *Barnabas* at *Lystra* because of the great miracles he saw them perform. In response, they tore their clothes and ran in among the people, crying out and saying, "Sirs, why are you doing these things? We also are men with the same nature as you, and we preach to you that you should turn from these worthless things <note>original: "vanities"</note> to the living God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all things within them." And what are those "worthless things" from which they must turn, if not the practice of giving <margin>Acts 17:29–30</margin> divine honor to mere creatures? The same Apostle, while at *Athens*, gave a very stern lesson against idolatry in the speech he delivered on *Mars Hill*: "Since we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Divine Nature is like gold or silver or stone, shaped by art and human design. And the times of this ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all men everywhere to repent." Certainly, *Paul* made this exhortation with the greatest possible earnestness; it is said in verse 16 **that his spirit was provoked within him** <term>original Greek: ὅτι παρωξύνετο τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ</term>, meaning his spirit was in a very sharp state, in a paroxysm <term>paroxysm: a sudden attack or violent expression of a particular emotion</term> of zeal, when he saw the city of *Athens* so entirely given over to idolatry.

<margin>Chapter 12, verse 2</margin> Again, in his first Epistle to the Corinthians, Paul identifies idolatry as the very defining characteristic of paganism <note>original: "Gentilisme"</note>, which Christ came to reclaim the world from: "You know that you were pagans, carried away to mute idols, just as you were led." <margin>Chapter 10, verses 14, 20, etc.</margin> Elsewhere in the same Epistle, he exhorts them more fully and vehemently: "Therefore, my dearly beloved, flee from idolatry. The things which the pagans sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons <note>original: "Demonia"</note> and not to God. You cannot be partakers of the Lord's table and of the table of demons. Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?" This warning was only about eating meat sacrificed to these demons <term>original: Dæmons</term>; how much worse, then, would it have been to bow down to their idols? <margin>Chapter 6, verses 14, 16</margin> He also speaks very sharply on this subject in his second Epistle to the Corinthians: "What fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness? What communion has light with darkness? And what agreement has the Temple of God with idols?" In his Epistle to the Galatians, <margin>Chapter 5, verse 20</margin> he plainly lists idolatry among the grossest "works of the flesh," alongside *murder, sorcery, and adultery*. Accordingly, in the Book of Revelation <margin>Chapter 21, verse 8</margin> (the *Apocalypse*), *idolaters*, together with *murderers and sorcerers*, are threatened with the lake that burns with fire and brimstone, and are shut out of the Holy City along with vile dogs <note>original: "obscene Dogs"</note>. <margin>Chapter 22, verse 15</margin> Therefore, *St. John* is certainly very much in earnest in his warning against *idolatry* <margin>1 John 5:20</margin> at the close of his general Epistle: "And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us an understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, through his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life. Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Amen." From these passages, I think it is abundantly manifest that the proclaiming of the *Gospel* aimed at the taking away of ido-

This means that both the *Moral* and *Ceremonial Law* were given by *Moses*. However, even that <margin>Galatians 3:21</margin> *Moral Law* was of the sort that could not *give life*, as the Apostle says. Instead, the gracious help of the Spirit of God promised in the Gospel is what *gives life* and the strength to live according to God's will. 

Furthermore, regarding the *Ceremonial Law*: both it, and indeed everything that happened to the Jews, were only *Types* and *Shadows* <term>Symbols or prefigurations of spiritual truths that would later be revealed</term>; but in Christ, we find the *Truth*. Those ceremonies were not what they appeared to be, and in that sense, they could be called "false"—just as someone who says that a *picture* of a man or a horse *is* the actual man or horse is speaking falsely. <margin>John 6:32</margin> Therefore, our Savior speaks the truth when he says, *Moses did not give you that bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread <margin>Verse 35</margin> from heaven.* Even though it is said of the *Manna* in Psalm 78, *He gave them bread from heaven to eat*, because it was only a shadow of the true bread from heaven (which is Christ), it is said not to be the actual bread from heaven. <margin>Hebrews 10:1</margin> Likewise, in the Epistle to the *Hebrews*, the *Law* is said *to have a shadow of good things to come*. ## Chapter IV. The Positive Ends of Christ's Coming.

1. The **positive goal of the Gospel**, as I have said and proved elsewhere, is **the elevating of the Divine life**. This is achieved either by giving all due honor and obedience to Christ, in whom this life lived so perfectly, or by promoting its growth—both in depth and in reach—among his members. The aim is for it to reach its full height where it already exists and to gain a foothold where it does not, so that the entire mass of humanity, if possible, might be leavened—not with the leaven of hypocrisy, but with the sincere doctrine and life-giving spirit of the Gospel of Christ.

# Of the True Concept of Idolatry. Book I.

...to a mere man because he is the *Vicar General of Christ* and *ecumenical Head of His Church on Earth*; and lastly, the adoration of the consecrated Bread in the Eucharist based on the idea that it is *transubstantiated* <note>The doctrine that the bread and wine in the Eucharist become the actual body and blood of Christ.</note> into the very body of Christ: I say, when these things are introduced into the Church as true doctrine and commendable practice, they will certainly constitute a major part of *Antichristianism*—and a principal one at that.

For the doctrine is not true, nor is the practice allowable; rather, it is gross and obvious idolatry (one of the most hated sins mentioned in Scripture), as you shall easily understand once I have, with all possible care, searched out the true concept and defining nature of it.

2. Although this term *Idolatry* is frequently used in the speech and writings of men, its meaning is often unstable and slippery. Some people, to excuse or downplay their clearly unacceptable rites and practices in the Christian religion, have narrowed the meaning of the word so much that, according to their subtle distinctions and restrictions, even the worst forms of Paganism would hardly be found guilty of *Idolatry*. Others—whether out of a terrified hatred of such a detestable crime, or out of an excessively partisan disgust for the opposing side—have stretched the meaning of the word so far beyond its natural sense that even harmless or commendable parts of divine worship appointed by authority are labeled with that hateful and insulting name. Their zeal and clumsy attempts to remove this major error from the Church have met with a similar lack of success; they have not so much achieved a cure as changed the disease, trading one great evil for several others of a lesser kind, such as *Scandal* <note>In this context, "scandal" refers to a "stumbling block" that leads others into sin or doubt.</note>, rash and *unjust judgment* <note>original: "Censure"</note>, and *Superstition*. These are very harmful and undesirable ailments in the Church of Christ, and they are the inevitable causes and promoters of unnecessary divisions <note>original: "Schisms"</note>. Indeed, if I had only said they had exchanged *Idolatry* for *Superstition*, it would have been enough to cover the rest. For *Superstition* is properly a fear of displeasing God in things that neither please nor offend Him, arising from an opinion that <term>indifferent <note>Theological term (adiaphora) for actions neither commanded nor forbidden by God.</note></term> things are either good or evil. Those who, whether out of ignorance or some worse motive, create in people's minds a superstitious hatred for such harmless and permissible actions, inevitably make them liable to cause offense and tempt them to make *rash* and *unjust judgments*.

3. Therefore, to clear the innocent as well as to identify the guilty, I will try to define the exact boundaries of this great sin of *Idolatry*. This way, we may know when it is committed and when it is not, and when it is appropriate to use that hateful name—and when it is instead an act of injustice and lack of charity to label a specific religious practice that way.

<margin>
Origen, *Against Celsus*, book 5.
</margin>

We often speak of *idolatrous nations* that worship the *sun, moon*, and *stars*, without considering whether they make any *images* of them or not. For these <term>visible and perceptible gods <note>original: "ἐμφανεῖς καὶ αἰσθητοὶ θεοὶ" (emphanēs kai aisthētoi theoi)</note></term>, as they...

### Chapter 5: Of the True Concept of Idolatry

<margin>Deuteronomy 4:15, 19.</margin>
...they are named <term>gods</term> <note>original Greek: θεοὶ (theoi)</note> by the Greeks, and it may easily be imagined how they enticed unrefined people to adore them before they had either the skill or the leisure to build temples and erect statues to them. For this reason, God gave a warning to His own people in *Deuteronomy*: *Take good heed to yourselves (for you saw no kind of likeness on the day that the Lord spoke to you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire), lest you corrupt yourselves and make a graven image, etc. And lest you lift up your eyes to heaven, and when you see the sun, the moon, and the stars, even all the host of heaven, you should be driven to worship them and serve them.* These heavenly bodies have been so strongly enticing to mankind that they were moved to bestow religious worship upon them. These were the first objects that gained the title of <term>gods</term> <note>original Greek: θεοὶ</note> because they are in perpetual motion, as *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher.</note> observed; this title was later applied to all other deities whatsoever. *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides, a prominent medieval Jewish scholar.</note> also places the first foundation of idolatry in the worship of these celestial bodies.

<margin>Herodotus, book 1, chapter 131.</margin>
5. However, nations that were sufficiently civilized, such as the *Persians*, managed to be idolaters without carved images or *idols*. For they sacrificed on the tops of mountains to the visible heavens under the name of *Jupiter*, as well as to the *sun*, *moon*, and *earth*, and to *fire*, *water*, and the *winds*. These are all perceptible objects, but they were worshipped without any physical figure or representation. And yet, I think no man—whether learned or an <term>uneducated person</term> <note>original: "Idiot" – in this period, the term referred to a common or unlearned person rather than a mental disability.</note>—will hesitate to label this nation *idolatrous*. The same applies to the ancient *Romans*, who worshipped their many gods without the use of any *idol* or *image* for nearly two hundred years together, as both *Varro* and *Plutarch* affirm.

<margin>* In the Panegyric Oration on the Birth of Christ.</margin>
<margin>* On Idolatry, chapter 15.</margin>
<margin>* 1 Chronicles 16:26.</margin>
6. Therefore, *idolatry* exists not only where an *idol* is worshipped, but wherever anything is worshipped which is not *God*, whether that thing is visible or not. In this sense, *Gregory Nazianzen* defines *idolatry* as <term>the transfer of worship from the Creator to the creatures</term> <note>original Greek: Μετάθεσιν τῆς προσκυνήσεως ἀπὸ τοῦ πεποιηκότος ἐπὶ τὰ κτίσματα.</note>. And *Tertullian* pronounces that whatsoever is exalted <term>beyond the measure of human honor</term> <note>original Latin: ultra humani honoris modum</note> with more than civil worship, becomes <term>by that very fact</term> <note>original Latin: ipso facto</note> an *idol*. When they are not truly <term>gods</term> <note>original Hebrew: אלהים (Elohim)</note>, they become <term>worthless things</term> <note>original Hebrew: אלילים (Elilim)</note> by being worshipped—that is to say, <term>not-gods</term> <note>original Latin/Hebrew: אל-אלים (non-Dii)</note> (as some would interpret the word). Instead, they are <term>idols</term> <note>original Greek: Εἴδωλα (Eidola)</note>, as the word is often rendered by <term>the Seventy</term> <note>The Seventy, or Septuagint, is the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, and also <term>hand-made things</term> <note>original Greek: χειροποίητα (cheiropoicta)</note>. And in the first book of *Chronicles*, the phrase <term>All the gods of the nations are idols</term> <note>original Greek: Πάντες οἱ θεοὶ τῶν ἐθνῶν εἴδωλα</note> shows plainly that the term *idol* is also to be applied to those things that are not carved images. For the nations worshipped the *sun* and *moon*, and the souls of deceased men, which are not imagery but natural things. Therefore, the translators sometimes render <term>worthless things</term> <note>original Hebrew: אלילים (Elilim)</note> as <term>gods</term>, <term>demons</term>, or <term>great lords</term> <note>original Greek: θεοὶ (theoi), δαιμόνια (daimonia), or μεγιστᾶνες (megistanes)</note>. The last of these must refer to those *invisible demons* themselves; since they are merely "worthless things" in the scriptural account, their worship must also be idolatry. This will be acknowledged without any hesitation by anyone upon whom either the sense of things or the force of words has left any impression.

For the doctrine is not true, nor is the practice allowable. It is, instead, gross and obvious *Idolatry* (one of the most abhorred sins the Scripture mentions). You shall easily understand this after I have, with all possible caution, searched out the true concept and definitive nature of it.

2. Although this term *Idolatry* is extremely common in the speech and writings of men, there is nothing with such an unsettled and elusive meaning. Some, in order to excuse or downplay their grossly unacceptable rites and practices in the *Christian* religion, have restricted the sense of the word to such narrow limits that, according to their precise distinctions and restrictions, even the foulest Paganism would hardly be found guilty of *Idolatry*. 

Others—whether out of a fear and hatred of such a detestable crime, or out of an overly-partisan disgust and detestation of the opposing party—have so stretched the meaning of the word beyond its natural sense that even harmless, and even commendable, circumstances of *Divine* worship appointed by Authority are stigmatized by them with that hateful and reproachful name. 

Their zeal and passionate lack of skill in removing this great error from the Church has had a correspondingly poor success; they have not so much achieved a cure as changed the disease. They have traded one great evil for several others of a slightly lower form, such as *Scandal*, rash and *unjust Censure*, and *Superstition*. These are very evil and undesirable disorders in the Church of Christ, and are the necessary authors and promoters of unnecessary divisions <note>original: Schisms</note>. 

Indeed, if I had only said that they had changed *Idolatry* into *Superstition*, it would have been enough, as superstition includes the rest. *Superstition* is properly a fear of displeasing God in things that neither please nor offend Him, arising from an opinion that indifferent things <note>Things that are neither commanded nor forbidden by God.</note> are either good or evil. Those who, either out of ignorance or some worse principle, create a superstitious hatred in the minds of men against such harmless and allowable actions, must inevitably make them liable to *Scandal* and tempt them toward *rash* and *unjust Censures*.

3. Therefore, both to excuse the innocent and to discover the guilty, I shall endeavor to exactly set out the bounds of this great sin of *Idolatry*. By this, we may know when it is committed and when it is not; when it may be called by that hateful name, and when, conversely, it is an act of injustice and uncharitableness to so label a specific action of religious worship.

# Chapter 5: Of the True Concept of Idolatry.

As they are named by the Greeks, it is easy to imagine how they tempted unrefined people to worship them before they had the skill or time to build temples and erect statues to them. This is why God gave that warning to his own people in *Deuteronomy*:
> *Take good heed to yourselves (for you saw no kind of likeness on the day that the Lord spoke to you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire) lest you corrupt yourselves and make a graven image, etc. And lest you lift up your eyes to heaven, and when you see the sun, the moon, and the stars, even all the host of heaven, you should be driven to worship them and serve them.*

So strongly enticing have these been to mankind, tempting them to bestow religious worship upon them. These were the first objects that gained the title of gods <note>original: "θεοὶ"</note>, because they are in perpetual motion, as *Philo* has observed; this name was afterwards applied to all other deities whatsoever. *Maimonides* <note>A prominent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> also places the first foundation of idolatry in these celestial bodies.

<margin>Herodotus, Book 1, Chapter 131.</margin>
5. However, nations that were quite civilized—namely the *Persians*—managed to be *idolaters* without *carved images* or *idols*. For they sacrificed on the tops of mountains to the visible heavens under the name of *Jupiter*, as also to the *sun, moon,* and *earth*, and to the *fire, water,* and *winds*. These were all sensory objects, yet they were worshipped without any physical figure or representation. And yet, I think no learned man, nor even an unlearned person <note>original: "Idiot"</note>, would hesitate to call this nation *idolatrous*. The same is true for the ancient *Romans*, who worshipped their many gods without the use of any *idol* or *image* for nearly two hundred years, as both *Varro* and *Plutarch* affirm.

<margin>* In the Panegyric Oration on the Birth of Christ.</margin>

6. Therefore, *idolatry* exists not only where an *idol* is worshipped, but wherever anything is worshipped which is *not God*, whether that thing is visible or not. In this sense, *Gregory Nazianzene defines *idolatry* as "the transfer of worship from the Creator to the creatures" <note>original: "Μετάθεσιν τῆς προσκυνήσεως ἀπὸ τοῦ πεποιηκότος ἐπὶ τὰ κτίσματα"</note>. And *Tertullian* pronounces that whatsoever is exalted "beyond the measure of human honor" <note>original: "ultra humani honoris modum"</note>, with more than civil worship, does "by that very fact" <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> become an *idol*. When they are not truly God <note>original: "אלהים" (Elohim)</note>, they become, by being worshipped, worthless things <note>original: "אלילים" (Elilim)</note>; that is to say, "not-gods" <note>original: "אל-אלים" (El-elim), as some would have the notation of the word</note>, but *idols* <note>original: "Εἴδωλα"</note>, as the term is often translated by the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, and also "things made by hands" <note>original: "χειροποίητα"</note>. And in the first book of *Chronicles*, the phrase "All the gods of the nations are idols" <note>original: "Πάντες οἱ θεוὶ τῶν ἐθνῶν εἴδωλα"</note> shows plainly that the word *idol* <note>original: "Εἴδωλον"</note> should also be applied to those things that are not carved images. For the nations worshipped the *sun* and *moon*, and the souls of deceased men, which are *natural things*. And therefore, the translators sometimes render the Hebrew word for idols <note>original: "אלילים"</note> as "gods" <note>original: "θεοὶ"</note>, "demons" <note>original: "δαιμόνια"</note>, or "nobles" <note>original: "μεγιστάνες"</note>. This last term must refer to those invisible demons themselves; since they are considered nothing more than worthless things <note>original: "אלילים"</note> in the *Scripture's account*, their worship must also be idolatry. This will be acknowledged without any hesitation by anyone whose mind has been shaped by the true nature of things or the force of words.

7. This might also have made the Seventy careless about always translating "God" <note>original: "אלהים" (Elohim)</note> as "gods" <note>original: "θεοὶ"</note> when speaking of the *heathen gods*. And whereas they <note>The "Seventy," referring to the translators of the Septuagint, the ancient Greek version of the Old Testament.</note> understood by *Baalim* <note>The plural of Baal, a common title for various local deities in the ancient Near East.</note> those false deities distinct from their images—as appears from the second book of <margin>* 2 Chronicles 28:2.</margin> *Chronicles*, where they translate the Hebrew text as "he made molten images for the Baals" <note>original: גלולים מסכות עשה לבעלים / ἐποίησε τοῖς Βααλείμ</note>—yet for the same reason, they several times translate the word simply as *idols* <note>original: εἴδωλα</note>. The *Baalim* themselves—whether they were the *sun* or the *souls* of deceased men—were considered nothing but *idols in the sense* we are discussing.

Finally, for this reason, I believe they also translate the Hebrew word for "idols" <note>original: עצבים (*atvabim*), often implying objects that cause grief or toil.</note> as *idols* <note>original: εἴδωλα</note> over a dozen times, and as *gods* <note>original: θεοὶ</note> only once. In contrast, a learned Doctor of our Church <note>Likely referring to a contemporary theologian or scholar familiar to the author.</note> understands the word according to its original meaning—signifying any cause of anxiety, grief, or frightful passion—to refer chiefly to the *demons* <note>original: δαίμονες</note> themselves. He argues that their harsh treatment and terrifying appearances to dismayed mankind brought about that kind of cowardice which the Greeks properly call *superstition* <note>original: δεισιδαιμονία (*deisidaimonia*), literally "fear of spirits."</note>, meaning a superstitious fear and disquieting dread of demons. This fear is not supposed to proceed from the *images* themselves; <margin>Grotius on the Decalogue.</margin> *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> noted that *Varro* <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, an ancient Roman scholar.</note> complained against those who had corrupted the purer worship established by *Numa* <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, who was said to have forbidden images in worship.</note> by introducing images. Varro said, "By doing so, they have both removed fear from their states and added error" <note>original: *Eos utique civitatibus suis & metum dempsisse, & errorem addidisse.*</note>. 

However, because anything that receives religious worship but is not God becomes an *idol*, the translators of the Septuagint may well be excused for their tendency to render these words as "idols" <note>original: εἴδωλα</note>, which, in certain contexts, would have been more accurately and specifically rendered as "demons" <note>original: δαιμόνια</note>. Their tendency to do so is another argument, as I have already suggested, for the legitimacy of the viewpoint and language of those who call the worship of anything that is not God "idolatry."

8. God himself also witnesses that this is the case by declaring himself affected by the *worship of that which is not God* in the same way he is by the bowing toward *images*. He forbids this, giving the reason: *For I the Lord your God am a jealous God* (Exodus 20). The original Hebrew is *El Kanna* <note>original: אל קנא</note>. And in *Deuteronomy* 32, he says, "They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God" <note>original: הם קנאוני בלא-אל (*hem kinuni ve-lo-el*)</note>. 

By this, we seem to be warned about the true nature of *idolatry*: the worship of an image is not *idolatry* simply because it is an image, but because that image is not God. No image is God, except for that true and living Image of the Father, *Jesus Christ*. Therefore, the true and general concept of Idolatry is *to worship anything that is not God*. By doing so, we forsake God himself and devotionally prostitute ourselves to every vanishing representation or far-cast shadow of Him. These are but *shadows of shadows* <note>original: εἴδωλα εἰδώלων (*eidola eidolon*)</note> in infinite myriads of degenerations from Him, and so we provoke His jealousy by these many *Baalim*, whereas He alone is to be our Lord and Husband. But this is a truth so plain and acknowledged that I did not need to spend so much time on verbal comparisons to give it further support.

# Chapter 6: Worshipping the True God by an Image is Idolatry.

### Chapter 6.

*1. Evidence from the Book of Exodus that the Israelites worshipped **Jehovah** in the form of the **Golden Calf**. 2. Proof that **Elohim** <note>original: אלהים; the Hebrew word for God, which is plural in form but often singular in meaning</note>, even when paired with a plural verb, refers to the true God; further evidence from Psalm 106 that God was worshipped in that **Calf**, and an explanation of what **Glory** <note>original: כבוד (*Kavod*)</note> signifies there. 3. Evidence that the **Golden Calf** was not a representation of the Egyptian bull-god **Apis**, but was actually a **Cherub**. 4. A brief explanation of **Aaron’s** role in making the **Golden Calf**, and the discovery of the source of the historian **Tacitus’s** ridiculous error. 5. Evidence from **Jeroboam’s** political strategies that the **Golden Calves** in **Dan** and **Bethel** were two **Cherubim** set up for the worship of the God of Israel. 6. Further proof from the stories of **Jehu** and **Elijah** <note>original: Elias</note>, and the instructions given to the **Assyrian Colonies** by an Israelite priest. 7. Evidence that **Micah’s Ephod** and **Teraphim** <note>household idols or ritual objects</note> were also intended for the worship of the true God. 8. Confirmation that both Micah and the Israelites in the wilderness were nonetheless **Idolaters** because they used **Teraphim** and **Cherubs** in divine worship. 9. Scriptural proof that **Jeroboam** was also an **Idolater** for setting up the **Calves** in **Dan** and **Bethel**. 10. Other testimonies to the same effect, including the **idolatry** committed regarding the **Brazen Serpent**.*

---

1. It now seems appropriate to inquire into this: *Whether, just as there is idolatry without the worship of images, there might also be the worship of images that is not idolatry, provided the images are worshipped in reference to the true God.*

I believe it is very clear from the children of Israel worshipping God through the **Golden Calf** made by **Aaron** that worshipping the true God by an image is indeed idolatry. First, it is evident they worshipped God through this **Calf** from what is written in Exodus 32:4, where it is proclaimed, *"These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt."* In verse 8, God tells **Moses** what has happened, saying, *"They have made themselves a molded calf, and worshipped it, and sacrificed to it, and said, 'These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.'"* However, it is obvious that this **Calf** did not literally bring them out of the land of Egypt; rather, they brought the calf—or at least the materials for it—with them. Therefore, they understood it only as a visible image and representation of the presence of the one who truly delivered them: **Jehovah**, the true God.

2. Nor should there be any doubt because the statement uses the plural number ("gods"), as if the *one true God* could not be meant. For the word ***Elohim*** <note>Hebrew: אלהים</note> is not only as appropriately applied to a single Deity as to a single image, but it is actually—and frequently—used to refer to the one God, **Jehovah**.

<margin>Nehemiah 9:18</margin>
When **Nehemiah** recounts this passage, he shows plainly that the meaning should be understood as singular. For the word *Cherub* properly signifies a *calf* or *ox* <note>original: μόσχος (*moschos*)</note>, derived from the word "to plow" <note>original: כרב (*karab*)</note>. It is one of those four animals in the *Chariot of God* described in the visions of both *Ezekiel* and *St. John*. It is remarkable in the book of *Ezekiel* that when he listed those four distinct forms—*a Man, a Lion, an Ox, and an Eagle*—in the first chapter, he repeated the same list in the tenth chapter but replaced the name *Ox* with *Cherub*: *And every one had four faces; the first face was the face of a Cherub, the second face was the face of a Man, the third the face of a Lion, and the fourth the face of an Eagle.* Therefore, the first must correspond to the *ox* specified previously. Furthermore, in the first chapter, he observes generally of them all that *their feet were like the feet of calves.* This is a clear hint that *Aaron’s* action was not as bizarre as it first appears; he was erecting a symbol of the Divine presence of the same kind that was to be placed later in the Ark: specifically, the figure of a *Cherub*, or *Golden Calf*. But to imagine that a man as holy as *Aaron* proposed worshipping the Egyptian bull-god *Apis*—essentially making an idol out of an idol—and then celebrated a festival to *Jehovah* using it, is so impious, illogical, and outrageous that it seems completely unbelievable.

4. Therefore, in short, the case seems to be this: God, through *Moses*, promised his people his visible presence to guide them into the Land of *Canaan*. This symbolic presence was to reside in the *Ark*, and especially among the *Cherubim*, upon which God was seen to sit by *Aaron* when he was admitted to the *sight* of God on the Mount. Being aware of the plan to represent the presence of God through *Cherubim* or *Golden Calves*, and seeing that *Moses* had stayed so long on the Mount...

<header>Other Modes of Idolatry. Book I.</header>

## CHAPTER VII.

1. *The worship of something that is not God through an image: a third mode of idolatry.* 2. *Regarding the worship of an image for its own sake.* 3. *How the common people among the Heathen came to mistake the idols themselves for gods.* 4. *The arguments used to create the belief that demons resided near their statues.* 5. *Indications of their presence there, and how the images themselves became objects of awe because of it.* 6. *The concept of the demon and the dedicated image merging into a single person.* 7. *That worshipping this combined entity was a fourth mode of idolatry.*

1. Thus, we have demonstrated *two* modes or manners of *idolatry*: namely, *the worship of something that is not God without an image, and the worship of the true God with one.*
From this, the proof of a *third* mode follows: *that the worship of something that is not God by means of an image is idolatry*. Indeed, I might say it is a *double-charged idolatry*.
For if giving divine worship to each separately is *idolatry*, then worshipping both of these unlawful objects at once is *double idolatry*. If the relationship of an external object of worship to the true God does not make that object lawful—even when it does not pretend to be the shape or image of the true God (as the *Golden Calf* certainly did not, nor did anyone think it was)—then surely a false god cannot make an *image* a lawful object of worship, even if the image actually resembled that god.

2. Nor can any *image* in itself, without reference to anything else, be a proper object of worship. For just as the true God is rightly called by the Psalmist the *God of gods* <note>original: אלהי-האלהים (Elohei ha-Elohim)</note>, so certainly an *idol* may well be esteemed the *merest nothing of all nothings* <note>original: אליל האלילים (Elil ha-elilim). In Hebrew, "elil" (idol) literally means "worthless" or "nothing."</note>, the emptiest of all vanities that could be proposed for religious worship. From this consideration arises another sort of idolatry, which is *the worship of an image absolutely, without reference to anything else*. (This would be idolatry in the strictest sense, based on the literal meaning of the word "idol-worship," if it were actually possible). It seems very difficult to worship an *image*, knowing it to be one, purely for its own sake, since the very nature of an *image* is to refer to something else.

...strange divinity in it, which is not there. According to some passages in Scripture, this seems to have been the condition of the common people among the Heathen. As it says in *Psalm* 135:15 and again in 115:4, <note>original: "עצבי הגוים" (Etzbei ha-goyim)</note> *the idols of the nations*, or the *Fear and Awe of the Gentiles* (that is, their Gods) are *but images of silver and gold, etc.* 

While these *images* were the fastest way to bring all religion into contempt among the more sharp-witted <note>original: "nasute"</note> and skeptical people, the golden splendor and magnificence of them apparently did so dazzle <note>original: "perfringe"</note> the eyes of the simple sort that they took them to be actual gods. This appears plainly in those passages from the *Psalms*, and very extensively in the *Epistle of Jeremiah*. However, this judgment by both *Jeremiah* and the *Psalmist* should be understood in a way that does not make us think the Heathen had no other objects of worship than the physical *idols* themselves. For (as I have hinted above) in all likelihood these <note>original: "עצבי" (etzbei)</note> awful objects of their superstitious worship were originally the *demons* <note>In this context, "demons" refers to any non-Christian spirits or minor deities, not necessarily "evil" spirits in the modern sense.</note> themselves—whether the *ghosts* of the departed or other spirits. These spirits sometimes, though not very frequently, miraculously showed their presence in these images or statues. As the fame of these miracles continued, it won over the superstitious reverence of the common people for these idols, making them believe they were living and powerful deities.

<margin>Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book 7.</margin>
4. *Origen* speaks of the binding of these demons near their statues, whether by magical incantations or because, like so many parasites <note>original: "smell-Feasts"</note> looking for a meal, they hovered near the altars to enjoy the savory fumes <note>original: "nidorous"</note> of the sacrifices, <note>original: "λίχνως μεταλαμβάνοντες τῆς τῶν θυομένων ἀποφορᾶς"</note> *greedily partaking of the rising smoke of the things sacrificed.*

<margin>Maimonides, *The Guide for the Perplexed*, Part 3, Chapter 40.</margin>
It is likely the deceptive priests would claim either of these things to the people (though not in such a disgusting way) to persuade them of the presence of the demons themselves in these consecrated places and images. Truly, the oily vapors from the burning of the sacrifices seem like a more suitable entertainment for them than the raw blood—which *Maimonides* says the *Sabians* <note>original: "Zabii"; an ancient Middle Eastern religious group.</note> believed to be the demons' food, and therefore ate the blood themselves to communicate with them.

<margin>Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book 3.</margin>
5. But as appears by *Origen* in his third book against *Celsus*, there were even clearer demonstrations of the presence of these demons in their temples and statues: through the giving of oracles, the healing of diseases, and the tormenting of the superstitious if they failed in even the smallest detail <note>original: "punctilio"</note> of religious service to them. Origen calls these <note>original: "δαίμονας μαντικοὺς καὶ ἰατρικούς"</note> *prophetic and healing demons*, whom he suggests are harsh monitors to those who transgress, <note>original: "πρὸς τὸ δεδίττεσθαι καὶ πολὺν καὶ ἀπαίδευτον"</note> *to terrify the vast and uneducated multitude.* Whether these terrors were created by the frauds of the priests or merely from the irritability of the demons, I will not dispute here. But without question, it struck a great dread into the simple people regarding the images themselves, as if there were a power and divinity within them.

We might add to these a fourth instance, which is *the burning of incense to the bronze serpent*. <note>The "brazen serpent" was a staff made by Moses that healed Israelites, but was later destroyed by King Hezekiah because the people began to worship it as an idol.</note> This act was certainly not intended to honor any foreign god, as it was a monument to those miraculous cures performed by Jehovah, the God of *Moses*. But it is already so clear that nothing can be clearer: *To worship an image, even if the honor is intended for the true God, is nonetheless flat-out idolatry.*

### CHAPTER VII.

*1. Worshipping something that is not God through an image is a third mode of idolatry. 2. Regarding the worship of an image for its own sake. 3. How the common people among the Heathen came to mistake the idols themselves for gods. 4. What arguments were used to create the belief that demons resided near their statues. 5. What signs indicated their presence there, and how the images themselves became objects of awe because of it. 6. The idea that the demon and the dedicated image merged into a single person. 7. And that the worship of this combined entity was a fourth mode of idolatry.*

1. Thus we have demonstrated *two modes or manners of idolatry*: namely, *worshipping that which is not God without an image*, and *worshipping the true God with one.*

From this, the proof of a *third mode* follows: *that the worshipping of something that is not God by using an image is idolatry.* In fact, I might say it is a *double-strength idolatry*.

For if giving divine worship to each of these separately is idolatry, then to worship both of these unlawful objects at once is *double idolatry*. If the relationship of an external object of worship to the true God does not make that object lawful—even when it does not pretend to be the shape or image of the true God (as certainly the *Golden Calf* did not pretend to be, nor did anyone think it was)—then surely a false god cannot make an *image* a lawful object of worship, even if the image actually resembled that false god.

2. Nor can any *image* in itself, without reference to something else, be a proper object of worship. For just as the true God is rightly styled by the Psalmist <term>אלהי האלהים</term> <note>original: "Elohei ha-Elohim"</note> *the God of Gods*, so certainly an idol may well be esteemed <term>אליל האלילים</term> <note>original: "Elil ha-Elilim"</note> *the absolute nothingness of all nothingness*—the emptiest of all vanities that could ever be proposed for religious worship. From this consideration arises another sort of idolatry: *the worshipping of an image absolutely, without reference to anything else.* This would be idolatry in the strictest sense of the word's definition, if such a thing were even possible. For it seems very difficult to worship an *image* while knowing it is an image, focusing only on the object itself; the very nature of an *image* is to refer to something else.

3. But people may possibly worship what is merely an *image* without referring to any other thing. The flashiness or the terrifying appearance of the statue might strongly affect the minds of the more simple-hearted, leading them to imagine some
<meta>The text continues on the next page, explaining how people imagine a "strange divinity" within these physical objects.</meta>

# Chapter VII: Other Modes of Idolatry

...strange divinity in it, which there is not. This seems to be the condition of the common people among the heathens, according to certain passages in Scripture. As in *Psalm* 135:15 and again in 115:4, the Hebrew phrase *Etzbei ha-goyim* <note>original: "עצבי הגוים"</note>, translated as "The sorrows" or "The terrors of the nations" <note>original: "Dolores or Terricula Gentium"</note>—that is, their gods—are described as nothing but images of silver and gold, and so on. Although these images were the quickest way to bring all religion into contempt among the more shrewd and keen-witted <term>original: "nasute"; meaning having a sharp sense of smell or being intellectually discerning</term>, the golden splendor and magnificence of them apparently did so dazzle <note>original: "perstringe"</note> the eyes of the simple people that they took them to be actual gods. This appears plainly in those passages of the *Psalms* and very extensively in the *Epistle of Jeremiah*. 

However, this judgment by both *Jeremiah* and the *Psalmist* should be understood in a way that doesn't force us to think the heathens had no other objects of worship besides the idols themselves. For (as I have hinted above) in all likelihood these *etzbim*—these awe-inspiring objects of their superstitious worship—were primarily the **demons** themselves, whether they were the ghosts of the departed or other spirits. These spirits sometimes (though not very frequently) miraculously showed their presence in these images or statues. When reports of this continued, it won over that superstitious reverence from the common people, leading them to believe the idols were living and powerful deities.

<margin>*Origen*, *Against Celsus*, Book 7.</margin>
4. **Origen** <note>A prominent early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD)</note> speaks of the binding of these demons near their statues, whether by magical incantation or because, like "smell-feasts" <term>parasites who hang around hoping for a meal</term>, they lingered near the altars to enjoy the smoke and odors of the sacrifices, "greedily partaking of the rising vapor of the things sacrificed" <note>original: "λίχνως μεταλαμβανόντες τῆς τῶν θυομένων ἀποφορᾶς"</note>.

It is likely the deceitful priests would claim either of these things to the people (though not in such a repulsive way) to persuade them that the demons themselves were present in these consecrated places and images. Truly, the oily vapors from the burning of sacrifices seem a more suitable entertainment for them than gross blood. Yet, <margin>*The Guide for the Perplexed*, Part 3, Chapter 40.</margin> **Maimonides** <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and physician</note> says the **Sabians** <note>original: "Zabii"; an ancient religious group mentioned in historical texts</note> believed blood was the food of the spirits, and therefore ate it themselves in order to commune with them.

5. But as appears by **Origen** in his third book against *Celsus*, there were even more obvious demonstrations of the presence of these demons in their temples and statues: by the giving of oracles, by the healing of diseases, and by the tormenting of the superstitious if they failed in even the smallest detail <note>original: "punctilio"</note> of religious service to them. Origen calls these "prophetic and healing demons" <note>original: "δαίμονας μαντικοὺς καὶ ἰατρικοὺς"</note>, whom he suggests are sharp monitors to those who transgress, "to terrify the common and uneducated people" <note>original: "πρὸς τὸ δεδίττεσθαι τὸν πολὺν καὶ ἀπαίδευτον"</note>. Whether these terrors were created by the frauds of the priests or merely by the spitefulness of the demons, I will not dispute here. But without question, it struck a great dread of the images themselves into the simple people, as if there were power and divinity within them.

6. But I have not yet reached my main point, which is the idea of such a close union between the **demon** and the **statue** that they were considered one sacred living being or person. For the people of **Tyre** certainly thought this about the statue of **Apollo**; they believed that by binding it with golden chains, they had tied **Apollo**...

Apollo himself so securely to them that he could not go away. Similarly, the *Athenians* seem to have believed this concerning the image of *Victory*; by clipping off her wings, they thought they could keep the goddess herself from flying away from them.

<margin>* Book 1, chapter 8.</margin>
This opinion might very well have been encouraged by certain supernatural events involving these kinds of images. For example, there is the image of the god *Adranus*: *Plutarch* relates in the *Life of Timoleon* that when the *Adranites* were engaged in a war, his statue was seen to sweat profusely and to shake the tip of his spear. *Valerius Maximus* also writes about how the statues of *Juno Moneta* and *Fortuna* spoke; one indicated her willingness to go to *Rome*, while the other expressed approval of how she was consecrated: "Rightly have you matrons seen me, and rightly have you dedicated me" <note>original: *Rite me matronæ vidistis, riteque dedicâstis*</note>.

The *Teraphim* <term>original: "Teraphim"; small idols or household gods used for divination in the ancient Near East</term> of the pagans—which were made according to a certain astrological figure or constellation of the heavens—were also erected to provide answers as oracles. In all likelihood, these are the "animated statues conscious of the future" <note>original: *Statuæ animatæ futurorum consciæ*</note> that *Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and magic</note> mentions in the *Asclepius*. There are many stories of such speaking statues, but I have already digressed too far.

7. The question that arises from considering why people thought these dedicated statues or images were real deities—whether due to rumors of truth or mere imagination—is this: *Can they be called idolaters for giving divine worship to them, not as images of something else, but (according to their belief) as true and living gods?* I believe there is very little difficulty in this point. For if worshipping something that is not God, under the concept of it being a saving and living deity, is not *idolatry*, then no one would be considered an idolater—except perhaps those who think they can excuse this "spiritual adultery" <note>original: "Fornication"; a common biblical metaphor for idolatry</note> by pretending they do not worship the image for its own sake, but in reference to the deity it represents. Meanwhile, they give religious worship to something that is no deity at all, but a dead object.

However, we have already proved that worshipping the *sun*, the *moon*, or any *demon*—even without an image—is idolatry (and I think no Christian would ever hesitate to admit this). Therefore, worshipping an image, or the combination of an image and a *demon* inhabiting it, as a deity—when it is not the true and only Almighty and Infinite Godhead, but a finite being of which there may be many others—is undoubtedly blatant *idolatry*. We may identify this as the fourth mode of idolatry.

## CHAP. VIII.

1. That the more enlightened Pagans <note>original: "Heathen"</note> were not so ignorant of the Deity that they failed to acknowledge the unity of His essence, His omnipotence, and His omniscience, would be an easy thing to prove, if it were not already generally accepted. "They are mistaken in the name, but they agree on one power—those who want Jupiter to be the chief," <note>original: *Falluntur in nomine, sed de una potestate consentiunt qui Jovem principem volunt*</note> says Minutius Felix. For *Jovis* <note>the Latin root for Jupiter</note> is so near to the Hebrew name *Jehovah* <note>original: יהוה</note> that to derive it from the Latin *juvo* (to help) rather than from *Jehovah* is like fetching the origin of the word *fur* (thief) from *furvus* (dark) rather than from the Greek word *phōr* <note>original: φὼρ</note> (thief), for which the author Gellius reprimands Varro.
