# The Fifth and Last Mode of Idolatry. Book I.

The question now arising from this is whether—if a simple soul, struck by the confidence and chanting of this fraudulent magician into a full belief that this statue has become the visible, yet true and eternal God of Heaven and Earth, should therefore worship that "divine combination" <note>original: *Divine Complicate*; referring to the belief that the god and the statue have merged</note> as it is claimed to be (though it is really a mere invention)—this act of worship is blameless and beyond reproach, or whether it constitutes a fifth mode of idolatry. For it might be said in his defense that it was well-intended, and that he meant his worship for the true God, which was not the case in the previous example. But, as I said before, if ignorance excuses one from idolatry, then philosophers will be the only men found capable of that crime. And in the former case, though they did not have a concept of God as true as that which belongs only to the One, yet they thought they had found a proper object of religious worship, if that might serve as their excuse. In this last case, the person has the right concept of the true God, yet he misses the mark in how he applies it, and instead adores a mere idol. And even though it is done in reference to the true God—meaning, it is really intended for Him—to serve Him through an idol is still idolatry; but to mistake an idol for Him is far worse.

4. In short, the sinfulness of any idolatry toward God consists chiefly, if not solely, in either a kind of injustice to Him, or a reproach against Him, or both. Now, I ask anyone whether it is not a greater insult to the true God to mistake a mere idol for Him than to apply that worship which we use for Him (and which always falls infinitely short of Him) to something that is only an idol. Is it not a lesser injustice to take that tiny bit <note>original: *mite*</note> of honor—for all that we can do is no more than that—which is due to God and give it to an idol, than to "take God from Himself," as it were, by assuming that something so infinitely debased below Him is actually Him? It would be a greater injustice to steal a prince out of his cradle and leave a changeling <term>a child believed to have been secretly substituted by fairies for the parents' real child</term> in his place, than to take the prince's cloak to wrap a changeling in. Similarly, it is a far lesser insult to fit a scepter and crown <note>original: *tiara*</note> to the hand and head of King Cyrus’s ape and then perform the Persian bow of respect to it, than to mistake this ape for King Cyrus himself. For the former might be interpreted only as a ridiculous excess of respect and homage, clumsily intended for the King himself by royally adorning and respectfully courting his ape. But the latter is the grossest and most foolish insult imaginable: specifically, because one lacks a properly formed idea <note>original: *prefigured Idea*</note> of a royal prince, failing to distinguish so heroic a person as King Cyrus from an ordinary ape or monkey. And yet, that mysterious statue mentioned above—into which the deceptive magician <note>original: *prestigious Magus*</note> or pagan priest would pretend to have vitally incorporated the true God of the universe—anyone would acknowledge to be more base than these lowest

# Chapter VIII: The Object of Religious Worship as both One and Invisible.

...of animals. It is so plain that this *fifth case* will constitute a *fifth* mode of idolatry, and an extremely flagrant <note>original: rank</note> one as well.

<margin>Pierio Valeriano, Hieroglyphica, book 49.</margin>
5. These *five instances* of idolatry shall serve as our reference points and clear patterns of that most heinous crime; there is hardly any case that cannot be reduced to these, either directly or by analogy. For the religious worship of *rivers*, *plants*, or *animals*—such as the Egyptians worshipped as natural things—is to be categorized under the first class; when worshipped as representatives of a more hidden divinity <note>original: Numen</note>, they belong to the second. *Pictures* also belong to the second category. Consecrated *pillars* and *stones*, even if they have no image on them, are to be considered the same as *statues* if divine worship is offered to them. Examples include the stone featuring only the footstep of Hercules, which the Thracians worshipped, and another four-square stone which Maximus Tyrius says was worshipped by the Arabians. To these, you may add the *Lapis Manalis* <note>a "pouring stone" used by Romans in rituals to call for rain or commune with the dead</note> of the Romans, and their *Terminus lapideus* <note>a stone boundary marker representing the god Terminus</note> in the Capitol.

<margin>Deuteronomy 4:12.</margin>
6. In brief, to keep you in suspense no longer, after reviewing all the details, the common concept <note>original: Notion</note> or *idea* of idolatry undoubtedly consists in this: *giving religious or divine worship to anything that is not truly God*—as certainly no visible thing produced by nature or art can be. Therefore it is said in Deuteronomy, *“You heard a voice, but saw no likeness.”* Corresponding to this is that principle <note>original: Dogma</note> of Pythagoras which Plutarch notes in his *Life of Numa*: "For the First Principle is neither perceptible nor subject to passion, but is invisible, undefiled, and intellectual." <note>original: "Οὔτε γὰρ αἰσθητὸν ἢ παθητὸν, ἀόρατον δὲ καὶ ἀκήρατον καὶ νοητὸν εἶναι τὸ πρῶτον."</note> This led Numa to reject all images in divine worship; instead, he built a temple that represented the world—that great and majestic temple of God—placing the "unquenchable fire" <note>original: τὸ ἄσβεστον πῦρ</note>, the Vestal fire, in the center of it. In this, he followed Pythagorean ideas, though he lived some ages before Pythagoras flourished. This is a witness to a happy combination of profound scientific skill and the purest religion within that philosophy later called "Pythagorean." It is superior to any other found outside the established Church of God, and we may well wonder where they obtained such knowledge, if not from the Church itself.

<margin>Deuteronomy 6:4.</margin>
<margin>Luke 4:8.</margin>
<margin>Hebrews 1:6.</margin>
7. But the purity of this philosophy declined whenever they allowed the worship of *angels*. For the proper object of our worship is *one*, as well as *invisible*: *“Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is One, and there is no God besides him.”* The immediate consequence of this is that he alone is to be worshipped, as our Savior Christ also ratified: *“You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.”* Furthermore, the author of the Epistle to the *Hebrews*, arguing for the divinity of Christ, cites the Psalms: *“Let all the angels of God worship him.”* If religious worship were not reserved solely for that which is God, this command would not prove Christ's divinity.

Lastly, even the Second Council of Nicaea <note>original: Nice</note>, which was excessively favorable toward images, nonetheless condemned the Arians for idolatry for holding that Christ was merely a creature and not truly God. And Nestorius was branded with the hateful title of *man-worshipper* <note>original: "ἀνθρωπολάτρης" (anthropolatrēs)</note> because he held that Christ was a mere man. Both the Arians and Nestorians held that Christ was to be worshipped despite being a creature; that...

The Synod concluded that it is absolute idolatry whether the worship is performed with an image or without one. Likewise, the Synod of Laodicea identifies the *praying to angels* as idolatry. *Epiphanius* <note>a 4th-century bishop known for his opposition to images and heresies</note>, speaking of the *Persians*, says they abhor images and yet they worship idols—meaning the *Sun*, *Moon*, and *Fire*. *Gregory Nazianzen* <note>a 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and influential theologian</note> also (as I have noted above) places idolatry simply in transferring that worship which is due to the Creator onto a creature; Thomas *Aquinas* and Robert *Bellarmine* <note>two of the most influential Catholic theologians and philosophers</note> also define it according to this same concept. Finally, Saint *Jerome* roundly affirms <margin>Book 2, Chapter 9.</margin> that *one is made an idolater if he believes in three Gods* <note>original: "Idololatram factum esse, si quis tres Deos credit"</note>. See Dr. *Rainolds* in his work *On the Idolatry of the Roman Church* <note>original: "De Romanae Ecclesiae Idololatria"</note>.

It is so plain that *idolatry* is not confined to the worshipping of an image, but includes the admitting of more objects of divine worship than that one true God. For the worshipping of any more than Him is what the Jews call *Avodah Zarah* <note>Hebrew: עבודה זרה, literally "foreign worship" or idolatry</note>, and is most frequently and significantly termed in Scripture as *Fornication*. This term looks more at the plurality of the objects of worship than the specific kinds of them. For this spiritual *fornication* is committed whenever we worship anything besides Him who is the Creator and Sustainer of all things.

## CHAPTER IX.

1. *The necessity of knowing what religious worship is in order to discover* idolatry. 2. *The flaws in dividing* worship *into* Latria <note>worship due to God alone</note>, Dulia <note>veneration given to saints and angels</note>, *and* civil honor <note>original: Cultus civilis; social respect given to humans</note>. 3. *That Christ only, who is the* God-man <note>original: θεάνθρωπος</note>, *has such a middle* excellence *that he may receive religious worship.* 4. *That the gap in* excellence *between* God *and* saints *or* angels *is so infinitely greater than the gap between* saints *or* angels *and* men; *therefore, it is extremely forced and irrational to assign one category of worship to the first two, rather than to the second and last—which, as they are fellow-citizens, might rightly be called* civil. 5. *That no kind of religious worship is due to* saints *and* angels, *as proved by the Angel's refusal to be worshipped by* Saint John. 6. *And also from the near affinity of our natures with theirs.* 7. *To whom* Origen <note>an early Christian scholar and theologian</note> *considers good men equal; nor does he allow the glorious stars to be worshipped, even if they were intellectual beings.* 8. *That the religious worship of* saints *and* angels *is not a duty of ours, as it cannot be reduced to the precepts of either* table <note>the two "tables" of the Ten Commandments</note>. 9. *That religious worship is only one thing and is due to* God *only, as proved from our Savior’s answer to the* Devil. 10. *Also from the author of the Hebrews, who argues for the* divinity *of* Christ *based on the religious worship due to him, along with several other testimonies.* 11. *An answer to an objection.*

1. Thus, we have found the full scope of what constitutes an object of idolatry: it is whatever is not truly God, or <margin>Chapter 4, verse 8.</margin> *everything that is not by nature God* <note>original: πᾶν τὸ μὴ φύσει ὂν Θεός</note>, as the Apostle speaks to the Galatians. But unless we also have the knowledge of what constitutes religious or *divine* worship—and when or how we give this worship to something that is not truly God—we shall still be at a loss.

2. There are some who, for the better disguising of their unjustifiable practices, have constructed a clever explanation; namely, that there are as many kinds of *Honor* or *Worship* as there are types of *Excellence*. They argue that because there are three kinds of *Excellence*—*Divine*, *Human*, and a middle ground between *Human* and *Divine* (such as the supernatural grace and glory of the *Saints* and *Angels*)—there are also three kinds of *Worship*: Divine worship <note>original: Latria</note>, Veneration <note>original: Dulia</note>, and civil worship <note>original: Cultus civilis</note>. But this division would have involved less deception and better logic if it had been divided into two parts; for then it would have appeared more plainly what kind of worship they mean by *Veneration*. For they do not want it to be *civil worship*, as it is a distinct category from it. It follows, therefore, that it must be *religious worship*, though they were afraid to speak openly about what they harbor in their hearts. For indeed *Religion*, which in its primary and proper sense is nothing other than the worship of the Deity <note>original: Cultus Numinis</note>, belongs by right <note>original: de jure</note> only to the true God; and if it is transferred to anything else, it is *idolatry* or *superstition*.

But if they had dealt honestly, and like truthful men and precise logicians, they should have divided *Honor* or *Worship* first into *Religious* and *Civil*, and then, according to the meaning they intended, subdivided *Religious worship* into Divine worship and Veneration. But since this was craftily aimed at and assumed, even if not plainly expressed—and indeed was the primary goal, to argue that *religious worship* is due to *saints* and *angels* as well as to *God himself*—I shall direct my answer only against this mistake.

3. First, therefore, I say that the basis for assigning *religious worship* to *saints* and *angels* is very weak—namely, because they are said to have a middle excellence between God and man. For it is plain they do not have this in a proper and strict sense; that is a privilege belonging to Christ alone, who is the acknowledged God-man <note>original Greek: Theanthropos</note>, and therefore may justly be worshipped with *religious worship*. Therefore, since there is nothing that truly has a middle excellence between God and Man—just as an animal-plant <note>original: Zoophyton; a historical term for organisms like coral that were believed to share the characteristics of both plants and animals</note> may be rightly said to have a middle excellence between an animal and a plant—except for the Man Christ *Jesus*, there is no creature capable of *religious worship* besides him. Nor is he, indeed, capable of it except by virtue of that mysterious union with the true Godhead, by which he becomes God as well as Man.

4. And then again, there is another deception, and indeed the more principal and original one, in dividing these *Excellences* immediately into three. It would have been more faithful and logical to have divided *Excellence* first into *Created* and *Uncreated* <note>original: Increated</note>; and then to divide *Created* Excellence into that of *Saints* and *Angels*, and that of *Men*. But if they had done this, the boldness and grossness of their assigning *religious worship* to that which is only a creature would have appeared at first sight. The Creator stands in opposition to the creature, as He is infinitely more excellent than any glorified creature whatever; or rather, His degree of excellence above the most glorious creature that exists is infinitely greater than the degree of excellence of *Saints* and *Angels* above *Men*.

From this, it appears how rash and forced a thing it is to try and hold together two different types of Excellence within the single category of receiving *religious worship*—especially when there is such an infinite distance between them. I am speaking of the *Divine Excellence* of God compared to that of *angels* and *saints*. In reality, *human excellence* and that of *saints* and *angels* are infinitely closer to one another; therefore, it is infinitely more appropriate for them to receive a type of worship that shares one common name. This may very well be termed *civil* honor, as the glorified *saints*, *angels*, and *good men* are all merely *fellow servants* and *fellow citizens* of that new *Jerusalem* which reaches from *heaven* to *earth*. As it is written: *But you have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels, and the spirits of righteous men made perfect.* This shows plainly that *saints*, *angels*, and *good men* on *earth* are all part of one community, citizens of the same city—the new *Jerusalem*. And as you know, fellow citizens do not give *religious worship* to one another, but only *civil* honor.

<margin>Chapter 19</margin>
5. Nor are they more than *fellow servants*, as the *angel* argued to *John* in the *Apocalypse* <note>original: "Apocalyps"; the Book of Revelation</note>: *And I fell at his feet to worship him. And if he refused *religious worship* even while present, how unlawful is it to offer such worship—even if it is only *veneration* <note>original: "Dulia"</note>—to a *saint* or *angel* who is absent? 

Furthermore, if the worship offered there was meant to be *divine worship* <note>original: "Latria"</note> and not merely *veneration*, why did the angel not say, "I am your *fellow creature*," rather than "your *fellow servant*"? Why would he be so unkind to the Church, or so harmful to his fellow angels, as to trouble the Church with doubts about the duty of worshipping angels and saints by so fastidiously declining the homage? Such an eminent example would likely be so influential that it would risk undermining the belief in the entire duty of *angel worship*. 

But I believe the distinction between *veneration* <note>original: "Dulia"</note> and *divine worship* <note>original: "Latria"</note> is so subtle that even the eye of an angel could never spot any such chink or smallest crack in *religious worship* by which it might be broken asunder. It cannot be so divided that even the smallest part of it falls to anything that is not truly God—which saints and angels certainly are not. Thus, it appears plainly, both from the meaning of Scripture and the infinite disproportion between God and His creatures, that only *civil* honor, and not *religious worship*, is appropriate for them.

<meta>This page continues the argument that religious worship is a singular category reserved for God alone. The author is refuting the idea that there are different "levels" of worship—one for God and another for holy beings—by examining the temptations of Christ and the history of early Church heresies.</meta>

<header>That Religious worship is but One. Book I.</header>

9. The kingdoms of the earth and their glory were *only committed to him* by another, <note>original Greek: ὅτι παραδέδοταί μοι—"since it has been delivered to me" (Luke 4:6)</note>. Therefore, the Devil did not possess them by his own power and, consequently, did not pretend to be the Most High God, from whom all things come. For this reason, the Devil could not be so unreasonable as to expect, nor so foolish as to demand, that our Savior should perform any worship to him as if he were the Most High God, since he had already confessed that he was not. 

Instead, his goal was to persuade Christ to perform *religious worship* to him—the kind of worship typically given to the many "gods" of the nations who rank below the status of the Most High. 

But the meaning of our Savior's answer is that there is no *religious worship* at all that belongs to anyone except God alone. Being out of patience (if I may put it that way) at the suggestion of such an impious act, Jesus calls him *Devil* because of such a monstrous suggestion; none but devils would either require or allow *religious worship* to be performed for them. 

Christ does not refuse to worship him simply because he was a *Devil*; rather, he concludes he is a *Devil* because, despite not being the true God, he still wanted to be *religiously worshiped*. Nor did Christ answer, "You shall only worship God and the good angels," but rather, "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve." Therefore, there is only *one single religious worship*, namely that which is due to God.

10. The same point is clearly inferred from the Epistle to the Hebrews. There, the author proves the divinity of Christ by citing the Psalms: *Let all the angels of God worship him*. This is unquestionably understood as *religious worship*, otherwise, it would not serve the author’s purpose. Yet, if there were two kinds of religious worship—supreme worship <note>original Latin: Latria</note> and secondary honor <note>original Latin: Dulia</note>—the argument would still be weak. 

It is quite plain that there is only one kind of *religious worship*, which is reserved for God alone. Furthermore, the Arians <note>Followers of Arius who believed Christ was a created being, not co-equal with God the Father.</note> could not have been justly considered idolaters by the Council of Nicaea, nor could Nestorius <note>A 5th-century bishop who was accused of separating Christ's divine and human natures too sharply.</note> be called a worshiper of a man <note>original Greek: ἀνθρωπολάτρης (anthropolatra)</note>, if there were more than one kind of religious worship. 

Neither Nestorius nor the Arians could have intended the worship they gave to Christ to be "supreme worship" <note>original Latin: Latria</note>, for that would have been an express acknowledgment that he was the true God—the very point they so stubbornly denied. Therefore, the Church Synod, Saint Cyril, and everyone else who judged the Arians as idolaters and Nestorius as a "man-worshiper," plainly bear witness that *religious worship is only one thing*.

11. Nor can the affectionate respect we show to the Bible when we kiss it while taking an oath, or the respect we show to the holy prophets of God, his priests, and faithful ministers when we revere them as such, disrupt our reasoning or serve as an example of another kind of *religious worship*. 

I absolutely deny that there is any *religious* respect or affection given to the Bible or to a "man of God" themselves. Instead, out of the *religious respect and affection* we have for God himself, a different kind of respect emerges toward things related to him. Toward people, this is *civil* respect. But toward inanimate objects, when compared to holy people, it is hardly bold to say it is a level of respect even lower than civil honor. These differences exist even where we have no specific names to call them by.

Chapter 10: The general notion of Religious worship.

And it seems to me just as absurd to conclude that because I respect the Bible or any holy man of God based on a *religious* regard I have for God himself, this respect for the Bible or the holy man is also a *religious* reverence or respect. This is like concluding that because a woman, out of the marriage-based affection and respect she has for her husband, also feels respect and affection for his pet spaniel (which she would not otherwise have), that the affection or respect she felt for the spaniel should either be, or be called, a "conjugal" <note>original: "conjugal"—relating to marriage</note> affection. Such an idea is obviously ridiculous at first sight.

## CHAPTER X.

1. *A correct categorization of worship into its various types.* 2. *The definition of religious worship.* 3. *That showing honor to any improper object—even if forced or faked—using signs reserved for acknowledging divine excellence is blatant idolatry.* 4. *And therefore there are no limited levels or specific degrees of religious worship; no Dulia or Hyperdulia, but it is all Latria.* <note>original: "Dulia" (service given to saints or angels), "Hyperdulia" (special service for the Virgin Mary), and "Latria" (worship reserved for God alone). The author argues these distinctions are false and all religious worship is Latria.</note> 5. *That religious worship is not applied to a thing by directing it toward it as a mere circumstance, but as an object; and therefore misapplying it to an object is what constitutes idolatry.* 6. *But it is not necessary that this application be intended as worship for God himself.* 7. *That the heathens themselves never committed such an act of idolatry as giving religious worship to something they knew was not the Supreme God, while treating it as if it were the Supreme.* 8. *That because religious worship is only one thing, every application of it to what is not God becomes idolatry.* 9. *That the repeated teaching of the divinity of Christ proves every created being is incapable of receiving religious worship.*

1. Because we are so well satisfied concerning the *oneness* of *religious worship*, we are able to create a more accurate and logical categorization of *honor* or *worship* than the one previously presented. We divide it immediately, first into *religious* and *civil*; and then *civil* into *political*, *economic*, and *moral*; and *political* again into *secular* and *ecclesiastical*, or else into *temporal* and *spiritual*—either set of terms being well enough known. By *moral worship*, I mean the honor or respect that passes between private individuals, or at least toward them as private persons, based on their *moral worth*, such as *generosity*, *wisdom*, *faithfulness*, and the like. The other terms are self-explanatory. Nor is it relevant to my goal to deal with any but the first: namely, *religious worship*, for the sake of understanding the nature of which I have taken all this trouble so far.

2. Which I conceive is rightly defined this way: *A devotional acknowledgment of the unique Name or Excellence of God, by the performance of some outward rite or ceremony dedicated to that end—specifically, to externally signify our inward acknowledgment of the divine Name or Excellence.* This is a true and the most general definition

...definition that can be made of *Religious worship*. For that religion which is centered on worshipping saints, angels, demons <note>original: "Dæmons"—referring to lower spirits or pagan deities</note>, images, and the like, is truly irreligion, idolatry, or superstition. It is no more to be called *religious worship* than vice should be called virtue, injustice called justice, or cowardice called bravery—regardless of whatever abuses of the word may have crept in through the unskillful and thoughtless.

3. Now, since giving *religious worship* to that which is not God is idolatry, and *religious worship* in its true and proper sense is nothing else but *a devotional acknowledgment of the divine eminence, by certain appropriate signs indicating this our recognition* <note>original: "agnition"—the act of acknowledging or recognizing</note>; it is demonstrably evident that where such a devotional acknowledgment is made through these signs to something that is not God, it is *by that very fact* <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> *idolatry*.

Indeed, even if these *appropriate signs* were used without devotion by the person toward the supposed object (which is a point worth noting and true, because a complete level of wickedness <note>original: "plenary pravity"—total depravity or full evil intent</note> or inward failure is not required for an action to be sinful) and were intended by other men to be directed there, or were simply understood by custom to be directed there, it would still be idolatry. Otherwise, the sin of *idolatry* could not be forced upon any man; nor would any Jew or Christian have hesitated to throw incense on the altar to any pagan deity, or even to sacrifice entire massive offerings <note>original: "Hecatombs"—ancient Greek sacrifices of 100 oxen; any large-scale slaughter or sacrifice</note> to them if their purses could have afforded it. And whoever died as a martyr for refusing to do so would have to be seen as mad or foolish rather than possessing any true and solid piety.

Therefore, just as it would be *blasphemy* to say *that Jesus Christ was not the Son of God, but an impostor*—even if it were forced by fear and the person's heart did not agree—so the use of the *appropriate signs* for acknowledging divine excellence for something that is not God is still the acknowledgment of that thing as God (just as that blasphemy was the denial of him being what he was). Therefore, it cannot be anything but outright idolatry.

4. And if idolatry is committed even without the person's devotion toward the improper object, then even if a person imagines this external *religious worship* to be accompanied by the smallest possible amount of *devotion* or inward intent, it will still be *idolatry*. This logical conclusion <note>original: "Consectary"</note> is particularly useful for convincing people of the foolishness of the excuses <note>original: "subterfuges"</note> found in these newly-coined terms: *Dulia*, *Hyperdulia*, and *Latria* <note>original: "Dulia" is the honor given to saints; "Hyperdulia" is the special honor for the Virgin Mary; "Latria" is worship for God alone. The author argues these distinctions are false.</note>. By these terms, they would suggest certain differences or degrees of religious worship—indeed, distinct *kinds* of it—whereas there can only be *one* kind, according to the true definition we have given. For every act or result of our religious affection for God that is expressed toward things or people is not immediately *religious worship*, as is clearly shown by its definition and what we already discussed in the previous chapter. But to return to the matter at hand.

5. Through this general concept of *religious worship*, we have now moved a significant step closer to discovering *when idolatry is committed*. Namely, it is committed *when we perform some rite or ceremony—that is to say, some external*

### Chapter X: The General Notion of Religious Worship

...an external *religious action*, appropriate for signifying our acknowledgment of the Divine Eminence, performed before, or rather toward, that which is not truly God. By "before" or "toward," I mean an intended direction (by ourselves, or by others, or at least by the interpretation of custom) of this religious action, as if toward an *object* we wish to honor by it. For that is the only thing by which the action becomes *idolatry*. There will always be a necessity of performing our religious rites before or toward something or other simply as a circumstance of place, which can be done without the least guilt or suspicion of that crime. Therefore, it is the intended and customary application of the appropriate signs of the acknowledgment of the Divine Excellencies toward an *object where the Divine Excellencies are not*—that is to say, to anything that is not truly God—which constitutes this heinous sin of *idolatry*. This much, I say, is required, and this much alone, without adding anything else, fully completes the nature of that sin.

6. As for those who imagine themselves so incredibly sly and subtle in sneaking <note>original: "foisting"</note> in this extra requirement—namely:
> "That the application of these
> "signs appropriated for signifying the honor we owe to God
> "must, in idolatry, be made to the creature *as if to God himself*; that is to
> "say, with the intent of gaining for the adored creature the status
> "of being the true God;"
they assuredly commit a gross piece of folly in daring to make such an assertion.

For just as a woman who gives to a man who is not her husband what is appropriate only to her husband (namely, the use of her body) is unquestionably a total adulteress—regardless of what mental restrictions or "directions of intent" she imagines during the act—so too, whoever applies the appropriate acknowledgments of the Divine Excellency (which is religious worship) to that which is not God, is undoubtedly a gross *idolater*. No matter how he tries to diminish the act with mental limitations and restrictions, once he directs this religious worship toward an improper object, the sin is committed. And just as her saying she did not do it "as to her husband" will not excuse her from *adultery*, the other person's saying he did not do it "as to God" will not excuse him from *idolatry*, which is *spiritual fornication*.

<margin>Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book 9, Chapter 2.</margin>

For among the many gods the pagans worshipped, there was only one worshipped as the Most High, whom the Latins called *Jupiter* and the Greeks called *Zeus*, who was considered the Father of the Gods. This gave occasion for *Aristotle* to use this expression concerning the distribution of duties and respect: *οὐδὲ τῷ πατρὶ πάντα, καθάπερ οὐδὲ τῷ Διὶ θύεται* <note>original Greek translated as: "For just as all sacrifices are not made to Jupiter [Zeus], so all honors are not to be given to a father."</note>. But those sacrifices that were not made to him (which were surely the majority) would not be considered idolatrous worship according to this hypothesis; nor would those made to his statue by people who did not mistake the statue for *Jupiter* himself; nor those that were sacrificed to *Jupiter* himself as the Father and...

8. To this you may add that, since we have already proved *that religious worship is one single thing*, applying it to any object on any terms—except to the only true God—is *by that very fact* <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> idolatry.

9. ## CHAPTER XI.

1. *Sacrifices, drink-offerings, and the burning of incense are designated signs of religious worship according to Grotius, as is whatever else the common agreement of nations has established as such.* 2. *Also vows, oaths, asking for supernatural gifts, and praying to saints or angels while they are invisible.* 3. *Or to ask them—even if they were visible—for any natural favor at an altar or in a temple dedicated to them.* 4. *Images set up and dedicated in temples or on altars are a form of divine worship; along with the prevention of an objection.* 5. *Songs and bowing <note>original: "Incurvations"</note> may also be so designed and performed in certain contexts as to become such signs.* 6. *That every act of idolatry is blasphemy; as is giving the Name of God to any creature.* 7. *A general classification of the designated signs of religious worship.* 8. *Prevention of an excuse <note>original: "subterfuge"</note> based on the claim that "religious worship" has a broader meaning than we have given; all our future proofs depend only on the truth of our definition of religious worship in the sense we have declared.*

Thus, he has not only provided us with examples but also a rule for how to find the proper signs of divine worship: namely, that at the very least, those things are signs which the common agreement of nations has made so. # Chapter XI. The appropriate Signs of Divine worship.

1. Regarding *sacrifice* to that which they call *Latria* <note>original: "Latria"; from the Greek word *latreia*, referring to the supreme worship and service reserved for God alone</note> (as if this sign of religious worship were exclusively proper to God, while others could be shared with other objects), we should take notice of one thing. If they mean by "sacrifice" the slaughtering <note>original: "Mactation"; the ritual killing of a victim for sacrifice</note> of living creatures, that manner of worship is no longer in use among Christians. Therefore, the absence of animal sacrifice must necessarily increase the importance of other signs of religious worship. It makes them even more clearly restricted to God alone and not to be shared with any created object—which would be true even if animal sacrifice still existed. But this is only a side note.

2. Hugo Grotius <note>a famous Dutch jurist and theologian (1583–1645)</note> acknowledges that *vows* and *oaths* are also part of this kind of worship, as is *praying for the Holy Spirit, for the forgiveness of sins, and for eternal life.* According to him, these things are not to be asked of an angel, even if that angel were visibly present. To this I will take the liberty of adding the religious invocation <note>calling upon or praying to</note> of any absent or invisible angel or spirit. Because God is the only giver of the *forgiveness of sins* and of the *Holy Spirit*, anyone who asks for such high things from any creature is attributing the unique excellencies of God to that creature. Similarly, anyone who prays to an invisible angel, saint, or spirit is acknowledging an *omniscience* <note>all-knowingness</note> and *omnipresence* <note>the state of being everywhere at once</note> in that saint or angel, which are the unique excellencies of God.

3. Furthermore, I would add that asking for things that *are* within the power of a creature to give—for example, asking for a proper medicine for a specific sickness, or for protection from danger while traveling—can still be an act of worship. If one asks for medicine from *Aesculapius* <note>the Greek god of medicine</note> in a temple and at an altar consecrated to his ghost, or asks for protection from *Hercules* <note>the Roman hero and god</note> at an altar dedicated to him, these requests for practical favors would still be *idolatry*. This is because the *common agreement of nations has established that building and dedicating temples and altars for prayers, vows, and sacrifices is a sign of divine worship*. As you know, this was the formal way of worshipping the Most High God, the God of *Israel*, while the Temple stood. His presence was understood to reside most specifically upon the *Cherubim* <note>winged celestial beings</note>, which were hidden from the people's sight so that they would not commit idolatry by worshipping them.

4. But the Gentiles <note>non-Jewish or pagan peoples</note> very corruptly used this aspect of religious worship. They directed their prayers toward open images or statues of "divine residence" consecrated for that purpose, where the god was expected to receive their offerings and prayers. So, even though all nations at all times did not use images to represent the divine presence, wherever it was used (which was extremely common), it is clear that it was part of the highest form of worship, the kind used toward the Supreme Deity <note>original: "Numen"</note>. We see that this method of divine presence through images was used not only in the worship of lesser spirits <note>original: "Dæmons"</note> but also for those called *celestial gods* <note>original: "Dii cæleſtes"</note> (whom the pagans surely did not believe were exiled from heaven just to live in these earthly statues). This is a sign that the *image* itself was considered the visible presence of the deity they adored. Consequently, this representation of the presence of the deity—whether the deity is personally...

...present or not, is that which by the *consent of nations* has passed into an ordinary mode of Divine worship.

The building of temples, altars, or other symbols of religious worship to those who are not gods does not stop these from being signs of such worship. In fact, since they have all been misused in that way, there would be no signs of Divine worship left at all if that were the case. Instead, we should conclude that since these things were consecrated for the worship or honor of the God of *Israel*, to consecrate similar things to anything else is an invasion of His rights and a manifest act of idolatry.

5. *Hymns* also, and *bowing* <term>original: "incurvations"</term>, depending on how they are framed, will unavoidably be *signs of Divine worship*. For example, if this *bowing* is directed at any particular invisible power while he is invisible, it is an acknowledgment of one of the unique excellencies of God: His *omnipresence* <term>original: "ubiquity"</term>. We may bow anywhere to the invisible God because He is everywhere; but to bow to any particular angel or spirit while he is invisible is inappropriate <note>original: "incongruous"</note> because he is not everywhere. Therefore, anyone who performs this worship to him as if it were appropriate does, by that act, *interpretatively* acknowledge an *omnipresence* in him, and thereby becomes an *idolater*.

*Bowing* also toward an *image* built for any creature—especially in a *temple* or on an *altar*, even if removed from both—is a sign of religious worship or service by infallible definition: *“You shall not bow down to them, nor serve them.”* That is to say, you shall not perform the service of *bowing*, nor any other religious service to them. For the Hebrew word *avodah* <note>original: "עבודה"; a term meaning service or labor, often used for religious worship</note> for *service* is *religious worship* <note>original: "Cultus religiosus"</note>, of which *bowing* in such circumstances is assuredly one kind. I mean, it is exhibited either to an invisible power or to its visible representation in an *image*. Regarding the latter, the *consent of nations* has also made images a specific sign of religious worship, especially in a *temple*, as I noted before.

And now regarding *hymns*: I say that the framing of a *song* to the praise of any created being—suppose the *Sun*, *Moon*, or a *spirit* <term>original: "Dæmon"</term>—is certainly giving *Divine worship* to them if there are titles in it that signify the unique excellencies of God. For example, if one should begin, *“O Almighty Sun”* <note>original: "O Sol Omnipotens"</note>, or, *“O All-knowing Moon”* <note>original: "O Luna Omniscia"</note>. Because of this, the poet *Martial* seems to me to be not only a flatterer of the emperor *Domitian*, but an *idolater* in that *eleven-syllable poem* <note>original: "Hendecasyllabon"; a common meter in Latin poetry</note>:

->*The edict of our Lord and God.* <note>original: "Edictum Domini Deíque noftri"</note><-

In this, he writes according to *Domitian’s* own example, who taught his ministers of state this form for letters: *“Our Lord and God so commands it to be done.”* <note>original: "Deus & Dominus nofter sic fieri jubet"</note> This might be more tolerable in pagan kingdoms where "gods" <note>original: "Dii"</note> usually meant no more than "angels" do among us. However, in Christian nations, where *God* is an *incommunicable name* <note>a name that cannot be shared with or applied to anyone else</note>—as the author of the *Book of Wisdom* suggests—calling any man "God" cannot be anything but *idolatry* or *blasphemy*.

6. But it is no less *idolatry* for being *blasphemy*, since every *idolatry* is so. For *idolatry*, by giving the specific signs of the acknowledgment of Divine excellence to a lowly creature (and every creature is lowly in respect to God), treats that creature as equal to God, and consequently...

# Chapter 11. The Appropriate Signs of Divine Worship.

...frequently makes God as vile as that creature. This is a manifest reviling and *blaspheming* of him, worse than calling a prince by the name of the basest vermin. I say, therefore, that in countries where the name of *God* usually refers to the *true God*, and not to angels, applying that title to any man is both *idolatry* and *blasphemy*. It would be the same as using any gesture toward him that was appropriate for divine adoration. This is why the Greeks would not show reverence to the King of *Persia* in the *Persian* manner <note>The Persian practice of *proskynesis*, or prostrating oneself before a ruler.</note>, because that was the very posture which in *Greece* they used for worshipping their gods.

7. These are the main, if not all, the *signs of divine worship* that easily come to mind. If I have missed any in my specific listing, they will be easily recalled—or at least kept safe—within the general concept I have provided for the *appropriate signs of religious worship*. Specifically, these are signs that have been established as such by the *consent of nations*, the *customs of particular countries*, the *natural meaning of the thing itself*, or by *divine definition*. 

Of the first sort are *food-offerings* <note>original: "Meat-offerings," referring to grain or food sacrifices</note>, *drink-offerings*, *burning of incense*, *erecting altars*, *dedicating images*, and the like. 

Of the second sort is *a particular posture of religious veneration specific to a country*, as in the example of the Greeks, which was mandatory for the people of that country. 

And of the third sort is *praying for the Holy Spirit, for the forgiveness of sins, for eternal life, or for whatever else is beyond the power of a creature to give*. Also, *the making of vows and oaths*, as these imply an absolute <term>knowledge of the heart</term> <note>original Greek: καρδιογνωσία (kardiognosia)</note> in those in whose name they are made. This implies not only a knowledge of the facts but a power to punish beyond the reach of human laws; we have no assurance of such power and knowledge in any particular spirit, but in God only. 

To these you may add *the invoking of any particular invisible powers while they are invisible*, even for things they are naturally able to help us with. *Hymns* also, or any forms of address whatsoever made to a creature, are signs of worship if the words signify the incommunicable excellencies of God. All of these, by their own nature and whatever is similar to them, are the *appropriate signs of religious worship*, even if the *consent of nations* did not agree; they are not owed to anything, nor lawful to be given to anything, except the true God. Therefore, the misapplication of them to any other object will certainly be the sin of *idolatry*. 

Lastly, an example of the final category is *bowing to images*, as it is declared in the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> to be a kind of service to them, as I noted before.

8. And now, so that no one may imagine they have found a loophole <note>original: "creep-hole"</note> to evade the power and clarity of our reasoning by pretending that *religious worship* has a broader meaning than what I have defined, I will warn him here in advance. I do not care what careless abuses a word may suffer, or what forced stretching is used to make proper terms cover and excuse improper actions or unsound opinions. Furthermore (and I want him to take special notice of this), the strength of our arguments does not depend on *religious worship* having only one single meaning (though I have sufficiently proved that it has only one), but rather on the truth of the definition we have given it, in the sense that is intended here.

Several Instances of Idolatry. Book I.

...intended. ### CHAPTER XII.

1. *A brief list of the components of the full instruction we have for identifying idolatry.* 2. *That the adoration of the Cross is idolatry.* 3. *As also the worship of any person of the Holy Trinity by an image or picture.* 4. *That religious worship given to saints or angels, even without the use of any image or picture, is idolatry.* 5. *That the mere invocation of any particular invisible power is also idolatrous.* 6. *Certain excuses regarding praying to saints answered.* 7. *Another subterfuge answered.* 8. *Worshipping saints by images is a double idolatry.* 9. *That it is idolatry to worship an image while taking it for the saint himself.* 10. *As also the adoration of any man alive upon Earth.* 11. *That the worship of the bread of the Eucharist <note>The bread used in Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper.</note>, when taken for the real body of Christ, is idolatry.* 12. *That all the above-mentioned acts are idolatrous, regardless of what men claim to cover their guilt.* 13. *And that "unlawful idolatries" <note>original Greek: "εἰδωλολατρεῖαι ἀθέμιτοι" (eidōlolatreiai athemitoi); a reference to 1 Peter 4:3.</note> in Saint Peter does not imply that any kind of idolatry is lawful.*

1. I believe we are now sufficiently instructed—partly by the acknowledged examples of idolatry committed by Heathens or Jews, and partly by knowing the proper object of idolatry. We also have a correct definition of *religious worship* and its appropriate *signs*, as well as how those *signs* are essentially applied. Therefore, we can discern and define infallibly what would be considered idolatry—and what would not—wherever it is practiced among Christians themselves.

2. For example, *to adore the Cross, or to give any religious worship to it, even if there were no image upon it, would be idolatry*. This follows the first instance of idolatry and those related to it, which show that idolatry can be committed even without an *image*. It is plain that idolatry is committed here because we assume that the appropriate *signs of divine worship* are being used in the adoration of the cross. When such signs are used for any created thing, it is *by that very act* <note>original Latin: "ipso facto"</note> idolatry.

### Chapter XII. Several Instances of Idolatry.

Any representation of God himself—Father, Son, or Holy Spirit—is nevertheless *idolatry* according to the second instance <note>The author refers back to a previous section or "instance" where he argued that using images to represent the true God is forbidden.</note>, in which worshipping the true God by an image is proved to be such.

4. Thirdly, the worshipping of *angels* or *saints*, and even the *Blessed Virgin herself*, with *religious worship*—even *without an image*—is *idolatry*. This includes the religious invocation of them, asking them for things that are only appropriate for God to give, such as the *remission of sins*, the *assistance of grace*, and *eternal life*. It also includes using any titles in *hymns* or *songs* dedicated to them that signify the *incommunicable excellencies of God* <note>original: "incommunicable Excellencies of God"; refers to attributes like being all-powerful or all-knowing that cannot be shared by created beings.</note>. Finally, it includes *making vows* and *swearing in their names*. This clearly follows from the first instance of idolatry and from those specific signs of divine worship that are naturally recognizable as such.

5. Indeed, the *invocation of help* from this or that *saint* is idolatrous, even if it is not done in the more obvious circumstances of offering petitions in a temple or before the image of the saint to whom we pray. For the *simple invocation of a specific invisible power* is, in itself, *idolatry* even without those other circumstances. This is because it indirectly attributes to that power what belongs only to the true God: namely, *omnipresence* or *ubiquity* <note>The state of being everywhere at the same time.</note>. After all, no one can be certain that an invisible power is in a specific place unless they assume that the power is in all places at once, which is the unique prerogative of God.

Therefore, the *simple invocation of any particular invisible power* is not the minor matter that some claim it to be. It is *absolute idolatry*. In fact, if examined rationally and philosophically, I believe it is the *most fundamental part of all the idolatry* committed by the pagans <note>original: "Heathen"</note> and the mother of all other forms. At the very least, every major or rationally convincing objection against giving the usual signs of religious worship to these specific invisible powers applies here and can be argued against *invocation*. The main point is that it implies the *omnipresence* of the invisible power being worshipped.

Because of this, the consecrating of a temple and altar, the creation of a symbolic residence or visible representation, and the offering of sacrifices (and similar acts) can only be appropriate for the *all-present God*. He is the only one whom worshippers can be sure to find "at home," so to speak, when they approach His house. But regarding other specific invisible powers, who knows whether they are at home or not? Perhaps they are pursuing someone, on a journey, or asleep somewhere—as *Elijah* <note>original: "Elias"; a reference to the prophet mocking the priests of the false god Baal in 1 Kings 18:27.</note> sarcastically argued concerning *Baal*. I would even add: who knows if they have been carried away captive and confined to some other place? No one can be certain where they are, or if they are ever truly present where their visible and symbolic residence is built, unless they are *omnipresent*—existing there by necessity because they are everywhere. If they are not, we can have no faith or assurance of their presence or their listening. Yet *prayer* and *invocation* assume a sense of faith and assurance of being heard. Since there can be no such assurance unless the invisible power being invoked is *omnipresent*, it is clear that anyone who invokes an invisible power implicitly suggests its omnipresence. Consequently, if that power is a specific and finite being, the person commits *idolatry* by doing so.

# Several Instances of Idolatry. Book I.

6. Nor can the demonstrability of this *reason* be eluded or evaded by those usual excuses of the Saints seeing and knowing all things by *particular revelation from God*, or by the *exalted uniqueness of their condition in that separate glorified state they are in*. For those who talk in this manner speak wildly, and utter unintelligible riddles without any ground or probability of reason or warrant from Scripture; these are merely later inventions and baseless assumptions to excuse the madness and extravagance of their idolatrous actions.

For regarding the latter assumption, it is plainly a dream to think the Blessed Virgin, for instance, merely by virtue of her glorified condition and separation from this terrestrial body, can hear from Heaven at such a vast distance the devout whispers or sighs of her affectionate supplicants, or see through the Earth their humble prostrations. For she is called upon by the inhabitants of this globe in all locations and distances—even by those who are *Antipodes* <term>Antipodes: People living on the opposite side of the globe, whose feet are "against" ours.</term> to one another. If she assists one, she must be at least the Earth’s diameter away from the other, through which distance neither her sight nor hearing can ever penetrate.

And as for the former hypothesis, how childish and ridiculous it is! They pretend that they supplicate the Saints to speak to God on their behalf, even though the Saints cannot speak to God until He tells them their errand first. He has already received the message from the supplicant, but must impart it to the Saints just so they can say it back to Him again. This shows the absurdity of making any addresses to them; and (considering how perfectly approachable and gracious, and how freely accessible God is through the only name and mediation of *Jesus Christ*) it is such a useless patch and clumsy fix in divinity that it cannot seem credible to any man of common sense. Therefore, there is no such special revelation to the Saints regarding our prayers to them. Consequently, the *invocation* of them (which belongs only to God, by reason of His *all-knowing omnipresence* <note>original: "omniscious Ubiquity"</note>) being thus misplaced upon these specific invisible powers, must be by interpretation an act of *idolatry*. This is because an act of worship is being performed for them that implies the object has an excellence found only in God.

7. Nor will their profession of those diminishing views concerning Saints in other respects (such as claiming they are not the true God but only glorified creatures, or that they are intercessors inferior to Christ, and the like) excuse them from *idolatry*. For the acknowledgment of any one divine excellence or unique quality of the Godhead in that which is merely a creature is undoubtedly *idolatry*, just as betraying even a single castle to the enemy is treason against a prince. Furthermore, the Pagans were esteemed as idolaters for worshipping *Mercury* and the whole order of the *intermediary* <note>original: "Medioxumous"; a Latin-derived term for middle-ranking deities who act as messengers between the supreme gods and humans.</note> or messenger-like *deities* or *demons*, despite their acknowledgment that these were inferior to the Supreme God. So, I cannot see any other conclusion than that the mere *invocation of Saints or Angels* is a palpable—even a fundamental—piece of *idolatry*. It is the foundation upon which all the pomp and equipment of idolatry was built; I mean the building of their temples, the erecting of altars and images, the burning of incense, sacrificing, and the rest. For all these things end in, or are the circumstances of, *invocation*.

# Chapter 12. Several Instances of Idolatry.

7. ...supplication, based on the faith and assurance of being heard. Such assurance cannot be rationally placed in any invisible power unless that power is *omnipresent* <term>omnipresent: present everywhere at the same time</term>. This act of *invocation* <note>original: "Invocation"; here meaning the act of calling upon a deity or spirit in prayer.</note> naturally and necessarily implies omnipresence; otherwise, the action makes no sense and would be entirely inconsistent and ridiculous. Any other assumptions about an invisible power are merely arbitrary, uncertain, and even incredible guesses, upon which no faith or assurance of being heard can be built.

8. Fourthly, just as this worship of *invocation* toward either a Saint or Angel *without the use of an image* is clearly *idolatry*, so invoking them—or worshipping them in any other way—*with an image* must be a double act of idolatry, and falls under the third category of the offense.

9. Fifthly, worshipping an *image*—for example, one of the Blessed Virgin or any other Saint—under the mistaken belief that the image is actually the Virgin herself or that specific Saint, is also *idolatry*, and is categorized as the fourth instance of it.

10. Sixthly, to worship any living person with religious worship—whether through gestures, titles, forms of address, or anything else that is a specific sign of the unique excellencies belonging only to God—is also idolatry, and belongs to the first instance.

11. Seventhly and lastly, to worship the *consecrated bread in the Eucharist*, even if one is fully persuaded that it has been *transubstantiated* <term>transubstantiated: the belief that the substance of the bread is changed into the actual body of Christ</term> into the body of Christ and is thus personally united with His divinity, is still a real act of *idolatry*. Despite the opinion held about it, this clearly falls under the last instance.

12. All these acts—or any others of the same nature that may be found even among Christians—done under the pretense of worshipping God and Christ, are surely acts of *idolatry*. This is according to the undeniable definition of the word: *the worshipping of that which is not God using the specific signs of religious worship, which either custom or the nature of the thing itself has made the proper ways of acknowledging Divine Excellence.*

<margin>1 Peter 4:3</margin>
13. Now that I have proved such acts are *idolatrous*, I do not need to spend more effort proving they are *unlawful*, because all idolatry is unlawful according to the consensus of Scripture and all people. To try to argue that some kind of idolatry is lawful because <margin>*</margin> Peter mentions "unlawful idolatries" <note>original: *Εἰδωλολατρεῖαι ἀθέμιτοι* (Eidōlolatreiai athemitoi)</note> is as weak and foolish as if someone heard a mention of "impious blasphemies" against God and concluded that the speaker believed some blasphemies against God were *not* impious. Therefore, it is plain that "unlawful" is added not to distinguish one type from another, but to emphasize or describe its nature. It is like saying "white snow" <note>original: *Alba nix*</note> or "a black crow" <note>original: *Corvus niger*</note>; in common speech, these are not intended to distinguish between white and black crows or types of snow, but are adjectives describing their very nature. Therefore, if such actions as we have listed are introduced into the Christian Church, they will prove to be a branch—and a major one—of *Antichristianism*. The doctrines that claim these acts are justifiable must be false and irrational.

## CHAPTER 13.

*1. That professing only one true God does not necessarily excuse a people from the guilt or the possibility of being idolaters. 2. That offering forms of worship proper only to the true God to a created being—even if we recognize it as a creature—is idolatry. 3. That the Jews were idolaters, even though they professed the only true God. 4. That believing the bread of the Eucharist is the real body of Christ does not excuse the person worshipping it from the charge of idolatry. 5. A comparison between the pagans who worshipped the sun and those who worship the bread. 6. A resolution to a logical fallacy <note>original: "Sophism"</note> the author once used to excuse this worship of the bread. 7. That simply because they do not believe bread remains in the Eucharist, the worshippers of the Host <note>original: "Host"; the consecrated bread used in the Catholic Mass.</note> are not excused from idolatry.*

I. Having thus demonstrated the falsity of the "Mystery of Iniquity" <note>original: "Mystery of Iniquity"; a biblical term often used by Protestant writers to describe hidden corruption or anti-Christian practices within the Church.</note> in this first point, I shall proceed, according to my intended method, to the *Fraud*. As I have already mentioned, this includes the deceptive pretenses and excuses, as well as the *self-interest* <note>original: "self-endedness"</note> of those who promote this unholy mystery.

And truly, the excuses and protections behind which they try to hide themselves are very thin and weak, while their *selfish motives* are obvious and undeniable. For instance, it seems to me a very poor defense for Christians to claim that they cannot possibly be idolaters because they openly and declaredly profess that there is only one true God, who possesses a nature infinitely superior to any creature. They argue that if they were idolaters, they would be contradicting themselves. Therefore, they claim that no one who professes Christianity could be an idolater—even if they offer religious worship to *Saints*, *Angels*, *Images*, *Crosses*, or a piece of *consecrated bread*—especially if they shamelessly insist upon it and try to convince the world they are not.

But the inadequacy of this excuse is all too apparent if we consider how easy and common it is for people to contradict the profession of their own faith. For how many people are there, even among those who truly believe *there is a life to come*, who do not live as if any such thing existed, and so contradict their belief through their actions? How many profess a belief and faith in the specific *providence* <term>providence: God's protective care and guidance</term> of God, yet in times of hardship <note>original: "streights"</note> do not rely on it? Instead, they turn to some unlawful practice or commit some wicked act to relieve their distress or secure themselves from danger. How many will passionately speak out against cruelty and injustice as things hated by God and man, yet are themselves notoriously unjust and cruel in the judgment of all impartial observers? These individuals will interpret their own actions more favorably and insist on their justification just as stubbornly as these professors of Christianity who insist they are not idolaters.

<header>Chapter XIII. Professing one God does not make a man incapable of Idolatry.</header>

<margin>Titus 1:16.</margin>
It can happen, therefore, that as the Apostle speaks to *Titus*, men may profess to know God, but in their works they deny Him. They may say there is only one true God, yet perform that homage—which is due to Him alone—to this or that creature, without saying or intending that this creature should be taken for the true God, or that they perform that religious worship to it as if it were the true God. This is a type of idolatry that never existed even among the heathens themselves, nor can it explicitly enter the mind of a man, any more than he can believe contradictions while he knows they are contradictions, or conscientiously go against the dictates of his own conscience while he believes those dictates to be true. It is quite plain that no people can conscientiously and devotionally give that worship—which they believe is due to God alone—to something they believe is not the true God.

2. However, due to negligence, poor education, or habitual superstition, it is not impossible that—because they do not know or do not notice that such ceremonies or forms of worship are properly due only to the true God—they may use them to honor what is merely a creature, or the image of a creature, whether it be a Saint or an Angel. Remembering that these are God's creatures cannot, in this case, save a person from *idolatry*. Their mistake regarding the nature of the worship they perform causes them to fall into idolatry, even though they perceive the object as a creature. Ignorance is no excuse where there is an opportunity to be better informed. Indeed, *incest* and *adultery* must be labeled and called by us *adultery* and *incest*, even if they are practiced in countries that allow them, and we must say those people are more immoral <note>original: "unclean"</note> than ourselves.

3. To this you may add that the Jewish people were sometimes *idolaters*, and were declared so by the prophets of God, even though they had not cast away the knowledge or acknowledgment of their *Jehovah* <note>The personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible.</note>, the only true God. Why then can *Christians* not be *idolaters*, even though they still profess to worship the only true God and *Jesus Christ* whom He has sent—the very same God once incarnate of the *Virgin Mary*, and thus living among men on Earth?

4. Specifically concerning the *adoring of the bread in the Eucharist* <note>original: "Eucharist"; the Christian ceremony of Holy Communion, where bread and wine are consecrated and consumed.</note> based on a belief that it is the very body of Christ, a Christian cannot defend himself from the charge of idolatry. Neither the general excuse mentioned before nor the specific excuse for this case—namely, that the person who adores it truly believes it to be the body of Christ or His physical presence—is sufficient. I say, he cannot clear himself from being guilty of real idolatry. His ignorance is no excuse, just as it wasn't in the previous examples.

For the meaning of his excuse is only this: that he gives this divine worship to the apparent bread because he truly believes it to be God, and therefore a rightful object of this worship; and that he gives no more worship than he thinks is due to the object. If there is any logic in human reason and understanding, this is the meaning of their plea. If this reasoning were sound and just, we would be acting very unjustly by accusing any nations or persons in the world of committing idolatry, provided they were sincere in the action. For could they, while acting devoutly or seriously, believe at the same time that they are offering divine worship to an improper object, and that the object is

5. There was infinitely more reason for the Pagans to take the *Sun* to be that true and eternal God who made and governs all things—as He is declared to be in the fragments of their ancient liturgies <note>Liturgies here refers to the formal public prayers or rituals of the ancient Greeks and Romans.</note>—than for any Christian to imagine a piece of *consecrated bread* to be so. And I do not doubt that the ancient heathens firmly believed the *Sun* to be God, just as any Christian can believe the *Eucharistic bread* to be the body of Christ. Yet, despite this, I think it never entered any Christian’s mind to doubt that the worshipers of the *Sun* were idolaters. How then is it possible for a *bread-worshiping* Christian to avoid being an idolater on the same terms? There is nothing intrinsic to the act that can excuse the one without also excusing the other.

As for the attempt to lessen the fault of either side based on external circumstances, I will briefly add this: the glorious brilliance of the *Sun*, his comfortable warmth, his notable effects, and his vast influence upon the world, were far stronger and more unavoidable inducements to make the Pagans think he was God than the phrase "This is my body" <note>original: "Hoc est corpus meum"</note> or any interpretation of it by the *Fathers* of the Church could justly be to make any Christian believe that the *Eucharistic bread* is the real body of *Jesus Christ*. Furthermore, just as *murder* and *adultery* may have various degrees of severity while the act itself remains the same, so also may these circumstances be more or less serious as men might imagine them; yet the act we are speaking of is certainly idolatry.

6. I must confess there was a time when I was wonderfully pleased with myself for imagining I had found such clear evidence—as I then thought—to prove that the adoring of the *Host* <term>the consecrated bread used in the Catholic Mass</term>, as it is called, was not idolatry in those who believed it was the very body of Christ. I thought it was as pardonable a mistake as one I committed myself when I was a boy, in asking a mischievous cousin of mine for a blessing. In the dusk of the evening, he happened to place himself in the chair where my father usually sat. As I passed by to go up to bed, I mistakenly begged for his blessing, as was the custom for children, thinking he was my father. But he rewarded my blind devotion with a ridiculous blessing and loud laughter, and I immediately discovered my error. (I do not know how far I have violated the rules of proper behavior by telling this trivial story about myself; but I hope the *Reader* will pardon this <term>talking about myself <note>original: "περιαυτολογία"</note></term>, as it serves my current purpose so well.)

### Chapter 13. [Sincere intention] does not make a man incapable of idolatry.

...intended it for; but just as this latter was entirely directed to my Father, so the former passed entirely to the person of *Christ*.

This self-deception was a great comfort and pleasure to my charitable nature as long as I thought carelessly about the matter. However, after making it my business to inquire more accurately into these things, I found the saying of *Solomon* <note>Solomon was the biblical King of Israel, traditionally regarded as the author of Ecclesiastes.</note> to be all too true: *He who increases wisdom increases sorrow* <note>Ecclesiastes 1:18</note>. I cannot defend this mistake in such a way without also excusing every idolater in the world who was sincere in their idolatry. For undoubtedly, they always believed they had a proper object for their worship; and what is *idolatry* if not the failure to have a proper object of worship? Therefore, if simply thinking we have a proper object excuses us from idolatry, then no devout and serious idolater was ever guilty of the sin—which is an enormous contradiction.

Furthermore, there is a great difference between a sudden, unavoidable mistake in a single action and a constant repetition of the same errors. This is even more significant when we consider the loud warning given in these recent ages against this obvious error of *Transubstantiation* <note>The Catholic doctrine that the substance of bread and wine is changed into the actual body and blood of Christ during the Mass.</note>. Men have strained their voices, calling out not only until they were hoarse <note>original: *ad ravim usque*</note>, but until they spat blood and gave up their own lives by freely and faithfully testifying against this idolatrous falsehood. Therefore, when men either adopt or persist in this gross error and its harmful effects, it must now be considered inexcusable idolatry in the judgment of everyone who believes that the *Eucharistic bread* is not the *body of Christ*. Of this *truth*, there is as much certainty as anything else in the world.

7. Finally, that excuse would not serve them either, if they should argue that they cannot be said to adore the *bread* because they do not believe it is present. This case is much the same as the previous one and needs no new answer. But I ask: Is it less idolatrous to adore the *accidents* <note>In the philosophy used by the Church at this time, "accidents" are the outward appearances of a thing—like color, taste, and smell—that remain even if the inner substance changes.</note> of the *bread*, which they acknowledge are present, or the *bread* itself? If the body of Christ is not present under these accidents, then their act of worship falls upon the visible accidents of the bread. If these accidents are less noble than the bread itself, their idolatry is even greater. 

Furthermore, the heathens who adored the *sun* did not believe that the physical object which is really the *sun* was there (for the *sun* is nothing but an inanimate and unintelligent mass of flaming matter). Instead, they thought it was the glorious Godhead itself, which they worshiped as an intellectual power that created and governed all things, as I have already suggested. Yet no one would say this excused them from idolatry in worshiping the *sun*. Where, then, is the excuse for those who claim to be guiltless of the *bread-worship* <note>original: *Artolatria*</note> they have fallen into, simply because they think the *bread* is not there—that is to say, they believe what they worship is not *bread*? For the pagans did not consider the *sun* to be what it actually is (according to our true understanding of it), even though the external appearance of the *sun* looks the same to both us and them, just as the external appearance of the *bread* looks the same to both the *bread-worshiper* <note>original: *Artolatra*</note> and his accuser.

<header>46 Excuses for their Idolatry answered. Book 1.</header>

### Chapter 14.

1. *The foolishness of distinguishing between an Idol and an Image when both are made objects of religious worship. 2. That nothing but what is essentially and infinitely excellent is a proper object of worship. 3. That the absence of the Saints from their images does not excuse the idolatry. 4. The unlikelihood that any true image of Christ exists, even if it were lawful to worship it. 5. That it is unlawful to worship it, even if there were one. 6. That the entire Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> is a moral law. 7. That the use of images for memory and devotion was also the plea of the Heathens. 8. That external objects in divine worship hinder its perfection. 9, 10. Other significant arguments against the pretended use of images in churches. 11. That there are many other ways of inspiring devotion in the people that infinitely surpass this use of images.*

1. That would also be but a weak excuse for the worshipping of the images of Saints—namely, that they are not *idols*, but the *images* of the holy Saints of God and Christ; and that an *idol* is the image of some Heathen deity, such as *Bacchus*, *Venus*, *Apollo*, and the rest, who were supposed to reside in the *idols* themselves, whereas the Saints are with Christ in Heaven. As if any image whatsoever to which religious worship is given were not an *idol*. For there is no difference between such an *image* and an *idol*, except that one is a *Greek* word and the other *Latin*; they both signify the likeness of something or other. The making of such things is merely a harmless piece of art; but whenever such likenesses or representations of things or persons receive divine honor or religious worship, they become *idols* by that very fact <note>original: *ipso facto*</note> in the worst sense.

Nor is there any sufficient reason why the image of *Bacchus* or *Ceres*, being worshipped *religiously*, should become an *idol*, while the image of *Peter* or *Paul* should not; or why the invocation of one should be idolatry, and the other not. For worshipping the true God by an idol is idolatry; therefore, worshipping that which is not God by an idol is double idolatry. And this is the case whether one is worshipping the image of *Paul* or *Peter*, or of *Bacchus* or *Apollo*.

<margin>
*Mystery of Godliness, Book 3.*
</margin>
2. For even *Bacchus*, *Apollo*, *Ceres*, and the rest were benefactors to mankind in the gratifications of the *animal life* <note>The physical or biological life, as opposed to the spiritual life.</note>, as I have noted at length elsewhere. But they were not infinite benefactors. *Mars*, in all likelihood, was a valiant warrior when he lived on earth, but he is not the *Lord of Hosts* <note>original: *Jehovah Zebaoth*</note>, God omnipotent; and *Apollo* was a wise and skillful man, but not all-knowing. Therefore, since they do not possess these divine excellencies infinitely and essentially, they are incapable of receiving divine honor.
