# Chapter XIV. Pretences for their Idolatry answered.

The reason for the unlawfulness of our performing *religious worship* to *Mars* or *Apollo* is not just that they were *benefactors* only in those things that concern the *physical life*, but that they were not the infinite and essential authors and originals of those perfections. And therefore *Saint Peter, Saint Paul*, and *Saint John*, and even the blessed *Virgin herself*—though they were excellent patterns and powerful persuaders to the love of God and all the duties and accomplishments of the *divine life*, and were singularly well-accomplished in it themselves—yet because they are not infinitely and essentially good and holy, they are as utterly incapable of *religious worship* (which in this case would become *idolatry*) as any of the others. And those who would commit this "spiritual fornication" <note>A common biblical metaphor for idolatry or unfaithfulness to God.</note> with them because they are so holy and so good, would be as ridiculously impious, in my view, as those radical groups who are reported to think nothing of physical adultery or fornication with a "holy brother" or "sister," while they refrain from such liberty with the profane and ungodly.

3. Nor can the assumption—*that the souls of the Saints are not present in the images of the Saints, as the pagan spirits were supposed to be in their idols*—offer the least show of a solid excuse. For the actual presence of the Saints would make the act of worship seem more excusable, as they would then be more capable of receiving such devout addresses and prayers. But these excuses are so flimsy that they are not worth dwelling upon.

4. The defense for *worshiping the image of Christ* may seem more plausible, because he was truly God and yet possessed a visible shape and figure. This indeed would be a valid argument for the lawfulness of making his *picture* or *likeness*, but it does not go so far as to warrant us to worship it.

Besides, who knows what the true features of our *Savior* were? How ridiculous and foolish, then, is that affection and pleasure we take in contemplating a picture we assume to be his, when in all likelihood it looks like neither him nor anyone else? For it is not probable that the sorrowful and burdened spirit of our Savior and his serious followers had so little to do as to concern themselves with having his picture drawn—he who was a <margin>* Isaiah 53.</margin> *man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief*. Furthermore, since the Divinity was <term>hypostatically united</term> <note>The theological doctrine that the divine and human natures of Christ are united in one person.</note> with Christ’s humanity only, and since his visible person had a specific and individual shape, and it is claimed that the right to worship his image arises from this union alone; if the image is not truly the image of Christ, then the grounds for worship fail. (It often happens, they say, that the *Virgin Mary’s* image is not actually hers, but is modeled after the most beautiful—though not always the most chaste—woman of the city). If it is the image of someone else, or an image made at random, or perhaps of nobody who ever existed, the basis for worshiping this image vanishes, so that no one can be certain they are not committing idolatry.

5. And besides, even if it were the true image of the human features of Christ, and this was the claimed ground for the lawfulness of worshiping it, we forget in the meantime that Christ himself is not a proper object of divine worship except as he is the *God-man* <note>original: 'θεάνθρωπος' (theanthropos)</note>—not a mere man, but God also. But what painter or sculptor can describe or carve out his divinity? Or what union is there between that divinity and his statue or

...picture? And finally, what permission do we have to break the commandment of God, which explicitly forbids us from worshiping an image or likeness of anything? In fact, it forbids the very making of an image or likeness for religious worship. The very title of the <term>First Table</term> <note>The first part of the Ten Commandments, which concerns duties toward God, as opposed to the "Second Table" which concerns duties toward other people.</note>, which is regarding the honor and worship of God, clearly shows that this is its true meaning.

6. For my part, I do not doubt that the *whole Decalogue is a moral law* <note>original: "Moral"; meaning it is an enduring rule of right and wrong, rather than a temporary ritual or civil law for ancient Israel.</note>, and that we are as strictly forbidden from *image-worship* as we are from *adultery* itself. Why would *Moses* mix duties of such different natures in one short Decalogue? This is especially unlikely since he delivered his positive laws—whether *ceremonial* or *political*—so extensively in other places. Simply forbidding the making of an image is not a command in itself; rather, it is a prohibition against making an *idol* of one. Therefore, the words, *“You shall not bow down to them, nor worship them,”* are added as an explanation to avoid any mistake. They plainly suggest that *idolatry* is what is forbidden there, not simply the making of images or pictures. Rather, images are forbidden to be made for the purpose of idolatrous worship, as I suggested before based on the nature of the title of the First Table, which concerns religion and our duty to God.

Furthermore, why were these *Ten Commandments* specifically said to be *written by God's own finger* on those *stone tablets*? It was meant to symbolically <term>indigitate</term> <note>To point out or indicate as if with a finger.</note> to us that it was that Law which is also written in our hearts by the finger of God, enduringly and permanently. If every person's mind were wiped and cleansed of the dirt and filth that covers it, those *eternal traits* of essential morality and reason would clearly and legibly appear there. Our minds would then agree with the Decalogue as a most just and righteous law.

<margin>Matthew 19:17</margin>
We know that our Savior has honored the *Decalogue* in a very special way by pointing to it as the way to eternal life. And the *general consensus* of the scholars of old has made it an abridgment of the *Moral Law*. Nor can anyone who duly considers its nature fail to acknowledge it as an everlasting law of God for His Church, even in its literal sense. But on behalf of Christianity (which requires a more spiritual worship than usual), to "spiritualize" the *Decalogue* so as to leave people free to practice *image-worship* seems to me like spiritualizing it into gross physical indulgence <note>original: "gross Carnality"</note>. It is both as impious and as ridiculous as "spiritualizing" the commandment against adultery into a holy permission to sleep with a neighbor's wife without sin or shame—which some claim is a high point of Christian liberty and perfection among certain <term>sectaries</term> <note>Members of radical or dissenting religious groups.</note>.

7. The last excuse that occurs to my mind on behalf of the religious use of *images* in churches is *that these are helps for memory and devotion*. The argument is that the minds of the <term>common people</term> <note>original: "vulgar"</note> are so dull and flagging, and so distanced from any sense or conception of the Deity and religion, that they must be prompted by these physical and visible <term>tools</term> <note>original: "engines"</note> that they can grasp. Thus, they can support their devotion and affection toward divine things by the helpful artifice of these external props. But this plea is shared by the heathens and backslidden Christians alike. That <term>defense</term> <note>original: "Apologie"; meaning a formal justification.</note> must surely be deceptive if it serves a confessedly bad cause just as well as a supposedly good one.

In ancient times, Maximus Tyrius <note>A Greek philosopher and rhetorician of the 2nd century AD.</note> defended the use of statues in religious worship in this way, claiming that they were only <margin>Dissertation 38. *Whether statues should be dedicated to the gods.* <note>original: "Εἰ θεοῖς ἀγάλματα ἱδρυτέον"</note></margin> signs of the honor we do to the Deity, and a sort of guiding hand and path toward remembrance <note>original: "σημεῖα τῆς πρὸς τὸ θεῖον τιμῆς, καὶ ὥσπερ χειραγωγία τις καὶ ὁδὸς πρὸς ἀνάμνησιν"</note>. But for those (he says) whose memory is more firm, and whose mental sight is more directly penetrative into the *Divine presence*, these have no need for such helps; however, he claims they are very few.

You may read much to this purpose in the work of this Sophist <note>A term for a professional orator or teacher of philosophy.</note>. Having taken notice of the several ways of *idolatries*—as we must call them—in various countries, he notes how there may be God in their mind <note>original: "θεῖον ἐν γνώμῃ"</note> all the while, even though their affection is stirred up toward him by some external representation. He compares this to how *lovers* remember their absent friends by their *pictures* or any other token that relates to them. He finally concludes his dissertation fairly and plausibly with this caution or admonition: "If the art of Phidias <note>original: "Φειδίου"; the most famous sculptor of ancient Greece.</note> stirs the Greeks to remember God, or the honor given to animals stirs the Egyptians, or a river stirs others, and fire stirs others, I am not offended by the diversity; only let them understand, only let them love, only let them remember; only let God be in their mind <note>original: "θεῖον ἐν γνώμῃ ἔστω μόνον"</note>."

8. But truly, in my view, to fix a person's sight upon a *river*, *cow*, or *statue* in such a way that they notice they are doing so (and if they do not notice it, to what purpose do they look at it?), is the quickest way to exclude God from the mind. For who can think of two things at once? Therefore, those *religious symbols* which will least of all take up our <term>animadversion</term> <note>The act of turning one's attention or notice toward something.</note>, or fix it upon themselves, but leave it free for God, are the fittest for the more perfect worship of him. 

What is even closer to our purpose: having no object in our worship except what is truly God will be the safest way to settle our mind with him. This allows us to think more truly, comprehensively, and devoutly of him than we possibly can while we pretend to see or conceive of him in any *statue* or *picture* whatsoever. For the understanding of his infinite *wisdom*, *goodness*, and *power*, his infinite *mercy*, *justice*, and *truth*, and the effects of these—the vastness of his *providence*, and the sense of his *ubiquity* <note>original: "Ubiquity"; the state of being everywhere at once; omnipresence.</note>—and that in him we live, and move, and have our being, is a more lively representation of the Deity than exquisite art or the costliest materials can afford.

But if anyone seeks an external image of God that can be perceived by the senses, behold, the best and most beautiful is this *entire universe* <note>original: "this All"</note> that we see—which is still a small matter as far as our sight can discern. How pitiful a representation, then, must any specific thing be—whether *natural* or *artificial*—for the purpose of displaying the *Divine Majesty*? And how unfit is it to claim to become an *object*, in any sense, of *religious worship*? How far short must it fall compared to the inward representation in the *virtuous mind*, whereas that in the mind so hugely exceeds the largest and most beautiful prospect the

## CHAPTER XV.

1. *That the general goal of this ungodly and useless idolatry and image-worship is the profit of the priest. 2. Several methods for making these images profitable to them. 3. The profitability of transubstantiation <term>transubstantiation: the Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the literal body and blood of Christ</term> as the cause for including it in the full development of "Antichristianism." 4. What a wonderful and powerful intercessor the priest seems to be based on this claim. 5. Various ways of promoting this profitable belief. 6. The incredible honor that seems to come to the priest from this amazing miracle. 7. That it seems to give him a just claim to be exempt from civil laws and saves him the effort of seeking truth and holiness. 8. That their excuses for idolatry are weak, while their selfish motives are obvious.*

1. WHEREFORE, since their excuses for idolatry and image-worship are nothing but mere deception <note>original: "Sophistry"</note>, let us consider what *selfishness* <note>original: "Self-endedness"</note> might keep up such unworthy practices. For unless there were some such "mystery of profit" underneath, it would be a wonder that the Christian priesthood should keep any such custom that is so clearly contradictory to the Word of God, so expressly and specifically against the Second Commandment, so great an offense to sober and conscientious Christians, and lastly such a huge stumbling block <note>original: "rock of scandal"</note> to both Jews and Muslims <note>original: "Turk"</note>.

<margin>+</margin> Emboldened by the advice or example of their seductive <term>original: "lenocinant," meaning alluring or enticing like a pimp</term> leaders, the people are encouraged not only to open their mouths to the saints in prayer, but also to open their hands with various offerings. These leaders have filled the uneducated minds of the people with a superstitious fear of the saints' displeasure if they approach them empty-handed. They may even use certain tricks to make the images seem to frown or smile upon the worshippers, depending on the <margin>scantness</margin> or largeness of their gifts. At the very least, they provoke competition among the givers by hanging up visible displays of what has been donated to the image, along with the names of the more devout and generous clients.

The claim that this or that saint has a specific power for performing certain miracles—such as healing particular diseases, helping in specific difficulties or urgent needs, or being granted a certain measure of pardons or indulgences <note>Indulgences were certificates sold by the church to reduce punishment for sins</note>—serves as a powerful lure. These beliefs strongly attract the devotion of the simple-minded, even leading them to make vows to the saints in times of danger and to go on pilgrimages to their temples or chapels. There, being brought into the visible presence of the saint (represented by a well-decorated statue or image), and acting out of a belief in help already received or in expectation of future aid, they feel compelled by shame to offer at least as much as they can afford. They do not doubt that the more generous clients of such a good and powerful patron will surely receive, one way or another, at least their money's worth <note>original: "a full penny-worth for a penny"</note>.

But in the meantime, they do not consider that imitating any specific virtue of those saints would please them more (if they have any awareness <note>original: "Εἴ τις αἴσθησις" (Ei tis aisthēsis)</note> of human affairs) and encourage them to do more good than if a person were to lay down all their wealth at the feet of one of their statues. Nor do they consider that a sincere prayer directed to God through Christ would gain more favor from the saints than if it had been directed to the saints themselves. Any good Christian would sooner relieve a poor man whom he happened to find earnestly expressing his needs to God in secret, than if that man had begged relief from the Christian himself.

3. We see plainly, therefore, what a *profitable* trade may be driven by maintaining the *Invocation of Saints* and *Image-worship*. And if some similar support did not uphold that mysterious concept of *Transubstantiation* <term>the doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the literal body and blood of Christ</term> and the idolatry depending on it, surely such a massive absurdity—one so at odds with Scripture and contrary to all sense and reason—would have no possibility of being part of that *concept of Antichristianism* which I am describing. For it could never have entered the Church of Christ on its own merit; it could only have been introduced because it served some other end or design. At the very least, it could not have been kept there once it was seriously examined, unless it were found to be very advantageous to those who maintain it.

the effect of his intention. He believes that once Christ’s personal presence is secured in this way, Christ will bring about the very designs the priest intended by bringing him there. Few doubt that someone who can summon a spirit to act as a "God from a machine" <note>original Greek: *Θεὸς ἀπὸ μηχανῆς* (Deus ex machina), a theatrical device where a god is lowered onto the stage to solve an impossible problem</note> in a difficult situation can also persuade that spirit to help achieve the goal for which he was summoned.

Therefore, suppose the priest has the power to bring this real "God from a machine" down into a physical presence through a divine charm, as they would describe it. In that case, who could doubt that since Christ is *physically* there, he will assist, favor, and fulfill any acceptable goal for which the priest brought him there by the power of the words of consecration? I say, if Christ is truly and physically there (body, soul, and divinity), and is visibly and personally offered up by the hands of the priest—in the eyes of the people—to obtain this or that favor from God, they cannot doubt the outcome. Having such a valuable pledge in his hand, the priest cannot fail to obtain anything from God that is not clearly sinful. For if God has palpably given him his own Son, how can he withhold anything else? Certainly, those who believe the priest in the first claim cannot easily disbelieve him in the second.

5. Consequently, the priest might safely claim that by virtue of offering Christ up really and personally in the *Mass*, and by directing the intention of his own action, this sacrifice will be effective for both the *living* and the *dead*. He claims it works for the sick and the healthy, for both man and beast; that he can use it to deliver souls out of Purgatory, free men from the plague, heal cattle, drive away fevers, prevent toothaches, recover lost goods, cure sore eyes, grant victory against enemies, secure a good husband or wife, and what not?

Thus, the sacrificer is seen as being endowed with such mighty power. If he is accessible enough to be persuaded to use this power—whether for love or for money—can he not have whatever he wants? From this, it is plain that if the priesthood wished to enrich themselves through this practice, it is entirely in their power to do so. It is not hard to imagine that they would receive money for such "holy" performances and "pious" causes. Therefore, it is no exaggeration in this portrait I am drawing of *Antichristianism* to suggest that the doctrine of *transubstantiation* <note>The belief that the bread and wine in the Eucharist become the actual body and blood of Christ</note> may be stubbornly and tenaciously defended simply to maintain and increase the *wealth* of an Antichristian priesthood. For if the doctrine is false—as it certainly is—it is the source of *idolatry*. Therefore, the founders or supporters of it may justly be called *Antichristian*, especially since it is assumed that they maintain it for the love of "filthy lucre" <note>original: "filthy lucre," meaning dishonest or shameful profit</note>.

6. However, *wealth* may not be the only goal and design of this monstrous doctrine. It may also be intended for the *exaltation of their own persons to a level of esteem and honor that is hardly human.*

To transform a piece of bread into the real person of Christ is little less than to "create our Creator." And if the Blessed Virgin, for being the Mother of God, deserves (in their judgment) what they call hyper-veneration <note>original Greek: *ὑπερδουλεία* (hyperdulia), a level of worship higher than that given to saints but lower than that given to God</note>—a kind of worship little inferior to the divine honor we give to God himself—what level of respect must these priests think they deserve?

<header>The *Selfish Motives* in this *Antichristian Idolatry*. Book I.</header>

imagine themselves to be the *creators* of that very God of whom the *Virgin Mary* is said to be the Mother?

Certainly, it would baffle people to conceive of a way to express sufficient honor and respect for such a wonder-working priesthood. In this one miracle—which they perform routinely and easily, even though our Savior was compelled to groan when he raised *Lazarus* from the dead—they outdo all the miracles Christ ever performed. By changing the dead element of bread into the living body and person of Christ, they create him who was the creator of all those miracles, even while he continues to exist. And (which is another great miracle), they do this without making the bread seem, to any of our senses, altered in any way from what it was before. What honor or privilege may they not claim for themselves, when they assure the people that they are the everyday performers of such a stupendous, incomprehensible, and impossible wonder?

7. Truly, if they have taken upon themselves such a boundless and miraculous power—which exceeds, and is even contrary to, the strongest laws of *physics*, *logic*, and *metaphysics*—can it seem like anything more than a modest claim for them to demand an exemption from all *secular* <note>original: "Politick"</note> laws as well, unless those laws are of their own making?

For how holy and sacred a person must he seem to the world, who can so easily and so frequently perform such an astonishing miracle? Therefore, how inappropriate would it be for the *secular* <term>secular: non-religious or civil authorities</term> powers to claim any authority over someone endowed with such divine power?
<margin>Aristotle's *Politics*, Book 3.</margin>
"For it is as if they would take upon themselves to rule over God himself" <note>original Greek: *Παραπλήσιον γὰρ κἂν τῷ Διὸς ἄρχειν ἀξιοῖεν*</note>; (as *Aristotle* says of those who are heroically virtuous). "For it is fitting that such a person should be like a god among men" <note>original Greek: *ὥσπερ γὰρ θεὸν ἐν ἀνθρώποις εἰκὸς εἶναι τὸν τοιοῦτον*</note>; that is to say, one who is so eminently and superlatively virtuous as he describes there. What, then, must he be considered who is thought to have a power—which is a more obvious object of the people's admiration—that is either equal or superior to God himself? For as wise men generally conclude, even God cannot do anything that involves a logical contradiction.

Therefore, if the corrupted Christian priesthood could persuade the people that they had the power to perform such a massive and incomprehensible miracle—which serves so greatly to increase their own reputation—it is no wonder they were zealous defenders of the deception. It gains them enormous credit and respect from those who believe it, and it saves them the labor of that *harder way* of winning respect: namely, *through unblemished holiness and an exemplary life, and through a true and sound knowledge of the mysteries of the religion they profess.*

8. Therefore, though the excuses and justifications for the *invocation* of *saints*, the *worshipping* of *images*, and the *adoring* of the *consecrated bread* <note>original: "Host"</note> are weak and trivial, we see that the *selfish motives* <note>original: "Self-ends"</note> behind these idolatrous practices are very substantial and obvious. But when both are put together, they constitute that *Antichristian fraud* (and it is surely a major one) that can be discovered in this first and primary *branch* <note>original: "Limb"</note> of *Antichristianism*, which is the *introduction of idolatry into the Church of Christ*.

<header>Chapter XVI. The Many Harms Resulting from Idolatry.</header>

### CHAPTER XVI.

1. *That Idolatry is the highest and most specific injury that can be committed against God. 2. That giving religious honor to Saints or Angels is really a way of reproaching and blaspheming them. 3. The exceedingly great harm done to the human soul by Idolatry. 4. That Idolatry turns men into bloody wolves and bears. 5. And is the mother and nurse of the foulest impurities. 6. That it is the source of all manner of wickedness and eternal death to the idolater. 7. The great harms it does to the Church of Christ. 8. How the Church is weakened by Idolatry at home. 9. And how its spread is hindered abroad. 10. And consequently, how the whole world is injured by it.*

1. WE will now briefly consider the *harm* <note>original: "Mischief"</note> of this horrid atrocity, which affects either *God* (as much as any harm can affect Him), the *Saints*, the *Idolaters* themselves, the *Church*, or the rest of the *World*.

The sin of Idolatry is the most specifically *injurious* to God of any sin, as it so directly touches His right to honor and worship—an honor He will not give to any other, nor allow to be taken from Him. Indeed, it is highly reasonable that it should be reserved entirely for Himself, as no other tribute is fitting for Him but this. For God, who is that infinite fullness of perfection, can lack nothing; but since we have all received everything from His fullness and possess nothing except what comes from Him, it is according to the sense of that eternal law of reason and sincere <note>original: "ingenuous"</note> gratitude, as well as the express commands of the sacred scriptures, that there should be specific acts of divine honor uniquely due to so infinite a benefactor. To take away <note>original: "alienate"</note> or profane this honor by applying it to any creature ought to be considered the most accursed and detestable <term>sacrilege: the violation or profanation of anything held sacred</term> that can be committed.

This robbing of God of His honor—concerning which He everywhere declares Himself so jealous and so wrathful an avenger—is the highest affront or injury that can be committed against the glorious Majesty of Heaven. This point is so admittedly true that there is no need to pursue it any further.

2. The next point seems more counterintuitive: that by honoring and worshipping the Saints to excess, we actually *injure* and abuse them; or that by giving them too much respect, we become guilty of disrespecting them. And yet, it is the absolute truth if examined thoroughly. For the zealous and careful offering of that honor which is done to them implies our belief or opinion that they accept it. But for them to accept that honor or worship which is due only to God (as all *religious* and *divine* worship is) would be to act as rebels and traitors to the Divine Majesty—usurping, or at least accepting, His rights and prerogatives. Instead of being Saints and faithful subjects of Christ and His Heavenly Kingdom, they would be transformed into *Titans* and *Giants* <note>These are references to Greek mythology, where the Titans and Giants attempted to overthrow the gods of Olympus.</note> or children of *Lucifer*, who—

Therefore, whoever claims that the Saints accept such homage or services proclaims to the entire world that they are proud and vainglorious—even that they are traitors and rebels against God. Thus, instead of honoring them, these people actually injure, reproach, and *blaspheme* them.

3. The *harm* <note>original: "Mischief"</note> done to the *idolaters themselves* is very great and easy to observe. *Image-worship* and *saint-worship* debase the mind, making it superstitious and cowardly <note>original: "pusillanimous"</note>. It creates a crude <note>original: "crass"</note> or gross conception of things, making the spirit coarse and carnal, leaning toward physical matters. Because this exercise of their affections toward divine things is so external and tangible <note>original: "palpable"</note>, it makes them more likely and ready to shift their focus to other visible objects. They quickly fall from caressing and embracing cold statues and images—those sensory and tangible ways of entertaining their devotions—to courting warm flesh and polluting themselves with sins of uncleanness, just as the ancient *pagan idolaters* were notoriously guilty of doing.

Indeed, all such ridiculous <note>original: "Ludicrous"</note> and superficial religion inevitably leaves the "body of sin" whole and untouched, and the inner mind dead and starving. As a result, full rein is given to every impulse of the flesh. Foul lust, bloody wrath, and zeal for those idols of fornication (much like the rage of hot-headed suitors on behalf of their mistresses) must rule and overrun everything. The coarseness <note>original: "crasseness"</note> of these superstitions, I say, leaves the mind undisciplined <note>original: "unmortified"</note> and unenlightened, yet it stirs up a zeal for them that is ignorant, bloody, and barbaric. This, it seems to me, is a sad condition for any soul to find itself in.

4. But the fact that this beastly rage accompanies the love of idols—to set aside several examples in the *Scriptures*—is a truth written clearly and testified by the blood of those countless groups of early martyrs. As everyone admits, they were put to death with great reproach and many kinds of torture for despising or opposing ancient pagan idolatry. And *idolatry*, whether *pagan* or *Christian*, will naturally make those truly devoted to it prone to the same cruel fury and madness. Although the cruelty of a *bear* or *wolf* seems more like a harm to those who suffer from them than an evil within the beasts themselves, few doubt that *Circe* <note>In Greek mythology, a sorceress who transformed men into animals; here used as a metaphor for the corrupting power of idolatry.</note>, who transforms men into these savage shapes, injures their human bodies. What a harmful *Circe* idolatry is, then, for transforming the mind into such beastly savagery!

6. But I think I am being too lenient in my charge against *idolatry* by appearing to limit its *harm* only to *uncleanness* and *cruelty*. For the author of the *Book of Wisdom* <note>A book of the Apocrypha, highly regarded in the early modern period for its moral teachings.</note> does not limit its effects to these, but expands them to include *dissimulation <note>deception or hypocrisy</note>, theft, unfaithfulness, riots, perjury*, and what not? *For the worship of idols,* he says, *which should not even be named, is the beginning, cause, and end of all evil.* And St. Paul, in the previously mentioned *Epistle*, identifies it as the fountain of all kinds of vices and wickedness. He does not conclude this recklessly, but very rationally: *For even as they did not choose to keep God in their knowledge, so God,* he says, *gave them over to a worthless mind, to do those things that are not fitting. They were filled with all unrighteousness, sexual immorality, wickedness, greed, and malice; full of envy, murder, quarreling, deceit, and craftiness. They are gossips, back-stabbers, haters of God, insolent, proud, boastful, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents, senseless, faithless, heartless, and unmerciful.* Such a great flood of wickedness breaks in upon people when they are addicted to *idolatry*. For by *apostatizing* <note>falling away from a religious faith</note> from *God* through this heinous sin, *God* also abandons them, as the *Apostle* implies.

<margin>Revelation 21:8.</margin>
Furthermore, the stupidity <note>original: "sottishness"</note> of idolatrous worship, which directs the emotions toward such gross and unsuitable objects, naturally puts the awareness of better things to sleep. It extinguishes the *true life of religion*, which is the renewing of the *mind* into the *image* or likeness of *God* and *Christ*. This true life consists of a *holy* and *peaceful love*, and a *pure, chaste*, and *unpolluted spirit, unstained by the vain desires of this present world*. Therefore, the introduction of *idolatry* into the *Church of Christ* must necessarily result in it being overflowed with all kinds of vice and wickedness. But that consideration belongs more to the next point: *the harm that results to the Church from idolatry*. I shall proceed to that immediately, after briefly mentioning one more *harm* that falls upon the *idolater* himself, and of which I think he will be most aware: *that he shall have his portion in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death—that is to say, that eternal death and destruction that will surely await all such enemies of God.*

7. I have already partly hinted at the *harm* that falls upon the *Church* from *idolatry*: namely, that it is the most likely way to corrupt her with all other kinds of vices. By that very fact <note>original: "ipso facto"</note>, it transforms her, who should...

8. And yet this is not all: there is still *an even greater harm remaining—an extremely significant one—done to the Church by this terrifying sin of idolatry: the prevention of her growth and spread throughout the world.*

It is part of our Christian faith, as we profess it in the *Nicene Creed* <note>The standard statement of Christian belief formulated in the 4th century.</note>, *that there is One Catholic and Apostolic Church.* This implies that the Church has a right to be *Catholic*—that is, to be universally spread over the face of the earth—and that the true and proper character of this Catholic Church is to be *Apostolic*. This means that whatever nation or people (or part of any nation or people) professes the doctrine and discipline delivered by Christ and his Apostles immediately becomes *part of the Catholic Church*. Conversely, those who profess and command doctrines and practices that are *Anti-Apostolic* run the risk of losing the true title of *Catholic* and of making themselves, in fact, no part of the Church of Christ. And certainly, idolatry is as *Anti-Apostolic* and as contrary to the *Apostolic Doctrine* as anything can be.

Therefore, the introduction of idolatry into the Church of Christ results in the cutting off of as many souls from the body of the Church as are persuaded to accept it. From this, it is obvious that *idolatry* is like a *gangrene* in the body of Christ, eating away as much of it as it infects.

9. But this is not the only *harm* of this kind done to the Church by *idolatry*—that is, *the narrowing of its reach by the tearing away of those who were its true members.* Just as significant as this is *the prevention or hindrance of making those people members who might otherwise have been persuaded to join.* For it is very clear that allowing *idolatry* into the Church of Christ will, for as long as it continues there, forever exclude both the *Jew* and the *Turk* <note>original: "Turk"; historically used to refer to Muslims, particularly those within the Ottoman Empire.</note> from it, as they are (rightly) such great haters of idolatry. This is to say nothing of the idolatrous Pagans themselves, to whom it would be ridiculous to preach (as the Apostles did) *to turn from lifeless idols to serve the living God*, when they could easily see in advance that it would merely be a matter of turning from their accustomed idols to the service of new ones.

It is a terrifying thing, therefore, to profess belief in the *Church Catholic* and yet, by the introduction of idolatry, to narrow it at home and hinder its expansion abroad by such horrible scandals.

Thus, we have seen an adequate description of the *first main branch* <note>original: "Limb"</note> of *Antichristianism*, namely, *idolatry*, which was brought into the Church of *Christ* under the pretense of honoring him and the saints. We have also uncovered the *falseness* and *unjustifiable nature* of that doctrine and practice, along with the blatant *deception* and great *harms* that accompany it.

## CHAP. XVII.

1. *That a multitude of minor observances can add up to an unbearable burden.* 2. *That no religious practice can be considered minor as long as it binds the conscience.* 3. *Though this general assessment of the burden of superstition—arising from the obligation of conscience and the vast number of observances—might suffice, he will also provide a more detailed sketch of this branch of Antichristianism.* 4. *Concerning ritual anointings and the excessive variety of priestly garments.* 5. *The pretense and self-interest involved in these ornaments and anointings.* 6. *The harm caused by these types of ceremonies to both priest and people.* 7. *A more complete description of their public worship service.* 8. *That respect for a priest is better earned and more surely found through the power of his life and teaching than through any theatrical pomp.* 9. *Which is so unsatisfying to serious people that it may risk causing them to leave.* 10. *The belief in a miraculous power within religious vestments.* 11. *The falseness and deception of this belief.* 12. *The bad consequences of it.*

Therefore, if our Savior Christ was so protective of his disciples that he did not want them trapped by superstition—not even in a practice as decent and simple as *washing their hands before eating*—it is certainly completely against his will for his followers to be entangled and enslaved by a countless number of less useful ceremonies. Whatever the nature of these ceremonies may be, if their sheer quantity equals the weight of the *Jewish rituals* <note>original: "Judaical Rites"</note> of the Old Testament, this general assessment is enough to identify it as a significant *part of Antichristianism* <note>original: "Limb of Antichristianism"</note>, regardless of which church allows such an excess.

That purpose was, undoubtedly, to free his followers from sin and the slavery of superstition.

4. # Chapter XVII: Of Multiplied Superstitions

...for the further decorating of themselves (as if they intended to outdo the ceremonial vestments <note>original: "Habiliments"</note> of Aaron himself), they add even more holy ornaments—let us say nine more. They also consecrate these priests with *holy oil* on their shaved heads <note>The "shaven crown" refers to the tonsure, a practice where a monk or priest's hair is partially shaved.</note> and on their hands. These hands become so sanctified that the most devout people would eagerly and zealously kiss the priest’s hand immediately after his ordination, hoping to share more fully in his devotion and holiness. What is this, I ask, but to adopt Jewish customs <note>original: "Judaize"</note> under the name of Christianity? It ensnares <note>original: "illaqueate"</note> the minds of men with the very superstitions that our Savior Christ came to set them free from. This observation is enough to show the *falseness* and groundlessness of such a system <note>original: "Oeconomy"</note> in the Church.

<margin>\* Appendix to the Defense of the Philosophic Cabbala, Chapter 5, Sections 2, 3, 4.</margin>

5. As for the excuse for these kinds of *Aaronic* ornaments, I can imagine none, unless it is the imitation of the *Levitical Laws*—which is a very poor excuse, since those laws were meant to be abolished by *Christ*. Furthermore, the robes of *Aaron* had a much deeper <note>original: "more profound"</note> and important meaning than something to be imitated for some trivial or superficial reason. Those robes, like other *Mosaic* symbols <note>original: "figures"</note>, were prescribed according to a specific pattern shown by God on the Mount. Since they were *shadows of things to come*, they naturally vanish in the high noon and vertical sunshine of the *Gospel*. Therefore, to introduce so many *new* shadows is to wrap the Church in darkness again and distract us from correctly understanding the meaning of the *old* ones. Those old symbols were certainly all "types" <note>A "type" is a symbolic person, event, or object in the Old Testament seen as foreshadowing something in the New Testament.</note> of the fuller knowledge of *Jesus Christ* and of the inward and spiritual holiness we have in him.

<margin>\* See the General Preface to the Collection of my Philosophical Writings, Section 3.</margin>

However, the advantage that this erroneous priesthood might seek for itself is this: by using these *theatrical disguises* <note>original: "Histrionical disguises"</note> and special decorations, they hope to appear more honorable in the eyes of the people. Common people—at least the simpler among them—are often impressed by outward shows. They might think the priests themselves are very holy because their ordination involves such grand ceremony, and because their *sacred anointing* makes it rival the *coronation* of princes. If they were truly thorough in imitating the great High Priest of the Jews, they would adorn themselves with what corresponds to his \* *Urim and Thummim* <note>The Urim and Thummim were objects used by the ancient Israelite high priest to determine God's will; here, the author equates them with intellectual and moral virtues.</note>—that is, *illumination of the mind and sincerity of the heart*. That would indeed be a worthy goal <note>original: "happy emulation"</note>, and it would excuse them from such a strict obsession with the rest of the ceremonies.

<margin>1 John 2:27.</margin>

For those who do not truly appreciate Christianity, it becomes an excuse for unbearable pride and conceit. It leads them to feel overly secure while neglecting the true and essential qualities of the Christian priesthood—that *anointing* which will teach them all things, even the Holy Spirit of God. That Spirit does not live in consecrated garments, but in the purer habits of the mind—in the "inner man" who is completely and thoroughly dedicated to God by the real renouncing <note>original: "abrenunciation"</note> of oneself, the flesh, the world, and the Devil, and by entirely giving oneself to the sincere love of

I say that the goal <note>original: "End"</note> of this deception <note>original: "Imposture"</note> is nothing other than the praising and glorifying of the priest and other religious orders of the Church—unless, of course, this high regard also brings with it some financial <note>original: "pecuniary"</note> benefits.

They will more quickly quench all the fiery arrows <note>original: "darts"</note> of the wicked one than whole pots of *holy water* squirted at him.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

1. *On the enchanting or exorcising of water, oil, salt, wax candles, etc., with a general warning about their harm. 2. On the exorcising of a golden rose and a lamb of wax. 3. That using the name of the true God in these exorcisms does not prevent them from being properly called enchantments. 4. Other instances of their being charmers and magicians, with an anticipation of an objection. 5. The falsehood, fraud, and mischief of these exorcisms. 6. The distribution of these exorcised elements into several superstitious uses. 7. On the assumption of the infant’s being possessed, and of baptismal spittle. 8. On extreme unction and other superstitious practices upon the dying man. 9. As also upon his corpse when it is laid out. 10. The fraud and mischief of these practices.*

1. The mention of holy water reminds me of another class of superstitions that might have been invented contrary to the faithfulness and simplicity of the school of Christ. These serve only to entangle <note>original: "illaqueating"</note> people’s consciences and misplace their dependence upon created things rather than the Creator. They also extinguish that comfortable inward sense of God’s invisible but all-powerful presence by interposing these vain and visible objects, which have neither the power nor the divine permission for the uses they claim. I mean the exorcising or enchanting (if you will) of certain natural elements, without any warrant from Holy Scripture, in order to grant them a supernatural power.

It is as if, for example, the priest should pretend—by exorcising the element <note>original: "Creature"</note> of salt by the living, true, and holy God—to make it become a holy and exorcised salt, for the health of both body and soul to as many of the believers as receive it; and for the chasing away of every evil phantom and unclean spirit by the sprinkling <note>original: "aspersion"</note> of it. Or by exorcising the element of water in the name of the Holy Trinity, to give it the power of chasing away the Devil, diseases, and every disturbing thing out of a house by sprinkling it. And he should recommend its use for sprinkling their rooms now and then, as well as their sick people, their fields, and vineyards, for health and increase. Or the exorcising of wax candles to give them the virtue of putting to flight the Prince of Darkness with all his followers, making them run away with fear and trembling from whatever place they are lit. Or the exorcising of the element of oil by God the Father Almighty, the Creator of all things, so that whoever uses it may put the troops of the Devil to flight and never be bitten by the ancient serpent. Also the exorcising of herbs or the boughs of trees; the exorcising of bells and the priestly garments <note>original: "Vestments"</note>. Is it not apparent that all these, and as many more as can be invented of this nature, are mere tricks <note>original: "Juggles"</note> and frauds?

## CHAP. XVIII.

1. *On the enchanting or exorcizing of water, oil, salt, wax candles, etc., with a general warning of their harm.* 2. *On the exorcizing of a golden rose and a wax lamb <note>original: "Lamb of Wax"; likely referring to an Agnus Dei, a wax disc blessed by the Pope</note>.* 3. *That using the name of the true God in these exorcisms does not stop them from being properly called enchantments.* 4. *Other examples of them acting as charmers and magicians; with an anticipation of an objection.* 5. *The falsehood, fraud, and harm of these exorcisms.* 6. *The distribution of these exorcized elements into various superstitious uses.* 7. *On the assumption that infants are possessed by demons, and on baptismal spit <note>original: "Spittle"</note>.* 8. *On Extreme Unction <note>term: Extreme Unction: the former name for the Roman Catholic sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, administered to those near death</note>, and other superstitious practices performed upon a dying man.* 9. *Also those performed upon his corpse when it is prepared for burial.* 10. *The fraud and harm of these practices.*

1. The mention of *Holy Water* reminds me of another category <note>original: "Classis"</note> of superstitions. These may have been invented contrary to the faithfulness and simplicity of the school of *Christ*, leading to the trapping <note>original: "illaqueating"</note> of men's consciences and the misplacing of their dependence upon created things <note>term: Creatures: in this context, physical substances or "created things" rather than the Creator</note> more than the Creator. They also extinguish that comforting inward sense of His invisible but all-powerful <note>original: "omnipotent"</note> omnipresence by placing these vain and visible objects in the way—objects which have neither the power nor the divine permission <note>original: "allowance"</note> for the uses they claim. I mean the *exorcizing* or *enchanting* (if you prefer) of certain natural elements, without any authority from Holy Scripture, to endow them with a supernatural power.

As if, for example, the priest should claim that by *exorcizing* the element of *salt* by the living, true, and holy God, he makes it become an *holy* and *exorcized salt*. He claims it provides health for both body and soul to as many believers as receive it, and that it chases away every evil vision <note>original: "Phantasm"</note> and unclean spirit by being sprinkled. Similarly, by *exorcizing* the element of *water* in the name of the Holy Trinity, he claims to endow it with the power of driving away the Devil and diseases, and every disturbing thing, out of a house by sprinkling it. He then recommends its use for sprinkling their chambers constantly <note>original: "ever and anon"</note>, as well as their sick relatives, their fields, and their vineyards, for health and growth <note>original: "increase"</note>. 

Then there is the *exorcizing* of *wax candles* to give them the power of putting the Prince of Darkness and all his followers <note>original: "Retinue"</note> to flight, making them run away with fear and trembling from whatever place the candles are lit in. Or the *exorcizing* of the element of *oil* by God the Father Almighty, the Creator of all things, so that whoever uses it may put the troops of the Devil to flight and never be bitten by the "old serpent" <note>a biblical reference to the Devil</note>. They also *exorcize* *herbs* or the *branches of trees*, as well as *bells* and the *priestly garments* <note>original: "Vestments"</note>. Is it not obvious <note>original: "apparent"</note> that all these, and as many more as can be invented of this nature, are mere tricks <note>original: "Juggles"</note> and frauds <note>original: "Impostures"</note>?

2. But the fraud would be more pleasing and complete, if we had some

...some fine consecrated object that was more portable and yet had a more universal influence, as well as being more durable and permanent than most of the previous examples. Therefore, the shape of some holy plant or animal exorcized in this way would be of great use and satisfaction—the *Rose of Sharon*, the *Lily of the Valleys*, the *Dove*, or the *Lamb*, names that are sacred to every Christian ear.

Therefore, a *Golden Rose* <note>term: Golden Rose: an ornament of gold traditionally blessed by the Pope on the fourth Sunday of Lent and presented to notable churches or Catholic figures</note>, filled with joy and gladness through the blessing of the holy High Priest of this church <note>referring to the Pope</note>, and full of the fragrance of the forgiveness of sins, the increase of faith (though the effect is never actually found), divine protection, and all prosperity, would be a gift fit to flatter a prince <note>original: "Posie to wipe the Nose of a Prince withall"; an idiomatic way of saying it is a prestigious but perhaps superficial or deceptive gift</note>. Likewise, a gentle *Lamb* made of some flexible material and elegantly shaped—suppose out of *wax*—but exorcized to have powers and virtues hardly inferior to the *Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world* <note>original: "Agnus Dei," referring to wax discs blessed by the Pope, believed to protect the wearer</note>. Since it is made capable, through a certain sacred exorcism or blessing, of preserving those who carry it from all the assaults of the flesh, the world, and the Devil; from plague, famine, and sudden death; from all dangers by land and sea; from lightning, storms, and miscarriage <note>original: "Abortion"</note>; it would be a suitable present for an Emperor or Empress.

Many such examples could be devised, all of which I must declare to be against the faithful simplicity and true power of the Gospel of Christ. They infringe upon the reverence due to the name of God and are a violation of the Third Commandment: *You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain*.

3. I believe those *forms of conjuration* found in books of magic—such as those by *Cornelius Agrippa* <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a famous German polymath and writer on the occult and "natural magic"</note> and *Petrus de Abano* <note>Pietro d'Abano (c. 1250–1316), an Italian philosopher and physician who was posthumously accused of magic</note>—evidently violate this precept. In these books, divine names like *Jah, El, Adonai, Elohim, Elohe Zebaoth, Elyon, Shaddai* <note>original: "Jah, El, Adonai, Elohim, Elohe Zebaoth, Elion, Sadai"; these are various Hebrew names for God used in the Bible</note>, and the like, are used as the building blocks of their vain and wicked art. This is a clear argument that a priest's exorcism in the names of God and His holy attributes does not excuse him from the guilt of enchantment, since magicians themselves use the names of the true God in their work.

As for the broader definition of *enchantment*, *Agrippa* defines it as nothing more than *the transfer of a certain miraculous power into the enchanted object through the words and breath of the enchanter* <note>original: "mirificent power"</note>. Nor will the use of phrases or passages from Scripture excuse the priest from this impiety, since these are both recommended and practiced by these magicians. Their *pentacles* <note>term: Pentacles: amulets or talismans used in magical rituals, often inscribed with symbols or scripture</note>—which they hang around their necks when they conjure and, for the sake of prestige, call the *Pentacles of Solomon*—are decorated and strengthened with such passages from Holy Scripture.

Therefore, it is clear that if anyone were to note all the specific characteristics of such an apostate church as the one I am describing, he could not fail, among other titles, to brand them with the name of *enchanters* or *sorcerers*.

4. They might deserve this label for other reasons which we have already hinted at; for instance, they teach people certain *prayers in an unknown* [language]...

## Chap. XVIII. Of Multiplied Superstitions.

...an unknown *language*, which they instruct them to recite for various purposes. After all, what are these but *charms*? And the claim of making *Jesus* of *Nazareth*—who was crucified at *Jerusalem* over sixteen hundred years ago—personally appear as flesh, blood, and bones upon the utterance of a few words, all covered by the thin clothing of certain *healing appearances* <note>original: "Panaceous Species"</note> or loosely-hanging *qualities* <note>original: "Accidents"; a philosophical term referring to the outward properties of bread and wine—like taste and color—that remain even after the "substance" is said to change</note>, is a piece of *magic* greater than that of the Witch of *Endor* and all the historical records of *necromancy* <note>original: "Necromancy"; the practice of communicating with or raising the dead</note> in the world. Since these claims are so widespread and general in the Church we are describing, who could fail to label them as a *Society of Magicians* or *Enchanters*?

The fact that these are mere pretenses and have no real effect does not mean they do not deserve such a title; the profession and the effort give the practitioners a sufficient right to it. Just as a man who has been casting his fishing line into the river for a good part of the day and brings home no fish may still be rightly called *Mr. Fisherman* or *Mr. Angler* upon his return—though not without some *mockery* <note>original: "Scommatism"; a taunt or jibe</note> behind his back. And he who professes to practice *medicine* <note>original: "Physick"</note> and has perhaps not yet cured anyone (except those who would have recovered just as well without him), even if he has killed many, is nonetheless called a *physician* by everyone. Generally, whatever men deliberately pretend to do—even if they cannot perform it—may justly be included in their description as a form of *mocking* <note>original: "Scommatical"</note> reproach, to complete the full account of their shame and correction.

5. I must confess I cannot easily find what grounds they might claim for such incantations as these. For the *blood of the Passover Lamb*, which the *Israelites* sprinkled on the doorframes of their houses, was not first "charmed" to give it the power to scare away the destroying angel. Instead, it was simply a present sign, as well as a *foreshadowing* <note>original: "Type"</note> of the sprinkling of the blood of *Christ*, who, as a lamb without spot, was to be sacrificed in future ages for the sins of the world. Nor were the *water* and *ashes of the heifer* mixed together with any exorcism or enchantment that we read of in the *Bible*. Nor did *Elisha* charm the *salt* before he threw it into the *waters* to heal them; he used it only as a symbolic gesture or sign in their healing. These are ceremonies that *Christianity* has nothing to do with, nor is there any reason to introduce more of the ancient *foreshadowings* <note>original: "Types"</note> or *figures* than those already chosen by him who was incapable of error.

Therefore, there is no basis at all for such practices. But the claim to such power—to so strangely and marvelously enchant things for such significant purposes—would do much for the honor of the priest. To the gullible people, he cannot help but seem like <term>a very great person</term> <note>original: "μέγας τις" (megas tis)</note>, someone very great and adorable. Furthermore, these exorcised goods would be as good as cash to anyone who believed in them.

But the worst part is that *faith and self-control* <note>original: "Temperance"</note> would be neglected. *Pots of holy water and enchanted wax lambs* would block those internal, living springs of the Spirit of God in the heart. They would help to extinguish that sense of innocence, which is a greater defensive tower for a believing Christian against all the fiery and thundering weapons of the "Prince of the Air" <note>referring to Satan</note> than anything else.

He asserts that these practices lack biblical foundation and distract believers from true faith and inner virtue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of the Roman Catholic Church, specifically targeting what he views as superstitious and "magical" rituals surrounding the sacraments of baptism and the anointing of the sick.</meta>

6. These are the most blatant and fundamental *superstitions* that resemble *magic* or *sorcery*. They can be applied to various uses and practices, such as the *Visitation of the Sick*, *Extreme Unction* <note>original: "Extreme Unction"; the Catholic sacrament of anointing the dying</note>, *funerals* or *burials*, *christenings*, *churchings* <note>original: "Churchings"; a formal service of thanksgiving for a woman after she has recovered from childbirth</note>, and *marriages*. In these rituals, *holy water*, *exorcised oil*, and *candles* might be frequently used. Some of these are truly a significant burden; for example, in the *anointing of the sick*, the priest must anoint their *eyes*, *ears*, *noses*, *mouth*, and *hands*—and even their *feet* and the *small of the back* <note>original: "Reins"; an archaic term for the kidneys or lower back, often considered the seat of emotions or physical strength</note>. This last part can cause a troublesome conflict between natural *modesty* and *religious zeal* in those who feel a deep sense of guilt for the sins committed by those parts of the body.

The *conjuring of the devil* out of the *infant* who is to be *baptized* would also seem like a terrifying thing to the *infant* himself, if he understood what an evil state the priest assumes he is in. The priest performs *three exsufflations* <note>original: "Exsufflations"; the ritual act of breathing or blowing on a person to drive away evil spirits</note> upon his face and uses an *exorcism ritual* <note>original: "Exorcistical form"</note> to cast out the foul demon. This demon is imagined to be incredibly arrogant to take possession of the child so quickly, especially since it should be obvious that *Jesus* Christ has a better claim to him, as the child of Christian parents. Here also (among other ceremonies) comes the use of *holy oil* to anoint the child on the forehead and chest, the putting on of *white garments* <note>original: "Vestments"</note>, and placing a *holy candle* in his hand. Furthermore—and considered even holier than any *oil* or *candle*—the *priest’s own spittle* is used to sanctify the child’s ears and nostrils by gently smearing it on those spots. Finally, to ensure that everything is sound and healthy, *holy salt* may also be placed in the child’s mouth, so that when he eventually learns to speak, his words might be more "savory" <note>original: "savoury"; a pun referencing the biblical idea of speech being "seasoned with salt" to show wisdom</note>.

Thus, you can see how the use of these first consecrated elements can go quite far, making the Christian sacrament of *baptism* exceed even *Jewish* ceremonies—and even *circumcision* itself—in its complexity. In reality, the use of *water* alone would be sufficient, and *one* dipping would be just as meaningful for the *unity* of the Godhead as *three* dippings are for the *Trinity*. Yet, Christianity casts such long and tedious shadows when the "Sun of *Righteousness*" <note>A biblical reference to Christ from Malachi 4:2, suggesting that as the light of Christ fades, rituals become more bloated and dark</note> begins to set within the Church.

7. And it would be surprising if something in this approaching darkness did not seem terrifying to *women*. For although it might seem like a grand thing for a priest to be thought to have such power over the *Stygian fiend* <note>original: "Stygian Fiend"; a demon from the underworld or the River Styx in Greek mythology</note> that he can *exorcise* him out of an *infant*, it is a grim thought for superstitious or depressed women to think they never give birth without delivering a devil and a child at once. They might fear that if their child should die before baptism, the devil (having bodily possession of him) will surely carry him to a place where even a mother's greatest love would not dare to visit. # The Antichristian Bondage and Burden: Book I.

...our religious prayer to them <note>original: "Invocation"</note>, might the act of praying to one not bring upon us the displeasure of the rest who are passed over <note>original: "pretermitted"</note>? And if I make one of them my personal patron, why might I not suspect that I have thereby made the rest my enemies by slighting them—if they were as eager for divine honors as we imagine <note>original: "conceit"</note> them to be?

And concerning their **holy relics** that are offered to be kissed by the devout, what pangs of conscience might arise from not heartily pressing our lips to the humbler and less attractive <note>original: "unlovely"</note> sort of them? How can a man sleep quietly when stung by the sense of such an irreligious piece of rudeness—suppose it were merely toward a holy, dirty handkerchief or some other old yellowed linen?

Since there is also said to be such great power in an **exorcised Cross** for the protection of health in both soul and body, and for driving away every evil phantom <note>original: "Phantasm"</note> (and the same logic applies to **relics**), what mental conflicts must this cause in a deeply religious person? If he has been able to but has not yet purchased such a safeguard for himself and his house—or, being pinched between poverty and the urgent demands of devotion, cannot decide whether he should buy it or not—he is at a loss. Or when he has bought it, he is unsure how many times a day he should crouch and creep toward it to draw out that secret power lodged within it by the "holy enchantment" or exorcism of the priest?

The same logic applies to **holy water** (how often it should be sprinkled) and to **exorcised boughs** <note>branches, such as palms, blessed by a priest</note>, and the like. And regarding the **communion of merit** <note>the belief that one can benefit from the spiritual "credit" earned by others</note> gained by being joined to this or that holy society <note>original: "Sodality"</note> or brotherhood: how anxious it would make a man regarding his choice, so that he might be best supplied with grace? And how ambitious he would be to enter into as many groups as he possibly can!

3. And regarding the **entanglement of vows**, how easy it would be for men to be caught in them, like a woodcock <note>a bird proverbially thought to be foolish and easily trapped</note> in a net? What a harsh and slavish thing it is to be under a **vow** of unlimited obedience to someone who—I cannot be sure—might command me (under the pretense of permission from an "infallible" power) to do something that my own conscience tells me is against the Law of God, of humanity, and of nature? I will not dwell here on the various occasions for making many rash vows based on different passions, emergencies, and pressures, in a Church where they are so much in fashion and where fulfilling them tends to enrich the Church (as does being released from a vow through a special paid dispensation), for these things are endless.

4. Great burdens of thought might also arise from a **superstitious trust in the power of the Eucharist, which is abused for ends it was never intended for.** It is commonly called the **Mass**. And if it had such power and effectiveness as this Church pretends—such as delivering souls from punishment in the afterlife, or for worldly success, for safe travel by sea or land, on horseback or on foot; for women who are barren, pregnant, or in labor; for fevers and toothaches; for hogs and hens; for recovering lost goods, and the like—what various misgivings of mind and anxieties of conscience would result in those who carefully considered these powers and privileges?

Therefore, where it is believed that by the power of those **five words of** <note>The "five words" likely refers to the Latin phrase "Hoc est enim corpus meum" (For this is my body) used by the priest during the consecration of the bread in the Mass.</note>

### Chapter XX. Of Multiplied Superstitions.

<margin>Matthew 10:31</margin>
Regarding Consecration <note>The prayer used to turn the bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ.</note>, if Christ stoops to give himself into the hands of the priest bodily and personally—to be lifted up and offered to his Father for the help and safety of a good man’s sheep, or poultry, or other minor concerns—how can that honest man be at peace? He believes in the irresistible power of such a stupendous **Sacrifice** and its certain effect (which would be even more certain in matters of greater consequence, for *Are you not of more value than sparrows?* <note>original: "Are you not of more value then Sparrows?" - a reference to the Latin Vulgate and English Bibles of the time.</note>). 

How can he not run to the priest as far as his purse-strings will stretch—and his conscience will often be racked and stretched just to save his purse-strings—on every occasion of the sickness of his cattle, the delay of his wife's pregnancy <note>original: "delay of his wife's belly"</note>, the dangers of pregnancy or childbirth, or when he or his family are traveling? He would do this for fear of being an accessory to any misfortune that might happen to them for lack of applying this certain means of prevention in time. And if any tragedy actually occurs, would he not imagine his neglect to be the sin of murder?

Indeed, how can men with a good conscience refrain from spending until they have nothing left but their very skin, laying out money for **Masses** <note>Religious services held for the benefit of the living or the dead.</note> for all their friends and relatives, and then making strict inquiry among the poor who might be neglected in that regard? Or, at the very least, how can they avoid being miserably distracted between the fear of impoverishing themselves and the compassion they feel for those they imagine may be tormented in the other world <note>Referring to the pains of Purgatory.</note> for want of such relief?

Such superstitious guesses <note>original: "surmizes"</note> as these will indeed bring "grist to the mill" in plenty for those who plant them in the heads of the people. But they will grind and grate so hard against the believers of such principles that they must live very uncomfortably under the load of such a false and corrupted <note>original: "adulterate"</note> religion.

5. This burden will be further increased by another additional uncertainty, which will cause a greater unsettling and wavering in all their decisions—even where their natural inclinations would otherwise lead them with more confidence to seek the help of religion and the assistance of her Sacraments. For, supposing the effect of a rite depended on the **Intention of the Priest** <note>A controversial doctrine suggesting a sacrament is invalid if the priest does not inwardly intend to perform it.</note>, our own cost and devotion would be utterly lost if he, out of malice or negligence, had his **Intention** diverted from the work. 

While this doctrine tends immensely to make the priest great, formidable, and a "little God" upon Earth—possessing the power, if not of damning people, at least of making the salvation doubtful for as many as depend upon the sincere exercise of his duty in baptizing, administering the Lord’s Supper, and absolving them of their sins—it is a terrible burden. To ensure he performs his duties faithfully, men feel obliged not only to pay him his dues or wages, but to honor him with every kind of compliance, lest he should do them or their loved ones some everlasting, incurable mischief. 

Yet, it is a plague and a torment of the mind beyond all expression to the poor, credulous laity <note>term: "Laiety" — the ordinary members of the church, as distinguished from the clergy.</note>. They are made to believe that God has put the power out of His own hand, and that unless His substitute wills it and intends it to be so, the Almighty Himself cannot graft a person into the body of the Church. Nor can the person receive the grace signified by the Lord’s Supper, nor receive clear Absolution <note>The formal release from guilt or sin pronounced by a priest.</note> for his sins, even if everything was performed externally by a person in holy orders according to the individual's own pious desire. This must necessarily haunt the religious person with a perpetual uncertainty about their own salvation and the salvation of others.

### CHAPTER XXI.

1. *Of the necessity of annual confession. 2. Of priestly absolution. 3. What is meant by "binding and loosing," and to what kind of people the forgiveness of sins is committed. 4. Erasmus's interpretation of that text in the Gospel of John. 5. Also Hugo Grotius's interpretation, which shows that private confession and absolution are groundless. 6. Voluntary and general confession is useful in the Church in some circumstances, leading to individual absolution from the priest. 7. Also a more detailed confession, if it is voluntary. 8. The selfish goals of the Church in demanding such a precise confession from men. 9, 10. The slavery and harm caused by such confessions. 11. The infinite distress caused to conscientious and honorable people by forcing incredible and impossible opinions upon them.*

1. The topic of absolution <note>The formal release from guilt or punishment for sin, pronounced by a priest.</note> reminds me of the claimed necessity of *confessing* at least once a year (specifically to the parish priest) all of a person’s sins. This includes not only sins actually committed, but even one's thoughts, desires, or inclinations toward committing them. This might indeed be rightly called a torture-chamber for consciences <note>original: "Carnificina conscientiarum"</note>. It is as debasing a form of servitude—and serves as poor a purpose—as if all the modest young women and respected matrons in the parish were required to strip themselves completely naked and humble themselves before their priest once a year. That would be seen as an unbearable form of tyranny.

And yet, this extorted *confession*—performed under the threat of damnation for concealing anything—is not merely the stripping of a person’s physical body. It is the stripping of their soul, so that the priests may see the naked heart. By the force of this superstition, they break into those secrets which are the sole privilege of Almighty God to know. He is the only rightful knower of hearts <note>original Greek: "kardiognostes"</note>; He can neither be harmed by seeing the most inward motions of His own handiwork, nor will He—knowing how we are made—do us any harm. Instead, He will judge all things with equity and will not despise the work of His own hands.

<margin>Matthew 18:18</margin>
<margin>John 20:23</margin>
2. The excuse for this *confession* is the supposed necessity of *absolution* by a priest; it is claimed that if a man lacks this through his own neglect, he must undoubtedly be damned. But that any such *absolution* is necessary—except in cases of legitimate excommunication <note>Being officially excluded from the sacraments and membership of the Church.</note>—cannot be proven by either Scripture or reason. For when it is said to Peter, to the Church, or to the Apostles, *Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven;* and, *Whosever sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whosever sins you retain, they are retained;* it is impossible that the meaning should be: "Forgive or retain, bind or loose, whether right or wrong, I will ratify everything in heaven that the successors of my Apostles do. Nor shall any forgiveness of sins be valid without them, even if they only follow in the external profession of the office and do not share the same Spirit as their predecessors." Where-

Therefore, such a large and accurate authority cannot belong to anyone except either the Apostles themselves, or to men of a true Apostolic spirit, who are entirely of one mind with God and therefore can only do what is right.

Since it is so rare and difficult to find such a confessor, it is an argument that such *Absolution* <note>The formal release from guilt or punishment for sin, pronounced by a priest.</note> is not necessary; for neither God nor Nature are lacking in providing necessities. But *Binding* by *Excommunication* <note>The act of officially excluding someone from the sacraments and services of the Christian Church.</note>, and the *Loosing* that corresponds to it, is a different matter, and concerns the external economy <note>original: "Oeconomy"; the management or administration of the church's practical affairs.</note> of the Church.

3. But to speak truly, that phrase of *Binding* and *Loosing*, cited above from Scripture, seems to refer not so much to people as to *things*. For the Greek text says "whatever you bind" <note>original: "ὃ ἐὰν δήσηϛ" (ho ean dēsēs)</note> and "whatever things you bind" <note>original: "ὅσα ἐὰν δήσητε" (hosa ean dēsēte)</note>, not "whom" or "who" or "whomever." This reflects the well-known phrases of the Jews, who called that which was declared unlawful "bound" <note>original: "אסור" (asur) / "ligatum"</note>, but that which was allowed as lawful they called "loosed" <note>original: "מותר" (muttar) / "solutum"</note>. Therefore, that passage does not refer to *Absolution* from sin, but to the making of laws and institutes for the Church by the Apostles, which Christ says he would ratify in Heaven.

But that other place (John 20) concerning remitting and retaining men's sins does undoubtedly refer to *Absolution from sin*. But notice to what manner of men this power is committed. *As my Father sent me, so send I you* (now Christ was sent full of grace and of the power of the Holy Spirit), and therefore, breathing upon them, he says, *Receive the Holy Spirit*, and did most certainly impart it to them. And based on that, the authority is derived upon them: *Whose soever sins you remit, they are remitted; and whose soever sins you retain, they are retained.*

4. From this, *Erasmus* <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), a famous Dutch humanist and theologian who critiqued Church abuses.</note> writes excellently on the passage: "Those who take pride in these later words and claim a kind of tyranny for themselves—why do they not remember the words that came just before? We are all swollen with a worldly spirit, yet we take pride in the authority given to us to forgive or retain sins. Defend the authority, but take care that the Spirit is present, through whom Christ granted that authority." <note>original: "Qui ex his posterioribus cristas erigunt, & Tyrannidem quandam sibi vendicant, cur non meminerunt eorum quæ mox præcesserunt? Toti turgemus mundano Spiritu, & tamen placemus nobis authoritate commissâ remittendi aut retinendi peccata. Tuere authoritatem, sed cura ut adsit Spiritus per quem Christus tribuit authoritatem."</note> This implies that where this Spirit is not present, the Authority is not present; and that a man cannot rationally be either comforted by the forgiveness, or dismayed by the retaining of sin, when it comes from such "Ghostly Fathers" as are devoid of the Spirit of Christ.

5. Moreover, *Hugo Grotius* <note>A Dutch jurist and theologian (1583–1645) known for his work on international law and biblical interpretation.</note> soberly and with judgment, I believe, interprets this place as referring to the *Remission of sins by Baptism*, or *Reception* back into the communion of the Church if anyone has fallen away after *Baptism*. However, the *Retaining* of sins refers to the *Non-admittance* of those into the Church who are not yet penitent believers, or the *Excommunicating* of them out of it after a lapse worthy of such a great punishment. But what does this have to do with an *annual absolution* which must force and squeeze out such an unnecessary and unreasonable confession? St. *James* says, *Confess your sins one to another*; his wording would be poorly chosen if it had been such an indispensable duty to confess to the priest—and in such a frequent and precise manner as has been described.

This annual prostration <note>original: "Provolution"; the act of throwing oneself down in front of another.</note>, therefore, of a penitent upon the floor at the feet of a formal confessor, with eyes and hands devoutly lifted up to—
