# Chapter 6: Of Prophetic Iconisms <note>term: Iconism | a symbolic figure or representation, especially in prophecy or dreams</note>

And compendiously <note>meaning: concisely</note> and all at once, *All flesh is distinguished into all wealth and gold;* <note>original Greek: Ἡ σὰρξ ὅλη εἰς πάντα πλῦτον ϗ χρυσὸν διακρίνεται</note> which is to say: **Flesh is universally referred to gold and riches in the interpretation of visions or dreams.**

17. **Flood.** See *Water*.

**Fornication.** See *Whoredom*.

<margin>* Pierius, Hieroglyphica, Book 29.</margin>
**Frogs.** A **Frog** is a hieroglyphic for imperfection, says Pierius <note>Giovanni Pierio Valeriano Bolzani (1477–1558), an Italian Renaissance humanist and author of a famous book on symbols and hieroglyphs.</note>, according to the understanding of the **Egyptian priests**. He suggests that the reason for this was the observation of the unfinished birth of this animal out of the slime of the **Nile**, which it casts up during its overflowing. After this, the creature is seen half-formed—part **frog**, part **mud**—as <margin>* Horus Apollo, Hieroglyphica, Book 1, Ch. 25.</margin> Horus Apollo <note>The supposed author of a 4th-century treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphics.</note> also expressly affirms: "Sometimes it is seen with one part as a frog, and the other part resembling earth." <note>original Greek: Ἔσθ᾽ ὅτε ὁρᾶται τῷ ἑτέρῳ μέρει αὐτῷ, βατράχῳ, τῷ δὲ λοιπῷ, γεώδει τινὶ ἐμφερής.</note>

But since it is generated from filth and mire, I would look upon it as a fitting emblem of that *wisdom which is not from above*, but is **earthly, sensual <note>original: animal</note>, and devilish**, <note>original Greek: ἐπίγειος, ψυχικὴ ϗ δαιμονιώδης</note> and is accompanied by bitter zeal and strife in the heart, as the Apostle [James] suggests just before. This is contrary to that *wisdom which is from above*, which is first pure—not mired with worldly lusts—then peaceable—not breeding contention, nor full of words and brawlings like the persistent, harsh, and disharmonious **croakings** <note>original: coaxations | a term derived from "koax," the sound of a frog in Greek literature</note> of **frogs**. (They are named in Greek from that very unpleasant noise, as if the word *batrachoi* [frogs] were shorthand for "those with rough cries," **from the shrillness and harshness of the noise they make**.) <note>original Greek: βοατραχεῖς, παρὰ τὸ τραχύτητα τῆς βοᾶς</note>

They are even less suited to war and bloodshed, or to the instigating of princes and men in power toward it; yet the hoarse and harsh croaking of these creatures may be a fit symbol of such behavior. This is especially true if these "trumpeters to war" are conceived to be men who are as soft and unwarlike as these naked and slimy animals—no more fit to fight than a frog—but who act only as heralds for war and confusion for their own interest. The zealous declamations and shouts they make are on their own behalf, just as all the noise a frog makes is with its tongue turned inward toward its own throat. From this, the creature seems a very lively emblem of such wretches as these. Artemidorus <note>A 2nd-century professional dream interpreter.</note> says in Book 2, Chapter 15: **"Frogs signify impostors and scoundrels <note>original: scurras</note>,"** <note>original Greek/Latin: Βάτραχοι δὲ ἄνδρας γόητας ϗ βωμολόχους προσημαίνουσιν· Ranae homines impoſtores & ſcurras ſignificant</note> which has no small affinity with our larger description of them.

18. **Gems and precious stones.** See *Crown*.

**God.** In Hebrew, the word *Elohim* signifies **magistrates** as well as **God**, as appears from several places of Scripture. And Artemidorus has noticed this analogy even from highest antiquity (Book 2, Chapter 37): **"For all the gods have a common relationship to masters. For this ancient saying is correct: 'That which rules has the power of God.'"** <note>original Greek/Latin: Κοινὸν γὰρ πάντες οἱ Θεοὶ λόγον ἔχουσι πρὸς δεσπότας. ὀρθῶς γὰρ ϗ τοῦτο τὸ παλαιὸν ἔχει, Τὸ κρατοῦν δύναμιν ἔχει θεοῦ. Quicquid dominatur, vim habet Dei.</note> And again in Book 3, Chapter 13: **"If any rich man should imagine himself to have become a god, it predicts a very great state office <note>original: principality</note>. For rulers, like the gods, have the power to do good or evil to people in a similar manner."** <note>original Greek: Θεὸς εἴ τις ὑπολάβοι γενέσθαι, πλούσιῳ ὤν, ἀρχὴν μεγίστην προαγορεύει. Ἐπίσης γὰρ τοῖς Θεοῖς ϗ οἱ ἄρχοντες δύνανται εὖ ϗ κακῶς τινὰς ποιεῖν.</note>

## CHAPTER 7.

1. **Hail**; its meaning according to Scripture. 2. And according to the ancient dream-interpreters <note>original: Onirocriticks</note>. 3. **Harvest**; the negative and positive senses of it. 4. **Head**; how it clearly signifies sovereign power, whether held by many or by one. 5. **Heaven** and **Earth**. 6. **Horn**. 7. **Horse**; **Islands**. 8. **King** and **Kingdom**. 9. That kinds or sorts of things are sometimes expressed as if they were individuals of the same kind. 10. **Leopard**; **Locusts**. 11. **Male-child**; **Mark**; **Measure**; **Mill**; **Month**; **Moon**. 12. **Mountain**; its several meanings.

1. **Hail**. Since winds and storms signify political commotions and wars—as is acknowledged by Hugo Grotius <note>A 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian famous for his work on international law and biblical interpretation.</note> and all other interpreters—such as in Daniel 7:2 (where the *four winds of heaven* are said to strive upon the *great sea*), a storm of **hail** may well signify war and the incursion of an enemy. This is especially true if they come from the **North**, as the frozen nature of this atmospheric phenomenon <note>original: Meteor</note> bears the character of that direction.

We have two eminent examples of this prophetic figure in Isaiah <note>original: Esay</note>. The first is in Chapter 28: *Behold, the Lord has a mighty and strong one, which as a tempest of hail and a destroying storm, as a flood of mighty waters overflowing, shall cast down to the earth violently. The crown of pride, the drunkards of Ephraim, shall be trodden under feet.* "These signify," says Forerius <note>Francisco Forério (1523–1581), a Portuguese Dominican scholar and biblical commentator.</note>, "the arrival of enemies who were to devastate the entire kingdom of Israel." <note>original Latin: Hæc significant hostium adventum, qui universum regnum Israel devastaturi erant.</note> But it is so plain that it required no interpretation. The other example is Isaiah Chapter 30: *And the Lord shall cause his glorious voice to be heard, and shall show the lighting down of his arm with the indignation of his anger, and with a flame of devouring fire, with scattering, and tempests, and hailstones. For through the voice of the Lord shall the Assyrian be beaten down, etc.* That is to say, the forces of the Lord will come against **Assyria** like thunder, lightning, and hail. It is quite clear that a hail-storm signifies the incursion and assault of an enemy, according to the style of Scripture.

2. A similar significance is also acknowledged by the **dream-interpreters** <note>original: Onirocriticks</note>. Artemidorus <note>A 2nd-century Greek professional diviner and author of the *Oneirocritica* (The Interpretation of Dreams).</note>, Book 2, Chapter 8, writes: "Rain, storms, and tempests bring disturbances, dangers, and losses to all." <note>original Greek: Ὄμβροι δὲ καὶ λαίλαπες καὶ χειμῶνες ταραχὰς πᾶσι καὶ κινδύνους καὶ ζημίας ἐπάγουσι.</note> He says something similar in Chapter 41, which has some similarity to the passage in Daniel. But to come closer to the point concerning **hail**, Achmetes <note>An author of a work on dream interpretation based on Arabic, Indian, and Persian sources.</note>, citing Indian, Persian, and Egyptian solutions for dream interpretation in Chapter 191, says: "Snow, hail, and frost signify afflictions, anxieties, and torments." <note>original Greek: Ἡ χιών, ἡ χάλαζα καὶ ὁ πάγος θλίψεις καὶ μερίμνας καὶ βασάνους σημαίνουσι.</note> Yet even more particularly regarding **hail**, and more to our present purpose: "If one dreams that hail falls on a place, he may expect a thorough and sudden incursion of the enemy." <note>original Greek: Ἐάν ἴδῃ τις χάλαζαν ἐν τόπῳ πεσοῦσαν, ἔφοδον ἀθρόαν ἐλπίζεται.</note> And further: "But if he dreams that the hail damaged the stems or **stalks** <note>original Greek: εἰ δ᾽ ἴδῃ ὅτι ἡ χάλαζα ἐλυμήνατο τὴν καλάμην τοῦ σίτου καὶ τῆς κριθῆς, σφαγαὶ ἀνάλογοι γενήσονται ἐν τῷ τόπῳ ἀπὸ πολέμου</note> of the wheat and the barley, proportional slaughters will occur in that place from war."

<summary>This page defines the prophetic symbol of "hail" as representing war and enemy invasion, drawing evidence from the Bible (Isaiah and Daniel) and ancient dream-interpretation manuals.</summary>
<keywords>Hail, Prophetic Symbols, Isaiah, Daniel, Dream Interpretation, Onirocritics, Artemidorus, Achmetes, War, Metaphor</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dictionary of prophetic symbols (iconisms) found in Chapter 7, completing the entry for "Hail" and moving through the definitions of "Harvest," "Head," and the beginning of "Heaven and Earth."</meta>

...the stalks of the grain <note>In this period, "corn" referred to any cereal grain, such as wheat or barley, rather than specifically maize.</note>, and according to how they are broken, the slaughter of men will occur in that same proportion in that place.

3. *Harvest.* The cutting down of *grain* signifies the death of men, as seen in the apparition of twelve men who seemed to mow the grain fields with scythes <note>original: "sithes"</note> in *Merchia* <note>Likely referring to the Marches, the border regions of England and Wales.</note>, which was followed by a pestilence. However, mortality caused by war is even more fittingly expressed by this symbol. *Achmetes* <note>The supposed author of an influential 9th-century Greek manual on dream interpretation.</note> writes in the *Indian Dream Interpreters* <note>original: "Onirocriticks"</note>: *Ἐὰν ἴδῃ ὁ βασιλεὺς χώραν θεριζομένην ἢ θερισθεῖσαν, κ᾿ ἐλογίζετο οἰκείαν εἶν᾿ αὐτὴν, ἀκούσεται ταχέως σφαγὴν τοῦ λαοῦ αὐτοῦ*; "If a King dreams he sees a harvest being reaped or already reaped in his own country, he will suddenly hear of the slaughter of his people" <note>original: Achmetes, quoting the Indian Onirocriticks in Greek.</note>. This comparison is also used in Scripture: *Jeremiah 51:33* <note>The original text cites Jer. 15:33, but the quote is from 51:33.</note>. *The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor; it is time to thresh her; yet a little while, and the time of her harvest shall come.*

But *Harvest* sometimes has a more auspicious sense, as in the words of our Savior in *John 4:35*:
> *Behold, I say unto you, lift up your eyes and look on the fields; for they are white already for harvest. And he who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit to life eternal, so that both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together.*

4. *Head.* It is as certain that the *head* of a beast in these prophetic figures signifies the person or persons in whom the *supreme power* resides as it is to find the fourth proportional in arithmetic when three numbers are given. For we have three terms of the analogy here as well: namely, a *Kingdom* and its *Sovereignty*, and a *Beast* (which is the prophetic figure of a *Kingdom*). Therefore, we cannot fail to say: as a *Kingdom* is to its *Sovereign Power*, so is this *prophetic* or figurative *beast* to its *head*. And conversely: as the *Kingdom* is to the *Beast*, so the *Sovereign Power* of the kingdom is to the *Head* of the beast. 

From this, we see plainly that the *head* of a beast corresponds to the *supreme power*, whether that power is held by one single person or by many. For just as the *power* is not considered in the abstract, neither are the *persons* considered apart from their *power*. Instead, both joined together concretely <note>original: "in concreto"</note> make up this *political head*. Therefore, if the *supreme* power exists only in *many* people, those *many* are the *head*. It is no less *one head* for consisting of *many persons*, just as the *body* is no less *one body* for consisting of *many persons*. Indeed, if a man were to follow the symmetry of his *imagination* <note>original: "Phancy"</note> rather than his *reason*, a *head* made of *many persons* would look more elegant and proportional than a single person. For example, if a *beast* were made of little wax pellets sticking together, a head made of only one pellet would not look as consistent as a head made of *many* pellets, identical to those the whole body consists of.

5. *Heaven and Earth.* By *heaven* and *earth*, we understand the *universe*, as Grotius has rightly noted regarding *Genesis* and abundantly proved regarding *2 Peter 3:13*. However, the prophets sometimes use *heaven* and *earth* to mean a *political universe*—that is, a *Kingdom* or *Polity*. There is no need for further proof of this than what is found in *Isaiah 51:15-16* <note>original: "Esay ch. 51. 15."</note>:
> *I am the Lord your God, who divided the sea whose waves roared, the Lord of Hosts is my name. And I have put my words in your mouth, and*

<header>A compendious Alphabet Book I.</header>

*I have covered you in the shadow of my hand, that I might plant the Heavens and lay the foundations of the Earth, and say unto Zion, "You are my people"*; that is to say, to make those who were only scattered individuals and slaves in Egypt before into a Kingdom or Polity, to be governed by their own Laws and Magistrates. Again, in chapter 65:17: *For behold, I create new Heavens and a new Earth, and the former shall not be remembered nor come into mind. But be glad and rejoice forever in what I create; for behold, I create Jerusalem as a rejoicing, and her people as a joy.* Regarding this text, Forerius <note>Franciscus Forerius (1523–1581) was a Portuguese Dominican theologian and commentator.</note> writes, "For I have decreed to establish a new world" <note>original: "Decrevi enim novum orbem condere"</note>, by which he means the Kingdom of Christ upon Earth—that is, his Church.

<margin>Isaiah 66:22.</margin>
According to this sense, he also interprets the passage: *For as the new Heavens and the new Earth, which I shall make, shall remain before me, so shall your descendants and your name remain*: "As long as the new world—that is, the Kingdom of God and the Church—should last, etc." <note>original: "Quam diu duraret novus Orbis, i. e. Regnum Dei & Ecclesia, &c."</note>. And Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch jurist and theologian known for his historical-linguistic approach to the Bible.</note> also—though he looks sideways and is very shy (he himself best knows why) regarding these previously mentioned places—cannot help but interpret *the new Heaven and the new Earth* in Revelation <note>original: "Apocal."</note> 21 as the state of the Church upon Earth. And Dr. Hammond <note>Henry Hammond (1605–1660) was a prominent English churchman and chaplain to King Charles I.</note>, in his commentary on 2 Peter 3, expressly acknowledges that *the new Heaven and the new Earth* mentioned there has a Political sense. This concept was worth clarifying because this general analogy helps us better understand what parts of the Universe signify figuratively; such as *to be called up into Heaven, or cast down to the Earth*, and similar phrases.

### 6. Horn.
*Horn* also signifies the Supreme Power of a Body Politic, which is compared to a Beast, the horn being the highest part of the Beast and the defender of its body. This is the interpretation given by the Angel in Daniel: *The great Horn is the first King*. And the *ten Horns* are interpreted as *ten Kings* by the Angel in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>. For they were the height and summit of their respective Kingdoms, though in some way subordinate to the seventh Head of the Beast.

### 7. Horse.
There is no explicit interpretation of that animal in Scripture. However, a noble Horse with its Rider naturally symbolizes Rule and Command. This also seems hinted to us from Psalm 45:4: <term>Prosper and ride</term> <note>original Hebrew: צלח רכב (tzelach rechab)</note>, which the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translate as <term>Prosper and reign</term> <note>original Greek: κατευοδῦ καὶ βασίλευε (kateuodu kai basileue)</note>.

But a *Horse* also signifies any success or fortune of the person who rides it. For instance, Achmetes <note>The traditional author of a manual on dream interpretation based on Persian, Indian, and Egyptian sources.</note> writes, drawing from Indian interpretations: "If one dreams that he rides on a *Pharas*" <note>original: Ἐάν τις ἴδῃ ἐποχούμενος τῷ φάρασ' (Ean tis idē epochoumenos tō pharas). The term "Pharas" refers to a high-quality horse, from the Arabic "faras."</note> (which is a noble steed) "which moves orderly and obediently, he shall obtain honor and renown proportionable to the Beast he rides on" <note>original Greek: ἀξίωμα καὶ φήμην (axiōma kai phēmēn)</note>. Afterward, he comments on the largeness, thickness, and length of the tail, declaring that the rider's power and followers shall be corresponding; but if the horse is bob-tailed or has thin hair, it signifies a lack of power. The halting of the *Horse* also signifies obstacles in the affairs of the Rider; and its defiance and stubbornness—if it be "unsubmissive and hard-mouthed" <note>original Greek: ἀνυπότακτος καὶ σκληροτράχηλος (anypotaktos kai sklērotrachēlos)</note>—signifies the Rider's own fault and affliction. Several other characteristics of the *Horse* are in a similar manner applied to the person riding it (Chapter 152).

And again, in Chapter 233: "A horse, that noble steed, signifies height and dignity..." <note>original Greek: Ἵππῳ, τῷ φάρασ' τῷ εὐγενεῖ εἰς ὕψος καὶ ἀξίωμα (Hippō, tō pharas tō eugenei eis hypsos kai axiōma)</note>

# Chapter 7: On Certain Prophetic Schemes

[It] was judged according to the interpretation of dreams <note>original: "κατὰ τὴν τῶν ὀνείρων ἐκρίθη κρίσιν"</note>. And shortly after: *If someone sees in a dream that he rode a dappled horse, he shall find great fame, high standing, and distinction before the people.* <note>original: "Ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις καθ' ὄναρ ὅτι ἵππῳ διθάκι κρούοντι φάρεας ἐπωχήπατο, εὑρήσει φήμην μεγίστην καὶ ὕψος καὶ αἰχμηρωσύνην ἐνώπιον λαοῦ."</note> And a little later: *But if anyone sees that while riding a dappled horse he holds a shield, he shall find fearlessness against enemies and power proportionate to the horse.* <note>original: "Ἐι δὲ ἴδῃ τις ὅτι ἐποχόμενος τῷ φάρεαι κατέχει ἀσπίδα, εὑρήσει ἀφοβίαν ἐξ ἐχθρῶν καὶ δύναμιν ἀνάλογον τοῦ ἵππου."</note> And lastly: *If anyone sees that he voluntarily dismounted from a dappled horse, he shall find a voluntary loss of power.* <note>original: "Ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις ὅτι ἑκὼν κατῆλθεν ἀπὸ ἵππου φάρεας, εὑρήσει ἑκούσιος ἐλάττωσιν ἐξουσίας."</note> 

From all of this, it is clearly evident that these **Horses** are the symbols of the **conditions** of their riders, or of the people over whom they are set (who are the "beast" they ride upon). This will make it easier to understand the visions of the **Four Horses** in the **Apocalypse** <note>The Book of Revelation</note>. Their riders are easily understood to be commanders—specifically Emperors—and what is signified by the horses relates either to the Empire or to the Emperors themselves.

***Hour.*** See ***Time.***

***Islands.*** That **Islands** may signify persons of greater dignity is suggested to us by their prominence or their way of rising above the plains <note>original: "Planicies"</note> of the sea. But that they may sometimes signify temples or consecrated places is also likely; their being separated from other land, just as these buildings are set apart from all other houses, may well lead a person’s imagination to believe this. See Mr. Mede <note>Joseph Mede (1586–1638), an influential English biblical scholar</note> on the **Sixth Seal.**

8. ***King and Kingdom.*** If **King** is looked upon as one distinct kind of sovereignty, when the word is used to mean "Supreme Governor," it may either be an <term>Icasmus</term> <note>a figure of speech based on comparison or likeness; an image</note>—for every supreme governor is to his political body as a king is to his—or else a <term>Diorismus</term> <note>a definition or specific distinction</note>. This is a kind of prophetic <term>synecdoche</term> <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole or a specific type represents a general category</note> which, as I have said, uses the specific species to represent the general genus. 

However, it may be as Mr. Mede seems to have abundantly proved (in his work *The Roman Empire is the Fourth Kingdom of Daniel*), that in Hebrew, the words for **King** and **Kingdom** are as broad in meaning as "Supreme Power" and the "Body that is subject to it," whether that body is a Kingdom or a Commonwealth. If so, then using "King" interchangeably for any supreme power—calling him a "king" <note>original: "βασιλεὺς"</note> as in Revelation 17—is simply a <term>Hellenism</term> <note>a Greek idiom or style of speech</note>. In that case, calling the **Seven Heads** there **Seven Kings** requires neither the explanation of a *Diorismus* nor an *Icasmus*, but only an <term>Henopaia</term> <note>a rhetorical device that unifies multiple things into one description</note>, describing those heads which represent a sovereignty shared by many.

9. And the fact that they are said to be **Seven Kings**, and not "seven sorts of kings," is not an unusual way of speaking. We say "four moral virtues," "five senses," "three physical principles," and "four passions," meaning four *kinds* of virtues, five *kinds* of senses, and so on. Similarly, the **Four Beasts** in Daniel that are said to rise out of the sea are four *kinds* of beasts, not four individuals of the same kind. And the **Two Witnesses** in the Apocalypse are two different *kinds* of witnesses, as Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian</note> himself acknowledges.

If it were not that common usage has made it familiar, calling seven sorts of kings "seven kings" would be a *Diorismus*, as the speech is more restrained and specific. An individual is more specific than the species, and the species more specific than the genus. Thus, there is very little difficulty in calling seven sorts of supreme governors **Seven Kings**, as the text of the Apocalypse does in chapter 17:10.

10. ***Leopard.*** Achmetes <note>An 8th or 9th-century author on dream interpretation</note>, chapter 272: *The leopard is judged to signify an irreconcilable enemy.* <note>original: "Ὁ πάρδος εἰς ἐχθρὸν ἀδιάλλακτον κρίνεται."</note>

It draws on classical dream interpretation and linguistic figures like synecdoche to clarify these biblical metaphors.</summary>

# A Concise Alphabetical Dictionary: Book I

It is interpreted <note>original Greek: "κρίνεται"</note> that a **Leopard** signifies an irreconcilable **enemy**. And in the same paragraph he says, *If a commander dreams that he fights with this animal*, he shall wage war with a powerful, deceitful, and fearsome enemy <note>original Greek: "εὑρήσει πόλεμον μετ’ ἐχθροῦ δυνατοῦ καὶ δολίου & ὑποφόβου"; Latin: "Cum hoste potente, fraudulento & formidoloso bellum geret"</note>.

***Locusts.*** That **Locusts** signify numerous armies of men pillaging and destroying a **country** is plain from *Joel 1:6*: *For a nation has come up upon my land, strong and without number, whose teeth are the teeth of a lion, and he has the fangs of a great lion. He has laid my vine waste, and stripped the bark from my fig tree; he has made it completely bare and cast it away; its branches are made white.* By **"nation,"** the **Jewish commentators**, along with **Vatablus** <note>François Vatable, a 16th-century French humanist</note> and others, understand a multitude of **locusts**; but that is only the symbolic type. The **Persians** and **Babylonians**, as well as other nations that were to lay waste to **Judea**, are signified by them, according to **Münster** and **Clarius**. **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius, a prominent legal scholar and theologian</note> also interprets this as the armies of **Phul** and **Shalmaneser**. Also, in the next chapter (verse 2), the gloominess and darkness of that day is attributed to the cloud of **locusts** that fly in the air; and their sudden landing on the place is compared to the **morning light spreading over the mountains**. And in verse 3: *The land is like the Garden of Eden before them, and behind them a desolate wilderness*; specifically because they devour all the green herbs wherever they go. That is the interpretation of several Hebrew expositors, as well as **Vatablus**, **Castalio**, **Drusius**, and **Lively**. But **Münster** and **Grotius** explain it as the numerous armies of the **Babylonians** and **Assyrians** that were to waste and destroy **Judea**.

**Achmetes** <note>An 8th or 9th-century author on dream interpretation</note> (chapter 300), according to the thinking of the **Indians**, **Persians**, and **Egyptians**, states: "In general, the locust is interpreted without variation as a multitude of enemies; for it is written that by divine command they go out to destroy a place" <note>original Greek: "Καθ’ ὅλου ἡ ἀκρὶς ἀπαραλλάκτως εἰς πλῆθος ἐχθρῶν κρίνεται· οὕτω γὰρ γέγραπται, ὅτι θείῳ κελεύσματι ἐκστρατεύονται εἰς ἀπώλειαν τοῦ τόπου"</note>. The latter part of this aphorism is to be referred to the **Indian** dream-interpreters <note>original: "Onirocriticks"</note>, and certainly alludes to the passage in **Joel**. And again: "If any King or ruler sees that locusts have gone out against someone, let him expect a powerful multitude of enemies there; and just as much as the locusts did damage, the enemy will do mischief in the same proportion" <note>original Greek: "Ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις βασιλεὺς ἢ ἐξουσιαστὴς ὅτι ἐξῆλθον κατά τινος ἀκρίδες, πλῆθος ἐχθρῶν μετ’ ἐξουσίας προσδοκάτω ἐκεῖσε, καὶ ὅσον ἐλυμήναντο αὑταὶ, τοσοῦτον βλάψουσι & αὐτοί"</note>.

<margin>Cassander's *Consultations*, Article 7.</margin>
11. ***Male-child.*** Just as the **Woman** who gives birth (in Revelation 12) is not a single woman but the Apostolic Church, so the **Child** must not be a single person, but a company of people; **Hugo Grotius** also agrees with this. **Andreas** says of this passage, "The male son is the people of the Church, the mystical Christ" <note>original Latin: "Filius masculus est Ecclesiæ populus"</note>. "For the whole Christ is both the Head and the Body," as **Cassander** has noted from **Saint Augustine**. If "male son" <note>original Greek: "υἱὸς ἄρρην"</note> may therefore be understood as a multitude under one head, why may not the "son of perdition" <note>original Greek: "υἱὸς ἀπωλείας"</note> in *2 Thessalonians 2:3* be understood in the same way?

***Measure.*** See ***Balance.***

***Mark.*** See ***Character.***

***Mill.*** **Achmetes**, quoting the dream-interpreters <note>original: "Onirocriticks"</note> of the **Indians** (chapter 194): "If anyone dreams he has a mill grinding, he shall prosper in his work and live in comfort and plenty, in proportion to the thickness and beauty of the millstones" <note>original Greek: "Ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις ὅτι ἔχει μυλῶνα ἀλήθοντα, εὑρήσει ἀγαθὸν καὶ εὐζωΐαν ἐκ τοῦ ἔργου αὐτοῦ ἀναλόγως τοῦ πάχους καὶ τοῦ κάλλους τῶν λίθων, &cc."</note>.

...stones, etc. And in chapter 195, according to the **Persian** and **Egyptian interpretations**: "In every case, overall, a birthmark is interpreted to signify life and wealth" <note>original Greek: "’Επὶ παντὸς καθ’ ὅλου ὁ μώλων εἰς ζωὴν & πλοῦτον κρίνεται"</note>.

12. ***Mountain.*** **Mountain** may have several significations. First, it may signify the **temples** or **holy places** of **idolaters**, which are frequently mentioned in Scripture under the title of **High Places**. In *Jeremiah 3:23*, according to the **Vulgate** <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note>: "Truly the hills were deceitful, and the multitude of mountains; truly in the Lord our God is the salvation of Israel" <note>original Latin: "Verè mendaces erant colles, & multitudo montium; verè in Domino Deo nostro salus Israel"</note>. Upon which **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch legal scholar and theologian</note> comments: "Those hills in which the idols were worshipped deceived us" <note>original Latin: "Colles illi in quibus Idola colebantur nos deceperunt"</note>. 

Secondly, **Mountains** signify **Cities**. *Isaiah 13:2*, concerning **Babylon**: *Lift up a banner upon the high mountain.* **Forerius** <note>Francisco Forerio, a 16th-century Portuguese Dominican theologian</note>, citing the **Chaldean Paraphrase** <note>Ancient Jewish translations and commentaries on the Hebrew Bible</note>, interprets this as "over the fortification which dwells peacefully" <note>original Latin: "super munitionem quæ habitat pacifice"</note>. The **Vulgate** has it as "upon a dark mountain" <note>original Latin: "super montem caliginosum"</note>. Upon which **Grotius** notes: "That is because ancient **Babylon** was situated in marshy places, from which rising vapor obscured the city" <note>original Latin: "Id ideo, quia vetus Babylon in palustribus locis sita erat, unde ascendens vapor urbem obscurabat"</note>. 

In *Jeremiah 51:25*: *Behold, I am against you, O destroying mountain... I will stretch out my hand upon you, and roll you down from the rocks.* Upon which **Münster** <note>Sebastian Münster, a German cartographer and Hebrew scholar</note> says: "He calls **Babylon** a 'mountain' because of the massive size of its buildings, even though the city itself was situated on a plain" <note>original Latin: "Vocat Babylonem montem ob ædificiorum molem, cùm urbs ipsa in planitie fuerit sita"</note>; and by analogy, he interprets the **Rocks** as "the defenses of the towering towers" <note>original Latin: "de præsidiis turrium eminentium"</note>. **Vatablus** and **Clarius** expressly agree with this. But all interpret this **Mountain** as the City of **Babylon**. 

In *Zechariah 4:7*: *Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you shall become a plain.* **Grotius** interprets this as **Babylon** being cast down by **Cyrus**. 

Thirdly, **Achmetes** <note>A 9th-century author on dream interpretation</note>, according to the sense of the **Persians**, **Indians**, and **Egyptians**, interprets **Mountains** as great and wealthy men. In chapter 144, while speaking of earthquakes and the things overturned by them, he says: "The mountain is interpreted as a high, wealthy man, in proportion to the size of the mountain" <note>original Greek: "Τὸ δ’ ὄρος ... ἐφ’ ὑψηλὸν ἄνδρα πλούσιον ἀναλόγως τῶ ὄρει κρίνεται"</note>. 

And lastly, it seems to refer to a whole Kingdom that has grown great, as in *Daniel 2*, where the *stone cut out without hands becomes a mountain and fills the whole Earth.*

# A Concise Alphabet: Book I.

1. **Nakedness.** It is either understood spiritually, as in *Revelation 3:18*, for being destitute of Divine Graces; or else in a more common meaning for distress, poverty, and disgrace. **Achmetes** <note>An 8th-century Christian author who wrote on the interpretation of dreams</note>, in his writing on the **Indian** interpretations of nakedness, says: "If someone dreams that they were made naked unexpectedly in some place, and that their private parts were revealed before the people, they shall be exposed and suffer great distress" <note>original Greek: "Ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις ὅτι ἐγυμνώθη ἀθέως ἐν τόπῳ τινὶ, καὶ ὅτι ἐφάνησαν τὰ κρυπτὰ αὐτοῦ ἐνώπιον λαοῦ, φανερωθήσεται καὶ θλιβήσεται μεγάλως"</note>. See also chapter 117 to the same purpose.

**Paradise.** **Achmetes**, in chapter 8, according to the sense of the **Indian** interpreters: "If a man dreams he enters **Paradise**, it foretells salvation for him." But it also broadly signifies worldly success and prosperity <note>original Greek: "Ἀλλὰ καὶ πλάτυ κοσμικῶ τοῦτο ἐπιτυχίαν σημαίνει"</note>. And shortly after, concerning the fruits of **Paradise**: "If someone dreams that they ate from the fruits of the trees, they will find wisdom and knowledge in their faith; because the fruits of paradise happen to be divine and useful concepts" <note>original Greek: "Ἐὰν ὤ ἴδῃ τις ὅτι ἔφαγεν ἐκ τῶν καρπῶν τῶν δένδρων, αὐτὸς εὑρήσει ἐν τῇ πίστει αὐτῷ σοφίαν καὶ γνῶσιν· διότι οἱ καρποὶ τοῦ παραδείσου λόγοι θεῖοι καὶ ἀγαθοὶ τυγχάνουσι"</note>.

2. **Philtre.** A *philtre* <note>original Latin: "Philtrum"</note> is a **love-potion** <note>original Latin: "Virus amatorium"</note>, a composition intended to force love from the person who drinks it. **Mr. Mede** <note>Joseph Mede, a 17th-century English scholar of the Apocalypse</note> argues that the passage in *Revelation 14:8* concerning the *wine of the wrath of her fornication* (which in the Greek is "from the wine of the wrath/poison of her fornication" <note>original Greek: "ἐκ τοῦ οἴνου τοῦ θυμοῦ τῆς πορνείας αὐτῆς"</note>) is a descriptive phrase for a **philtre**. Therefore, he translates it as "from the wine of the sorcery of her harlotry" <note>original Latin: "ex vino veneficii scortationis suae"</note>. 

For just as the **Hebrew** word *hemah* <note>original Hebrew: חמה</note> signifies both "wrath" and "poison," so the **Greek** word *thymos* <note>original Greek: "θυμὸς"</note> signifies the same. This is clear from *Deuteronomy 32:33*: "Their wine is the poison of dragons, and the cruel venom of asps," which the **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> renders as: "Their wine is the wrath of dragons, and the incurable wrath of asps" <note>original Greek: "θυμὸς δρακόντων ὁ οἶνος αὐτῶν, καὶ θυμὸς ἀσπίδων ἀνίατος"</note>. There are also several other places in Scripture to the same purpose. See **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch legal scholar and theologian</note> on the text; "the wine of wrath" <note>original Greek: "Ὁ οἶνος τοῦ θυμοῦ"</note> is therefore the same as "poisoned wine" <note>original Latin: "Vinum venenatum"</note>, in the sense that it may be a "love potion" <note>original Latin: "Virus amatorium"</note>. For what other kind of potion should be in the hand of a **whore**? Especially one who is said "by her sorcery" <note>original Greek: "ἐν τῇ φαρμακείᾳ αὐτῆς"</note> and enchantment to have deceived the nations of the earth—that is to say, by her enchanted cup, "in the wine of the sorcery of her fornication" <note>original Greek: "ἐν τῷ οἴνῳ τῆς φαρμάκου τῆς πορνείας αὐτῆς"</note>. For the Greek word *pharmakon* <note>original Greek: "φάρμακον"</note> signifies "poison" as well as "wrath."

3. But that magical rites and charms were used in the mingling of these **love-potions** is widely renowned throughout the writings of the poets. As in **Juvenal**, *Satire 6*:

> "I will speak of the *hippomanes* <note>A substance supposed to have aphrodisiac properties, often described as a growth on a foal's forehead or a discharge from a mare</note>, the incantation, and the brewed poison." <note>original Latin: "Hippomanes carménque loquar coctúmque venenum."</note>

And towards the end of that *Satire*:

> "This man brings magical songs; that one sells **Thessalian philtres** — — — — — — —" <note>original Latin: "Hic magicos affert cantus, hic Thessala vendit Philtra"</note>

Which plainly implies that **philtres** are made by witchcraft. And **Virgil**, concerning the superstitious gathering of *hippomanes*—believed to be potent for this purpose—in *Georgics 3*, suggests the same:

> "The *hippomanes* which evil stepmothers often gathered, and they mixed herbs with words that were not harmless." <note>original Latin: "Hippomanes quod saepe malae legere Novercae, Miscuerúntque herbas & non innoxia verba."</note>

And, lastly, **Ovid** in his *The Art of Love, book 2*:

> "The herbs of Medea and **Marsian** poisons mixed with magical sounds will not make love last." <note>original Latin: "Non facient ut vivet amor Medeïdes herba, Mistáque cum magicis Marsa venena sonis."</note>

<summary>This page explains the symbolic and scriptural meanings of "Nakedness," "Paradise," and "Philtre," emphasizing the linguistic connection between wrath, poison, and sorcery in the context of the biblical Whore of Babylon.</summary>
<keywords>Nakedness, Paradise, Philtre, Love-potion, Sorcery, Achmetes, Joseph Mede, Hugo Grotius, Juvenal, Virgil, Ovid, Hippomanes, Symbolism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Concise Alphabet" of prophetic symbols, specifically concluding the entry on "Philtre" and moving through "Pillar," "Rain," "Red," and beginning "Resurrection."</meta>

# Chapter VIII. On Prophetic Iconisms <note>original: "Iconisms"; the study of symbolic figures or icons</note>.

All of these passages, along with several others, sufficiently inform us about the nature of a **Philtre** <note>a love potion</note>. It is a magical potion, superstitiously mixed according to certain rites and laws of sorcery or witchcraft, regardless of what the ingredients may be. Therefore, "the wine of wrath" <note>original Greek: *ὁ οἶνος τοῦ θυμοῦ*</note>, translated as "Wine of Witchcraft" <note>original Latin: *Vinum Veneficii*</note> or **Philtre**, which is a "love poison" <note>original Latin: *Virus amatorium*</note>, agrees very well with "sorcery" <note>original Greek: *φαρμακεία* (pharmakeia)</note>. This relates to the sorcery of the Whore mentioned in **Revelation 18:23**. Since she is accused of this, and no other signs of that wickedness appear upon her except for **this cup in her hand**, it is in all likelihood to be found there.

4. **Pillar.** **Pillars** signify princes or nobles in a kingdom, "magnates" or "the greatest of the kingdom" <note>original Greek: *μεγιστᾶνας* (megistanas) or *τοὺς μεγίστους τῆς βασιλείας* (tous megistous tēs basileias)</note>, as you may see in **Achmetes** <note>an 8th-century interpreter of dreams</note>, chapters 148 and 160.

**Rain.** **Rain** may signify the **refreshment of pure and heavenly doctrine**. As in **Deuteronomy 32:2**:
> *My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distill as the dew, as the small rain upon the tender herb, and as the showers upon the grass.*

It also signifies **peace** and **righteousness** through the goodness of the sovereign power. **Psalm 72:6-7** describes the Kingdom of Christ this way:
> *He shall come down like the rain upon the mown grass, as showers water the earth. In his days shall the righteous flourish, and abundance of peace so long as the moon endures.*

Similarly, **Hosea 10:12** mentions the Lord's coming and raining down righteousness upon them. **Achmetes**, drawing from Indian interpretations in chapter 171, says: "Rain is an emblem of mercy from God in answering our prayers" <note>original Greek: *Ἡ βροχὴ εἰς αἰτήσεως ἐκπλήρωσιν καὶ ἔλεον διακρίνεται*</note>. Therefore, he says:
> *If anyone dreams that his field is rained upon, he shall find riches, and joy, and mercy from God* <note>original Greek: *εὑρήσει πλοῦτον καὶ χαρὰν καὶ ἔλεον ἀπὸ Θεοῦ*</note>.

And a little later, he interprets "pure rain" <note>original Greek: *τὴν βροχὴν καθαρὰν*</note> to be "common benefit" <note>original Greek: *κοινὴν εὐεργεσίαν*</note>. According to this is the verse from the Psalmist:
> *You, O God, sent a gracious rain on your inheritance, and refreshed it when it was dry.*

**Red.** It is so obvious that **Red** symbolizes bloody cruelty and barbarous persecution that it seems unnecessary to note it. Everyone acknowledges that the "great red dragon" <note>original Greek: *δράκων μέγας πυρρὸς*</note> in **Revelation 12**, with seven heads, is called so because of his bloodiness. But not everyone has noted that his seventh head growing out of this **red** body signifies that this Beast will also be cruel under the seventh head, and that this cruelty itself is part of the "Image of the Beast."

5. **Resurrection.** That the **resurrection** of the dead has a **political** sense as well as a theological or physical one may appear plainly from **Ezekiel 37:9-10**:
> *Then he said to me, "Prophesy to the wind, prophesy, son of man, and say to the wind, 'Thus says the Lord God: Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain that they may live.'" So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived and stood upon their feet, an exceedingly great army.*

That this is to be understood in a **political** sense—concerning the restoration of the people of **Israel** to their own land out of bondage and captivity—is plain from the very mouth of God himself in the following verses:
> *Then he said to me, "Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel. Behold, they say, 'Our bones are dried, and our hope is lost; we are cut off for our parts.' Therefore prophesy and say to them, 'Thus says the Lord God: Behold, O...'"*

<summary>This page defines the prophetic symbolism of "Pillars" as nobles, "Rain" as divine doctrine or mercy, "Red" as cruelty, and "Resurrection" as a political restoration of a nation.</summary>
<keywords>Philtre, Pillar, Rain, Red, Resurrection, Achmetes, Ezekiel, Revelation, political symbolism, dream interpretation</keywords>

> *My people, I will open your graves, and cause you to come out of your graves, and bring you into the land of Israel.* <note>Ezekiel 37:12-13</note>

From this, it is plain that to be "cut off," to be "slain," and to "rise from the dead" has (as I said) a *Political* sense as well as a *Natural* or *Theological* one. In this context, *Resurrection* is the recovery <note>original: "Recuperation"</note> of such rights and liberties as have been taken away, and a deliverance from persecution, affliction, and bondage. Achmetes <note>an 8th-century author on dream interpretation</note>, in chapter 5, according to the *Indian* doctrine, says: "If anyone sees a resurrection of the dead in a dream, in whatever place they see it, there justice shall be practiced" <note>original Greek: *Ἐάν τις ἐν ὀνείρῳ θεάσηται ἀνάστασιν νεκρῶν, ἐν ᾧ τόπῳ θεωρήση τις, ἐκεῖ δικαιοσύνη πραχθήσεται*</note>. And in chapter 6, according to the doctrine of the *Persian* dream interpreters <note>original: "Onirocriticks"</note>: "If someone sees in their sleep a rising of the dead, in the place where the vision occurred, there shall be a release from bonds and a deliverance from afflictions" <note>original Greek: *Ἐάν τις ἴδῃ καθ᾽ ὕπνους νεκρῶν ἔγερσιν, ἐν ᾧ τόπῳ ἡ ὄψις, ἐκεῖ δεσμῶν λύτρωσις κὶ θλίψεων ἀπολύτρωσις ἔσται*</note>. And lastly, according to the *Egyptians* in chapter 7: "If someone sees in their sleep a rising of the dead, it signifies freedom for prisoners and the end of wars" <note>original Greek: *Ἐάν τις ἴδῃ καθ᾽ ὕπνους νεκρῶν ἔγερσιν, δεσμίων ἐλευθερίαν κὶ πολέμων παῦσιν σημαίνει*</note>. The sense of all these put together is: *That dreaming of men rising from the dead signifies the execution of Justice, and deliverance from war, bondage, and affliction.*

6. **Rivers.** A **River** has two ways it can be considered. The first is in respect to its origin and its return there, which is hinted at in **Ecclesiastes 1:7**: 
> *All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again.* 
According to this consideration, if we suppose the **Sea** to be a symbol <note>original: "Type"</note> of the extent of jurisdiction or the empire of any powerful ruler (as it indeed is), then **Rivers** will signify any powers sent out from there <note>original: "Emissary Powers"</note>. These might be armies, provincial magistrates, or whatever agents abroad act on behalf of this chief power. These may, according to exact analogy, be called **Rivers** because they and their affairs flow back to the main "Sea"—the greatness of that jurisdiction to which they belong.

Achmetes, in chapter 178, according to the mind of the *Indians*, *Persians*, and *Egyptians*, says: "The sea and the deep represent the person of a great king; and just as all rivers flow into it, so all the wealth of the world flows into him" <note>original Greek: *Ἡ θάλασσα κὶ ὁ βυθὸς εἰς πρόσωπον ♃ μεγάλου κρίνονται βασιλέως· κὶ ὥσπερ οἱ ποταμοὶ πάντες βάλλουσιν ἐν αὐτῇ, οὕτω κὶ πᾶς ὁ πλοῦτος τοῦ κόσμου εἰσρεῖ ἐν αὐτῷ*</note>. And again, to the same purpose: "If the king sees that new, unusual rivers have flowed into the sea, he shall receive wealth and joy from nations far away" <note>original Greek: *Ἐὰν ἴδῃ ὁ βασιλεὺς ὅτι νέοι ποταμοὶ εἰσέβαλον εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν ἀσυνήθεις, πλοῦτον ἐξ ἐθνῶν μακρόθεν κὶ χαρὰν αὐτὸς δέξεται*</note>. This means that *new Rivers running into the Sea signify new revenues coming to the King or Kingdom from people far off—supposedly those made into provinces by his power.*

7. The other way to consider **Rivers** is their clarity <note>original: "limpidness"</note> and their ability to irrigate. In this respect, they have either a spiritual sense or a more worldly <note>original: "Mundane"</note> one. The spiritual sense appears from what our Savior said in **John 7:38**: 
> *He that believes in me, out of his belly shall flow rivers of water. This he spoke of the Spirit, which those who believed in him should receive.* 
The fruit of this Spirit, as it is shared with the Church in general, is *Righteousness, Peace,* and *Joy*. This agrees with the dream-interpretation <note>original: "Onirocritical"</note> solution of Astrampsychus <note>an ancient author of a book on dreams</note>:

->A clear spring dissolves the sorrows of the mind.<-
<note>original Greek: *Πηγὴ διαυγὴς τὰς νόου λύει λύπας*</note>

Regarding this water, Christ says in **John 4**: *Whoever drinks of the*

# Chapter VIII. Of Prophetic Symbols <note>original: Prophetick Iconisms</note>

But waters also represent worldly abundance: *Jeremiah* 31:12: *Therefore they shall come and sing in the height of Zion, and shall flow together for the goodness of the Lord, for wheat, and for wine, and for oil, and for the young of the flock and of the herd; and their soul shall be as a watered garden, and they shall not sorrow any more at all.* Achmetes, in chapter 176, according to the *Egyptian* interpretations <note>original: Solutions</note>, says: *Rivers that water the soil are interpreted as the livelihood of men* <note>original Greek: Οἱ ἄρδοντες τὴ γῆν ποταμοὶ εἰς τ’ ζωὴν διακρίνονται τῶν ἀνθρώπων</note>. *If someone sees a river that usually waters the country dried up, it portends death, sorrow, and affliction* <note>original Greek: Ἐὰν ἴδη τις τ’ ἄρδοντα τὴ γῆν συνήθως ποταμὸν ξηρανθέντα, εὑρήσει ὁ τόποϚ λιμὸν ϗ μέριμναν ϗ θλίψιν</note>.

8. *Saints.* The first title of "Saintship" belongs to the *Israelites*, who were a separate people, set apart from other nations and made holy to the Lord by adhering to the Law he gave them, not contaminating themselves with the idolatrous customs <note>original: Institutes</note> of the Gentiles. <margin>*Deuteronomy* 33:2.</margin> *The Lord came from Sinai, and rose from Seir unto them; he shined from mount Paran, and he came with ten thousands of saints.* This means, according to the commentator Vatablus, *with the people of Israel, of whom there were indeed many thousands; although not every individual was a saint, yet the thousands were holy because God had sanctified them and set them apart for himself as his own people* <note>original Latin: cum populo Israel, quorum fuerunt quidem multa millia, licèt non singuli Sancti, tamen sancta fuerunt millia, quòd Deus illos sanctificasset, & in populum suum illos sibi segregasset</note>. And further in the following verse: *Yes, he loved the people; all his saints are in your hand.* This is clearly spoken of the *Israelites* according to the sense in *Exodus* chapter 19, verses 5–6, where they are called a *peculiar treasure above all people, and also a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.* They are said to be this if they obey his voice and keep his covenant.

From this, it is easy to understand that those Christians who are purely evangelical succeed to this title; they do not contaminate themselves with any idolatrous practices against the command and covenant of God. They are *Saints* in this specific and separate sense, because they do not join in the rituals of the Gentiles but keep themselves to the commands of their one Master, Christ. If they do this sincerely and constantly (and truly there is little doubt of the sincerity of those who did not hesitate to lay down their lives for the truth), even if they are not seen as wise or fashionable <note>original: plausible</note> by the world’s standards, and are not free from the flaws of human frailty, they are undoubtedly those *Saints* so frequently mentioned in the *Book of Revelation* <note>original: Apocalyps</note>. They are the true *Israel of God*, regardless of the hardships or low social status <note>original: low condition of fortune</note> they may endure, which might hide their true worth. For the *Witnesses* were to be clothed in sackcloth for one thousand two hundred and sixty days.

*Scorpion.* See *Serpent.*

*Scorched by the Sun.* Achmetes, in his *Book of Dream Interpretation* <note>original: Onirocritica</note>, chapter 167, says: *If someone dreams that the sun has scorched them greatly, they will be punished by the king in proportion to that scorching* <note>original Greek: Εἰ δὲ ἴδῃ τις ὅτι πλεῖστα ἀπέκαυσεν αὐτὸν ὁ ἥλιος, εὑρήσει τιμωρίαν παρὰ τοῦ βασιλέως ἀνάλογον τῆς καυσπηρίας</note>.

It also briefly introduces dream interpretations regarding being scorched by the sun as a sign of royal punishment.</summary>

# The Definitions and Illustrations Book I.

...teaching <note>original: ching</note>, according to the doctrine of the *Egyptians*, *Indians*, and *Persians*.

9. *Sea*. Waters signify *people*, as the Angel tells *St. John*; the gathering together of people into one body politic <note>original: Body Politick</note>, kingdom, or jurisdiction may appropriately be called a *Sea* in the political world, just as the gathering together of the waters is so termed in the natural world, in *Genesis* 1. And the whole collection <note>original: University</note> of kingdoms, or a great part of them, may according to this analogy be called either the *great Sea* or *Ocean*. This is also figured out in the vision of *Daniel*, chapter 7: *I saw in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven strove upon the great sea.* Where by *winds* undoubtedly is meant *war*, just as the *great sea* represents a collection of several kingdoms in which this bluster and tempest of *war* is made, with one kingdom fighting against another to enlarge their dominions.

This analogy of the *Sea* is also acknowledged in the interpretations of the *Indians*, *Persians*, and *Egyptians*. Achmetes <note>An 8th or 9th-century author on the interpretation of dreams</note>, chapter 178: "If any dream he is Master of the Sea, he will be entire successor in the whole Kingdom" <note>original Greek: Ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις ὅτι ἐδέσποσε τῆς θαλάσσης, κληρονόμος ἔσται τῆς βασιλείας πάσης·</note>. And so likewise of the winds: "If a King see the Sea troubled by a wind from a known quarter, he will be molested by some Nation from that quarter" <note>original Greek: Ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐὰν ἴδῃ τὴν θάλασσαν σφόδρα ταρασσομένην ὑπὸ ἀνέμου γνωρίμου, ἐκ τοῦ κατοικεῖσθαι πρὸς τὸν ἄνεμον ἔθνους ταραχθήσεται·</note>. "But if he see the Sea calm, he will enjoy his Kingdom in peace" <note>original Greek: Εἰ δ’ ἴδῃ γαληνιῶσαν τὴν θάλασσαν, εὐφρανθήσεται ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ αὐτοῦ·</note>. This interpretation of the *Sea*, therefore, will further confirm that of the *Rivers*.

*Serpent*. That notorious *serpentine* shape which deceived *Adam* and *Eve* and caused them to fall <note>original: lapsed them</note> into rebellion against God, cannot but assure anyone that in Scripture, all the *serpentine* kind described in prophecy do, in all likelihood, refer to the Kingdom of the *Devil*.

*Ship*. That a *ship* as well as a *mill* may be a hieroglyphic <note>original: Hieroglyphick</note> of *profit*, anyone may easily conceive if he thinks of merchandising. Achmetes, according to the mind of the *Egyptians* and *Persians*, chapter 180: "If one dream he builds Ships, he shall grow rich proportionately to the number of the Ships he builds" <note>original Greek: Ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις ὅτι κτίζει πλοῖα, πλούτου περιποίησιν ἀνάλογον τῶν πλοίων ἕξει·</note>. But from the previous chapter, according to the doctrine of the *Indian* interpreters: "If one dreams he built a merchant ship, he shall create a gathering of men for religious mysteries" <note>original Greek: Ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις ὅτι ἐτεκτόνει πλοῖον ἐμπορευτικόν, συναγωγὴν ἀνδρῶν διὰ μυστήρια ποιήσει.</note>. This is an interpretation as far-fetched as if it came from the *Indies* indeed. Nor is it easy to guess why a *ship* should suggest the gathering of men for celebrating religious mysteries, unless we conceive a *ship* to represent a temple. Why we should do so, I do not know, unless because they are separate <note>original: disterminated</note> and solitary buildings, as *temples* are; not joined to one another, any more than a temple is joined to other houses. But since it is called a merchant ship <note>original Latin: Navis mercatoria</note>, it may be that the profit the priest receives from sacrifices or offerings to idols is being alluded to. And whether any darker, recessed areas in the *ship* may represent the inner sanctuaries <note>original: Adyta; the most sacred, private parts of a temple</note> in temples, I do not know. Such particularities I leave to every man’s fancy to pursue at leisure.

### Chapter 8: Of Prophetic Symbols <note>original: Iconisms</note>

*Slain. See Resurrection.*
*Slaughter. See Death.*

10. **Sun, Moon, and Stars.** The *Sun* and *Moon* have either a *spiritual* meaning or a *secular* one. Of the *spiritual* meaning of the *Sun*, there is an example where Christ is called the *Sun of Righteousness*, as he is by the Prophet *Malachi*. Also, the Apostle says to the *Ephesians*: *Awake, you who sleep, so that Christ may give you light*. The *Moon* also may have a *spiritual* meaning, assuming it represents <note>original: typifie</note> the *Mosaic* dispensation <note>The religious system and laws given to the Israelites through Moses</note>. It may very well do so, both because it is a light (though a far dimmer light than that of the Gospel) and also in allusion to the New Moons and other Jewish festivals, the order of which depended on that planet. See Mr. *Mede* <note>Joseph Mede (1586–1639), an influential English biblical scholar and expert on prophecy</note> on *Revelation* <note>original: Apocal.</note> 12.

To which you may add that, just as the *Law of Moses* is compared to the *Moon*, so may the *Light of the Gospel of Christ* be compared to the *Sun*. It is plain from *David* in <margin>Psalm 119:105.</margin> *Psalm 119* that the *Word of God* is compared to *Light*: *Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my path*. And that great lamp of the universe, the *Sun*, is the clearest light men can walk by. From this, the common expression of the *sunshine of the Gospel* was framed by a very justifiable analogy; it further assures us that the *light of the Gospel* may also be one spiritual meaning of the *Sun*.

11. The *secular* meaning of the *Sun* and *Moon* occurs when they represent the power and glory of this world. This is meant either generally and at large, as in *Jeremiah 15:9*: *Her Sun is gone down while it was yet day*, which the *Targum* <note>Ancient Aramaic translations or paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible</note> renders as *Their glory passed from them in their lifetime*. A similar example is in *Amos 8:9*: *I will cause the Sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the Earth in the clear day*. Vatablus <note>François Vatable (d. 1547), a French humanist and scholar of the Hebrew Bible</note> interprets this: "When you are at the highest degree of happiness, then I will cast you down from there and make you most unhappy" <note>original Latin: *Cum eritis in supremo felicitatis gradu, tunc inde vos dejiciam & infelicissimos reddam*</note>. Again, in *Isaiah* <note>original: Esay</note> 60:20: *Your Sun shall no more go down, neither shall your Moon withdraw herself*. That is to say, you shall have uninterrupted glory and prosperity, as it follows immediately after: *The days of your mourning shall be ended*. In such places as these, *Sun* and *Moon* do not have a meaning limited to any particular rank in a kingdom, but signify generally its glory and prosperity.

12. But in other places, there may be a more specific meaning for these *lights*. For as there is a *political universe* as well as a *natural* one (as I have already shown), which has its own *heaven* as well as *earth*, there must be something in the *political heaven* answering to those chief conspicuous parts of the *natural heaven*: the *Sun, Moon, and Stars*. It follows that whoever is chief in a *political world* must be the *Sun* of it. This appears even in a smaller instance concerning a household <note>original: Body Oeconomical</note> in *Genesis 37:9*, namely the dream of *Joseph*, that the *Sun and the Moon and the eleven Stars made obeisance to him*. Interpreting <note>original: unriddling</note> this, *Jacob* says to his son, *What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow down ourselves to you to the earth?* Therefore, if these symbols signify so distinctly in a *family*, which is but a small household body, it is much more to be expected that they signify the same in a *body politic* <note>A state or organized political community</note>.

<meta>This page continues the "Alphabet of Prophetic Symbols," specifically concluding a point about teaching from various ancient cultures before moving on to the symbols for "Sea," "Serpent," and "Ship."</meta>

-># The Definitions and Illustrations Book I.<-

...teaching, according to the doctrine of the Egyptians, Indians, and Persians.

9. **Sea.** Waters representing people, as the Angel tells St. John; the gathering together of people into one body politic, kingdom, or jurisdiction may fitly be called a **Sea** in the political world, just as the gathering together of the waters is so named in the natural world in *Genesis 1*. The entirety <note>original: "university"</note> of kingdoms, or a great part of them, may according to this analogy be called either the **great sea** or **ocean**, as is also depicted in the vision of Daniel, Chapter 7: *I saw in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven strove upon the great sea.* In this passage, "winds" undoubtedly refers to **war**, while the "great sea" represents a collection of several kingdoms in which this blast and tempest of war occurs, as one kingdom fights against another to enlarge its borders.

This analogy of the **Sea** is also acknowledged in the interpretations of the Indians, Persians, and Egyptians. *Achmetes* <note>Achmetes refers to a popular medieval manual on dream interpretation (the *Oneirocriticon*), which attributed its wisdom to ancient Eastern sources</note>, chapter 178, states: *If anyone dreams he is master of the sea, he will be the heir of the entire kingdom* <note>original Greek: "Ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις ὅτι ἐδέσποτε τὴν θάλασσαν, κληρονόμ. ἔσται τῆς βασιλείας πάσης"</note>. And likewise regarding the **Winds**: *If a king sees the sea greatly troubled by a wind from a known quarter, he will be molested by some nation from that quarter* <note>original Greek: "Ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐὰν ἴδῃ τὴν θάλασσαν σφόδρα ταρασσομένην ὑπὸ ἀνέμῳ γνωρίμῳ, ἐκ τοῦ κατοικεῖθ. πρὸς τὸν ἄνεμον ἔθνει ταραχθήσεται"</note>. *But if he sees the sea calm, he will enjoy his kingdom in peace* <note>original Greek: "Εἰ δ᾽ ἴδῃ γαληνιῶσαν τὴν θάλασσαν, εὐφρανθήσεται ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ αὐτοῦ"</note>. This interpretation of the Sea, therefore, further confirms the interpretation of **Rivers**.

**Serpent.** That notorious **Serpentine** shape which deceived Adam and Eve and caused them to fall into rebellion against God ensures that in Scripture, every kind of **Serpent** described in prophecy most likely refers to the Kingdom of the **Devil**.

**Ship.** Anyone can easily understand that a **Ship**, as well as a **Mill**, can be a symbolic image <note>original: "hieroglyphick"</note> of **Profit**, if they consider the nature of merchandising. *Achmetes*, following the thinking of the Egyptians and Persians in chapter 180, says: *If one dreams he builds ships, he shall grow rich in proportion to the number of ships he builds* <note>original Greek: "Ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις ὅτι κτίζει πλοῖα, πλούτου περιποίησιν ἀνάλογον τῶν πλοίων ἕξει"</note>. However, in the preceding chapter, according to the doctrine of the Indian interpreters, it says: *If anyone dreams that he builds a merchant ship, he will create a gathering of men for religious mysteries* <note>original Greek: "Ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις ὅτι ἐτεκτόνει πλοῖον ἐμπορευτικὸν, συναγωγὴν ἀνδρῶν διὰ μυστήρια ποιήσει"</note>. 

This is an interpretation that is indeed as far-fetched as if it came from the "Indies." It is not easy to guess why a **Ship** should suggest the gathering of men for celebrating religious mysteries, unless we imagine a ship represents a **Temple**. Why we should think so, I do not know, except perhaps because they are detached <note>original: "disterminated"</note> and solitary buildings, as temples are—not joined to one another, any more than a temple is joined to other houses. But since it is specifically called a "merchant ship" <note>original Latin: "navis mercatoria"</note>, it may be that the profit a priest gains from sacrifices or offerings to idols is being alluded to. And whether any darker, recessed areas in the ship represent the inner sanctuaries <term>Adyta</term> <note>The most sacred, private inner chambers of a temple</note> of temples, I do not know. Such details I leave to every man's imagination to explore at his leisure.

### Chapter VIII. Of Prophetic Iconisms <note>original: "Iconisms" — symbols or imagery</note>.

*Slain. See Resurrection.*
*Slaughter. See Death.*

10. **Sun, Moon, and Stars.** The *Sun* and *Moon* have either a *Spiritual* meaning or a *Secular* one. Regarding the *Spiritual* meaning of the *Sun*, there is an example where *Christ* is called the *Sun of Righteousness*, as he is by the Prophet *Malachi*. Also, the Apostle says to the *Ephesians*: *Awake, you who sleep, so that Christ may give you light.* The *Moon* may also have a *Spiritual* meaning, assuming it represents the *Mosaic* dispensation <note>The religious system and laws given through Moses</note>. This is a fitting symbol because the Moon is a light, yet a far dimmer light than that of the Gospel; it also alludes to the New Moons and other festivals of the *Jews*, the timing of which depended on that planet. See Mr. *Mede* <note>Joseph Mede (1586–1638), an influential English scholar of biblical prophecy</note> on *Revelation* 12.

<margin>Psalm 119:105.</margin>
To this you may add that, just as the *Law of Moses* is compared to the *Moon*, so may the *Light of the Gospel of Christ* be compared to the *Sun*. For it is plain that the *Word of God* is compared to *Light* from the words of *David*: *Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my path.* And that great *Lamp of the Universe*, the *Sun*, is the clearest light men can walk by. From this, the common expression of the *sunshine of the Gospel* was created by a very reliable analogy; it further assures us that the *Light of the Gospel* may also be one *Spiritual* meaning of the *Sun*.

11. The *Secular* meaning of the *Sun* and *Moon* is when they signify the *Power and Glory* of this world. This can be used either generally and broadly, as in *Jeremiah* 15:9: *Her Sun has gone down while it was yet day*, which the *Targum* <note>An ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> translates as, *Their glory passed from them during their lifetime.* A similar example is in *Amos* 8:9: *I will cause the Sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the Earth in the clear day.* *Vatablus* <note>François Vatable, a 16th-century French biblical scholar</note> interprets this as: *When you are at the highest level of happiness, then I will cast you down from there and make you most unhappy* <note>original Latin: "Cùm eritis in supremo felicitatis gradu, tunc indè vos dejiciam & infelicissimos reddam"</note>. Again, in *Isaiah* 60:20: *Your Sun shall no more go down, neither shall your Moon withdraw herself*; that is to say, you shall have uninterrupted glory and prosperity, as it follows immediately after: *The days of your mourning shall be ended.* In such places, the *Sun* and *Moon* do not refer to a specific rank in a kingdom, but signify the glory and prosperity of that kingdom in a general sense.

12. But in other places, these *Lights* may have a more specific meaning. For just as there is a *Political Universe* as well as a *Natural* one (as I have already shown), which has its *Heaven* as well as its *Earth*, there must be something in the *Political Heaven* that corresponds to the most conspicuous parts of the *Natural* one: the *Sun, Moon, and Stars*. It follows that whoever is the leader in a *Political* world must be its *Sun*. This appears even in the smaller example of a household <note>original: "Body Oeconomical"</note> in *Genesis* 37:9, namely the *Dream of Joseph*, where *the Sun, the Moon, and the eleven Stars bowed down to him.* Interpreting this, *Jacob* said to his son, *What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow down ourselves to you to the Earth?* Therefore, if these symbols have such distinct meanings within a *family*, which is only a household unit, it is much more expected that they would have such meanings within a *Body Politic* <note>A state, kingdom, or organized political society</note>.

12. Achmetes <note>original: "Achmetes" — likely referring to Achmet son of Seirim, an 8th-century author on the interpretation of dreams</note>, according to the traditions of the *Indians, Persians,* and *Egyptians* (chapter 167), states: "The Sun is interpreted invariably as the person of the King, and the Moon as the person of the second-in-command after the King." <note>original: "Ὁ ἥλιος εἰς πρόσωπον βασιλέως κρίνεται ἀπαραλλάκτως, καὶ ἡ σελήνη εἰς πρόσωπον τοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ βασιλέως δευτέρου ἐξουσιαστοῦ."</note> (In the next chapter he calls him "the second or the lesser King" <note>original: "τὸν δεύτερον ἤτοι τὸν ἐλάττονα βασιλέα"</note>). He continues: "Venus represents the person of the Empress <note>original: "Αὐγούστης" — Augusta</note>; and the rest of the great stars represent the great men of the King," <note>original: "ἡ Ἀφροδίτη εἰς πρόσωπον τῆς Αὐγούστης· καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ τῶν μεγίστων ἀστέρων εἰς τοὺς μεγίστους ἄνδρας τοῦ βασιλέως"</note> whom he describes in the following chapter as "the noble and wealthy and those near to the King." <note>original: "τοὺς εὐγενεῖς καὶ πλουσίους καὶ τοὺς ἐγγὺς τοῦ βασιλέως"</note> The sense of all this is, in brief, that in the interpretation of *Visions* or *Dreams*, the *Sun* unchangeably represents the King, the *Moon* the person next in power to him, the *Planet Venus* the *Queen*, and the rest of the larger *Stars* the *Princes* or *Nobles* of the *Kingdom*.

13. This is not to be understood so rigidly that if there were no *Queen*, any third person in dignity might not be represented by Venus. For this *Venus* is also *Lucifer* <note>The "Morning Star"</note>, which the Hebrews call *Helel* <note>original: "הילל"</note>, under which the mighty King of *Babylon* is represented in *Isaiah* 14:12: *How are you fallen from Heaven, O Lucifer, son of the Morning! How are you cut down to the ground, who did weaken the Nations!* This seems to go against the analogy of the *Onirocritics* <note>original: "Onirocriticks" — interpreters of dreams</note>, who say the *Sun* signifies the King "invariably" <note>original: "ἀπαραλλάκτως"</note>. However, they do not say a Star may not also signify him, especially when he is not being compared with his own Nobles and Princes, but with other Kings. After all, a plurality of Suns is unnatural. Therefore, in that case, the parable is to be drawn from the Stars only, and the chief King is the greatest and most glorious *Star*. For this reason, when the *Roman* Empire had two *Caesars* who were not subordinate to one another, they could not well be called *Suns*, but *Stars*, though glorious ones. This agrees well with Mr. *Mede's* <note>Joseph Mede (1586–1638), a famous scholar of prophecy</note> interpretation of that great *Star* that fell at the sound of the third Trumpet, which he views as the end of the *Western Caesarship* <note>original: "Cesariate"</note>.

<margin>* Revelation 2:28.</margin>
<margin>* Chapter 22:16.</margin>
14. But that there is a more mystical sense of *stars* as well may appear in that promise of Christ: *I will give him the Morning-star*. Yet where Christ says, *I am the root of David and the bright Morning-star*, I do not know but that this may be understood in a *Political* sense; for all kingdoms had not then, nor have yet, submitted to him. However, where *Stars* signify *Angels*, that is more Cabbalistical <note>original: "Cabbalistical" — relating to mystical Jewish traditions of interpretation</note>. *Revelation* 1:20: *The seven Stars are the seven Angels of the seven Churches.* They signify the same in *Job* 38:7: *When the Morning Stars sang together, and all the Sons of God shouted for joy.* Those among them who did not keep their positions, but fell into this earthly pollution, may well be called *Fallen Stars*, or "stars fallen from heaven to the earth" <note>original: "ἀστέρες ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ εἰς τὴν γῆν πεπτωκότες"</note>. According to this, *Revelation* 9:1—"and I saw a star fallen from heaven to the earth" <note>original: "καὶ εἶδον ἀστέρα ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ πεπτωκότα εἰς τὴν γῆν"</note>—is nothing but a circumlocution for some fallen Angel or Devil, who afterwards is called the *Angel of the Abyss*, a great officer in the kingdom of darkness. That this is the meaning is plain, because it is written not as "falling" <note>original: "πίπτοντα"</note>, but as "having fallen" <note>original: "πεπτωκότα"</note> in the past perfect tense.

<margin>* Book 2, Hieroglyphics 1.</margin>
It may not be irrelevant also to add what *Horus Apollo says of this Hieroglyphic: "A star among the Egyptians sometimes signifies a god, and sometimes the soul of a man." <note>original: "Ἀστὴρ παρ' Αἰγυπτίοις ποτὲ μὲν θεὸν σημαίνει, ποτὲ δὲ ψυχὴν ἀνθρώπου ἄρρενος"</note>

<header>Chapter 9. Of Prophetic Symbols <note>original: "Iconisms"</note>.</header>

## CHAPTER 9.

1. *Tail*; *Temple*. 2. *Throes*; *Throne of God*. 3. *Thunder*—a symbol <note>original: "Iconism"</note> of Divine assistance for the defeating of the enemies. 4. *Other more mystical meanings of it*. 5. *Time*; *Hours*; *Days*. *That a day signifying a year is a prophetic symbol*. 6. *The association of months and days with the history of the wicked and the righteous, with a conclusion from the latter regarding a flexibility of calculation <note>original: "latitude of compute"</note> in the 1,260 days in the Apocalypse*. 7. *Trees*; *Vintage*; *Water*. 8. *White clothing*; *Wilderness*; *Winds*. 9. *Whore and Whoredom*. 10. *The perfect analogy that idolatry bears to these terms*. 11. *Wine-press*. 12. *That it also signifies spiritual destruction and slaughter*. 13. *Woman and Women*. 14. *Worship*; *World*. 15. *That the prophetic style is so clearly intelligible that the effort to understand prophecies is most unfairly criticized for having any insurmountable difficulties*. 16. *Certain rules to test interpretations of prophecies: which are more reliable and authentic, and which are less so*.

1. Tail. The tail of a beast is that part that follows or comes behind; therefore, the "train" <note>the followers or retinue</note> of a great prince or ruler corresponds to it by analogy. But, it seems to me, the analogy is most exact in serpents of a great length, which have a long train following them. However, it is significant enough in other animals as well, as the dream interpreters <note>original: "Onirocriticks"</note> have noted. Achmet, chapter 152: 
<note>original Greek: "Ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις ὅτι ἐπωχεῖτο τοιούτῳ ἵπῳ (he means τῷ φάρας) μέγα, δασὺ, κὴ μακρὸν οὐραῖον ἔχοντι, εὑρήσει ἀκολόθως τῆς ἐξουσίας αὐτοῦ ἀναλόγως τῷ πλήθει κὴ μήκει τοῦ οὐραῖο."</note> 
> *If anyone dreams he rides on a noble steed (such as the Persians called a Pharas <note>An Arabic/Persian word for horse</note>), having a large tail, thick with hair and long, he shall have a retinue or train of men or officers proportional to the fullness and length of the tail.*
This analogy holds true for everyone from nobles to princes and emperors, or any sovereign power over a state or kingdom. In such cases, their forces and people are their *train* or *tail*.

Temple. Leaving aside the more mystical or moral meanings of "Temple," in the prophetic style it sometimes signifies a people consecrated to God by an outward profession of faith, and thus set apart from other nations, just as consecrated places are set apart from other buildings or plots of ground. *1 Timothy 3:15: That you may know how to behave yourself in the house of God, which is the Church.* And *Revelation 3:12: Him who overcomes I will make a pillar in the temple of my God.* Both Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous Dutch theologian</note> and Dr. Hammond <note>Henry Hammond, an influential English churchman</note> interpret this as the *Visible Church*; Grotius refers it to the church in *Sardis*, and Dr. Hammond to the *Universal <note>original: "Catholick"</note> Church*.

2. Throes of Childbirth. The pains of childbirth are a figure or image of great efforts to bring something to pass, involving much difficulty, pain, and danger. Successfully reaching the goal is the "delivery" of what they were pregnant with, and a "deliverance" from the pain and danger they labored under. There are several examples of this symbol <note>original: "Iconism"</note> in the pro-

prophets. *Jeremiah 30:6, 7. "Why do I see every man with his hands on his loins, like a woman in labor, and all faces turned pale? Alas! for that day is great, so that none is like it; it is even the time of Jacob’s trouble, but he shall be saved out of it."* Also *Isaiah 66:7. "Before she was in labor, she gave birth; before her pain came, she was delivered of a male child."* Interpreters usually understand this as the sudden birth of the Church—that is, the sudden conversion of the Gentiles to it. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch legal scholar and theologian.</note> understands it as the deliverance of Judea by Maccabeus.

**Throne of God**. The *Throne of God* signifies a great and magnificent throne, according to a common Hebrew idiom <note>original: "Hebraism"</note>, where nouns joined with *El*, *Elohim*, or *Jehovah* <note>original Hebrew: אל, אלהים or יהוה; these are various names for God.</note> acquire a sense of excellence, intensity, or greatness. Thus, the "Trees of God," the "Cedars of God," and the "Mountains of God" are great and high trees, cedars, and mountains; the *Fire of God* is an intense *Fire*, and so on. Accordingly, the *Throne of God* is a high and exalted throne, a Royal or Imperial Seat from which the *Political World* is ruled, just as God rules the entire universe from Heaven.

3. **Thunder**. *Thunder* and *Lightning* signify the scattering and dispersal of the forces of *War*. *Isaiah 29:6. "You shall be visited by the Lord of Hosts with thunder and earthquake and great noise, with storm and tempest and the flame of devouring fire."* And *Job 39:25. "He smells the battle from afar, the thunder of the captains and their shouting."* It is very frequently used to describe God’s defeating of the enemies of his Church. *1 Samuel 2:10. "The adversaries of the Lord shall be broken to pieces; out of heaven he shall thunder upon them."* Again, chapter 7, verse 10: *“And as Samuel was offering up the burnt offering, the Philistines drew near to battle against Israel: but the Lord thundered with a great thunder that day upon the Philistines, and struck them until they came to Beth-car.”* Whether this is understood figuratively here or as a literal event in Israel's history <note>original: "Israelism"</note>, it serves as an image or symbol of the Church's deliverance from her enemies for all posterity. David also describes his deliverance from his enemies in this manner in *Psalm 18: "The Lord thundered in the heavens, and the Highest gave his voice, hailstones and coals of fire. Yes, he sent out his arrows and scattered them, and he shot out lightnings and defeated them."*

4. But there is also another more *mystical* meaning of *Thunder*: *Prophecy* or *Revelation from God* is signified by it, by way of allusion to the "Daughter of a Voice" <note>original Hebrew/Latin: בת קול / Filia vocis</note>, which is one kind of prophecy. Such was the voice from Heaven testifying about our Savior Christ in *Matthew 3:17*, as well as in *John 12:28*, where the people standing by said, *“It thundered.”* See the scholar Drusius on that passage. Besides this, *Thunder* inherently signifies *Prophecy*, as one is the Voice of Heaven and called the voice of God, and the other is an oracle from God.

<margin>* John 12:28, 29.</margin>

There is yet another sense that *Thunder* may be capable of: namely, some special and notable proclamation <note>original: "Promulgation"</note> of the Gospel to a people who have not yet heard it, consented to it, or rightly believed it. This is an allusion to the Law given to the Israelites in *Thunder* and *Lightning*—not to mention it also respects the way God witnessed from the clouds to his Son Christ, declaring him with a voice of thunder...
