# Chapter XIV. and Thirteenth Chapters of the Apocalypse.

9. For this expression does not concern itself at all with any such claim, but only considers the succession and *series* of time in which this *Idolatrous Empire* is included. It has given a name to the *Beast* based on its last succession—not in reference to *St. John’s* own time, but in reference to the first *series* of time under which the *Idolatrous Empire* *was to be*, then of the time it *was not to be*, and lastly of that *series* of succession it *was to be again*, and then *finally to perish*. This *Character* [or identifying mark] from these *series* of times compared with one another could have been made in *Daniel’s* time just as well as in *St. John’s*. These periods have no necessary connection or link <term>ligation</term> <note>original: "ligation"; a binding or connection.</note> with the time of the Prophet himself, but only with one another. For as far as is expressed in this verse, the meaning refers only to a sequence of existence, non-existence, and re-existence. These changes are indeed tied to one another, but they are not yet fixed to the Prophet’s time or anyone else’s time.

Although I have taken such care to prove this point, it is an idea so easy to accept that *Alcazar* <note>Ludovicus ab Alcasar (1554–1613) was a Spanish Jesuit theologian who wrote a significant commentary on the Book of Revelation using a "preterist" approach, which views the prophecies as having already been fulfilled in the early centuries of the Church.</note> in his *Exposition* assumes it without asking permission or giving any explanation. For he understands the revived or re-existing *Beast* to be the persecuting Empire under *Julian* the *Apostate* <note>Emperor Julian (reigned 361–363 AD), known as "the Apostate" because he rejected Christianity and attempted to restore traditional Roman paganism.</note>, whom he identifies as the eighth King. By acknowledging that the *Visions* were shown to *John* in *Domitian’s* <note>Emperor Domitian (reigned 81–96 AD) was traditionally considered a fierce persecutor of Christians; John was said to have been exiled to Patmos during his reign.</note> time, when the *Roman Empire* was actually persecuting Christians, he clearly implies that the phrase [*The Beast which you saw, was, and is not*] is not to be understood as referring to existence or non-existence at the exact time of the Vision. (After all, it would have been false to say the *Beast* "is not" during *Domitian’s* time). Instead, it refers only to the changes and successions of the *Condition* of the Empire. "Therefore," he says, "since the persecutions were to be interrupted, this very interruption is what the Angel signifies by repeating three times in the seventeenth chapter, when he says of the Beast: 'He was and is not,' 'He was and is not'; which is the same as if he said, 'Now he is, and now he is not.'" <note>original: "Cùm igitur... persecutiones interrumpende forent, hâc ipsâ interruptione significatur quod Angelus ter repetit capite decimo septimo, dum ait de Bestia, Fuit & non est, Erat & non est; Quod idem est ac si diceret, Modò est & modò non est."</note> This phrase signifies no set time of existence or non-existence, but only the cycle of them.

This commentary is on the seventeenth chapter; he speaks to the same purpose regarding the thirteenth, where he asserts that by the *Beast that was, and is not*, the Angel only suggests that there would be an *Intermission* [a pause] of persecution. I might also add that our Protestant commentators <note>original: "Expositours"</note> generally follow the same assumption, as *Paraeus* <note>David Paraeus (1548–1622) was a prominent German Reformed theologian and professor at Heidelberg.</note> has noted. But this point, I hope, is abundantly cleared.

10. And what has been said of this first description of the *Beast*—*Was, is not, and shall ascend out of the bottomless pit and go into destruction*—is also to be understood of the second: *Was, is not, and yet is*. Namely, that it is the *Name, Nature, or Character* of the *Beast*, not any claim concerning his present existence or non-existence. For regarding that Idolatrous Empire which is pointed out <term>indigitated</term> <note>original: "indigitated"; from the Latin 'indigitare', to point out or indicate.</note> here, it could not be properly said when *St. John* wrote that it "was, but is not," because at that time it still continued in an uninterrupted existence. Nor could it be said of it, *Is not, and yet is*, for at that time it was not the *Image* of the *Pagan Idolatrous Empire*, but that very Empire itself. And it is remarkable that this *Beast* is described as being destined to come hereafter out of the bottomless pit, and that the world shall marvel at him when he appears again upon the stage, beholding the *Beast that was*,

<meta>This page continues the logical and linguistic analysis of the phrase describing the Beast in Revelation 17:8. The author argues that the specific wording "is not, and yet is" serves as a riddle or paradox designed to explain how the Roman Empire's idolatry would vanish and then return in a modified form.</meta>

and is not, and yet is. Therefore, since neither "was" nor "is not" have any connection or binding <term>ligation</term> <note>original: "ligation"; a binding or connection.</note> with the era of St. John—given that it is clear that "is" does not—the prophecy is not about a beast that existed then, but one yet to come. It seems very unlikely to me that the title or name of the Beast would be repeated so quickly in the same verse with such a slight variation, unless it were done intentionally as a key to the first title's meaning, guiding the thoughtful reader toward the interpretation I have proposed. But to read "and shall be" <note>original Greek: "kai parestai"</note> instead of "and yet is" <note>original Greek: "kaiper estin"</note> would make the prophecy a dull and pointless repetition <term>tautology</term> <note>original: "tautologie"</note> and destroy a specific clue pointing to its true meaning. But we proceed.

11. The phrase "is not, and yet is" can only be understood by looking closely at the logical laws of contradiction. This is the "mysterious dress" used here to provoke wonder <note>original: "amusement"; in this context, it means to be puzzled or have one's attention captured by a riddle.</note>; without this element of paradox, it would lack both meaning and literary grace. Therefore, the same thing must be both claimed and denied about the same subject in different ways. Therefore, just as the phrase "was, and is not" naturally means he is no longer what he used to be—and as "is not" must be understood to the same degree as "was" (for example, if "was" refers to his entire existence, then "is not" must mean he has ceased to exist entirely; but if "was" only refers to a specific condition or quality of his existence, then "is not" only removes that specific part and nothing more)—likewise, "is not, and yet is" must be understood in equal measure. The thing being affirmed and denied must be the same: either his entire existence must be both claimed and denied, or the same specific condition.

12. The first option (total existence and non-existence at once) cannot be the case, as it would be a literal contradiction and a blatant falsehood. In the second option (the condition), if the condition were exactly the same, it would be just as impossible and irreconcilable a contradiction. For example, imagine a man who is King, is deposed for a time, and then is restored to his throne with as much power as ever. It would be a total contradiction and a massive lie to say "he is not King" at the same time as saying "he is King." 

This exposes the weakness of Hugo Grotius's <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a influential Dutch legal scholar and theologian who argued that many biblical prophecies referred to historical figures of the early Roman Empire rather than future events.</note> interpretation. He claims that Emperor Domitian is the Beast that "is not, and yet is." But you could never say of Domitian while he was Emperor that he was *not* Emperor, nor could you say he *was* Emperor during a time he was not. Being Emperor was exactly the same condition both times he held the title (if indeed he held it twice). Grotius has no way out of this logical trap except by changing the text to read "and shall be" <note>original Greek: "kai parestai"</note>.

<margin>Parallel 2. Argument 5.</margin>
However, when this sameness is slightly imperfect and leans more toward resemblance than exact identity, then this riddle becomes appropriate. Although the riddle <term>enigma</term> <note>original: "Ænigma"</note> seems to baffle a person with a contradiction, it actually reveals a truth. This is clear in my interpretation of the Beast that "is not, and yet is": the ancient, pagan, idolatrous Roman Empire *is not* (it ended), and yet it *is* (it returned in a new form). Both parts are true. In terms of the style of its idolatry, it is the same Beast, but in terms of the specific figures being worshipped, it is not the same. Therefore, as I noted before, it is also called the "Image of the Beast."

13. Therefore, this second title of the Beast—"Was, and is not, and yet is"—

# Chapter 13 and the Thirteenth Chapters of the Apocalypse

...is] being thus plainly discovered not to signify mere existence, but rather a condition and the order of succession. This provides further assurance that our interpretation of the former title of the Beast is also true. The omission of an insertion or subjunction such as *“This is his Name or Property,”* or something similar, is a mere prophetic <term>ellipsis</term> <note>original: "Ellipsis"; a grammatical device where words are omitted but understood from context.</note> and a deliberate device for concealment. This is justifiable on two grounds: either because it was spoken in a state of rapture and ecstasy, and therefore expressed elliptically; or else because there are examples of such an ellipsis in other places of Scripture regarding the very same subject, such as in Revelation 1 and Exodus 3.

But to argue that in those other passages they do not cause the same obscurity or confusion as they do here is to acknowledge exactly what I am contending for: that the ellipsis is used here intentionally for concealment. However, this concealment is commendable and not at all impossible to overcome, because this ellipsis is not without scriptural precedent. It was perhaps made with some allusion to those very texts where the Name of God is "I am that I am" <margin>Exodus 3:14.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: "Eheyeh asher eheyeh"</note> (translated in Latin as *“I will be who I will be”* <note>original: "Ero qui ero"</note>) and "He who is, and who was, and who is to come" <note>original Greek: "ho on kai ho en kai ho erchomenos"</note>. The scholars Zegerus and Cornelius à Lapide compare these with this name of the Beast to show the great difference between them. The latter concludes that the reign of the wicked is fitly expressed by "Was, and is not" <note>original Latin: "Erat, & non est"</note>; but the Name of God—who alone possesses immortality and whose Kingdom is a Kingdom for all ages—is expressed by "He who is, and who was, and who is to come" <note>original Latin: "Qui est, & qui erat, & qui venturus est"</note>. He says much more to that purpose in comparing this Name of God with the Name of the Beast, for that is what he also calls this description of him:

-> “Just as God's Name is Jehovah, that is, ‘He who is’; so the Beast's Name is ‘He who is not.’ Second, God's Name is ‘He who was and is’; the Beast's is ‘He who was and is not.’ Third, God's Name is ‘He was and will be’; the Beast's is ‘He will be no more.’” <-

So says Cornelius. The last of these points exactly matches our understanding of the phrase "goes into perdition" <note>original Greek: "eis apōleian hypagei"</note>. But we have been excessively thorough and diligent in clearing up a point which we had already fully demonstrated by proving that this Beast—whose <margin>Chapter 11, Sections 13, 14, etc.</margin> name, title, or description (call it what you will) is [*Was, and is not,*] etc.—is the **Roman Empire** after it had formally accepted Christianity and then degenerated into a kind of "After-Paganism" <note>The author uses this term to describe a state where Christian worship becomes corrupted by practices that resemble old Pagan idolatry.</note>.

14. My reason for interpreting the Beast’s "re-existence" as the Empire turning idolatrous, rather than it being molded into some entirely new political government (as many other commentators do), is because this is more consistent with my third rule of interpreting prophecies. Furthermore, in a political sense, the Empire cannot be said to have ever yet ceased to be; there has never been a time since its beginning when a person could truly say, "*It is not*." And lastly, the "Whore" or the "Two-horned Beast" will not be contemporary with the Beast that *was, and is not, and yet is*, unless this Beast’s beginning starts on the terms I have declared—namely, that the "rising again" of the Beast was the Empire's relapse into a kind of Paganism and idolatry.

15. But we shall now continue identifying these parallels: "*Was, and is not, and shall ascend out of the bottomless pit.*" That is to say, *it was* during that period of time before the Dragon fought with Michael and was slain, but it ceased to be upon that defeat. And therefore it is said in the Thirteenth Chapter that the *Dragon gave him his power*; that is, he succeeded as heir to the powers of the Dragon. The Dragon’s forces (for that is what "powers" <note>original Greek: "dynameis"</note> signifies here, as in the phrase "Lord of Hosts" <note>original: "Kyrios dynameōn"</note>) were left to his conduct and management.

# His Joint-Exposition of the Seventeenth Book I.

<margin>
Parallelism 2, Agreement 3.
</margin>
This restoration of the Beast that had the deadly wound—returning to life by means of the Dragon's assistance and the specific weapons of his warfare, such as idols, images, and false miracles—corresponds very closely to his re-ascending here out of the *bottomless pit*. For the word **abyss** <note>original Greek: "abyssos"</note> may signify the *Sea*, or *Abolition*, or *Evanescence* <note>original: "Evanescence"; meaning the state of fading away or disappearing.</note>. From this, the truth of the third agreement of our second parallelism is made clear.

<margin>
Parallelism 2, Agreement 6.
</margin>
16. But if we understand the **abyss** <note>original: "abyssos"</note> to signify the *Sea*, as it usually does (and as I believe it does here in reference to the Empire itself), this corresponds to the Seven-headed Beast’s rising out of the *Sea* in Chapter 13, verse 1. This is the sixth agreement of our second parallelism.

Parallelism 2, Agreement 7.
</margin>
17. *And go into perdition.* Just as it is said in Chapter 13, verse 10: *He that leads into captivity, must go into captivity; he that kills with the sword, must be killed with the sword.* This is the seventh agreement of our second parallelism.

<margin>
Parallelism 2, Agreement 8.
</margin>
18. *And those who dwell on the earth shall wonder, whose names were not written in the book of life.* This matches what we read in Chapter 13, verse 3: *And all the world wondered after the Beast*; and verse 8: *And all that dwell upon the earth shall worship him, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb, etc.* This is the eighth agreement of our second parallelism.

19. *When they behold the Beast that was, and is not.* He is said here—or rather at the beginning of this verse—*not to be*, which corresponds to him being described as slain in Chapter 13, verse 3: *And I saw one of his heads as if it were wounded to death*; so says the English translation. But the Greek has it, **as if slain even to death** <note>original Greek: "hōs esphagmenēn eis thanaton"; translated into Latin as "cæsa ad mortem"</note>. The word **as** <note>original Greek: "hōs"</note>, which we render as "as it were," does not imply that his head was not truly slain and struck with such a fatal blow that it died. For besides the fact that this wound is called **a deadly wound** <note>original Greek: "plēgē tou thanatou"</note> more than once, it is evident that the particle "as" does not always weaken or lessen the meaning. This appears in Chapter 5, verse 6, where we find **a Lamb standing as if it had been slain** <note>original Greek: "arnion estēkos hōs esphagmenon"</note>; that Lamb, despite the phrasing, was really and truly slain. Therefore, the word "as" refers to the symbolic nature of the vision, not to any incompleteness of the death or slaughter represented. Therefore, this Head was really slain and killed, which implies the Body was dead also, and that the Beast ceased to be—just as it is said here that *he is not*. I have already noted this to be the third agreement of our second parallelism.

Parallelism 2, Agreement 3.
</margin>

# Chapter 14 and the Thirteenth Chapters of the Apocalypse.

Thirteenth; and there can be no objection against the overly-hidden sense in this notable *omission* <note>original: "Ellipsis"</note>, because although the joint <note>original: "commissure"</note> is as invisible as one in fine steel-work, the obvious agreements of this second parallelism between the Seven-headed Beast in this chapter and the Thirteenth Chapter would certainly reveal the meaning to the perceptive and informed reader.

<margin>Parallelism 2, Agreement 5.</margin>
20. *Is not, and yet is.* Regarding this phrase, I have already shown that it makes no sense unless we understand it not as a perfect identity, but rather as a resemblance or similarity. This resemblance, for the sake of elegance, is given the title of "identity," as if something very similar were exactly the same thing. In this way, he who came in the spirit of *Elijah* was called *Elijah*; and someone who was remarkably *Epicurean* or *Platonic* might be called "Epicurus reborn" or "Plato reborn," as if the one were really Epicurus and the other Plato. It is also a common expression to say *that a man will never die as long as his son—one who is exactly like him—is alive*. This acknowledges that the father may be dead and alive at once: dead in his own person, but alive in that living image of himself, his surviving son. *Although Servius Sulpicius could leave no clearer monument than a son who was the image of his own character, constancy, piety, and talent.* <note>original: "Quanquam nullum monumentum clarius Servius Sulpitius relinquere potuit quàm effigiem morum suorum, constantiæ, pietatis, ingenii, filium."</note>

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 30:4.</margin>
Regarding such a son as this, there is a saying by the *author of Sirach* <note>original: "Siracides"; referring to Ben Sira, the author of the deuterocanonical Book of Sirach or Ecclesiasticus.</note>: *Though his father dies, yet he is as though he were not dead; for he has left one behind him that is like him.*

So then, just as Servius Sulpicius may be said to be dead and alive at once—dead in his own person, but alive in his son who is so perfect a likeness of him—so it may be said of the Beast, that he *is not*, and *yet is*. This is because he is not really that ancient Pagan Empire (which was the Beast killed by the introduction of pure Christianity); yet he *is*, in that he is revived by the Empire becoming once again paganly idolatrous, and so vividly representing its state during the time of the Dragon. *For a thing is said to exist when its model, image, type, or figure exists.* <note>original: "Res enim dicitur existere cùm ejus Exemplar, Imago, Typus, aut Figura existit." The quote is attributed to Cornelius à Lapide, a 17th-century Jesuit biblical commentator.</note> How vivid an image or resemblance this degenerate Empire is to the one under the Dragon, I could display here in detail, but I will instead defer it to the following chapters. In the meantime, this should suffice in general to prove the fifth agreement of our second parallelism.

**Verse 9. AND here is the mind that has wisdom,** <note>original: "ὧδε ὁ νοῦς ὁ ἔχων σοφίαν"</note>

That ancient *Sophia*, which *Siracides* would have found similar to *Tsaphah*, had a double sense: one according to external appearance, and the other according to an inward truth. Therefore, just as "here is wisdom" <note>original: "ὧδε ἡ σοφία"</note> signifies "here is such a kind of hidden wisdom as I have described," so "here is the mind that has wisdom" <note>original: "ὧδε ὁ νοῦς ὁ ἔχων σοφίαν"</note> signifies "here is a meaning that implies a special example of the ancient *Sophia*," which used to hide great and important truths under outward <term>Hieroglyphics</term> and Types.

# Chapter 14 and the Thirteenth Chapter of the Apocalypse. 297

That Old *Rome* is indicated here by these seven hills, interpreters generally agree; that city being so famously noted for them by both historians and poets. This is seen in the works of *Dionysius of Halicarnassus*, *Pliny*, *Plutarch*, as well as *Varro*, *Tertullian*, and others. Among poets, it is mentioned by *Virgil*, *Horace*, *Ovid*, *Claudian*, and the *Sibylline Oracles*. Since these references are so well known and obvious in the works of commentators, I think it is unnecessary to provide any specific examples.

<margin>Part 2, Chapter 5.</margin>
But there are those who take pleasure in finding records of *Constantinople* also being noted for its seven hills. Bishop *Montagu* does this in his *Appeal to Caesar* <note>original: "Appello Cæsarem"</note>; where he says this city is called "the city of seven hills" <note>original: "πόλις ἑπτάλοφος"</note> by *Nicetas*, the "City of Seven Hills" <note>original: "Urbs Septicollis"</note> by *Paulus Diaconus*, and that it is acknowledged as such by *Janus Douza* and by Mr. *Richard Knolles* in his *Turkish History*. To this, I will add what I find in the *Theater of Cities* <note>original: "Theatrum Urbium"</note>, that *Scholarius*, the Patriarch of *Constantinople*, in his *Explanation of the Prophecy concerning the destruction of the Turkish Kingdom* <note>original: "Enarratio Vaticinii de Turcici Regni interitu"</note>, titles the city "seven-hilled" <note>original: "ἑπτάλοφος"</note>. *Dilichius*, also in his description of the city, not only mentions the seven hills but also describes the magnificent structures that stand upon them. And lastly, *Ludovicus Gotofredus* says, speaking of this city, "Its walls are of incredible height, encompassing seven hills within their circuit" <note>original: "Muri ejus sunt incredibilis altitudinis, complectentes ambitu suo septem Colles"</note>.

So, although there is no mention of the *Seven Hills* of *Byzantium* or *Constantinople* as ancient or early as those of *Rome*, it may be reasonably assumed that because of the Emperor’s wish to have the city called *New Rome*, they would also "find" seven hills in it (in imitation of the old Imperial City), whether there were exactly seven or not. I mean that even if there were more than *seven*, or if fewer, they took the opportunity to imagine one and the same hill as being more than one due to some slight unevenness in the terrain. Yet I cannot help but believe there is a reasonable basis for this title; and since it has been established among the writers of its history, I will not deny that it may also be called the *City of Seven Hills* <note>original: "Urbs Septicollis"</note>. This will not be an inconvenience to our interpretation, but rather a further confirmation of our explanation of the *Two Horns* of the Beast, which I understand to be the two Imperial Patriarchates: the *Roman* and the *Constantinopolitan*. This shows the extent of that *false-prophetic* Beast—that it reached over the whole Empire, the *Eastern* <note>original: "Oriental"</note> as well as the *Western* <note>original: "Occidental"</note>.

<margin>Parallel 1, Agreement 8.</margin>

According to this sense, the phrase "The seven heads are seven mountains" <note>original: "Αἱ ἑπτὰ κεφαλαὶ ὄρη εἰσὶν ἑπτά"</note> would be rendered "The seven heads are two sets of seven mountains" <note>original: "Septem capita septeni sunt montes"</note>, meaning the seven heads signify the two groups of seven mountains—one at *Rome*, the other at *Constantinople*. From this, the eighth agreement of our first parallelism is clarified.

This ancient *Sophia*, which Sirach found to be like the word "to hide," had a double sense: one based on external appearance, the other based on inward truth. Therefore, just as "here is wisdom" signifies "here is the kind of hidden wisdom I have described," so "here is the mind that has wisdom" signifies "here is a meaning that provides a special example of ancient wisdom," which used to hide great and important truths under outward symbols <note>original: "Hieroglyphicks"</note> and types.

### Chap. XIV. and Thirteenth Chapters of the Apocalypse. 297

That *Old Rome* is pointed out <note>original: "indigitated"</note> here by these seven hills, interpreters generally agree; that city being so famously noted for them by both historians and poets. This is seen in the works of *Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Pliny, Plutarch*, as well as *Varro, Tertullian*, and others. Among poets, it is mentioned by *Virgil, Horace, Ovid, Claudian*, and the *Sibylls* <note>The Sibylline Oracles: a collection of oracular utterances written in Greek hexameters ascribed to the Sibyls, prophetesses who uttered divine revelations</note>. Since these references are so well known and obvious in commentaries, I think it is unnecessary to provide any specific examples.

<margin>Part 2, Chapter 5.</margin>
However, there are those who take pleasure in finding records of *Constantinople* also being noted for her seven hills. Bishop *Mountague* does this in his *Appello Caesarem* <note>original: "I Appeal to Caesar"</note>, where he says this city is called a *seven-hilled city* <note>original Greek: "πόλις ἑπτάλοφος"</note> by *Nicetas*, a *seven-hilled city* <note>original Latin: "Urbs Septicollis"</note> by *Paulus Diaconus*, and that this is acknowledged by *Janus Douza* and by Mr. *Richard Knolls* in his *Turkish History*. To which I will add what I find in the *Theatrum Urbium* <note>Theater of Cities</note>: that *Scholarius*, Patriarch of *Constantinople*, in his *Explanation of the Prophecy concerning the downfall of the Turkish Kingdom* <note>original Latin: "Enarratio Vaticinii de Turcici Regni interitu"</note>, styles the city *seven-hilled* <note>original Greek: "ἑπτάλοφος"</note>. *Dilichius*, in his description of the city, not only mentions the seven hills but also describes the magnificent structures that stand upon them. And lastly, *Ludovicus Gotofredus* says, speaking of this city: *Its walls are of incredible height, surrounding seven hills in their circuit* <note>original Latin: "Muri ejus sunt incredibilis altitudinis, complectentes ambitu suo septem Colles"</note>.

So, although there is not such an ancient or early mention of the Seven Hills of *Byzantium* (or *Constantinople*) as there is of those of *Rome*, it may be probably conceived that—at the Emperor's pleasure to have the city called *New Rome*—they would also find seven hills in it in emulation of the old Imperial City. This would be true whether there were exactly seven or not; I mean, though there might be more than *seven*, or if fewer, they might take the occasion to imagine one and the same hill (due to some small unevenness) to be more than one. Yet, I cannot well doubt that there is a tolerable ground for this title. Since it has been accepted by the writers of her history, I will not deny that she may also be considered a *seven-hilled city* <note>original Latin: "Urbs Septicollis"</note>. This will be no inconvenience to our interpretation, but a further confirmation of our exposition of the *Two Horns* of the Beast, which I conceive to be the two Imperial Patriarchates <note>The primary jurisdictions of the Christian church in the Roman Empire: the Roman (Western) and the Constantinopolitan (Eastern)</note>: the *Roman* and the *Constantinopolitan*. This shows the extent of that *false-prophetic Beast*—that it reached over the whole Empire, both *Oriental* <note>Eastern</note> and *Occidental* <note>Western</note>.

# His Joint-Exposition of the Seventeenth Book I.

The succession of each type of ruler is grouped by a common rhetorical device where many are treated as one <note>original: "Henopaia," likely referring to the Greek *henopoeia*, a figure of speech where multiple things are spoken of as a single unit</note>. I believe it is demonstrable by reason that seven different sorts of governors may be called *Seven Heads* just as easily as seven individual persons. This is because there is a greater difference between types of government than between individuals of the same type. 

Therefore, I wonder why *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note> should call the idea of seven forms of government (taken concretely, as everyone does) "monstrous talk" <note>original Greek: "τερατολογία"</note>. If there is such a sevenfold difference in the supreme powers throughout the succession of an empire, and if that empire is considered as a "Beast," it will be *by that very fact* <note>original Latin: "ipso facto"</note> seven-headed whether we like it or not. So far from being monstrous talk, it is a natural and inevitable truth.

2. Now, the division of the succession of the supreme powers of the Empire is naturally made this way: this power was held either by *many* or by *one*. It was held by *many* in the cases of the *Consuls*, the *Military Tribunes* <note>original: "Tribuni Militum"</note>, and the *Decemvirs* <note>original: "Decemviri"; a ten-man commission in ancient Rome</note>. It was held by *one* in the cases of the *Kings*, *Dictators*, and *Emperors*. I will further divide these *Emperors* into three categories: *Pagan*, *Christian*, and *Pagano-Christian* <note>Referring to a period the author views as a corrupt or "paganized" form of Christianity</note>. So, the entire line of succession for these supreme powers is divided first into two equal parts (many or one), and then each of those two is subdivided into three, and then one part of the second subdivision is divided into three again. Thus, the whole line naturally falls into eight parts, which agrees with both the history of events and the declaration of the prophecy.

For there are plainly numbered *Eight Kings*, though there are only *Seven Heads* of the Beast. This is because under the *Christian Emperors*, the Empire was not a "Beast," and therefore there could be no "Head" of a beast at that time.

3. Nor do I know of any tolerable solution to this riddle of *Eight Kings* and yet only *Seven Heads* other than this. The short duration of the *Christian succession* cannot be the reason they are excluded from the number of the "Heads," since the rule of the *Decemvirs* was over forty times shorter. Therefore, it is not the length of time, but because the Empire during their succession was not a Beast; they were neither fit to be, nor actually were, the "Heads" of one. Instead, they were only Heads or Kings of the undegenerated Empire that had not yet returned to paganism. This was, therefore, the time of the "Death of the Beast," when he "was not," and therefore he was to have no Head, nor could he have any.

4. Nor is there the least ground for any petty objection <note>original: "Cavil"</note> against our last subdivision, which divides *Emperors* into *Pagan*, *purely Christian*, and *Pagano-Christian*. One might argue there is not a fundamental enough cause for this last distribution, but on the contrary, there is such a strong opposition between the first two members (Pagan and Christian) that one pushes out the other; the "seventh King" is the one who wounds and kills the "sixth Head." 

Furthermore, because a religion becomes the law of an empire when it is made the official state religion, it can be rationally understood that there is a political difference between a *Christian* and a *Pagan Emperor*. Lastly, however one views it, it is plain to all men that there is a very eminent and notorious difference between a *Christian* and a *Pagan Emperor*. This difference is of more concern to the Church of God than any political distinction of government. We may be assured that God takes the most notice of that which most concerns His Church; therefore, He would be just as likely to distinguish the succession of supreme governors by this religious difference as by any other.

# Chap. XIV. and Thirteenth Chapters of the Apocalypse.

5. In fact, I think I may safely add that it is likely that once the Angel reached the division of the Heads (or rather Kings) into *Christian* and *Pagano-Christian* <note>The author uses "Pagano-Christian" to describe what he views as a corrupt or "paganized" form of Christianity, likely referring to the Roman Catholic Church of his time.</note>, he completely ignored the political differences in forms of government within the Empire. That concept was now irrelevant to his purpose, and he satisfied himself solely with distinguishing them based on religion. But until that point, he numbered them according to their distinct political forms, because they all agreed in pure paganism up to that time. 

So, the meaning of "[*The Beast that was, and is not; his Head is the eighth King*]" <note>Quoting Revelation 17:11</note> seems to be this: that the supreme power—regardless of its political structure or title—which rules over the revived Beast (that is, over the Empire as it returns to idolatry) is considered the Eighth King or the last Head of the Beast. This succession, wherever you find it, whether it be the Pope or the Emperor, is what the Vision focuses on, rather than pointless distinctions and technicalities. This assumption aligns with our third Rule for interpreting prophecy.

The argument for the distinction between the first two parts of my last subdivision is so easily applied to the last part compared to the second—that is, comparing the *Pagano-Christian* to the *Christian*—that I only need to mention it and move on. 

I will delay the proof of my first subdivision (into *Consuls, Military Tribunes, Decemvirs, Kings, Dictators, and Emperors or Caesars*) until after I have finished my *Joint-Exposition* <note>Joint-Exposition: A combined or systematic explanation of these prophetic texts.</note>.

6. ***Five have fallen, one is.*** <note>Quoting Revelation 17:10</note> The five that had fallen by St. *John’s* time were the Kings, Consuls, *Decemvirs* <note>Decemviri: A ten-man commission in ancient Rome.</note>, Dictators, and *Military Tribunes*. The "one that then was" refers to the continuous succession of the *Pagan Caesars*.

And here it is appropriate to note that St. *John* so plainly asserts that one of the seven Heads of the Beast was alive and not yet slain when he had this Vision. This means the Beast itself was still alive and in existence; therefore, the Beast had not yet reached the state of "[*was, and is not.*]" This is a proof as certain as mathematics that the phrase "[*was, and is not*]" does not signify a fixed or determined state of existence or non-existence, but only the order in which they appear, as I have explained. Consequently, there is an *ellipsis* <note>original: "Ellipsis"; a grammatical omission where words are understood but not stated for brevity.</note> as I suggested in the phrase "[*The Beast that you saw, was, and is not*]" etc. Our interpretation is demonstrably evident in every point. But I will proceed.

7. ***And the other has not yet come.*** <note>original Greek: Ὁ ἄλλος οὔπω ἦλθεν</note> He does not say "the seventh has not yet come" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἕβδομος οὔπω ἦλθεν</note>, but "*the other*." This is because this *Seventh* head is not properly in the same line as his predecessors, since they were all Pagans. He is called "*the other*" because of the extreme difference or distinction he has from those who went before him, as if it were a different species entirely. As *Porphyry* <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> defined it: "Every difference added to a thing makes it different, but while some differences make it different in a general or common way, those that are most specific make it *other*." <note>original Greek: Ὅτι πᾶσα διαφορὰ προσγινομένη τινὶ ἕτερον ποιεῖ, ἀλλ' αἱ μὲν κοινῶς τε καὶ ἰδίως ἀλλοῖον ποιοῦσιν, αἱ δ' ἰδιαίτατα, ἄλλο</note> He then adds: "Those differences that make a thing *other* in every respect are called *Specific differences*." <note>original Greek: αἱ μὲν ἐν πᾶσιν ἄλλο, εἰδοποιοὶ κέκληνται</note> These "Specific Differences" are the greatest differences possible. This provides a solid basis for our last subdivision.

2. *Even he is the Eighth*: So our English translation says, but this sense is not as balanced or adequate as it could be. The Greek text says, "And he himself is the eighth, and is of the seven" <note>original: "καὶ αὐτὸς ὄγδοός ἐστι, καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἑπτά ἐστί"</note>, which is most easily and naturally rendered in Latin as, "And that very one is the eighth, and yet is from the seven" <note>original: "Et ipsissimus ille octavus est, & tamen è septem"</note>, or more briefly, "And he is the eighth, and of the seven" <note>original: "Et ipse octavus est, & de septem"</note>. This means that this Beast that *was, and is not*—specifically, his Head (for this is clearly a <term>synecdoche</term> <note>a figure of speech where a part, like the "Head," represents the whole Beast</note>)—is both the *Eighth King* and also one of the *Seven*. Specifically, he is one of those seven kings understood as the "Heads of Blasphemy" or Idolatrous Heads.

It is remarkable with what caution and precision things are written down in this holy and mysterious Book of Revelation. For first, when the author came to the *Sixth Head*, he did not say "the sixth is," but rather "one is," to prepare for counting the next one under the name of "the other" <note>original: "ἄλλος"</note>. This is a very significant and necessary expression, as I have already noted, to emphasize how his nature was completely different from all who came before him; he was not properly part of that same idolatrous line. For what commonality or connection did the pure Christian *Caesars* have with the purely Pagan ones?

But now, when he comes to this last Head—which for clarity I must call *Pagano-Christian* (since the entire Empire from head to foot is assumed to be such)—the author thinks it right to call this king the *Eighth*. This is because he is derived from a double line: he succeeds all the predecessors before him, both Christian and Pagan. Therefore, by counting "the other" <note>original: "ὁ ἄλλος"</note> (the Christian line) in the succession from which he also descends, he is rightly called the Eighth King. And yet, considering that he is a paganizing or idol-worshipping head just like the previous ones, he is also said to be *one of the Seven*. Specifically, he is one of those seven kings represented by the *seven* blasphemous heads of the Beast, of which there were seven and no more. In my view, this is the easiest and most certain interpretation that anyone could desire for any passage of Scripture.

3. We should not doubt this interpretation because of the apparent awkwardness of that *synecdoche*, where the whole Beast stands for a part (the *Head*). This way of speaking is not only justified by this figure of speech but is also confirmed by biblical examples. As in Daniel 2:38: *You are this Head of Gold*. And yet, *this Head of Gold* was a symbol for the entire Kingdom of *Babylon*. Therefore, it is plain that the entire *Head of Gold* represents a chief part of that kingdom. Also, in Daniel 4:20, 22: *The tree which you saw, which grew and was strong, etc. It is you, O King, who have grown and become strong, etc.* Even though that tree was a symbol of his entire kingdom and its vast dominion, the King is again called the *Tree*, when in fact he was only a part of it—the *root*. As it is said, "The king is the foundation of the people" <note>original: "βασιλεὺς is said to be βάσις λαοῦ"</note>, and the chopping down of the tree to the ground was a figure representing his removal from the kingdom for a time. Besides all this, the passage makes no sense without this *synecdoche*; for how can any single Head truly and properly be the entire Beast?

4. Therefore, the *Eighth King* refers to the succession of Christian *Caesars* during the time when the Empire returns to pagan practices—that is, when it practices idolatry within Christianity. Although their succession is long and there may be more than one person ruling at a time in some ages, they are represented as a single king through <term>henopoeia</term> <note>a rhetorical device where multiple things are spoken of as one unit</note>. For the division into *seven*...

# His Joint-Exposition of the Seventeenth Book, Part I.

This distinction was not determined by individuals, but by differences in kind, as I have declared above. Therefore, the fact that Eastern and Western Emperors reigned at the same time in the Empire does not cause any problems <note>original: "breaks no squares"</note> in this prophetic method of calculation. This system does not count individuals, but rather categories and successions organized into a single individual shape or appearance. This is the reason why there is no mention of a succession of specific persons, nor an enumeration of years, in this Book of Revelation <note>original: "Apocalyps"</note>, even though it treats things that fill a period of almost two thousand years, even on this side of the Millennium <note>the thousand-year reign of Christ mentioned in Revelation 20</note>.

<margin>Paragraph 2. Agreement 9.</margin>
5. **And is of the Seven.** This also suggests that the Seven Heads of the Beast are idolatrous heads, just as they are declared to be in Chapter 13, verse 1. This serves as evidence for the ninth agreement of our second comparison <note>original: "Parallelism"</note>.

<margin>Paragraph 2. Agreement 7.</margin>
6. **And goes into perdition**, that is, into final destruction, as is also suggested in the thirteenth chapter, verses 5 and 10, where his time is set at 1,260 days, after which death is assigned to him. This is the seventh agreement of our second comparison, as I have already noted.

<margin>Paragraph 2. Agreement 11.</margin>
**Verse XII. And the Ten Horns which you saw are Ten Kings, which have received no kingdom as yet**; that is to say, in Saint John’s time. He lived during the reign of the Sixth Head, under which the Beast fought and was slain by Michael <note>the Archangel</note>. In that battle, the Beast is also represented with seven heads and ten horns, but with no crowns upon these horns, because their actual coronation does not occur until the Seventh Head. Therefore, the phrase "which have received no kingdom as yet" corresponds to that symbolic image of the horns without crowns upon them. This is the eleventh agreement of our second comparison.

<margin>Paragraph 2. Agreement 12.</margin>
2. **But receive power as kings one hour with the Beast**; that is to say, with the Beast whose name is "[Was, and is not, and yet is]". This refers to the Beast considered under the succession of the seventh or last head—the head that was healed or revived from the mortal wound it suffered. The kings receive power and are actually crowned as kings at the time this Beast returns to existence. Therefore, the ten horns of this healed Beast are represented with ten crowns on them in Chapter 13:1. This corresponds exactly to this present text: "They receive power as kings one hour with the Beast," and is a clear proof of the twelfth agreement of our second comparison.

3. **"But they receive power as kings for one hour with the beast."** <note>original Greek: "Ἀλλ’ ἐξουσίαν ὡς βασιλεῖς μίαν ὥραν λαμβάνουσι μετὰ τοῦ θηρίου"</note> The meaning, I believe, is: **But they are receiving power at about the same time as the Beast.** For the present tense may suggest that the action is still in progress <note>original: "in fieri"</note>. Nor does it rule out that they may be receiving this power over a period of time (though not in such a passive way that it doesn't involve some bold effort of their own to obtain it; for "to receive rule" <note>original: "λαμβάνειν ἀρχὴν"</note> and "to receive a city" <note>original: "λαμβάνειν πόλιν"</note> have a stronger and more active meaning than that). I say they may be receiving this royal power for some time together; though some succeed sooner than others, none are long without their prize. For I would understand "one hour" by a specific definition <note>original: "Diorismus"</note>: it does not signify a literal hour, but rather any short space of time, the length of which circumstances will clarify for us.

# Chapter 14 and the Thirteenth Chapter of the Apocalypse

It is best to understand it this way. Therefore, I would translate it, *But they receive power as Kings about the same time as the Beast*: as it is understood in Exodus 9:18: *Behold, tomorrow about this time I will cause it to rain a very great hail.* The Greek has it, "Behold, I will rain hail tomorrow at this hour" <note>original: "Ἰδὲ ἐγὼ βρέχω ταύτην τὴν ὥραν αὔριον χάλαζαν"</note>. And that "one hour" <note>original: "μίαν ὥραν"</note> will signify "the same hour" <note>original: "τὴν αὐτὴν ὥραν"</note> is plain from Exodus 36:9 and several other places of Scripture.

The sense, therefore, is this: that about the time the Beast should revive and be worshipped (that is, obeyed)—or, in plainer English, about the time the Empire should relapse again into idolatry and resume the ancient pagan rites, though applying them to Christian objects—about that very same time, the Empire would be rending into ten kingdoms. These ten kings would be seizing and receiving power as kings, all of them appearing and succeeding in their enterprises within a short time from the first degeneracy of the Empire into pagan idolatries and superstitions, which may be within the space of forty or fifty years. (See Mr. Mede’s <note>Joseph Mede (1586–1638) was an influential English scholar who specialized in interpreting biblical prophecy.</note> diagram of the ten kings).

<margin>Paragraph 2. Agreement 13.</margin>
**Verse XIII. These have one mind, and shall give their strength and power to the Beast.** And therefore, in the thirteenth chapter, he is also adorned with this gift, where he is described as *the Beast with seven heads and ten horns, and upon his horns ten crowns*; which shows that even when they were actually kings, they were voluntarily the strength of this Beast. For what strength in the Empire could have constrained them, since they were the very strength of it? From this appears the thirteenth agreement of our second comparison <note>original: "Parallelism"</note>.

But the sense of this verse is briefly this: These ten kings *shall be of one mind*, that is, of one mind in matters of religion. They shall be of the religion of the Empire—that is to say, of the *Pagano-Christian religion* <note>The author uses this term to describe a form of Christianity that he believes has incorporated pagan-like idolatry.</note>—whereby the Empire had again become a *Beast*. They *shall give their power and strength unto this Beast*; that is to say, they shall be ready even by force of arms, if need be, or by whatever other power or authority they have, to maintain this Beast in its beastly, idolatrous condition and pagan-like superstitions. Or else, understanding it as a <term>synecdoche</term> <note>a figure of speech in which a part is made to represent the whole or vice versa</note> throughout, they shall give the Pagano-Christian Emperor (who is the head of this Beast) aid or provide him with the assistance of their armies or forces, if necessary, against all opposers of this Pagano-Christianity. For the Emperor is looked upon as the chief champion and commander-in-chief <note>original: "Generalissimo"</note> of all the Pagano-Christian forces. And though those kings are distinct and absolute in their own dominions, yet looking upon them as held together as one because of the religion of the Empire (of which the Emperor is by status the chief champion), these ten kings may be considered as coming into a kind of subordination to him. They are conceived to be the horns of this head—I mean, of this commander-in-chief or Emperor of that army which *makes war with the Lamb*. But the power which influences all is the *Whore* <note>A reference to the "Whore of Babylon" from Revelation, traditionally interpreted by Protestant Reformers as the corrupted Church of Rome.</note> who rides the Beast.

Regarding the Universal Patriarch <note>The Pope</note>, there is no inconsistency in allowing him to be represented in two places since he plays two roles. We can conceive of him being symbolized as much by the last Head of the Beast as by the costly, adorned Head of the *Whore* <note>In this period of Protestant commentary, the "Whore of Babylon" was frequently identified with the Roman Catholic Church.</note>. But my approach is more distinct and more compatible with the opinion of *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a famous Dutch jurist and theologian who argued that the Roman Empire continued to exist through the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, who stands so firmly for the idea that the Imperial Majesty continues to this day. It also seems reasonable to me to interpret prophecy according to the style and language of history; for *prophecy* is nothing else but *history written in advance*. Therefore, since the *succession of Roman Emperors*, the title of the Empire, and the body of the Empire still continue (though much reduced in size), and are viewed that way in history, I think the most natural way to interpret this is according to the common, acknowledged language and perspective of historians.

But, as I said, if the Pope is understood to take the place of the Emperors as soon as—or as often as—he appears to surpass them even in secular power, and proves to be the real Head of the Empire, acting as the *Caesar* as well as the *Patriarch*; that interpretation is also very acceptable and beyond reproach. For the supreme power of the Beast *that was, and is not* <note>A reference to Revelation 17:8.</note> is viewed by the Angel as one and the same Head, provided it remains the Head of that "Pagano-Christian" <note>The author's term for a church that claims to be Christian but has adopted (in his view) pagan-like idolatry and rituals.</note> Beast throughout. The spirit of prophecy takes no notice of useless distinctions and differences. Therefore, that supreme power which is found to be *Pagano-Christian* is still considered one "Head" in the style of this prophecy, as I noted above. And whatever is beneath it, even if it were invested with the title of *Emperor*, will fall under the number of the *Ten Horns* after the division of the Empire into many kingdoms—*supposedly ten*, at least, or thereabouts. For I view the number as signifying something symbolic rather than being strictly mathematical.

<margin>Paragraph 2. Agreement 14.</margin>
**Verse XIV. *These shall make war with the Lamb*.** What is said here of these *Ten Kings* is said of the *Beast* in the thirteenth chapter: *That he should make war with the Saints*, which is the same thing as to war against the *Lamb* <note>Jesus Christ</note>. As it was said to the apostle Paul: *Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?* <note>Acts 9:4. The author argues that attacking the Church is equivalent to attacking Christ himself.</note> And since these *Ten Kings* are the horns of the Beast, what is done by them is done by the Beast. So, the Beasts in both chapters make war with the Saints, according to the fourteenth agreement of our second parallelism.

As for the 16th and 17th verses of the thirteenth chapter, their meaning is this: that no person, of whatever social rank, who did not follow the *Pagano-Christian profession* (which is what is meant by *receiving a mark in the hand or in the forehead*), should have any trade or business in the empire or territories of any of these ten kings. This is a kind of besieging them with famine, and therefore it is appropriately counted as an act of *war*. This ban on all trade and commerce is an effect of *excommunication* by the "Two-horned Beast" <note>A figure from Revelation 13 often identified by Protestants as the Catholic clergy or the Papacy's spiritual power.</note>. Examples of this kind of warfare are common everywhere in history. Concerning the *Name* of the Beast and the *Number* of his name mentioned in those 16th and 17th verses, I shall speak on the last verse of this present chapter.

<margin>Paragraph 2. Agreement 15.</margin>
2. ***And the Lamb shall overcome them.*** This matches what is said in the thirteenth chapter, verse 10: *He that leads into captivity shall go into captivity.* This fifteenth agreement of our second parallelism is very clear.

If we compare this with what is written in the thirteenth chapter, verse 7, it seems to indicate a scope no less than that of the whole Empire. For the Beast described there is certainly the entire Empire, and it is said of him, "And power was given him over every tribe and tongue and nation" <note>original Greek: *καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ ἐξουσία ἐπὶ πᾶσαν φυλὴν καὶ γλῶσσαν καὶ ἔθνος*</note>. It is true that in this present verse we do not find the exact phrase "all peoples and multitudes" <note>original Greek: *πάντες λαοὶ καὶ ὄχλοι*</note>; for here the Angel is delivering a rule for the art of interpreting prophecies, and therefore could not easily say that "waters" signify *all* peoples and multitudes. However, his use of so many more words than in the previously cited verse, and all in the plural number, seems to aim at an extent just as large as the other. This is further confirmed by his calling these peoples, multitudes, nations, and tongues "the many waters" <note>original Greek: *τὰ ὕδατα τὰ πολλά*</note> at the beginning of this prophecy, which seems to point to the whole Empire, as I have suggested above. To this you may add that both Grotius and Alcazar <note>Hugo Grotius and Luis del Alcázar were prominent 17th-century biblical commentators</note> understand this passage to mean the universal extent of the Roman Empire. Cornelius à Lapide <note>a Jesuit theologian</note> also agrees in his commentary on the text: "The waters which you saw," he says, "signify all nations and peoples over whom Rome shall rule" <note>original Latin: *Aquæ quas vidisti significant omnes gentes & populos quibus Roma imperabit*</note>.

<margin>Parallel 1. Agreement 7.</margin>
I have already mentioned that the *Two Horns* of the Second Beast signify the same thing. As for whether his "exercising all the power of the first Beast in his presence" refers as much to the geographic extent as it does to the types of power, I leave that to further investigation. Enough has already been produced to prove the seventh agreement of our first parallelism.

*Verse* XVI. *And the Ten Horns which you saw upon the Beast, these shall hate the Whore, and shall make her desolate and naked, and shall eat her flesh, and burn her with fire.* To "burn with fire" is a <term>diorismus: a vivid, specific description used to define or distinguish a concept</term>, and it signifies only to consume and destroy, and to cause her to cease to be what she was. I shall wait until the last part of our discourse to explain what kind of execution is implied by "making her desolate and naked" and "eating her flesh."

In the meantime, having so clearly discovered that this *Whore* is not a city built of wood and stone, but a hierarchical political system <note>original: "Polity"</note> that has degenerated into a kind of idolatrous paganism—the very same as the *Two-horned Beast* or the false-prophetic body—I must confess I see no necessity for any war aimed at the burning of the ancient city of *Rome*. This prophecy may be fulfilled without any such military noise, ruins, or garments rolled in blood. This is something to be seriously considered for the peace and welfare of Christendom. For the hatred of these *Ten Horns* against the *Whore*, and their persecution of her, does not imply the raising of armies or marching in formation against fortifications, walls, and houses, nor taking a long expedition to the physical city of *Rome*. This "city" is larger than the borders of *Italy*. It is a false-prophetic system that has spread through all the territories of the Empire—a water-nymph whose skirts are so large that she has sat floating upon the entire Imperial ocean for many ages. Therefore, she is not the kind of entity to which the punishments of "burning" or "drowning" apply in that crude and literal sense that is commonly understood. But we shall discuss these things in their proper place.

# Chapter XV and the Thirteenth Chapter of the Apocalypse

Verse XVII. *For God has put in their hearts to fulfill his will, and to agree and give their Kingdom unto the Beast.* This seems to be exactly the same as the thirteenth verse—*These have one mind* <note>original Greek: *μίαν γνώμην ἔχουσι*</note>, which corresponds to *acting with one mind* here <note>original Greek: *ποιῆσαι μίαν γνώμην*</note>—and *shall give their power and strength to the Beast*. But the most astounding mystery <term>original: "Arcanum"; a profound secret or mystery</term>, which should not be thought upon except with the greatest humility and reverence, is that God is here credited with this plan and joint purpose of these Kings. He is said *to put this in their hearts*, and it is called *the fulfilling of his purpose* <note>original Greek: *τὴν γνώμην αὐτοῦ*</note> to give their kingdom to the **Beast**. The simple meaning of this is that they contribute their kingdoms to form this **Ten-horned Beast**, just as the children of **Israel** might be said to contribute to the creation of the golden calf.

<margin>Acts 17:30</margin>
2. This seems to be a remarkable act of Divine Providence, which even the words of Saint **Paul** hardly match. Speaking of the gross idolatry of the Pagans that reigned in the world for so many ages, he says, *And the times of this ignorance God overlooked <note>original: "winked at"</note>, but now commands all men everywhere to repent.* But here, God is said not merely to overlook the matter, but to *put it into the hearts of these Kings*, etc.

Therefore, it seems most similar to the *hardening of Pharaoh's heart*, so that he would not let **Israel** go; or the Jews crucifying our Savior Christ, whom <margin>Acts 2:23</margin> **Peter** says they took, and by wicked hands crucified and slew, *being delivered up by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God* <note>original Greek: *τῇ ὡρισμένῃ βουλῇ καὶ προγνώσει τοῦ Θεοῦ ἔκδοτον*</note>. Therefore, it appears that such unavoidable circumstances and inviting opportunities—which God, by his permissive or more active Providence, brings into the world to test or rather reveal what is in the hearts of the wicked—are regarded as suggestions or transmissions and movements upon the hearts of men from God himself. Because these events will naturally take effect in those who have fallen into this lower state of fate, the minds of men are determined to act in this or that way by such a providential framework of affairs, which God at least allows, if not contrives. We need not understand the hardening of **Pharaoh's** heart by God in any other way than this: the primary cause was God permitting the **magicians** to imitate, if not equal, most of the miracles of **Moses**. For as the text says, *And the magicians did so with their enchantments, and Pharaoh’s heart was hardened.*

It is just as easy to conceive that the False-prophetic **Beast** might be permitted (with the active assistance of the powers of darkness) to perform such miracles and use such methods of deceiving the **Ten Kings** that they would certainly be led toward the idolatrous religion of the Empire. But the fact that they were so certain to be deceived is the fault of their own spiritual fall and its consequences, not any injustice on God's part.

# His Joint-Exposition of the Seventeenth Book I.

...in the same manner with the current of the times, and how God has overlooked <note>original: "winked at"</note> the times of this ignorance. But let them be assured that the night is far spent, and the day is at hand when God will no longer overlook things, nor will men be so universally asleep and in so deep a stupor <note>original: "sopor"</note>, but that they will be easily awakened by that voice of Saint **Paul** commanding all men everywhere to repent; or, if you will, the voice of **John the Baptist**: *Repent, for the Kingdom of God is at hand*. Otherwise the stream of Fate and Providence will turn, and that doom shall be fulfilled upon her in the most unwelcome sense: *Therefore shall her plagues come in one day—death, and mourning, and famine; for strong is the Lord God who judges her.* For her time of prosperity is set, as is plain by what follows in this present verse of this seventeenth chapter:

In the works of Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BC), often called the "father of Roman poetry."</note>, there are infinite examples of this.

->Which the ancient people, the Latins, first held <note>original: *Quam preimum Cascei popolei tenuere Lateinei*</note><-
So there is very little ground for that fancy <note>original: "conceit"</note> of Grotius.

6. Nor can these examples be dismissed because of their antiquity. The ancient Romans pronounced words in a way most similar to the Greeks, as appears in those diphthongs *ae* and *oe*, and in the letter *y*, which later Romans did not distinguish from *i*. To the Greeks, however, it was a short *u*, and they had no other way to represent it. That the Greeks sounded it like *u* appears from several words derived from that tongue: as in *Sus* (swine), *Super* (above), *Fucus* (seaweed/dye), *Turba* (crowd), and *Trutina* (balance/scale), which come from the Greek words *hys* <note>original: ὗς</note>, *hyper* <note>original: ὑπὲρ</note>, *phykos* <note>original: φῦκος</note>, *tyrbe* <note>original: τύρβη</note>, and *trytane* <note>original: τρυτάνη</note>. Therefore, they were represented all at once without distinguishing between different times.

### Chapter XVI. That there had been five sorts of Roman Magistrates, etc.

1. If I add to this a solid refutation of the interpretations by **Ribera** <note>Francisco Ribera, a Jesuit scholar who argued the Antichrist was a future individual, not the Papacy</note> and **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch jurist who interpreted these prophecies as referring to the early Roman Empire</note> regarding the seven-headed beast, I think nothing will be missing for the greatest assurance of the truth of our interpretation that anyone could desire.

Nor will they doubt that it is the same "Beast" throughout, just as the historian **Florus** considers it as one "man" and distinguishes his *ages*. He allots the first 250 years from **Romulus** to the *infancy* of the *Roman people* or *Empire*; then 200 years more to its *youth*; and then 250 years more (reaching to the time of **Augustus**) to the *manly age* of the Empire. The next 200 years he calls the **old age of the empire** <note>original: "Senectutem Imperii"</note>. This shows plainly that he looks upon the whole succession as one and the same Empire, though under several stages of growth—though it lived much longer than to be considered "old" in **Trajan’s** time. Therefore, since history itself views the whole succession of the *Roman people* as one *body politic*, there is no harshness at all in describing this body by the number of heads that reached from the first beginning of this succession to the final period of the Empire.

# That there had been five sorts of Supreme Power - Book I.

Regarding **Kings** and **Consuls**, there is no debate at all. Now, concerning these **Consular Tribunes** <note>original: *Tribuni Consulares*</note>, they are named this way to distinguish them from the **Tribunes of the People** <note>original: *Tribuni Plebis*</note> and the **Military Tribunes** <note>original: *Tribuni Militum*</note> as they are usually called; neither of those two were the supreme powers of the Roman State or Empire. The Tribunes of the People were magistrates of the commoners <note>original: *plebis*</note> rather than of the Roman people as a whole. In fact, during those few years when they blocked the election of other magistrates, the city was considered to have no government at all. "Rome was without magistrates for four years," <note>original: *Quatuor annis sine Magistratibus Roma fuit*</note> says **Sextus Rufus** regarding that time. **Diodorus Siculus** also calls this condition of the city "anarchy" <note>original: *ἀναρχίαν*</note>. Likewise, a passage <margin>Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book 13, chapter 12.</margin> by **Marcus Varro** found in **Gellius** plainly shows that they could not be a supreme power:

> "In a magistracy, some have the power of summoning, others the power of arrest, and others neither. The power of summoning belongs to the Consuls and others who possess supreme authority <term>imperium: the formal power to command</term>; the power of arrest belongs to the Tribunes of the People and others who have an attendant <term>viator: a minor official or summoner</term>; neither summoning nor arrest belongs to the Quaestors and others who have neither a bodyguard <term>lictor: an officer attending a magistrate</term> nor an attendant." <note>original: *In Magistratu habent alii Vocationem, alii Prensionem...*</note>

From this, it is plain that the Tribunes of the People are counted among those "who do not have supreme authority," <note>original: *qui non habent imperium*</note> and therefore they are not supreme powers.

4. No more supreme are the Military Tribunes when simply styled as such, as appears <margin>Livy, book 8.</margin> from the words of **Livy**: "For in military discipline, the soldier obeys the authority of the Centurion, the Centurion that of the Tribune, the Tribune that of the Lieutenant, and the Lieutenant that of the Consul." <note>original: *Disciplina enim militari, miles Centurionis...*</note> But the "Military Tribunes with Consular Power" are those **Consular Tribunes** which I <margin>Fenestella, *On Roman Magistrates*, chapter 16.</margin> have already named. Of these, **Fenestella** says: "In this magistracy (as the name itself indicates), the same power as that held by the Consuls was indeed conferred, with only the names changed and consideration for the common people beginning to be taken." <note>original: *Penes quem sanè Magistratum...*</note>

5. That the **Decemviri** <term>Decemviri: a commission of ten men</term> was a supreme power is plain from **Livy**. <margin>Livy, book 3.</margin> "In the three hundred and second year after Rome was founded, the form of the state was changed again from Consuls to the Ten Men, just as it had previously passed from Kings to Consuls, with the supreme authority being transferred." <note>original: *Anno trecentesimo altero quàm condita Roma erat...*</note> It is also clear from **Sextus Rufus**: "For forty-nine years Rome lacked Consuls: under the Ten Men for two years; under the Military Tribunes for forty-three; and Rome was without magistrates for four years." <note>original: *Quadraginta enim novem annis Roma Consules defuerunt...*</note> This is found in Rufus’s *Summary* <note>original: *Breviarium*</note>, where a recent edition has grossly corrupted the text, reading "for nine years" instead of "for forty-nine years," and later "three" instead of "forty-three." That editor forgot that the historian had said shortly before that the people of Rome were under Consuls for four hundred and sixty-seven years (specifically from Brutus and Poplicola to Pansa and Hirtius), but that he counts only four hundred and seventeen Consuls within this span. How then can only nine years make up the difference? But I mention this only in passing. From this, it clearly appears that the supremacy of these Military Tribunes as well as the Ten Men is confirmed by this author, as the Consular power ceased during their time. And as for the short duration of the Ten Men's reign—who lasted only two years—that can no more remove them from the list of government forms than **Otho’s** reign of only three months could remove him from the list of Roman Emperors.

### Chapter 16: Roman Magistrates in St. John’s Time, and No More.

9. This conclusion must seem very easy and natural to anyone who considers how "collective" and <term>henopoetical (unifying several distinct things into one symbol)</term> these prophetic symbols are. 

Considering the collective and unifying nature of these symbols on one hand, and the clear, explicit historical list of **five** distinct types of government before the Emperors on the other, a person must feel unshakable certainty. The Spirit of Prophecy would reckon neither more nor fewer than **five** kinds of governors before the Emperors. Having cleared up this point, I will move to the second: a fuller explanation of how appropriately that corrupt state of the Empire—symbolized by the **Beast that was, and is not, and yet is**—is also called the **Image of the Beast**.

> Help me now, Goddess, help me; for many a painted tablet in your temples shows that you have the power to heal.

The historian **Polydore Vergil** acknowledges that the same thing is done in the Church of **Rome**. As a memorial for having their leg, arm, ear, breast <note>original: "pap"</note>, or any other part cured by this or that Saint, they hang images <note>original: "effigies"</note> of these body parts openly near the shrines, or at least in their chapels or temples.

10. Their superstition regarding **Holy Water** is also well worth noting. This *lustral water* <note>original: "Aqua lustralis," water used for ceremonial purification</note> was common among the ancients:

(The Greek priest sprinkles the captives with lustral water.)
<note>original Latin: "Spargit aquâ captos lustrali Graia Sacerdos"</note>

But its supposed power is most justly and wisely mocked by the poet **Ovid**:

<margin>Fasti, Book 2.</margin>
> Ah, you are far too easy on yourselves, you who think that the grim crime of murder can be washed away by river water.
> <note>original Latin: "Ah nimiùm faciles, qui tristia crimina cædis / Flumineâ tolli posse putatis aquâ."</note>

But **Aeneas** was not of that mind in **Virgil**'s work. Speaking to his father **Anchises** when he was about to offer a sacrifice, he argues this way:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 2.</margin>
> "You, father, take the sacred objects and our ancestral household gods <note>original: "Penates"</note> in your hand. For me, having just come from such a great war and recent slaughter, it would be a sin to touch them until I have washed myself in a running stream."
> <note>original Latin: "Tu, genitor, cape sacra manu patriosque Penates; / Me bello à tanto digressum & cæde recenti / Attrectare nefas, donec me flumine vivo / Abluero."</note>

And again in another place:

> Aeneas takes the entrance, and sprinkles his body with fresh water.
> <note>original Latin: "Occupat Æneas aditum, corpusque recenti / Spargit aquâ."</note>

And at the burial of **Misenus**:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 6.</margin>
> He also carried pure water three times around his companions, sprinkling them with a light dew from a branch of a lucky olive tree, and thus he purified the men.
> <note>original Latin: "Idem ter socios purâ circumtulit undâ, / Spargens rore levi, & ramo felicis olivæ, / Lustravitque viros."</note>

**Tibullus** also writes in his second book of Elegies:

> Pure things please the gods; come with clean clothing, and take pure spring water in your hands.
> <note>original Latin: "Casta placent Superis; pura cum veste venite, / Et manibus puram sumite fontis aquam."</note>

There was a spring near the **Capene Gate** <note>Porta Capena, a gate in the walls of Rome</note> sacred to **Mercury**, where the ancient **Romans** used a laurel bough to sprinkle themselves. Merchants especially used it to purify themselves from their sins—specifically the sins of cheating <note>original: "couzenage"</note> and lying. **Ovid** described the ceremony so vividly and pleasantly, including a wise note on the ill effect of such pretended purifications (which only encourage people to be corrupt), that I cannot resist transcribing the story, even though it is somewhat long.

<margin>Fasti, Book 5.</margin>
> There is a spring of Mercury near the Capene Gate; if it helps to believe those who have tried it, it has divine power. Here comes the merchant with his tunic tucked up, and being in a pure state, he draws water in a jar to carry away. A laurel branch is soaked in it; with the wet laurel, he sprinkles all the goods that will soon have new owners. He even sprinkles his own hair with the dripping laurel and recites his prayers in a voice accustomed to deceiving. "Wash away the perjuries of past time," he says, "Wash away the treacherous words of past bad faith."
> <note>original Latin: "Est aqua Mercurii portæ vicina Capenæ... Ablue præteriti perjuria temporis, inquit, / Ablue præteritâ perfida verba fide."</note>

### Chap. XVII. In the Gross Degeneracies of the Lapsed Empire.

> Whether I have made you a witness to a lie, or have falsely invoked the powerless divinity of Jupiter who will not hear; or whether I have knowingly deceived another God or Goddess, let the swift South Winds carry away my wicked words. Only give me profits; give me joy in the profits I have made, and make it a pleasure to have cheated the buyer.
> <note>original Latin: "Sive ego te feci testem, falsóve citavi / Non audituri numina vana Jovis; / Sive Deum prudens alium Divámve fefelli, / Abstulerint celeres improba verba Noti. / Da modò lucra mihi; da facto gaudia lucro, / Et face ut emptori verba dedisse juvet." This is Ovid's description of a merchant's prayer to Mercury.</note>

That is, he asks of **Mercury** <note>The Roman god of both merchants and thieves</note> that, by virtue of this superstitious devotion and by sprinkling himself with water sacred to his deity, he may cheat and grow rich with a cheerful conscience, and without the fear of the gods' displeasure.

The examples of **lustral water** <note>original: "Aqua lustralis," water used for ritual purification</note> are infinite, and the Church of **Rome's** imitation of this superstition is extremely frequent in their washings and sprinklings with **holy water**. It is to be feared that this is done with just as much hypocrisy and safe trading in sin—based on a vain presumption of the power of such superstitious and imaginary purifications—as the poet has described here.

11. The **Tubilustria** <note>A Roman festival dedicated to the purification of sacred trumpets</note> or the hallowing of trumpets has a significant similarity to the Catholic **baptism of bells** <note>original: "Christening of Bells"</note>. But this agreement would be even more exact if, just as these consecrated bells are believed to have the power to drive away evil spirits by their ringing, those trumpets were believed to chase away ghosts and spectres by being sounded. Whether or not those trumpets were understood to have such a special power, the ringing of brass instruments with the assistance of **holy water** is plainly declared to have that power in **Ovid’s** *Fasti*:

<margin>Fasti, Book 5.</margin>
> He touches the water again, clangs the Temesean bronze, and asks the ghost to leave his house.
> <note>original Latin: "Rursus aquam tangit, Temeseáque concrepat æra, / Et rogat ut tectis exeat umbra suis." Temese was an ancient Italian city famous for its copper mines.</note>

And that the sound of brass—whether pans, cymbals, or whatever they may be—was superstitiously thought by the Heathen to have power against witchcraft and enchantment (which are the works of the evil devil), **Tibullus** seems to suggest in this couplet:

<margin>Book 1, Elegy 8.</note>
> Incantation also tries to pull the Moon down from her chariot; and it would succeed, if the clanging bronze did not ring out in response.
> <note>original Latin: "Cantus & à curru Lunam deducere tentat; / Et faceret, si non æra repulsa sonent." Ancient people often beat bronze during eclipses to "rescue" the moon from magic.</note>

How close this comes to the Catholic superstition of driving away evil spirits by the jangling of **baptized bells**, I leave for anyone to judge.

12. And now for their **festivals**. What was Pope **Boniface VIII's** institution of a **Jubilee** every hundredth year but an imitation of the Romans' **Secular Games** <note>original: "Ludi Seculares," a three-day festival of sacrifices and theatrical performances marking the end of a "saeculum" or era</note>? For otherwise, if he had imitated **Moses**, fifty years would have been the regular interval of that festival. To note what is more general, singing, dancing, drinking, and staggering were the usual accompaniments of all the Pagan holidays:

> Unmindful of us, they led the festive dances.
> <note>original Latin: "Immemores nostri festas duxere choreas."</note>

And again in the same poet:

> Some beat the ground with their feet and sing songs.
> <note>original Latin: "Pars pedibus terram pulsant, & carmina dicunt."</note>

**Tibullus** also describes their festivals as consisting of idleness and drinking until they stagger:

<margin>Book 2, Elegy 1.</margin>
> Let wines celebrate the day; on a feast day, there is no shame in being soaked, nor in having feet that stumble poorly.
> <note>original Latin: "Vina diem celebrent, non festâ luce madere / Est pudor, errantes & male ferre pedes."</note>

**Erasmus**, in his *Colloquies*, sadly complains that this is the manner of celebrating...
