# The Lifelike Image of the Revived Beast — Book I.

celebrating the Feasts of the Saints in the Church of **Rome** in his time.

It was a custom among the Pagans in the celebration of the Feasts of their Gods to *put on the gods* <note>original: "Deos induere"</note>, as **Tertullian's** phrase is. This meant that someone or other would take on the persona or act the part of the God whose Feast they were celebrating. I have been specifically informed that this custom also took hold in the Church of **Rome** during the Festivals of their Saints, where someone acts the part of the Saint to entertain the people with pastime, or a kind of superstitious merriment. See **Polydore Virgil**, *On the Inventors of Things*, book 5, chapter 2.

13. But let us move on to briefly examine a few specific Festivals of the Heathens. The *fetching in of May*, as they call it—conducted by the playful youth of both sexes—what is it but an imitation of the Roman <margin>On the Inventors of Things, book 5, chapter 2.</margin> **Floralia** <note>A Roman festival in honor of Flora, the goddess of flowers</note>? As **Polydore** has also observed: "among whom," he says, "Flora, the goddess of all fruits, was celebrated lewdly in the month of May" <note>original Latin: "apud quos sic Flora, cunctorum fructuum Dea, mense Maio lascivè colebatur?"</note>. The **Cerealia** <note>A major festival in honor of Ceres, the goddess of grain</note> of the Pagans were celebrated at night, with the Priests running up and down with torches in their hands. In imitation of this superstition, **Polydore** <margin>Book 5, chapter 2.</margin> says that in **Umbria** and other parts of **Italy**, on the evening before the **Calends** <note>The first day of the month</note> of **March**, boys kindle fires in the field and run up and down on the lands with torches made of dry reeds, "so that they might pray for the fertility of the fields, with the earth already giving birth to its offspring" <note>original Latin: "ut precantes fœcunditatem agrorum cum terrâ jam fœtum parturiente"</note>. Regarding their **Palilia** <note>An agricultural festival aimed at purifying herds and shepherds</note>, **Ovid’s** instruction in <margin>Fasti, book 4.</margin> his *Fasti* is:

> Let the shepherd purify the well-fed sheep at the first light of dusk;
> Let water sprinkle them first, and a branch sweep the ground.
> <note>original Latin: "Pastor oves saturas ad prima crepuscula lustret: / Unda priùs spargat, virgáque verrat humum."</note>

But this is only a preparation for the **lustration** <note>A ritual purification</note> of the sheep; the main ceremony follows:

> Let blue smoke be made from pure sulfur,
> And let the sheep bleat when touched by the smoking sulfur.
> <note>original Latin: "Cærulei fiant puro de sulphure fumi, / Tactáque fumanti sulphure balet ovis."</note>

The Friars of **St. Anthony** have changed this lustration by **fumigation** <note>Purification using smoke</note> into the sprinkling of **Holy Water**, not only upon sheep, but horses and oxen, at a set time of year. Both practices agree in the superstitious purification of mute creatures. The *leaping over certain fires* that people do on **St. John the Baptist's** day is a more exact imitation of the old Pagans leaping over their fires at the previously mentioned **Palilia**, or the Festival of **Pales** <note>The Roman goddess of shepherds and livestock</note>.

<margin>Fasti, book 4.</margin>
> And soon, through the burning piles of crackling straw,
> Leap your vigorous limbs with a swift foot.
> <note>original Latin: "Móxque per ardentes stipulæ crepitantis acervos / Trajicias celeri strenua membra pede."</note>

And this Roman <term>Hierophanta</term> <note>A priest or interpreter of sacred mysteries</note>, **Ovid**, tells the reason for it immediately after:

> Devouring fire purges all things.
> <note>original Latin: "Omnia purgat edax ignis."</note>

So it is plain that such customs as these, which have been retained in the Church of **Rome**, are but the footsteps of Heathenish superstitions and purifications. The use of **baptismal spittle** itself seems to be a clear instance of this, as may appear from a passage in **Persius**:

<margin>Satire 2.</margin>
> Look, a grandmother or a god-fearing aunt takes the
> boy from his cradle; she first purifies his forehead and wet lips 
> with her middle finger and purifying spittle, 
> being skilled in warding off the "evil eye": 
> Then she shakes him in her hands, etc.
> <note>original Latin: "Ecce avia, aut metuens Divûm matertera, cunis / Exemit puerum, frontémque atque uda labella / Infami digito & lustralibus antè salivis / Expiat, urentes oculos inhibere perita: / Tunc manibus quatit, &c."</note>

### Chapter 17: On the gross degeneracies of the fallen Empire

Such marvelous virtue did the old women of **Rome** believe resided in spittle to protect against witchcraft and the approach of the Devil. They performed this ceremony on the *Day of Purification* <note>original: "Dies Lustricus"</note> of the child, which is also called the *Naming Day* <note>original: "Dies Nominalis"</note>, as they gave the child his name on that day. This "purifying spittle" <note>original: "Saliva lustralis"</note> completely corresponds to the "baptismal spittle" used in the **Roman** Church. But I mention this only in passing.

In the ancient **Saturnalia** <note>A Roman festival in late December where social norms were overturned</note>, the masters waited on their servants, entertaining them with good cheer, as the poet **Lucius Accius** records in his verses:

> "Throughout almost all the fields and cities, they joyfully celebrate with feasts, and each master provides for his own servants." <note>original Latin: "per agros urbésque ferè omnes / Exercent epulis læti, famulóque procurant / Quisque suos."</note>

<margin>On the Discovery of Things, book 5, chapter 2.</margin>
<margin>Polydore Virgil, On the Discovery of Things, book 5, chapter 2.</margin>
From this, **Polydore Virgil** notes that the Christmas custom of making one servant a **Master of Misrule**—whom both his master and his fellow servants must obey—took its origin. In the *Lesser Quinquatria* or the *Megalensian Games* <note>Roman festivals involving theater and public games</note>, men ran up and down in masks <note>original: "vizards"</note> madly and lewdly, committing many immodest acts. This wildness lasted only a day or two in those ancient **Roman** festivals; but it is not only imitated but surpassed in the **Roman** Church during their **Carnival**. That madness of committing outrages in masks (as if they could hide themselves under them from the sight of God) lasts not two days, but two entire months in some places. At this time, they also indulge themselves excessively in eating and drinking, as if they intended to turn their bodies into cellars and storehouses against the approaching fast of **Lent**, so that they might better withstand that "siege." Therefore, this **Carnival** seems to be a joining of those two lewd Pagan solemnities together: I mean their *Megalensian Games* and the *Bacchanalia* <note>Festivals of Bacchus, known for drunken revelry</note>. 

The foul and abominable misdeeds of those festivals—involving unclean and impudent gestures, and all manner of obscenity in words or actions—are so great and varied that they are beyond an ordinary man's imagination without reading the history of these Pagan enormities. Yet, as history from eyewitnesses of these "Pagan-Christian Bacchanalias" assures us, this **New Romanism** has surpassed old **Rome** in every kind of impudent vileness during this festival. Thus, the Beast <note>A reference to the Beast of Revelation, symbolizing the corrupt Roman Empire revived in the Papacy</note> is not only *restored* but has grown stronger in this regard.

I might go on and observe what corresponds in the Church of **Rome** to the *Vinalia* <note>Wine festivals</note>, *Robigalia* <note>A festival to protect crops from blight</note>, *Terminalia* <note>Festival of boundaries</note>, *Parentalia* <note>A festival honoring deceased ancestors</note>, *Proserpinalia* <note>A festival for Proserpina</note>, and other feasts of the Gentiles; but this forest is so wide that I might more easily lose myself in it than get through it.

14. But I will not omit that the Beast has a kind of revival even in their **Funerals** for the dead.

<margin>Persius, Satires, 3.</margin>
> "From here comes the trumpet and the candle, and at last the 'little blessed one' <note>referring to the deceased</note> is laid out on a high bed." <note>original Latin: "Hinc tuba, candela, tandemque beatulus alto / Compositus lecto"</note>

That this solemnity also included funeral songs, and that there were hired professional mourners <note>term: Præficæ; women hired to weep and sing dirges at Roman funerals</note> to stir up grief with their doleful melodies, is something that everyone has noticed. But that pomp of carrying torches is also vividly described by **Virgil**:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 11.</margin>
> "The Arcadians rushed to the gates and, according to ancient custom, snatched up funeral torches; the road shines with a long..." <note>original Latin: "Arcades ad portas ruere, & de more vetusto, / Funereas rapuere faces: lucet via longo"</note>

# The Lively Image of the Revived Beast: Book 1

How closely the modern funerals of the Roman Catholics imitate this ancient nocturnal spectacle, even the slowest imagination can see. However, I do not place a great deal of importance on such things.

15. It would be too long a task, and unnecessary, to give a full account of the various *Religious Orders* in both the Old and New *Roman religion* <note>original: "Romanism"</note>. It is enough to notice that just as there were different types of societies of priests, both male and female, in the old Pagan religion—some devoted to *Mars*, some to *Venus*, some to *Vesta*, and others to various deities—so there are in the Church of *Rome* several orders of priests and religious persons. Some are devoted to the service of one saint, others to another; some to the service of the Blessed Virgin, others to *Saint Francis*, and so on for the rest.

16. However, we cannot fail to notice that the *tonsure* <note>original: "shorn Crowns"</note> is no modern invention, but was a ceremony of the ancient priests of *Isis* or *Diana*. Nor is the *vow of virginity* so recent that it belongs only to the nuns of the current *Roman religion*. The priests of *Vesta*, *Apollo*, *the Argive Juno*, *Diana*, and *Minerva* were all committed to perpetual *virginity*. Furthermore, the priests of *Cybele*, the Mother of the Gods, ensured a constant state of celibacy by castrating themselves <note>original: "execting their virilities"</note>. I must admit that this practice is not imitated with that same exactness in *Modern Rome*, but *chastity* is vowed with such confidence that it is as if they had either made themselves *eunuchs* in the literal sense suggested by *Origen* <note>An early Christian theologian who, according to tradition, castrated himself for the sake of the Gospel</note>, or else had been born eunuchs for the Kingdom of God. 

But while they fall short of the *Galli* <note>the self-castrated priests of Cybele</note>, they have surpassed the *Luperci* <note>priests of the Roman festival Lupercalia</note> with their *penitents* <note>original: "Ninevites"</note> and *flagellants*, whose lashes are not laid upon those they meet, but upon themselves. This harsh self-severity is actually more likely derived from *Egypt* than *Ancient Rome*. The worshipers of *Isis* beat themselves while their burnt offerings are consumed; "While the sacrifices are burning, they all beat themselves," says *Herodotus* <note>original Greek: "καιομένων δὲ ἱρῶν τύπτονται πάντες"</note>. Alternatively, it may come from the self-cruelty of the priests of the *Syrian Goddess* <note>original: "Dea Syria"</note>, or from the rigid discipline of *Diana* at *Lacedaemon* <note>Sparta</note>, who could only be appeased by bloody whippings, as I have noted elsewhere.

17. There are so many similarities between the superstitions of the *Roman Church* and ancient Paganism that it would be a tiresome task to try to list even the smallest part of them; therefore, I will willingly end the account here. However, I will not overlook one main parallel that comes to mind.

The Pagan priests claimed to provide a *revelation* <note>original Greek: "Ἐπόπτεια"</note> or *eyewitness sight* <note>original Greek: "Αὐτοψία"</note>—the ability to show a physical manifestation of their gods in the *inner sanctuaries* <note>original: "Adyta"</note> of their temples. The poet *Claudian* seems to refer to this when he writes:

18. I will conclude with one final comparison: the sacrificial ceremonies of the pagans versus the supplications or *processions* of the Church of *Rome*, as described by *Polydore Virgil* <note>An Italian scholar and historian (c. 1470–1555) who wrote extensively on the origins of traditions.</note> in his account of both.

The pagans, in their superstitious and idolatrous *processions*, carried images of their gods. To better entertain the uneducated crowds, a certain silly image also went in this procession, which the Latins call *Citeria*. They usually derive the name from the Greek words for "magpie" and "to speak" <note>original: *Κίττα* (Kitta) and *ἐρεῖν* (erein)</note>, referring to the bird’s talkativeness; for this image was made to snap its jaws and chatter like that bird. "Why should I argue further with that man, whom I believe is carried in the procession at the games as a *Citeria*?" <note>original Latin: *Quid ego cum illo differtem ampliùs, quem ego denique credo in pompa vectitatum ire ludis pro Citeria?*</note>. These are the words of Cato against *Marcus Caecilius*. *Plautus* <note>A famous Roman playwright known for comedies.</note> mentions another terrifying idol carried in these superstitious shows, which he calls *Manducus*. "What if I hire myself out for the games as a *Manducus*, so that I might loudly rattle my teeth?" <note>original Latin: *Quid si ad ludos me pro Manduco locem, quapropter clarè crepito dentibus?*</note>. For it was a huge, ugly image with a wide mouth split open to the ears, gaping horribly and gnashing its teeth to the great terror of the simple-minded. Of this *Mormo* <note>A terrifying spirit or "bogeyman" in Greek and Roman folklore used to frighten children.</note>, *Juvenal* says it scares the children of the country folk in their mothers' laps with its wide gapes:

-> "When the rustic infant, in its mother's lap," <-
-> "Shrinks from the gaping mouth of the pale mask." <-
<note>original Latin: *Cùm personæ pallentis hiatum / In gremio matris formidat rusticus Infans.*</note>

Such were the religious spectacles and processions of the ancient pagans.

"In the pomp," he says, "of our prayers or *processions*, some ludicrous show usually goes first, such as ranks of soldiers, both horse and foot. There are other playful sights, among which the ancient Prophets are played by actors, and boys with wings go along singing as if they were part of the heavenly choir of angels. "Beasts are also brought into the parade, and there an ape or monkey, wearing a *Monmouth cap* <term>Monmouth cap: a knitted wool cap popular in the 16th and 17th centuries</term> buttoned up on one side, rides upon some large mastiff dog or stunted pony. There are also men carrying torches in their hands, and boys and girls are forbidden to look out of the windows. Besides this, the priests or others represent the persons or act the parts of various saints, carrying their images or relics along with them in the procession. The air is also filled with fragrances as they go, and the ground they pass over is strewn with flowers. Finally, certain people are assigned the job of speaking to the crowd to tell them to make way, so that the parade may march on without any hindrance."

Can any two eggs be more alike than this *Roman* procession is to the ancient, superstitious parade of the pagans? Therefore, *Polydore’s* conclusion is very solid and beyond reproach: "Thus the Romans used to do, as did many other nations, from whom such rites undoubtedly flowed down to us." <note>original Latin: *Ità Romani factitabant & aliæ pleraque gentes, à quibus ad nos ritus ejusmodi dubio procul manavit.*</note>

## CHAP. I.

*1. The great usefulness of showing the folly of Ribera's and Grotius's interpretations of these two chapters of the Revelation <note>original: "Apocalyps"</note>. 2. That, according to Ribera, the Beast is the Devil. 3. The seven Kings are the wicked kings of the seven Ages of the world. 4. That five of these Ages had passed by St. John's time; that the Reign of Antichrist is the seventh; and that Pagan Rome <note>original: "Rome Heathen"</note> is the Whore. 5. The general usefulness of our Joint-Exposition. 6. That the Beast is not the Devil, as proved by several circumstances. Nor are the seven Heads seven such Ages, because of the deadly wound in the sixth Head. 7. Nor is the Whore Pagan Rome any more than the Two-horned Beast. 8. That the Devil cannot be the "Beast that was, and is not, etc.," proved by arguments not relying on our Joint-Exposition. 9. Further proof from that part of his Name ["and yet is"], with a defense of that reading. 10. A refutation of Ribera's interpretation of the seven Heads based on the groundless and objectionable nature of his division of the world's duration into seven Ages. 11. And, lastly, from the seven hills, which necessarily identify those seven Heads with the Roman Empire. 16. That these interpretations of Ribera, as well as those of the rest of the Roman interpreters, were very weak even in Grotius's own judgment, which led him to invent new ones.*

1. So far, we have dedicated our efforts to fully demonstrating the true and genuine meaning of these two main chapters of the Book of Revelation. However, because of the hypocrisy and reluctance of those whose personal interests bias them, they will likely try to dismiss the weight and evidence of such a clear demonstration. They may pretend that learned men have provided entirely different interpretations of these prophecies, and that it is therefore uncertain what they signify. To address this, I will introduce the two most prominent interpreters—whom the Church of **Rome** relies on and praises most—namely, **Ribera** <note>Francisco Ribera (1537–1591) was a Jesuit theologian who developed the "futurist" interpretation of prophecy to shield the Pope from being identified as the Antichrist.</note> and **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch scholar whose interpretations of Revelation often aligned with Catholic views to promote church unity.</note>. I will show plainly how foolish <note>original: "fond"</note>, forced, and indeed impossible their interpretations are, so that even biased men may be ashamed hereafter to take shelter in such wretched excuses <note>original: "subterfuges"</note>.

# Chapter I: The Seventeenth Chapter of Revelation <note>original: "Apocalyps"</note>.

2. *Ribera's* explanation of the Beast with seven heads and ten horns—which *was, and is not, and yet is*—and of the *Whore of Babylon* who rides him, is briefly this: "The Beast is the *Devil*, considered in relation to his condition of reigning or not reigning in the world. <note>original: "*In Bestia non Diabolus intelligitur, sed Diabolus regnans*" — In the Beast, it is not simply the Devil who is understood, but the Devil reigning.</note> Therefore, where it is said, '*The Beast which you saw, was, and is not*,' he interprets it this way: The Devil in the ages before Christ was the *reigning Devil*, but in Saint *John’s* time he was not the *reigning Devil*, because then *the Prince of this world was cast out*. Consequently, in this sense he is said to be the Beast that *was, and is not*, but will be the *reigning Devil* again in *Antichrist*, who is the Seventh Head, during whose reign he comes up again out of the bottomless pit."

3. "The Seven Kings are the wicked kings of the Seven Ages of the world, from *Adam* to the Last Judgment. The first Age is from *Adam* to *Noah* <note>original: "Noe"</note>, in which *Cain* and the *Giants* are particularly blamed. The second is from *Noah* to *Abraham*, in which *Nimrod* is censured <note>original: "perstringed"</note>. The third is from *Abraham* to *David*, in which the Kings of *Egypt* <note>original: "Ægypt"</note> and other nations are noted as persecutors and opponents of the People of God. The fourth is from *David* to the Babylonian Captivity, in which the Jewish people were much afflicted by the Kings of *Assyria*. The fifth is from the Babylonian Captivity to the coming of Christ, in which they were much afflicted by the *Chaldeans* and *Greeks*. The sixth is from the coming of Christ to the coming of *Antichrist*, in which the Church has been much persecuted by the *Roman* Emperors and by the *Turks* and *Saracens*, and may be still more by others who may arise hereafter. The seventh is from the coming of *Antichrist* to the Last Judgment, in which *Antichrist* with his ten horns (that is, ten kings) shall persecute the Church worse than ever."

4. "Five of these Heads (that is, of these Ages with their wicked kings) had passed by Saint *John’s* time; one Age was then current and still continues; the other (that is, the Seventh and Last) has not yet come, but when it does come, it must continue only a little while—that is to say, three and a half years, or forty-two months. *Antichrist* is that Beast in the thirteenth chapter, according to his interpretation. And lastly, regarding the *Whore who rides this Beast that was, and is not*, he says it is *Pagan Rome* <note>original: "Rome Heathen"</note>." This is a clear and faithful presentation of *Ribera’s* explanation, as anyone may see who refers to his commentary on the passage. Let us now see how much—or rather, how little—truth there is in it.

5. In examining this, as well as the following explanation, we may see the usefulness of our demonstrating so plainly that one and the same thing is absolutely understood by the *seven-headed Beast* in the thirteenth chapter and by the *seven-headed Beast* in the seventeenth, as well as by the *Whore of Babylon* and the *two-horned Beast*. For this fact alone will easily expose the trivialities and failings of these interpretations.

6. That the Beast *that was, and is not* cannot be the *Kingdom of the Devil* <note>original: "*Regnum Diaboli*"</note> (as *Ribera* says) or *the Devil reigning in the world through his members, who began to reign in men almost from the beginning of the world* <note>original: "*Diabolus regnans in mundo per sua membra, qui ab initio ferè mundi regnare cæpit in hominibus*"</note> is provable from the Beast with seven heads in the thirteenth chapter, which is the same Beast,

# A Confutation of Ribera upon Book I.

and whose time of continuance is but forty-two months. This is a sign that *Ribera* is completely mistaken in his interpretation. For the same numerical Beast must have the same duration of time. Again, he claims the Beast in the Thirteenth Chapter is *Antichrist*, but calls this one the *Devil*; this is another inconsistency in his narrative. Furthermore, whereas the Beast in the Thirteenth Chapter is said to *come out of the Sea*, it is clear, according to the usual meaning of that symbol <note>original: "Type"</note> in the prophetic style, that it represents a body politic <note>A collective group or organized political entity</note> consisting of men. But how can the *Devil* be such a thing with his dark legions? They are not *men*, but *demons*, nor can they be *led captive* or *killed with the sword*, as is said of the Beast mentioned there. Moreover, the Dragon—that is, the Devil—is said to *deliver his forces* to the *Seven-headed Beast* in that chapter; how then can the Beast be the Devil himself?

To all this, you may add that the *Sixth Head* of the Beast in that chapter is wounded to death and is not healed until the revival of the Beast and his recovery in the *Seventh Head*. But how can the wicked kings of the Sixth Age be said to be wounded to death? Or how can it be said that the Beast does not revive until the Seventh Head, when the Church of Christ was so dreadfully persecuted in the primitive times, and is to this very day so cruelly infested by the *Turks* <note>The Ottoman Empire</note>, as it was previously by the *Saracens* <note>The Arab Muslim caliphates</note>? These actions are no signs of the Sixth Head being *wounded to death* any more than the previous heads—indeed, even less so. Lastly, how can the Devil in this Seventeenth Chapter be the *Image of the restored Beast* that had received the deadly wound? For when the Devil reigns again, he will not "Pagano-Christianize" (if I may use the term), but will instead act as a gross Pagan or a Jew, as our adversaries themselves admit. Therefore, he would not be an *Image*, but either the thing itself, or something entirely different.

7. And regarding the *Whore who rides on the Beast*, I might ask in what sense *Heathen Rome* has *two horns like a lamb* (with other similar questions), but I will omit those for the sake of brevity. I will instead point out how unbecoming <note>original: "indecorous"</note> it is to imagine *Heathen Rome* riding the Devil; it is much more appropriate to conceive of her as being *ridden*—that is to say, guided, driven, and incited by him.

8. But we shall now prove by other arguments, independent of the Thirteenth Chapter, that the *Beast that was, and is not*, is not the Devil. First, if the Devil is a "Beast," what makes him so is his wicked nature, his persecution of the Church of God, and his effort to establish a kingdom of idolaters against God. Now, the Devil has never ceased to be these things from the beginning of the world to this very day. This is the very nature of the "Beast," and that nature has never been killed in him, nor was it ever absent, nor will it ever be. Therefore, it never was—nor ever will be—true of him to say that he is the *Beast that was, and is not*. To be reigning and then to cease reigning does not make him a Beast and then "no Beast"; it only makes him a "non-reigning" Beast. But even that is false: he has never at any time ceased to be a reigning Beast.

### Chapter 1. The Seventeenth Chapter of the Apocalypse.

Christian, yet the Kingdom of the Devil was no less than all the rest of the habitable world, in comparison to which the other is but a small spot of ground; and yet what great portions have been removed from it? Besides his rule within Christendom itself by introducing such a universal spirit of Antichristianity into it, consisting of gross idolatries and bloody persecutions of the dear servants of God. Now let anyone consider and say whether the Devil is a *Beast not reigning* or a *reigning* Beast <note>original Latin: "Beſtia non regnans, or regnans"</note> in the world from Christ’s time to this day. See how groundless this interpretation by *Ribera* is, which understands the Beast that *was, and is not* as referring to the Devil in general, rather than the *Roman Empire* in the sense we have explained.

That it is the *Fourth Empire*, which is the *Roman*, is plainly indicated by the *ten horns*; these are the symbols <note>original: "Enſigns"</note> of the *Fourth Beast* in the Book of *Daniel*, which I think no man has been yet so grossly mistaken as to interpret as the Devil.

9. Besides, this Beast is not only styled *The Beast that was, and is not*, but there is also added to his title "[*and yet is*]." This entire title cannot be true of the Devil reigning in Antichrist's time according to *Ribera*’s interpretation. For if he were reigning then, he would be the exact same Devil in every respect; one could not say he is *not* reigning, even if it were then true that he *is*. So only that part of the title would apply to him—namely, that *he was, and is*. This is another clear exposure of the falseness of *Ribera*’s exposition.

Nor is there any escape in the alternative readings of the text. For copies generally have it, <term>is not, and yet is</term> <note>original Greek: "οὐκ ἔστι, καίπερ ἔστι" (ouk esti, kaiper esti)</note>. This seems like such a contradiction that it has caused some to omit the phrase <term>and yet is</term> and others to change it into <term>and shall be present</term> <note>original Greek: "καὶ παρέσται" (kai parestai)</note>; neither of these versions reaches the meaning of the Apostle. But seeing that the reading we follow is so generally accepted, notwithstanding its seeming harshness and contradictoriness, it is an undeniable argument that it is indeed the true and genuine reading. It shows that the unquestionable authenticity of the manuscripts has allowed it to prevail over the other two readings, which the excessive boldness and lack of skill of some had ventured to put in place of the true one.

10. Again, concerning his exposition of the *Seven Heads*, many things can be criticized. First, his dividing the entire history of the world into *Seven Ages* is groundless and completely arbitrary; there is nothing in either tradition or Scripture to support it. There is, indeed, an ancient tradition of *Elijah* <note>original: "Elias"; referring to the "House of Elias," a Jewish tradition that the world would last 6,000 years</note> that divides the duration of the world into three parts: *two thousand years of emptiness, two thousand years under the Law, and two thousand years of the Messiah*, followed by the great *Sabbath* <note>original: "Sabbatism"</note>. But of such a division as *Ribera* has made here, there is no news nor example in antiquity. And in the steps he takes, he has rudely ignored *Moses*, as if he were not a man important enough to be noticed among the milestones <note>original: "Joints"</note> of this division. Certainly, Moses is one of the most eminent *epochs* <note>original: "Epochas"</note> of time, as appears by that tradition of Elijah, and therefore he ought to have been mentioned before the author reached *David*. Likewise, *Enoch* was so famous for his being taken up into heaven <note>original: "Aſſumption"</note> that his birth ought to have been noted before reaching *Noah* <note>original: "Noe"</note>. There are other equally justifiable divisions which would be easy to observe. But these short hints may suffice.

<margin>Ribera's exposition is faulty in this regard.</margin>...suffices to show how slippery and fictional a commentary Ribera’s exposition is in this regard.

11. Secondly, how can the kings in each of these ages make up only *one head* for an *age*? These kings have no subordination to one another; they are absolute and entirely separated in their respective kingdoms. They have no political coordination or correspondence as heads of a single political body. There is no justification or example for such a thing in the *prophetic style*. If you argue they are *one head* because they belong to one body—*the Devil*—then the entire succession of wicked and persecuting kings throughout all these ages would be *only one head*. Consequently, the Beast would have only one head, not seven. In the prophetic style, distance of time and succession do not create different heads or beasts; rather, a distinction in their nature is required.

12. Thirdly, it is very awkward and inconsistent to make these wicked kings the "heads" of the Devil, when the Devil is actually their prince and head. He is above them both by his superior nature—being an *angel*, though a wicked one, while they are merely wicked men—and by right of jurisdiction. All those who rebel against the kingdom of God join the kingdom of the Devil. Therefore, the exposition in this respect is as awkward and absurd as painting a horse with its head on its *tailbone* <note>original: coccyx</note> and its tail hanging down in front of its chest.

> If you were admitted to see such a sight, my friends, could you restrain your laughter? <note>original Latin: *Spectatum admissi risum teneatis, amici?*</note>

13. Fourthly, if the seven kings are the wicked kings of the seven ages of the world up to the very Day of Judgment, who is that eighth king? In what age of the world will he appear? There seems to be neither room nor time left for him. Truly, *Ribera* has chosen a very clever dealer <note>original: "subtil Merchant"</note> who will slip into all times and places, if possible, for his own advantage. He says this eighth king is *the Devil*. But I say the Devil is the Beast itself according to Ribera's own hypothesis. This eighth king is said to be one of the seven heads. How can the same entity be both the entire Beast and yet only one of its heads? Clearly, his exposition in this regard contradicts common sense and the basic principles of human understanding.

14. Fifthly, the seventh age of the world—which measures the reign of the Antichrist—is most ridiculously out of proportion with the others. According to *Ribera’s* calculation, it lasts only three and a half years. This would be more tolerable if it were proportional to the great exploits the Antichrist is supposed to achieve in that short time. He is supposed to subdue the whole world, or at least the ten kings who (according to their fiction) will rule the world when the Antichrist begins his campaign. After first launching an expedition against three kings—namely, the king of *Egypt*, the king of *Libya*, and the king of *Ethiopia*—and killing them, the other seven will submit to him and become the seven heads of the Antichrist. They even claim that when the first of these is mortally wounded in his service, the Antichrist will miraculously raise him from the dead. Thus, through a bizarre transformation, they have changed the ten horns into seven heads, making the horns of the Antichrist grow before the heads. They are pitifully desperate in their deceptive <note>original: "prevaricatory"</note> interpretations of God's oracles.

### Chapter 1: The Seventeenth Chapter of the Apocalypse

And not content to adorn this great ruler with that one single miracle of raising the dead, they also grant him the power of literally bringing down fire from Heaven and making his own statue speak. They place his royal palace in *Judea*, derive his ancestry from the Tribe of *Dan*, place his throne in the very Temple of God at *Jerusalem*, and proclaim him the expected *Messiah* of the *Jews*, to whom they are all to gather themselves. He must besiege *Rome* and burn it, and call nations from all quarters of the Earth to conspire toward the total extermination of the Christian name from under the canopy of heaven. And, as it seems, despite all the vigilance of the Pope, his whole council of Cardinals, their active agents, and all the military forces of Christendom, he will almost entirely succeed. All of this—which would be the miracle of miracles—is supposed to happen within the space of three and a half years. Indeed, what is even more miraculous is that this *four-part Antichrist* <note>original: "quadrimular"; likely referring to his dominion over the four corners of the world</note> shall not only overrun Christendom but also subdue the *Sultan* <note>original: "Grand Signior," a title for the Ottoman Sultan</note>, overrun the *Persian Empire*, make the *Great Khan* <note>original: "Tartarian Cham," referring to the ruler of the Mongol/Tatar Empire</note> submit to him in the North, and extort loyalty from the remotest kingdoms of *Africa*. This is such a piece of prophetic fiction as no man would ever present even in the most exaggerated fantasy stories. Therefore, Ribera’s explanation concerning the *Seven Heads* of the Beast is incredible in this regard as well.

<margin>15.</margin>
Sixthly and lastly: the *Seven Kings* can only belong to that Beast to whom the *Seven Hills* belong in some way or another. Both are said to be signified by the *Seven Heads* of the Beast, and therefore both have a proper and specific reference to him. Since they are his symbolic heads, what they represent must necessarily belong to him. But it is plain that the *Seven Hills* belong to the *Roman Beast*—that is, to the *Roman Empire*. Therefore, it is necessary that the *Seven Kings* belong to it as well. From this, it follows that these kings cannot be the kings of the "Seven Ages" of the world. For *Rome* was not built until about the Year of the World <note>original: *Anno Mundi*</note> 3200, when even the Fourth Age of the World (according to *Ribera’s* own reckoning) was almost over. So his explanation is impossible in every way, and goes against all sense and reason. And yet it is the very best interpretation the *Roman Catholics* <note>original: "Romanists"</note> have, and the one in which they think they have the safest shelter, as seen in the works of *Cornelius à Lapide* and *Lessius*, who stick to this version rather than any other they have found so far.

<margin>16.</margin>
*Grotius*, seemingly pitying the weakness of all these explanations, has minted a brand new one from his own forge. Although we have examined it elsewhere and found it lacking and counterfeit, it is a matter of such great importance that we will give it a second trial. If it is found to be clearly false again, and more fully exposed as being full of gross inconsistencies and impossibilities, I cannot imagine what more could be needed to give us the greatest assurance anyone could desire regarding the truth of the interpretation we have made of these 17th and 13th chapters of the Apocalypse.

# A Refutation of Grotius upon Book II.

1. **The meaning of the Scarlet Beast with seven Heads and ten Horns, and of the Woman riding him, according to Grotius.** 2. **A refutation of Grotius's interpretation, based on our Joint-Exposition.** 3. **Two main grounds or necessary supports of Grotius’s interpretation: The first, that Saint John reckons the Seven Heads beginning with Claudius, along with a refutation of that idea.** 4. **The second, that this Vision was written in Vespasian's time; 1. Let us therefore more accurately examine the interpretation of *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian who proposed a "Preterist" view of Revelation, seeing it as already fulfilled in the early Roman Empire</note>, the sum of which is this:

# Chapter II. The Seventeenth Chapter of Revelation.

2. These are the main points of **Grotius’s** interpretation of the seventeenth chapter of **Revelation**: the general outlines of which do not match those of the thirteenth chapter. This alone should make his theory suspicious to those who carefully consider the great evidence—or rather, the demonstration—that these two chapters deal with the exact same subjects, but are designed so that one may shed light on the other.

Therefore, regarding the Dragon in the twelfth chapter with **seven heads bearing seven crowns** (which clearly shows that the meaning of **kings**, not **hills**, is to be understood there), who was mortally wounded in one of his heads in 그 fight and then healed so that all the world wondered at him: I would ask **Grotius**, which of these Emperors was mortally wounded in a battle with **Michael**, and was then revived again to the astonishment of the world? Again, there are only seven kings in the thirteenth chapter; how can there be eight in the seventeenth? Thirdly, according to him, the eight kings in the seventeenth chapter are all idolatrous, but the label of idolatry is only on seven heads in the thirteenth, which implies the Beast had no more than that. These things make no sense unless they are explained according to the interpretation I have already presented.

Furthermore, if the Beast in the seventeenth chapter is **Roman pagan idolatry**, why does it continue for only forty-two months in **Grotius's** view? For that is the duration of the **seven-headed beast** in the thirteenth. He also acknowledges that the ten horns of one Beast are not the same as the ten horns of the other. I will omit for now that **Roman Dominion** <note>original: *Dominatio Romana*</note>, which he says is the **Whore of Babylon** in the seventeenth chapter, is not the same as **Magic** <note>original: *Magia*</note> in the other chapter; even though I think it is clear enough that the **Whore of Babylon** and the **two-horned beast** are symbols of the very same thing. But I confess it may seem too overbearing <term>original: "magisterial"; acting as a dogmatic master or authority</term> to make my own interpretation, however true, a rule for others. Therefore, I shall entirely release **Grotius** from such unequal terms and examine his interpretations of these two chapters of **Revelation** based on free and common principles that all men appeal to.

3. And that, first, in a more general way, by searching into the validity of two main grounds which he assumes: The one, *that Saint John begins the counting of the seven heads of the Beast with Claudius*; the other, *that this vision of the Whore of Babylon and the Beast that "was, and is not," was written by Saint John in Vespasian's time*. These grounds are so necessary for his interpretation that without them it is not only inconsistent, but impossible; because **five are said to have fallen, and one currently is**, etc. This interpretation, therefore, necessarily requires and implies that "the one who is" was **Vespasian**, and that he was reigning when this vision was either seen or written. Therefore, his reasons for these grounds deserve a more diligent examination. For the first of these, he alleges two reasons. First, that **Claudius** was the first persecuting Emperor—meaning the first who persecuted the **Christians**. Yet this is contrary to the entire consensus of **ancient history**, which fixes the first persecution upon **Nero**, dismissing that expulsion of the **Jews** from **Rome** as a thing either insignificant or as not properly belonging to...

# A Refutation of Grotius regarding Book II.

...the Christians as such, but as they were Jews. But as far as I can see, **Caius** (the predecessor of **Claudius**) afflicted both Jews and Christians with his outrageous excesses more than **Claudius** ever did. **Grotius** himself wrote about this in his notes on 2 Thessalonians 2: "The greatest grief and fear took full hold of both Jews and Christians." <note>original: *Mæror metúfque maximus & Judæorum & Christianorum plenum habuit effectum*</note>. Therefore, this era <term>epoch</term> could just as well have begun with **Caligula** as with **Claudius** according to this logic, which shows the interpretation to be merely arbitrary. Besides, if the era begins with **Claudius** because he was a persecutor, why did the record not stop when the persecution ended? For **Galba**, **Otho**, **Vitellius**, **Titus**, and **Vespasian** are none of them infamous for any persecution.

The other reason this era is fixed to the reign of **Claudius** is because **St. John** himself was banished to **Patmos** during **Claudius's** time, and therefore **St. John** counts from the time of his banishment, just as **Ezekiel** counts from the era <term>epoch</term> of his captivity. But this is a very weak argument. For **Ezekiel** did not calculate the time from his own specific captivity, but from the captivity of **Jeconiah**, as you may see repeatedly in **Gaspar Sanctius's** commentary on **Ezekiel**. Furthermore, it is one thing for a man to calculate what happened to himself (as **Ezekiel** did) from the time of his private captivity, and quite another to reckon the succession of kings or emperors from such a private starting point. And what is even worse, it is not at all probable that **St. John** was banished to **Patmos** during the reign of **Claudius**. This is not only because he did not suffer as a **Jew**, but as a witness of **Jesus**, but also because he has not recorded that starting date. It would have been very necessary—and poorly omitted—if so much importance were placed on it to ensure the truth of the main visions of **Revelation** <note>original: Apocalyps</note>.

Add to this that **St. John** was not in **Rome**, and was therefore unaffected by this edict of **Claudius**. Even if he had been there, or wherever else he was, there is no mention made of any confinement to specific places in these expulsions. We see in **Acts 18** that **Aquila** and **Priscilla**, who were expelled from **Rome**, lived safely enough in **Corinth**, where **St. Paul** joined them and worked at his trade with them. Finally, it goes against the entire weight of ancient authority—**Irenaeus**, **Origen**, **Tertullian**, **Eusebius**, **Jerome** <note>original: Hieronymus</note>, **Nicephorus**, **Victorinus**, **Primasius**, **Andreas**, and **Arethas**—and against the universal agreement of both Catholics <note>original: Papists</note> and Protestants, who declare with one voice that **St. John’s** exile to **Patmos** occurred under **Domitian**. But I do not need to dwell on these points for now, since the refutation of his second argument will make this one disappear as well.

4. That second argument is: *That the vision of the Whore and the Beast was written by **St. John** in **Vespasian's** time*. But unless it was actually *seen* then, it serves no purpose; for it is not the voice of **St. John**, but of the angel, who says, "*Five have fallen, and one is*." Therefore, the vision, as well as the writing of it, must have occurred in **Vespasian’s** time. It must also have happened on the island of **Patmos**, because right at the beginning of this book of visions, he says once and for all that they happened to him on the Isle of **Patmos**, and he never suggests otherwise throughout the entire book. From this, it is hard to believe they occurred anywhere but in that seclusion. ### Chapter 2: The Seventeenth Chapter of the Book of Revelation

...of the island during Vespasian’s time. From this, I would infer that the vision of the **Whore** and the **Beast** was not seen by **John** during Vespasian’s time. This completely destroys **Grotius’s** exposition <note>Grotius: Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian who argued that the prophecies in Revelation had already been fulfilled in the early centuries of the Church.</note>, as I noted before.

5. This point alone, which he himself admits, should be enough to end this debate. However, since this is a matter of such great importance, I will examine it more thoroughly and demonstrate the utter insufficiency and weakness of **Grotius’s** position. Therefore, sticking closely to the universal consensus <note>original: "Catholick suffrage"</note> of antiquity and of all writers—Protestants and Catholics alike—let us again consider what reason **Grotius** has for exiling **Saint John** to **Patmos** during the reign of **Claudius**. For **Claudius’s** act of expelling the **Jews** from **Rome** is very different from banishing **John** to **Patmos**.

First, **Grotius** would have to prove that "Christians" are meant by the term "**Jews**" in that context. There are significant reasons to believe that the **Jews**, not the **Christians**, are the ones intended there. First, because the **Christians** sought a kingdom in heaven, not on earth; but the **Jews** were obsessed with finding a **Christ** or **Messiah** who would make them masters of the world. Therefore, only they could seem dangerous in **Rome**, as their riots were aimed at gaining earthly power. Second, in the **Book of Acts**, this decree by **Claudius** is mentioned as applying only to the **Jews**. **Aquila** and **Priscilla**, being **Jews** (for there is not the slightest hint that they were **Christians** at that time), are said to have left **Rome** for **Corinth**. Third, the fresh memory of **Tiberius’s** decree against the accusers of **Christians** might still have influenced his successors, so that no such harsh sentence would be passed against them so suddenly—especially since they were a people, as I said, whose thoughts were on heaven and who were not looking for earthly opportunities <note>original: "did not lie at catch for things on Earth"</note>. And lastly, none of the ancient writers ever blamed **Claudius** for any injury done to the **Christians**. If they had been banished and **Saint John** himself confined to **Patmos** (which would have been a very severe punishment, and to human nature little better than death), the shame of such a great cruelty would undoubtedly have been passed down to us by the Church, and **Claudius** would not have escaped being labeled a persecutor.

Nor do those words of **Suetonius** <note>Suetonius: A Roman historian who wrote *The Lives of the Twelve Caesars*.</note> prove that the decree applied to the **Christians**: "Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome, who were constantly rioting at the instigation of Chrestus" <note>original: *Claudius Judæos impulsore Chresto tumultuantes Româ expulit*</note>. This only proves that there was a decree against the **Jews**. For who can believe there is any truth in his claim that they rioted "at the instigation of Chrestus," given that **Christ** was no longer alive on earth, much less in **Rome**, to incite the **Jews** to riot? It is more likely that the **Jews** were occasionally annoyed with the **Christians** in **Rome** and made a great fuss about their acknowledgment of a **Messiah** who was crucified—someone from whom there was no hope of regaining their liberty or making them powerful in this world. Therefore, because there was such a stir among the **Jews** concerning their "**Chrestus**" or **Messiah** in opposition to the **Christians**, vague rumors might have led **Suetonius** to phrase it as he did. But this insight into the nature of the **Jews** might have caused **Claudius** to expel them from the city—perhaps even to favor the **Christians**, as well...

# A Rebuttal of Grotius on Book II

<margin>Orosius, Book 7, Chapter 6.</margin>
...as for his own security. This passage in **Suetonius** <note>Suetonius (c. 69–122 AD) was a Roman historian who wrote about the early emperors.</note> is so far from proving that this edict applied to the **Christians**, that **Orosius** <note>Paulus Orosius (c. 375–418 AD) was a Christian historian and theologian.</note> gives this judgment of it: "It is by no means clear whether he ordered the Jews—who were rioting against Christ—to be restrained and suppressed, or whether he also intended the Christians to be expelled at the same time as people of a related religion" <note>original: *Utrum contra Christum tumultuantes Judæos coërceri & comprimi jusserit, an etiam Christianos simul, velut cognatæ religionis homines, voluerit expelli, nequaquam discernitur.*</note>. So, there is very little certainty that **Claudius** did any harm at all to the **Christians** through that edict mentioned in **Suetonius**.

6. But even if we suppose that the decree reached the **Christians** in **Rome**, it is merely an arbitrary guess to think it reached other parts of the Empire. Furthermore, if it did reach other parts of the Empire, it was not a forced confinement—as I hinted above—but rather a general banishment from one specific place. In that case, it is most likely it only applied to those involved in riots, or at least from towns where they might have caused riots. This would have been highly unlikely in the place where **Saint John** lived, as the sweetness and peaceableness of his spirit would tempt any sensible governor to keep him there to help maintain order. And yet, this theory is so far-fetched that it suggests he is the *only* man treated so harshly; no one can produce an example of anyone else being banished in **Claudius's** time. Yet, all the **Apostles** were certainly busy enough performing their duties to spread **Christianity** throughout the Empire.

7. But you might say that this record of **Claudius** expelling the **Jews** from **Rome**, when combined with the testimony of **Epiphanius** <note>Epiphanius (c. 310–403 AD) was a bishop and church father known for his works against heresies.</note>—who claims John was banished to **Patmos** under that same Emperor—is a "double cord" of evidence that cannot easily be broken. I would more easily grant that if either of those points had any strength on their own. However, I have shown the first has none, and I shall now do the same for the second.

There are two passages cited from **Epiphanius**. The first is from *Heresies 51*, Section 33, where he writes the following about **Saint John**: "But he was prophesying in the times of Claudius Caesar at the farthest, when he arrived in Patmos..." <note>original: Αὐτὸς δὲ προφητεύων ἐν χρόνοις Κλαυδίου Καίσαρος ἀνωτάτω, ὅτε εἰς τὴν Πάτμον ἔπληξεν</note>. But these words are not spoken definitively regarding **Saint John** being in **Patmos** during **Claudius's** reign; they only state that he was in **Patmos** and prophesied there. Regarding the timing, he says it was "at the farthest" in **Claudius's** reign. That is the meaning of the Greek word *anotato* <term>original: ἀνωτάτω; meaning "at the highest" or "at the furthest point back in time"</term>—it was the earliest that he could be thought to have prophesied in **Patmos** as an exile. He does not say he *definitely* prophesied then. 

So, it is a vague and conjectural statement concerning the time. It only says that this is the maximum distance back in time within which he might be thought to have prophesied, without denying that the actual time of his prophesying might have been later—for instance, in **Domitian's** <note>Emperor Domitian (reigned 81–96 AD). Most traditional accounts date John’s exile to his reign.</note> time. **Petavius** <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a French Jesuit theologian and scholar.</note> is so confident of this that he wrote a short marginal note next to the phrase "During the reign of Claudius" in the text: "In error; should be Domitian" <note>original: *Mendosè, pro Domitiano*</note>. He took it for granted that **Epiphanius** was speaking more definitively than I believe he actually does. I believe both **Grotius** and others who cite this passage for the same purpose were aware of the meaning of *anotato* that I have suggested, which is why they left it out of their citations, as it weakens their argument.

Furthermore, it is no proof that **Epiphanius** dogmatically defines **Saint John's** prophecy as occurring in **Claudius's** time. If he were not convinced of that opinion, he would have followed the standard view, which would have been more effective to use against the **Montanists** <note>The Montanists were an early Christian movement that claimed to receive new prophetic revelations.</note>, who sought to diminish the truth of the Apocalypse...

# Chapter 2: The Seventeenth Chapter of Revelation

...**Revelation**, because of the *Epistle to the Church of Thyatira*, which they claim was written before there was even a church established there: for in their view, the later it was written, the better. But even assuming the Church Father was uncertain which account was true, and not being entirely sure if the **Montanists** <note>The Montanists were a 2nd-century Christian movement that emphasized new prophetic revelations.</note> would prove that there was no church at **Thyatira** during **Domitian's** <note>Domitian (reigned 81–96 AD) is the emperor traditionally associated with John’s exile.</note> time either; is it likely that he would stubbornly settle on **Domitian's** reign rather than the other? Indeed, he seems to favor the objection when it is presented this way, because he believes he gains an advantage over his opponents; by their own logic, they are forced to acknowledge that **Saint John**, or the author of this book of visions, was truly endowed with the spirit of prophecy. "For if they say there was not a church at Thyatira in existence at the moment Saint John wrote, they plainly show that Saint John did prophesy and suggested beforehand that there would be one" <note>original: Ἐὰν γὰρ εἴπωσιν, οὐκ ἔνι νῦν ἐκκλησία εἰς Θυάτειρα, δεικνύει πεπροφητευκέναι τὸν Ἰωάννην</note>. Therefore, **Epiphanius** found little reason why he should choose the common opinion over his own based on the state of the current controversy.

8. The other passage from **Epiphanius** is found in *Against Heresies*, Book 51, Section 12, where he tells us how **Saint John** was driven and compelled to write the Gospel by the prompting of the Holy Spirit. Although he very much declined the task "out of reverence and humility" <note>original: δι’ εὐλάβειαν καὶ ταπεινοφροσύνην</note>, he was forced by that inner drive in his old age, "when he was more than ninety years old, after his return from Patmos, which happened in Claudius Caesar's time" <note>original: μετὰ ἔτη ἐνενήκοντα τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ζωῆς, μετὰ τὴν αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς Πάτμου ἐπάνοδον τὴν ἐπὶ Κλαυδίου γενομένην Καίσαρος</note>. Here, the mention of his return from **Patmos** is added as a confirmation of the Apostle's great age at that time.

Now let us see what help this "great witness and most diligent inquirer into history" <note>original: Magnus testis & Historiarum diligentissimus Inquisitor</note> (as **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch legal scholar and theologian whose theories on Revelation the author is refuting.</note> calls him—just as he calls **Petavius**, <note>Denis Pétau (Petavius) was a Jesuit scholar who often disagreed with the chronology Grotius used.</note> who plainly contradicts him on this very point) can offer our learned interpreter in this case. For this passage, even if the previous one had any strength, completely nullifies <term>original: "obtund," meaning to blunt or weaken</term> it. It shows that **Epiphanius** was not at all diligent in chronology (as **Alcazar** <note>Luis del Alcázar (1554–1613) was a Spanish Jesuit theologian.</note> has also correctly observed) by claiming **Saint John** was over ninety years old in **Claudius's** time. In contrast, the common tradition of the Church is that he was very young when he began his apostleship. **Saint Jerome** says that Christ chose him when he was only a youth or a child. **Baronius** <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607) was an influential Catholic historian.</note> calculates that he was exactly twenty-five years old at the time of the Crucifixion of our Savior. The Scripture itself also implies that he was quite young, in that Christ says to his Mother concerning John, *Woman, behold your son*; which would imply that he was at least as young as Christ himself. Christ was born of the Virgin when she was only fifteen years old, as **Nicephorus** relates from a letter by **Euodius**, the Bishop of **Antioch**. But according to **Epiphanius's** chronology, **Saint John** would be at least twenty years older than the Blessed Virgin, regarding whom Christ nevertheless said to John, *Behold your Mother*. And even worse, if **Saint John** was ninety years old when he left **Patmos** under the reign of **Claudius**, it would push the birth of Christ back nearly forty years,

These absurdities show that Epiphanius is not as great or as unquestionable a witness in history as Grotius would make him out to be. Therefore, the scholar Petavius once again decisively notes in the margin, opposite Epiphanius’s mention of "the return that occurred under Claudius Caesar" <note>original: "ἐπάνοδον τὴν ἐπὶ Κλαυδίου γενομένην Καίσαρος"</note>, that "under Cocceius Nerva, John was recalled from exile" <note>original: "Sub Cocceio Nerva Joannes revocatur ab exilio"</note>. This is certainly the truth, and it agrees with the age Epiphanius assigns to Saint John at the time he wrote the Gospel. For assuming he was born around the same time as our Savior, or a little later, the writing of the Gospel would fall during the years of Nerva’s reign, or at least a few years after Domitian, as you will find recorded in historical chronologies.

<margin>Section 4.</margin>

9. But even if we assume Epiphanius’s testimony is valuable in this case, the same Epiphanius who testifies that John was on Patmos under the reign of Claudius also testifies that he left it during the same reign. As I have already noted, this ruins Grotius’s plan. Grotius wants Saint John to be prophesying during Vespasian’s time; otherwise, everything falls apart regarding his interpretation of the seventeenth chapter of Revelation <note>original: "Apocalyps"</note>. But I believe I have clearly proved that nothing can be gained from Epiphanius to support Grotius’s theory. These passages from the Church Father are either mere conjectures, oversights, or errors by the scribe, who apparently wrote the name "Claudius" more easily than those of the other two Emperors. This is evident in that second citation: Saint John was indeed about that age when he left Patmos during the time of Cocceius Nerva, but not during the time of Claudius.

10. So, Grotius does not have even a single witness to support his new invention. And even if he had this one, what is one witness compared to the entire consensus of antiquity and the Church? Indeed, what is Epiphanius’s testimony compared to that of a single Father like Irenaeus? Irenaeus lived two hundred years closer to Saint John’s time than Epiphanius did, and he expressly asserts, according to the historian Eusebius, that the Book of Revelation was given to Saint John at the end of Domitian’s reign. For when speaking about the Name of the Beast, Irenaeus writes:

> "For if his name were meant to be openly proclaimed at this present time, it would have been declared by the one who saw the apocalypse. For it was seen not long ago, but almost in our own generation, toward the end of Domitian's reign" <note>original: "Εἰ γὰρ ἔδει ἀναφανδὸν ἐν τῷ νῦν καιρῷ κηρύττεσθαι τοὔνομα αὐτοῦ, δι᾽ ἐκείνου ἂν ἐρρήθη τοῦ καὶ τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν ἑωρακότος. οὐ γὰρ πρὸ πολλοῦ χρόνου ἑωράθη πρὸς τῷ τέλει Δομιτιανοῦ ἀρχῆς."</note>.

11. I have no doubt that this is the genuine meaning of these words, and that he is not speaking only of the vision of the Beast under the name of "The Apocalypse," but of the entire collection of visions known by that name. Otherwise, for the sake of clarity, he would not have said "the one who saw the apocalypse" <note>original: "τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν ἑωρακότος"</note>, but "the one who saw *his* apocalypse" <note>original: "τὴν αὐτοῦ ἀποκάλυψιν ἑωρακότος"</note>—especially considering "Apocalypse" had already become a well-known title for this volume of visions. Furthermore, the *Name* of the Beast was not seen by Saint John, but rather the *Number* of his name. Therefore, while the Latin version says, "The name of the Antichrist through him..." <note>original: "Antichristi nomen per ipsum..."</note>

"It would certainly have been published by him who saw the Apocalypse, for it was not seen long ago" <note>original: "ipsum utique editum fuisset qui Apocalypsin videret, neque enim ante multum temporis visum est"</note>; I would easily believe that *seen* <note>original: "visum"</note> was mistakenly written for *visions* <note>original: "visa"</note> by the carelessness of the scribe. For unless the translator of **Irenaeus** had understood "he who saw the Apocalypse" <note>original: "qui Apocalypsin videret"</note> as referring to the whole collection of visions, and not just the Beast and his name, he would have instead said "the Revelation" <note>original: "Revelationem"</note> and, to be sure, added "of it" <note>original: "ejus"</note> to make the sense more distinct and certain: "he who saw the Revelation of it" <note>original: "qui Revelationem ejus videret"</note>. And lastly, even if we suppose this testimony proved only that the vision in the thirteenth chapter of **Revelation** <note>original: "Apocalyps"</note> was seen at the end of **Domitian's** reign (which I do not believe for a moment), it will not serve **Grotius's** purpose. This is because the seventeenth chapter is later, both in the order of its placement in the Apocalypse and by its very nature. Since it is the clearest vision concerning the Beast with seven heads and ten horns and contains the key for correctly understanding the others, it ought to come last; the commentary is naturally later than the text, according to common sense and reason.

12. Therefore, seeing as there is no proof at all that **Claudius** persecuted the Christians—much less that he exiled **John** to **Patmos**—but that **Domitian** was a notorious persecutor, and universal antiquity attests that Saint **John** was banished to **Patmos** under him and received the Apocalypse there, there is nothing to stop our conclusion. We may infer that the whole volume of those visions was written there by him toward the latter end of **Domitian's** reign, as **Irenaeus** has affirmed (the second persecution not beginning until the tenth year of **Domitian**). I mean the latter end of his real and uncontroversial reign, when he succeeded his brother **Titus**, not that imaginary one during his father’s absence, for he was not truly Emperor then. And even if we should admit he had two reigns, if the "end of his reign" is mentioned generally, as it is here in **Irenaeus**, it must either signify the end of all the time he reigned or the end of his more notorious and acknowledged reign—which in this case are the same thing, and therefore most certainly understood. So, there is no avoiding the authority of **Irenaeus** by this trick. Not to mention that there is no persecution recorded in all of **Vespasian's** reign, and therefore no **Patmos** for Saint **John**, and consequently no prophecy, as I have noted above. So, there is not the least shadow of probability that the Apocalypse was written at any other time than what **Irenaeus** has declared.

13. The Apocalypse itself also witnesses against this dream of Saint **John** being on **Patmos** under **Claudius's** reign in that general preface to all the visions:
> I, **John**, who am also your brother and companion in tribulation, and in the kingdom and patience of **Jesus Christ**, etc.
This shows it was a time of great distress among the Christians and of sharp <term>original: "smart"</term> persecution. This was true for no one but **John** if this occurred in **Claudius's** time—at least not in **Asia**, where the churches he wrote to were located.

But there is yet another more relevant place for our purpose: I mean the martyrdom of **Antipas**, Bishop of the Church of **Pergamum**, who suffered under **Domitian** about the tenth year of his reign. That which I note as most remarkable in his story is that he was urged by the governor of the place to renounce Christianity because it was but a novelty, arguing to him "that older things are more honorable" <note>original: "ὅτι τὰ πρεσβύτερα τιμιώτερα"</note>, the very same argument...

argument that Catholics use to tempt our modern "Antipas" or opponents of the Pope. But the point I am making is this: the mention of Antipas's martyrdom as a past event at the very beginning of this Book of Visions clearly shows that they were all seen after the start of the second Persecution, which occurred under Emperor **Domitian**, more than twenty years after **Titus** destroyed **Jerusalem**. 14. He interprets the **Seals** and **Trumpets** as events that happened many years *before* this prophecy was even written. This makes the **Revelation** about as sensible as if it were a "prediction" of things that have already happened! Yet the preface to the entire book explicitly states: ***The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave to him, to show his servants*** what must soon take place <note>original Greek: "ἃ δεῖ γενέσθαι ἐν τάχει"</note>, ***such things as are shortly to come to pass***. But according to **Grotius’s** interpretation of the **Seals** and **Trumpets** (which are a major part of the prophecy), as well as the battle between **Michael** and the **Dragon** and several other visions, the preface should have read: *The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave to him, to show his servants what things happened a while ago*. Since these things were written so cryptically <note>original: "Ænigmatically"</note>—as if the author intended to hide what had already clearly happened in real life—the title should have been "The Hiding" <note>original: "Obvelation"</note> or "The Darkening" <note>original: "Obscuration"</note> rather than the **Revelation**. Such is the nature of a single absurdity: once it is accepted, it leads to the creation and multiplication of many others.

# Chapter III. The Seventeenth Chapter of the Apocalypse.

1. Therefore, because the foundation of **Grotius’s** explanations is so false and unstable—and such that it must collapse if pressured—the structure cannot be sound or well-formed, but is instead forced, distorted, and misshapen. For if prophecy fits times it was not intended for just as well as those it was, it will be shrouded in such invincible darkness that it will lose both its usefulness and authenticity.

We shall show, therefore, that just as **Grotius** has relied on a false premise, his explanations of these **seventeenth** and **thirteenth** chapters are correspondingly forced and inapplicable. He has left the clear path and rushed recklessly through obstacles, tearing up all boundaries just to gather a "bouquet" of ideas that both smell bad and wither in his hand the moment he picks them.

2. Even if we suppose that the visions of the **seventeenth** and **thirteenth** chapters were given to Saint **John** during **Vespasian’s** reign (which I consider undoubtedly false), let us take a brief look at the inconsistencies and flaws in his interpretation. 

First, he claims the **Seven Heads** of the Beast are **seven emperors**, five of whom were gone by **Vespasian’s** time: **Claudius**, **Nero**, **Galba**, **Otho**, and **Vitellius**. I have already shown that there is no reason at all for him to begin his calculation <note>original: "compute"</note> with **Claudius**. **John** was not banished during his reign, nor was **Claudius** as wicked an emperor as his predecessor **Gaius Caligula**. Furthermore, the Church does not date its persecutions before **Nero**, and there were no complaints against **Nero’s** successors until **Domitian**. Why should these specific men be considered "**Heads of Blasphemy**" <note>original: "Heads of Blasphemy"; a reference to the beast in Revelation 17:3, which is described as being "full of names of blasphemy."</note> more than any other emperors? Therefore, it is entirely baseless and fabricated to claim that only *five* heads preceded **Vespasian**, when he was actually the tenth since **Julius Caesar**. It is also absurd to include only two of his successors, **Titus** and **Domitian**, when at least thirty followed him, during whose reigns eight of the major persecutions of Christians occurred.

3. **Grotius** has no excuse for this shortened calculation except that it conveniently allows **Domitian** to be the "**Beast that was, and is not, and yet is**" <note>original: "Beast that was, and is not, and yet is"; a famous riddle from Revelation 17:8.</note>. This is because **Domitian** had acted as emperor during his father's absence, "was not" emperor when the vision was allegedly given, and "yet was" (meaning he was alive) and would "**ascend out of the bottomless pit again**"—that is, become emperor again after the deaths of his father and his brother **Titus**. **Grotius** congratulates himself on this point, greatly insulting the early Church Fathers. Being much closer to **Domitian's** time than **Grotius**, they still could not see this prophecy being fulfilled in him. If **Grotius** is right, it would seem the prophecy was useless to the Church, providing them with no warning at all.

4. To speak my mind freely on this notion <note>original: "Conceit"</note>, it seems to make the **Spirit of Prophecy** interested in predicting trivial things rather than useful and important matters. I have already proved through historical timelines that this assumption about the date of the vision is false (which removes the main support for this interpretation). Additionally, there are several inconsistencies <note>original: "Inconcinnities"</note> in his argument, historical gaps, and nothing that isn't forced or suspicious.

# A Refutation of Grotius on Book II.

For, in the first place, I will deny that **Domitian** was ever really and truly emperor in his father's time. He was merely a <term>pragmatical</term> <note>original: "pragmatical" — in this context, meaning meddlesome or a busybody</note> and **active young man**, and did, as his father **Vespasian** complained, <note>original: "terminos ætatis & concessa filio egredi" — overstep the boundaries of his age and what was permitted to a son</note>. That is to say, he went somewhat beyond his limits, which he could do without being emperor, just as he might be greeted by that title as a form of flattery in the court. But a polite greeting is not a formal installation into imperial power. Otherwise, **Titus** would also have been emperor during his father's time; for the soldiers, upon his taking of **Jerusalem**, greeted him as emperor with a universal shout of congratulations. Furthermore, he even wore a diadem at **Memphis** during the consecration of the **Egyptian Apis** <note>The sacred bull of ancient Egyptian religion</note>, and there were great rumors and suspicions that he had seized the eastern part of the empire against his father's wishes. It would be too large a task to delve deep into history here; but I do not doubt that, when all the records are considered, **Titus** would be found to be as much an emperor in his father's time as **Domitian**—and likely much more so. Therefore, he would be a more fitting candidate for the **Beast that was, and is not**, than **Domitian** in that regard. However, neither of them is fit, because neither was truly and really an emperor before their father's death.

Besides this, it is quite contrary to the prophetic style to call a **Single Person** a **Beast**, which in that style always signifies a **Body Politic** <note>A collective group of people acting as a single political entity, such as a state or empire</note>. Furthermore, to say **he is not, because he is not Emperor**, is hardly true. That elegant contradiction—[**that he is not, and yet is**]—as interpreted by Grotius (meaning he is a man, though not an emperor), is a weak and watered-down comparison to the explanation I have given. I have shown that the Image of the **Beast** is the **Beast** and yet is not the **Beast** <note>The author refers to his own interpretation where the "Beast" represents a system of power rather than an individual</note>. But they could not say during **Vespasian's** time, nor in **Domitian's** own time, that **Domitian** was emperor and yet not emperor at the same time.

And, lastly, his **ascending out of the bottomless pit** is a prophetic phrase. It is the same as to **ascend out of the Sea**, or the **multitude of Waters**, which is a description applied to **Bodies Politic**, because they consist of multitudes of men. It is not appropriate to say this of a **Single Person**, any more than the term **Beast** is appropriate in the prophetic style.

5. Secondly, the Angel's interpretation of the **Heads of the Beast** is that they are so many kings, of whom, says **Grotius**, **Domitian** is the eighth: <term>he himself is the eighth king</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτὸς ὄγδοός ἐστιν — autòs ogdoós estin</note>. Therefore, **Domitian** is plainly and unavoidably the eighth head, according to **Grotius's** interpretation and the earlier explanation of the Angel, which cannot be rejected. From this, it would follow that the Beast has **eight heads**, which directly contradicts all the visions of the Beast, which always show him as **seven-headed**.

Thirdly, **Grotius** nonetheless makes **Domitian** the Beast himself. This is an impossibility: that one and the same being should be both the whole Beast and a single Head of the Beast. Besides, what a strained meaning—or rather, what an obvious piece of nonsense—it would be to claim that **Claudius**, **Nero**, **Galba**, **Otho**, **Vitellius**, **Vespasian**, and **Titus** were the **Heads of Domitian**. They were all of equal supremacy—meaning **Domitian** was equal to those seven previous **Caesars**—and they were not in power when he was the Beast; therefore, it is impossible for them to be his **Seven Heads**.
