[Truth overcomes] all things, *Esdras* 4 <note>Refers to 1 Esdras 4:41 from the Apocrypha: "Great is Truth, and mighty above all things."</note>. These courageous defenders <note>original: "stout Champions"</note> shall therefore draw their swords against the beauty of his wisdom; that is to say, they shall use the "Sword of the Spirit," which is the Word of God—even that sword that comes out of the mouth of the one who rides on the white horse <note>A reference to Christ in Revelation 19:11–15</note>. This sword consists of pure reason and Scripture, used against the finely-crafted subtleties, whether academic <note>original: "Scholastick"</note> or political, and all the plausible and impressive pretenses of Papal <note>original: "Pontifician"</note> wisdom. The glory of the Gospel shall darken the "Seat of the Beast" <note>The Papal throne or authority</note>, just as sunshine obscures or puts out the light of an artificial fire. Thus shall the Papal power perish from the midst of the nations.

6. And then, regarding that more-than-imperial majesty and splendor in the Pope's vestments <note>original: "Habiliments"</note>, it is said of this King of *Tyre*, *"Every precious stone was your covering: the sardius, the topaz, and the diamond"* <note>Ezekiel 28:13</note>. This is similar to what is said of the **Whore of Babylon**, that she was *decked with gold, precious stones, and pearls.*

Although this Papal power is represented by the image of a woman in the **Revelation** <note>original: "Apocalyps"</note> to better illustrate the **seductive secrets** <note>original: "Meretricious Mysteries"</note> of that Church, its arrogance—and specifically that of the Pope—also seems to be symbolized by the **King of Babylon**. For is it possible that anyone should doubt that, since *Babylon* is such an acknowledged symbol <note>original: "Type"</note> of the **Antichristian Church**, the head of this Church is likewise symbolized by the **King of Babylon**?

7. Let us hear, therefore, what *Isaiah* <note>original: "Esay"</note> says of this exalted ruler in the fourteenth chapter, verses 12 and 13:

> 12. *How you are fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! How you are cut down to the ground, you who weakened the nations!*
>
> 13. *For you have said in your heart: "I will ascend into heaven; I will exalt my throne above the stars of God; I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, on the sides of the north."*

How every nation is weakened by the power of the Pope, we have outlined <note>original: "adumbrated"</note> in our *Idea of Antichristianism*. His ascending into "heaven," in the prophetic style <note>original: "stylo Prophetico"</note>, and his exalting himself above the "stars of God" (which refers to the stars of the greatest magnitude in this symbolic heaven), is the same as his climbing into Imperial power and advancing himself above all the kings and princes of the **Roman Empire**. His "sitting upon the mount of the congregation" refers to his sitting in the Temple of God. Thus, there seems to be a double allusion: both to the mountain of the Temple of God at *Jerusalem*, and to the mountains (or perhaps one specific mountain) at *Rome*, which is the chief city of the Church of Christ. This "sitting upon this mount of the congregation," or the Church of God, matches perfectly with the prophecy of **his sitting in the Temple of God**.

Nor is the phrase ["on the sides of the north"] included for no reason, though it seems a small detail in the literal text. It appears to foretell that the dominion of the Pope was to spread most notably northward; we know he could never make much progress with the **Southern Churches**, as the **African Church** always resisted him very stoutly—besides other considerations which I will omit for the sake of brevity.

...that day shall not come unless a falling away comes first <note>original Greek: *ean mē elthē hē apostasia prōton*</note>, before that prominent *Apostasy* occurs (for that is how *Alcazar* <note>Luis del Alcázar (1554–1613), a Spanish Jesuit theologian</note> interprets the definite article "the" in this place)—that lapse into idolatrous worship which is rebellion against God and Christ; *and that Man of Sin be revealed, the Son of Perdition.*

That this is to be understood as referring to that notable Antichrist is the common opinion of the ancient church fathers, and even of *Alcazar*, *Ribera* <note>Francisco Ribera (1537–1591), a Jesuit doctor of theology who pioneered the futurist interpretation of prophecy</note>, and *Bellarmine* <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), an influential Italian Jesuit and Cardinal</note> himself. However, we argue that this *Antichrist* will prove to be the *Pope along with his clergy*. It is a weak defense to claim that the *Man of Sin* must refer to only one single person; in prophetic writing, a *Man* (as well as a *Woman*) can easily signify not only a succession of individual men but an entire political body. This is done through a "union of many into one" <note>original: "Henopoeia," a figure of speech where a collective is spoken of as a single entity</note>. Thus, it refers here to the succession of fallen Popes and their *Clergy*, who are called the *Son of Perdition* because they are to be destroyed by the brightness of Christ’s coming and the power and light of the Gospel. *Not by worldly power nor by might, but by my Spirit, says the Lord of Hosts.*

*Verse 4. Who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God or what is worshipped; so that he, as God, sits in the Temple of God, showing himself that he is God.*

That the *Bishop of Rome* fulfills every tiny detail of this prediction will be obvious to anyone who looks back at what we have written in our *Idea of Antichristianism*, and what is generally known to all who have even a slight knowledge of the history of Christian affairs. For it is plain from history that he *opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God* in some significant way. He opposes and exalts himself above *Christ*—who is truly God—in all of Christ's roles: *King, Priest,* and *Prophet*, as I have abundantly shown. Consequently, he exalts himself above all the saints. Indeed, he is specifically set above the *Saints* and *Angels*, as Bishop *Downham* <note>George Downame (died 1634), Bishop of Derry, who wrote extensively against the Papacy</note> proves at length in his treatise *Concerning the Antichrist* <note>original Latin: *De Antichristo*</note>, book 4, chapter 4. As for the *Emperors*, he treads on their very necks and makes them his servants; he kicks off their crowns with his feet, and then puts them back on with his feet. It is so plain that this Prince of the "Crowning City" <note>Rome</note> exalts himself "above everything called God or an object of worship" <note>original Greek: *epi panta legomenon theon ē sebasma*</note>. That is to say, he exalts himself above all powers whatsoever, whether heavenly or earthly. Among the earthly powers are the "Venerable ones" <note>original Greek: *Sebastoi*</note> or *Augusti*, the *Roman Emperors*.

<margin>
*Idea of Antichristianism*, Book 2, Chapter 11.

A hint is enough; a more complete expansion of his enormous pride is set down in the aforementioned *Idea*, which is nonetheless obvious and well-known both by common reputation and in history. So it is that he, *as God, sits in the Temple of God, showing himself that he is God.* "Demonstrating himself that he is God" <note>original Greek: *Apodeiknynta heauton hoti esti Theos*</note>; that is to say, doing and accepting such things as—if they rightly belonged to him—would prove that he were God. But by doing so, he "shows himself to be God" <note>original Latin: *ostentare se Deum esse*</note>; he puts on a display as if he were God. *The Temple of God* here is to be understood either literally; and then it is plain how well it fits with the Pope’s...

<header>Chapter XVIII. On the Prophecy of the Man of Sin.</header>

The Pope receives honor fitting for God on the high altar in St. Peter’s Church at Rome after his election, where he is adored. Or, if the "Temple of God" is understood figuratively as the people who bear the name of Christ and are dedicated to him, he sits and rules there too, as if he were God—claiming to be infallible and uncontrollable, making laws obsolete or granting dispensations even against the laws of God himself.

> Verse 5. *Do you not remember that, when I was with you, I told you these things?*

> 6. *And now you know what holds him back, so that he might be revealed in his own time.*

That is to say, you know what hinders him from revealing and showing himself to the world. For all things exist in the confused potential of the universe but remain hidden, like a rose in winter, until they appear in their own season <note>original Greek: *en tō autou kairō*</note>. But that which hindered this appearing of Antichrist was, according to the general opinion of the ancient church, the integrity of the Roman Empire. Until the Empire broke into ten kingdoms, Antichrist was not to exist—and perhaps not to appear, in another sense, until even later. To prove that "the one who restrains" <note>original Greek: *ho katechōn*</note> is the Roman Empire, Alcazar <note>Luis del Alcázar (1554–1613), a Jesuit theologian</note> cites many witnesses including Malvenda, Tertullian, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Theophylact, and Oecumenius. To these he adds Anselm, Haymo, Strabo, Thomas Aquinas, Lyranus, Cajetan, Bellarmine, Suarez, and Pamelius.

> Verse 7. *For the Mystery of Iniquity is already at work; only he who now restrains will continue to do so, until he is taken out of the way.*

Tertullian, Chrysostom, and most other commentators (as Alcazar confirms) understand this "working of iniquity" in the Apostles' time to be only a "type" or "figure" of what would occur under Antichrist. They believe there was something then actually in existence, or perhaps "a-brewing," that was a preliminary representation of the state of the Church under Antichrist. Alcazar argues it was Roman Paganism or the worship of idols. However, that was no *Mystery of Iniquity* <note>The author implies paganism was openly evil, whereas a "mystery" implies something hidden or deceptive within the church</note>. But he might argue that paganism was a "type" of what would eventually become a "mystery"—and a marvelous one at that—namely, the living image of Paganism revived within Christianity. Therefore, the future Mystery "worked" through its earlier type. For the Empire, revived into idolatry, is called the Beast that *was, and is not, and yet is* <note>referencing Revelation 17:8</note>. This concept is not entirely far-fetched.

But I am more inclined to think that the Apostle might have been speaking of something already present in Christianity—meaning among its professors—that bore some resemblance to the great Antichrist who was to appear in his proper season. He may have intended this "present working of the Mystery of Iniquity" to refer to the misconduct of some Christians, or their leanings toward it, having caught a strong taste of the Antichristian spirit—particularly the spirit of fighting for power and status. Whether Simon Magus <note>A figure from Acts 8 who tried to buy spiritual power; often cited as the first heretic</note> might be hinted at here, I shall consider in the proper place.

But this Antichristian heat of ambition had to play for smaller stakes until "the one who restrains" <note>original Greek: *ho katechōn*</note>—the Roman Emperor most properly so-called, meaning the one who holds his imperial seat at Rome—was removed or destroyed. This series of Caesars ended with Romulus Augustulus <note>The last Western Roman Emperor, deposed in 476 AD</note>. After this, the Pope played his pranks in these Western parts of the Empire and gathered much wealth and power to...

> *Verse 8. And then shall that Wicked one be revealed, whom the Lord shall consume with the Spirit of his mouth, and destroy with the brightness of his coming.*

That Wicked one—the lawless one <note>original Greek: *ho anomos*</note>—is the one who exalts himself above the Laws of God and Christ, and who can grant dispensations from them as he pleases. His destruction comes through the preaching of the Gospel and the victorious evidence of Truth—by clear and convincing Reason spread throughout the world by those who speak by the Spirit of God and by a Principle of Life within them. For their mouth is the mouth of God, and their breath is like a flaming torrent to consume the ungodly Deceiver.

The remainder of this prophecy we have explained already, and therefore we do not need to repeat our explanation here. No prophecy can be more explicitly applied to any event than this one is to the Papal Power and its deception. Therefore, since the effect is already present in the world, who can doubt that this is the prediction of it? This is especially true since we have the common agreement of the ancient church that it is to be understood as someone who appears after the Roman Empire breaks into pieces. If anyone asks Tertullian <note>Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155 – c. 220 AD), an early Christian author</note> who "the one who restrains" <note>original Greek: *ho katechōn*</note>—he who hindered the revealing of Antichrist—is, he shall have this direct answer from him: "Who but the Roman State? Its departure and division into ten kings will bring in the Antichrist, and then the Wicked One will be revealed." <note>original Latin: *Quis nisi Romanus Status? cujus in decem reges abscessio dispersa Antichristum superinducet, & tunc revelabitur Iniquus.*</note> This is exactly what the faithful servants of Christ have discovered to their great sorrow and affliction.

2. This *Man of Sin*, therefore, is that *little horn* with the *eyes of a man* in it (both expressions suggesting the human strategy <note>original: "policy"</note> of the Papal Power). He is that *King different from the ten*, being an ecclesiastical <note>term: "Ecclesiastick"—relating to the Christian Church or its clergy</note> prince who rises up behind them to outgrow and overtop them by his cleverness. St. Paul calls him the *lawless man* <note>original Greek: *ho anomos*</note>, just as Daniel describes him as a *changer of Times and Laws*, as he is not content to be restricted or bounded by those that already existed, even though they were the decrees of God and his Christ. In that *horn* there is also a *mouth speaking great things*, even *against the most High*; that is, treasonous words against the sovereignty of God and Christ. This *Man of Sin*—this *Papal Body*—does exactly this, exalting their head, the *Pope*, *above everything that is called God or is worshipped*. Finally, just as the *little horn* in Daniel is to be burned by the fiery stream issuing from before that dreadful Judge, so is this *Man of Sin* to be consumed by the *Spirit of the mouth of the Lord* and by the *fiery brightness of his coming*. These considerations may assure us that one and the same person is intended by the *little horn* in the seventh chapter of Daniel and that prosperous King in the eleventh chapter who exalts and magnifies himself *above every God*. Both figures align with this present prophecy of the *Man of Sin* and *Son of Perdition*.

It is so plain that this prophecy should not be understood as referring to either Gaius <note>The Emperor Caligula</note> or Simon Magus, as Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian who favored a preterist interpretation of prophecy</note> groundlessly imagines. I will now examine his opinion, only because that author's name carries so much influence with some men; otherwise, it would hardly be worth the effort of reviewing.

<header>Chapter 19. A Refutation of Grotius’s Interpretation, etc.</header>

## CHAPTER 19.

1. *A summary proposal of Grotius's interpretation of the preceding prophecy. 2. That the coming of Christ in this prophecy cannot be understood as the destruction of Jerusalem. 3. Neither can apostasy be attributed to Caius <note>Caius Caligula, Roman Emperor from 37–41 AD</note>, nor can he be said to sit in the Temple of God; nor does "the one who restrains" <note>original Greek: ho katechōn</note> fit well with Vitellius. 4. That Caius's purpose of placing his statue in the Temple was no "mystery of iniquity," but gross profaneness. 5. Grotius’s ridiculous distortion of the sense of the prophecy in making Caius the "Man of Sin" and "Son of Perdition," supposedly concealed by Vitellius standing in the way; and yet upon Vitellius’s removal, not Caius, but Simon Magus is claimed to be the man revealed and destroyed. 6. That in all likelihood the story of Simon Magus is a fiction, and from what occasion it arose. 7. That even if it were true, it is not applicable, as this wicked man Simon was not consumed by the Spirit of Christ's mouth, but only his coach and horses. 8. That Grotius makes Paul prophesy of things already past, his Epistle being written ten years after Caius’s death, with a full answer to Grotius’s first argument to the contrary. 9. An answer to the second. 10. A demonstration from Scripture and Grotius’s own concessions that this Second Epistle was written ten years after Caius’s death, and also that the fall of Simon Magus from his fiery chariot was eight years before this prophecy.*

1. THE sum of Grotius’s interpretation of this second chapter of the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians is this:

> "First, He interprets the coming of **Christ** as the destruction of **Jerusalem**.
> 
> "Secondly, The *apostasy* or *falling away* and the *revealing of the Man of Sin* he understands as referring to **Caius Caligula**, who indeed was a very impious emperor and intended to have his own statue set up in the Temple of **Jerusalem**.
> 
> "Thirdly, 'the one who restrains' <note>original Greek: ho katechōn</note>, or 'that which restrains' <note>original Greek: to katechon</note>, he identifies as **Lucius Vitellius**, Governor of **Syria** (and consequently of **Judea**), who was a friend to the **Jews**. Therefore, during his time, it was not an opportune moment for **Caius** to propose setting his own statue in the holy Temple.
> 
> "Fourthly, By the working of the *mystery of iniquity*, he understands the persuasions of **Helicon** and other **Egyptian** impostors who were close with **Caius** and were preparing the way for this grand act of impiety.
> 
> "Fifthly, But when he who hinders is taken out of the way—that is, **Lucius Vitellius**, who until then prevented **Caius** from this impious purpose of placing his statue in the Temple at **Jerusalem**—then shall that *Wicked one* be revealed (who has dealt secretly until now with his fellow-conspirators **Helicon** and the rest). You will certainly expect him to say **Caius**; but no, **Simon Magus**, says Grotius. Was there ever such a ridiculous absurdity <note>original Greek: aperispepsia; literally a lack of consideration or thoughtlessness</note> in any serious interpretation of authors, much less of Holy Scripture?
> 
> "Sixthly and lastly, This is because the rest of the prophecy seems to speak of a conjurer or magician, such as **Simon Magus** was famed to be, whom at **Rome**, riding in the air with his fiery chariot and horses, **Peter** [defeated]...

> “[Simon Magus was] by his prayers to Christ made to fall to the ground. And thus was *Simon* consumed by the Spirit of the Lord’s mouth, and by the brightness of his coming, as *Grotius* would have it.”

2. This is a brief account of his exposition <note>An explanation or interpretation of a text</note>, in which there is hardly one sound joint <note>A logical connection or part of an argument</note>. Regarding the first point—which interprets the **coming of Christ** as the destruction of **Jerusalem**—anyone who considers that this letter is truly the *Second Epistle to the Thessalonians* (as I will prove later) <margin>* Ch. 4. v. 15, 16, 17.</margin> will see the problem. In the *previous epistle*, the Apostle speaks of the **final coming of Christ**, which is joined with the **resurrection of the dead** and our **being gathered together** to meet the **Lord in the air**. Therefore, one cannot—without doing great violence to the meaning—understand "this coming of Christ" and our "gathering together unto him" in this second epistle as anything other than the same event and time described in the first. 

This is even more certain because of the Apostle’s serious appeal <note>original: "Obtestation"</note> regarding this coming of the Lord. He urges them that they should not **be shaken in mind nor troubled**; "not to be shaken in mind or troubled" <note>original Greek: *mête saleuthênai apo tou noos mête throeisthai*</note>. These words suggest such a high degree of distress that it is as if they were at their wits' end at the thought of the matter. However, the sacking of **Jerusalem** could not have concerned those living at **Thessalonica** to such a great extent. And, lastly, the phrase [**nor by word, nor by letter, as from us**] seems to refer to the previous epistle. In that letter, the Apostle spoke through a common reading <note>original Greek: *anaginôsis*</note> as if he and the rest then alive would meet the Lord in the air, which gave the **Thessalonians** reason to believe that the **Day of Judgment** would occur very shortly. He therefore rectifies this mistake in this present epistle. From this, it is plain that the coming of Christ is not understood here as the destruction of **Jerusalem**, but as the Last Judgment.

3. The second part of the argument is also weak. **Caius** <note>Emperor Caligula</note> could not properly be called an "apostate" from the God of **Israel**, since he was never in a covenant with Him. Nor did he ever actually set his statue in the Temple at **Jerusalem**, which is the main point **Grotius** aims at; much less did he sit there himself, which the words of the text plainly suggest. Furthermore, the Greek phrase "so that he sits in the temple of God" <note>original: *hōste auton eis ton naon tou Theou kathisai*</note> does not mean to **place himself** in the Temple of God, but to **sit there**. Every part of this interpretation is extremely strained.

The third point would make enough sense if the facts were agreeable. Yet there seems to be a small flaw in this as well. If **Vitellius** <note>The Roman governor of Syria who delayed Caligula's order to place a statue in the Temple</note> were the one intended and nothing more, the phrase **the one who restrains** <note>original Greek: *ho katechōn*</note> would likely have been used in both places, as that is the most fitting way to describe a specific person.

4. As for the fourth point, it is very improper to call **Caius's** private and concealed purpose of setting his statue in the Temple of God at **Jerusalem** a **Mystery of Iniquity**. Mere privacy and concealment do not automatically make something a **Mystery**; otherwise, every secret <note>original: "clancular"</note> attempt at theft, murder, or adultery would be a **mystery of iniquity**. Instead, a **Mystery** is something that—even when spoken of in words—is still mysterious in its own nature and has some hidden depth, whether it is a bad **Mystery** or a good one. 

But this plan of **Caius's** to place his statue in the Temple at **Jerusalem** is no such thing; it is only a plain and obvious piece of impiety, such as everyone would understand at first sight. Therefore, the biblical passages cited by **Grotius**—namely, *Romans 11:25* and *1 Corinthians 15:51*—[are not applicable].

...are nothing to this purpose. For those are difficult and deep mysteries mentioned there, even after they are revealed.

5. I have already noted the excessive dislocation <note>original: "luxation"; a medical term for a joint out of place, used here as a metaphor for a logical flaw</note> in the fifth point of his argument, and indeed I think it cannot be hidden from anyone. For who would expect, according to the common way of speaking, anything other than what the Apostle began with? He started his prophecy concerning the **Man of Sin**, whom he also calls the **Son of Perdition**, adding further that **he is to be revealed**, that there are secret preparations being made for it, and that only **Lucius Vitellius** <note>A Roman politician and father of Emperor Vitellius; Grotius claimed he was the "restraining force" mentioned by Paul</note> hinders his revelation in his own time—a hindrance that will last until the said **Vitellius** is taken out of the way. 

I say, who would not expect the eighth verse—*And then shall that wicked one be revealed, whom the Lord shall consume with the Spirit of his mouth, and destroy with the brightness of his coming* (just as he was called before both the **Son of Perdition** and the **Man of Sin**) — to be understood as the same person the Apostle began with? And yet, Grotius claims the **Man of Sin** and **Son of Perdition** is **Caius** <note>The Emperor Caligula</note>, while the wicked **Man** whom the Lord destroys here (and who is therefore plainly the **Son of Perdition** in the highest sense) is **Simon Magus**. Grotius has placed the text upon such a violent rack to extort false answers from it, and to make it accuse **Caius** and **Simon Magus** so that the Pope may escape the suspicion of being identified as **Antichrist**. In doing so, Grotius’s judgment or his conscience is placed in a very dangerous position.

6. And finally, now that he has turned to **Simon**; though I admit the story of his fiery horses and chariot is not impossible, and even less so his fall to the ground by the prayer of **Peter**, yet long before I knew this use for the story, the narrative always seemed very incredible to me. This is despite the fact that I believe in the existence of **Spirits** and **Apparitions** as firmly as most people do. It always looked to me like a stage trick <note>original: "gambal trick"</note>, such that I could not help but place it among the earlier legends or pious fictions of the Church, invented by some idle monk to entertain the credulous and superstitious. 

A passage so notorious as this happening in the City of **Rome** could not have been kept out of the *Lives of the Caesars*, and particularly the life of **Nero**. In Nero's life, **Suetonius** only makes this short mention among those theatrical shows in Chapter 12: "Icarus, at his very first attempt, fell down close to Nero's bedroom and splattered him with blood" <note>original Latin: *Icarus primo statim conatu juxta cubiculum Neronis decidit, ipsumque cruore respersit.*</note>. It seems this monastic legend was framed out of this unlucky performance of a poetic fiction, in which the storytellers add and alter whatever they please. This greatly undermines the credibility of the story.

7. The most detailed and plausible narrative Dr. **Hammond** has chosen comes from **Arnobius**: "They had seen the chariot of Simon Magus and the fiery four-horse team blown away by Peter's breath, vanishing when the name of Christ was spoken. They had seen him fall headlong by his own weight and lie there with broken legs. Afterward, having been carried to Brundisium, exhausted by his tortures and shame, he threw himself down again from the top of a very high roof" <note>original Latin: *Viderant currum Simonis Magi & quadrigas igneas Petri ore difflatas, & nominato Christo evanuisse: viderant pondere præcipitatum suo, cruribus jacuisse præfractis: post deinde perlatum Brundam, cruciatibus & pudore defessum, ex altissimi culminis se rursum præcipitasse fastigio.*</note>. 

Now, these words ["The fiery four-horse team blown away by Peter's breath and vanishing"] agree well with ["Whom the Lord shall consume with the breath of his mouth"]. For, as **Grotius** excellently and truly noted, "The Apostles are the mouth of Christ" <note>original Latin: *Apostoli sunt os Christi*</note>—an analogy I used to explain the vision of the **Rider of the white Horse**. But when I see the **Horses and Chariot** scattered and consumed, but **Simon Magus** himself falling whole, except for the breaking of his

shins, which, it seems, were later at Brunda <note>original: "Brunda", likely referring to Brundisium, an ancient port in Italy</note> so well again that he could stand on his legs to throw himself headlong from some precipice. He could even go up to the higher stories of a house—for who would have carried him so high when a lower room would have better suited a lame man? If this accident had been the goal of this prophecy, undoubtedly *Simon* himself would have been consumed, not only his *chariot* and *horses*.

8. Therefore, even if we admit Grotius’s chronology—who, for his own advantage, pretends that this *Second* Epistle was written before the *First*, and during *Caius’s* <note>Caius is the Emperor Caligula, who reigned 37–41 AD</note> reign—you see how distorted, forced, and incompatible his exposition is with the text. The same failure occurs here as in his other mistimed interpretations of prophecy. But to sweep all this away at once, I say that both these Epistles were written about the ninth or tenth year of the reign of Claudius—that is, many years after *Caius’s* death. Therefore, *Grotius* makes *Paul* prophesy about things that had already happened. That this is the constant tradition of the Church cannot be denied. But this is not the first time that *Grotius* has exceeded all bounds of modesty to reach for an argument that vanishes in his hand as soon as he grasps it. I know he has some excuses to prove the Second Epistle was written before the First, so that he might imagine it written as early as he pleases; but the arguments he produces only cut his own fingers <note>A metaphor meaning his own arguments damage his own case</note>.

The first argument comes from the conclusion of this Second Epistle: *The salutation of Paul with my own hand, which is the token in every epistle; so I write: namely, <note>original: "viz."</note> The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all, Amen.* This, written with *Paul's* own hand, is his *mark* or token in every *epistle*. Yet *Grotius* would infer from this that this epistle was written first, because there is no such mark in the preceding epistle—supposing that those among the *Thessalonians* who were still alive already knew his handwriting. But I answer:

First, that the preceding epistle *has* this mark. For does it not end with *The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all, Amen*? And as he said before, this is written with his own hand in every epistle. Therefore, the mark is present in both these epistles.

Secondly, unless he had sent them some earlier epistle with this mark, they could not use it to prove that this one was his.

Thirdly, he did send an epistle to them before this one, as appears from *Chapter 2, verse 15*: *Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions you have been taught, whether by word or our epistle.* Therefore, this mark cannot demonstrate which letter came first, for it would have been in that other one that actually preceded it—which is a contradiction. Even *Grotius* himself does not deny that the epistle mentioned here came before this one, but he capriciously and groundlessly pretends it has been lost, rather than admitting it is the "First Epistle" according to the biblical Canon.

Fourthly, this "first" epistle, according to the Canon of the Church, is the very same epistle mentioned in *Chapter 2, verse 15*. This is clear from the subject of this second chapter, which is obviously nothing more than a clarification of his meaning concerning *the coming of Christ*. He had written about this in the preceding epistle, *Chapter 4, verse 13* to the end, and *Chapter 5, verses 1, 2, and 3*, where there are expressions suggesting that the Resurrection and the Last Judgment were near at hand, even hanging over their heads.

# Chapter XIX. Of the Prophecy of the Man of Sin.

And therefore, fifthly and lastly, **Paul** so earnestly gives them notice that this Second Letter is his. He ensures they can recognize it by his well-known mark, written—as in every one of his letters—with his own hand, so that they might be calmed by his authority, since they were so perplexed and troubled by a misunderstanding of his meaning. This evidence, in fact, clearly works against **Grotius’s** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a famous Dutch jurist and theologian who proposed that the "Man of Sin" referred to the Roman Emperor Caligula.</note> own argument.

9. His second argument for the priority of this Second Letter is this: That the Christians at **Thessalonica** were so few when **Saint Paul** wrote that they did not yet form a *Church* or *leadership body*, and could not form a number sufficient to constitute an authoritative church. His reason is: "Because the Apostle here did not command that men who were not living according to the rules be excommunicated—which would have required a proper assembly—but only that they be avoided, which is the right of individuals." <note>original: "Quod homines non ex regula viventes Apostolus hic non excommunicari præcepit, quod justi cœtûs fuerit ; sed vitari, quod jus singulorum est."</note> For an answer to this, I shall only set down the words of the Apostle in chapter 3, verses 14 and 15: *And if any man does not obey our word by this letter, note that man, and have no company with him, so that he may be ashamed: Yet do not count him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.* The words in the original are, "do not associate with him" <note>original Greek: μὴ συναναμίγνυσθε αὐτῷ</note>, and "admonish him as a brother" <note>original Greek: νουθετεῖτε ὡς ἀδελφόν</note>. The former phrase also occurs in 1 Corinthians 5:11: *But now I write to you* "not to associate," <note>original Greek: μὴ συναναμίγνυσθαι</note> *if any man who is called a brother is a fornicator, etc., with such a person you should not even eat.* This is an explanation of what it means to not associate. Regarding this, **Grotius’s** own note is: "Among the Hebrews, the custom was not to eat common food with one who was under <term>Niddui</term> <note>Niddui is a Hebrew term for a formal type of excommunication or social distancing practiced in the Jewish tradition.</note>, that is, with him who was excommunicated." <note>original Latin: "Hebræis mos erat cibum communem non sumere cum eo qui erat in נידוי, with him that was excommunicated."</note> So "not associating with him" implies excommunication, and shows that the Christians in **Thessalonica** were a *Church*, just as **Paul** styled them when he wrote this Second Letter to them.

And regarding the phrase "admonish him as a brother," is it not also in the first letter to the **Thessalonians**, chapter 5:14: "admonish those who are unruly"? <note>original Greek: νουθετεῖτε τοὺς ἀτάκτους</note> Yet **Grotius** acknowledges that there was then a *Church* in **Thessalonica** properly so called. From this it is plain that he has no reason at all to change the order of these letters. Therefore, constant tradition and the authority of the Church must stand: the *Second* letter must be the *Second* letter in the Church's sense—that is to say, written after the First. This is also apparent from those internal arguments I produced in answer to **Grotius’s** first reason.

10. Furthermore, the *First* Letter, according to **Grotius’s** own acknowledgment, was written after **Paul** had been at **Thessalonica**. However, **Paul** had not been at **Thessalonica** before the council that was held at **Jerusalem** by the Apostles, as appears from Acts chapters 15 and 16 and the whole sequence of the History of the Apostles. Nor was this council of the Apostles at **Jerusalem** held until fourteen years after the conversion of **Saint Paul**, as appears in Galatians 2:2, where **Grotius** himself acknowledges that **Paul** then went up to that meeting: "I find nothing more credible than that the very journey of Paul mentioned in Acts 15:2 is noted here." <note>original Latin: "Nihil credibilius reperio quàm notari hic illud ipsum Pauli iter cujus mentio Act. 15. 2."</note> But after this journey to **Jerusalem**, **Paul** chose **Silas** (that is, **Sylvanus**) and **Timothy** (as appears in Acts 15:40 and 16:1) to be his companions, whose names are included at the beginning of the Second Letter to the **Thessalonians** as well as the **First**.

Therefore, both the Second and the First letters were written fourteen years after **Paul’s** conversion, and consequently about the tenth year of **Claudius’s** reign. That is to say, about ten years after **Caligula’s** death, and

### CHAP. XX.

1. *The superiority of this latter interpretation over that of* **Grotius**. 2. *A summary proposal of the same.* 3. *The first part of this exposition is the same as* **Grotius's**, *and therefore already proven wrong; the second part is weakened.* 4. *The third part is refuted by further discovering the improbability of the story of* **Simon Magus**; *his having been sufficiently revealed before, and the fact that he was never found sitting in any Temple to receive divine honors.* 5. *That "the one who restrains"* <note>original: "ὁ κατέχων" (ho katechōn)</note> *is not good grammar in this case, nor was the wickedness of the* **Gnostics** *a "mystery," but rather open impiety and hostility against the Church.* 6. *The awkwardness of interpreting the word "whom"—in the phrase "whom the Lord shall consume," etc.—as referring to two different subjects: one to be destroyed by the breath of* **Christ’s** *mouth, and the other by the brightness of his coming, in separate places and times.* 7. *If the history of* **Simon Magus** *had been true and the application fit this prophecy, the most ancient Church Fathers would not have failed to notice it; # Chap. XX. of the Prophecy of the Man of Sin.

Although this application is ingenious, it presents such great difficulties that it cannot help but hinder belief in cautious readers. But such as it is, I shall first briefly set it down and then examine it, so that it may more fully appear that there is no interpretation that can compete with the one which the general consensus of Protestants agrees upon, which usually leans toward the sense I have declared.

2. “First then, he, like **Grotius**, interprets the coming of **Christ** as the **destruction of Jerusalem**.
“Secondly, **The Apostasy** or **Falling away** he understands as a defection from the Faith to the heresy of the **Gnostics**; or else the Apostles leaving the **Jews** and no longer complying with them.
“Thirdly, **The revealing of the Man of Sin** is **Simon's** <note>original: "Simon his"; referring to Simon Magus.</note> appearance at **Rome** at the time he rode in his fiery chariot, together with the **Gnostics'** persecution of the Christians.
“Fourthly, **That which withholds** <note>original: "That which withholdeth"; referring to the restraining force mentioned in 2 Thessalonians 2:6.</note> is the Apostles not giving up on preaching to the **Jews**, nor yet leaving them as stubborn and hopeless.
“Fifthly, **The Mystery of Iniquity** which already works is a smothered opposition against **Christ** and Christians, and an express renouncing of Christianity in this sect of **Gnostics** under **Simon** and **Carpocrates**, ready to break out as soon as the Apostles said goodbye to the **Jews**, their countrymen.
“Sixthly and lastly, **The Spirit of God’s mouth** is the prayer of **Peter** by which **Simon Magus** was cast to the ground; and the **brightness of his coming** is the destruction of **Jerusalem**, by which the persecuting **Jews** and **Gnostics** were overthrown.

3. This is the sum of his interpretation, which we will briefly run over. Against the first part, the same things must be said as were said against **Grotius’s** view, and I need not repeat them. That alone is enough to completely overthrow both their interpretations in the judgment of any unprejudiced reader.

Regarding the second point, **Grotius** asserts so confidently that **Simon Magus’s** unhappy display happened in the beginning of **Claudius's** reign—which this **Apostasy** must precede—and since this latter interpretation names no time when this **Apostasy** happened, it makes the application altogether uncertain; but if **Grotius** is right about the timing, it is impossible. And as for that other sense of **Apostasy**, I suspect it is unjustifiable. *A departure* <note>original: "’Απόστασις" (Apostasis)</note> indeed can signify a simple departure as well as a defection, but *an apostasy* <note>original: "ἀποστασία" (Apostasia)</note> signifies a defection only.

4. The third point is the grand basis of the entire exposition; but I have already hinted at the incredibility of the story. It will be further suspected by anyone who is not overly credulous if they consider what is added to it in the works of **Baronius** <note>Caesar Baronius was a 16th-century Catholic cardinal and historian.</note>: namely, that **Peter**, by the extraordinary miracle he performed in bringing down **Simon Magus** headlong out of the air by his prayers, was so far from gaining any respect from **Nero** (the spectator of the combat), that he was imprisoned for such a stupendous achievement. Certainly, if the people honored **Simon Magus** as a god for the magical power he boasted of, they would have given much more honor...

4. Beyond this, Simon Magus could not properly be called the "Man of Sin who was to be revealed" at the time this Epistle was written. He had already, at the beginning of the Emperor Claudius's reign, shown himself to be an impious blasphemer by pretending to be a God and receiving divine honors in Rome. There is no evidence to suggest anything other than that he remained that wicked from then until the end of his life.

Regarding his "sitting in the Temple of God," what seat or "see" <note>A "see" refers to the center of authority for a bishop or religious leader.</note> did he have anywhere? Or what temple was ever built for him? It is said that a statue was erected to him, but this happened at the beginning of Claudius's reign, and thus before this prophecy was written. But a statue is not a temple. Furthermore, it might be a fictional statue if the guess of Petrus Ciaconius <note>Petrus Ciaconius (1525–1581) was a Spanish scholar known for his work on ancient Roman inscriptions.</note> is correct. He suggested that the story arose from an old Pagan inscription on a piece of marble dug up in the year 1574 in the place where Simon's statue was said to be. The inscription read "Sacred to Semo Sancus, the god of oaths" <note>original: "Semoni Sango Deo Fidio sacrum"; Semo Sancus was a Roman deity whose name was often confused by early Christian writers with Simon Magus.</note>, as you can see in the works of Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607) was an influential Catholic historian.</note>.

5. Regarding the fourth point: it is not good grammar to use the masculine phrase "he who restrains" <note>original: "ὁ κατέχων" (ho katechōn)</note> when the author refers to a thing rather than a person. Furthermore, it seems unbelievable that the Apostles would ever be responsible for such a disaster by stopping their compliance with the Jews—if they could foresee by a prophetic spirit (or if Saint Paul told them) that doing so would cause such great harm. This compliance was supposedly a strong barrier against the flood of Gnosticism and the persecution of the Church.

Concerning the fifth point: there is a similar objection to the one raised against Grotius's interpretation. It seems to define anything concealed as a "mystery," which is a false understanding of the word. For a clear and intended opposition or renunciation of Christianity that is merely kept secret (which is the case proposed here) is no more a "mystery" than a hidden murder or adultery, as I stated previously.

6. As for the sixth and final point: it seems forced and unnatural to interpret the execution carried out by the "spirit of the mouth of the Lord" as applying to Simon Magus in Rome, and the "destruction brought by the brightness of his coming" as applying to the Gnostics caught up in the destruction of Jerusalem. This is especially true when we consider that Simon Magus and the Gnostics did not form a single political group. Instead, as Baronius suggests, the Gnostics seemed to descend from the Nicolaitans <note>The Nicolaitans were an early Christian sect mentioned in the Book of Revelation, often accused of heresy.</note> and thus had no relation to Simon Magus.

Moreover, the text speaks of these as continuous actions: "Whom the Lord shall consume with the spirit of his mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of his coming." This is simply the bright flame and fiery spirit coming from his mouth, similar to the description in the Book of Esdras <note>Referring to the apocryphal book 2 Esdras (or 4 Ezra) 13:10.</note>. It is directed at one and the same target: the "Man of Sin," who is the same as the "little horn" in the Book of Daniel, who is to be destroyed in this way.

### Chap. XX. Of the Prophecy of the Man of Sin.

It is a **strange** thing that the early Church Fathers, who had a closer view of those events in the world, could not discern the completion of the prophecy in *Simon Magus* and the *Gnostics*. It would be odd if we, who stand at the furthest distance from the events, should be the most clear-sighted in seeing how they apply to the prophecy. I have already said enough to show how improbable it is that this should be the main meaning of *St. Paul’s* prediction. 

But if I could believe that the condition of *Simon* and the *Gnostics* was in some sense criticized <note>original: "perstringed"; meaning to touch upon briefly or censure.</note> here—as I must confess this pious and sensible interpreter has made a very strong case for—I would look upon them as a preliminary model <note>original: "preludious Type"</note> for the *great Antichrist*. I would think that the passage [*For the Mystery of Iniquity is already at work*] should be understood as referring to them. This is possible even though the rest of the prophecy is, in many ways, inapplicable to *Simon* and belongs only to the *great Antichrist* himself. Indeed, this magician may be only a type or figure of him, and truly a significant one.

For as Simon is a magician, so is that great Antichrist an outstanding sorcerer and the head of a numerous society of sorcerers and enchanters.

Secondly, just as *Simon* gave his name to and provided the first example of that wicked sin of <term>simony</term> <note>The sin of buying or selling spiritual offices or positions in the church.</note>, so these pretended successors of *Peter*—both the leaders and their entire ecclesiastical body—have notoriously imitated *Simon’s* example in buying and selling spiritual matters.

Thirdly, part of the apostasy of *Simon* and the *Gnostics* was "Judaizing" <note>Adopting Jewish customs or laws while claiming to be Christian.</note> while they made a show of Christianity. It is conspicuous to all the world how much the Antichrist and his followers "Judaize" through their ceremonies and their boasting of "works" and dead formalities.

Fourthly, *Simon* and the *Gnostics* were notorious for filthiness and impurity. The same has been true of the great Antichristian synagogue, both in its leadership and its members.

Fifthly, although *Simon* and the *Gnostics* were so clearly offensive in their lives and behavior, they were <term>Gnostics</term> <note>original: "γνωστικοὶ" (gnostikoi); meaning "the knowing ones." These were early groups who claimed to have secret, superior knowledge of divine matters.</note>—extraordinary pretenders to, and boasters of, the certainty of their knowledge in divine matters, which they held in great esteem. And is this not the special character of the Pope and his Church? They pretend to be infallibly wise and perfectly orthodox in knowledge and opinion, yet they are foully negligent and scandalously permissive regarding all kinds of immoral living.

Sixthly, *Simon* and the *Gnostics* were opponents and persecutors of the true Church. The Papal hierarchy and its instruments do the same.

Seventhly, the followers of *Simon* polluted themselves with idols. So do those who adhere to the leadership of *Rome*.

Eighthly and lastly, *Simon* exalted himself above everything that is called God and received divine honors in his own person on Earth. This is also notorious in the case of the *Roman* Bishop <note>The Pope.</note>.

So, while such things were happening in the world, and being done by people who made some show of Christianity, *St. Paul* might well say of that great *Mystery of Iniquity* that it is already on foot. In some sense, it was already acting through *Simon* and his followers, serving as a type and prelude to the—

#### Prophetic Strictures concerning Antichristian Impurity. Book II.

...the strange antics of the great *Antichrist*, and that nothing is missing but the removal of that great *obstacle* at *Rome*—the Western *Caesarship* <note>original: "Cæsareate"; the office or rule of the Roman Emperor.</note>—and then the Lawless One <note>original: "ὁ ἄνομος" (ho anomos)</note> himself, that great *Antichrist* indeed, will reveal himself, of whom *Simon* is but a figure. See *Chapter 18, Verse 7*. This explanation is somewhat more plausible than that of *Alcazar* (who understands the *Mystery of Iniquity* already at work as being pure *Paganism*), but whether it is the most accurate of all, I leave to the judicious reader to consider.

In the meantime, I believe I have sufficiently clarified the truth of those main prophecies in Scripture that concern the enormous *Arrogance* and *Pride of Antichrist*, which is so clearly opposite to the first branch of the Divine life: *Humility and Lowliness of Spirit*.

8. The next branch is *Purity*, whose opposite is *Uncleanness*. I have already touched upon the predictions of the causes that lead to that vice. But as for the vice itself—being so inseparable a companion of *Idolatry*, which is *Spiritual Adultery* or *Fornication*—I believe the Spirit of Prophecy was more brief in particular foreshadowings or predictions of it for that very reason. But I do not doubt that it is involved in that description of the *great city* in *Revelation 11: "And their bodies shall lie in the street of the great city which is spiritually called Sodom, etc."* And no one can be ignorant of how unclean a city *Sodom* was.

Again, those who are excluded from the *Holy City* (which is perfectly opposite to this city called *Sodom*) are called *Dogs* and the abominable <note>original: "ἐβδελυγμένοι" (ebdelygmenoi)</note>. By this term, as I have noted above from *Grotius*, are understood sodomites and the effeminate <note>original: "ἀρσενοκοῖται καὶ μαλακοὶ" (arsenokoitai kai malakoi); archaic terms for those engaging in same-sex acts, often used in older translations of the New Testament</note>. *Whoremongers* are also named in the same *list*. But I have spoken sufficiently of these texts in my *Idea of Antichristianism*.

In the passage where the *Church* is said to become a *wilderness*, it may also be an intimation of the excess of those actions of the animalistic life <note>original: "Animal life"; refers to the base, physical, or unredeemed nature of man, as opposed to the spiritual life.</note> that proceed from cruelty and lust. But these hints shall suffice concerning this second opposition to the Divine Life in its various branches.

The reason for his ruin in that vision is declared to be his barbarous and Antichristian cruelty. *Isaiah 14: "Because you have destroyed your land, and slain your people."* That is to say, the people of Christendom—the land over which you claim an ecclesiastical sovereignty as being the Vicar of *Christ*—and yet you most bloodily murder and martyr his truest and most faithful servants.

Again, *Daniel 7*. The *little horn* there, which is a figure of the same *Papal power* <note>original: "Pontifician Power"</note>, is said *to wage war with and to wear out the saints of the Most High*; that is, to consume them and destroy them with perpetual persecutions.

### Chapter 20: Foreshadowings of Antichristian Cruelty

10. A third sign is found in **Revelation 11** concerning the Witnesses: *The Beast that ascends out of the bottomless pit shall make war against them, overcome them, and kill them; and their dead bodies shall lie in the street of the great City which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where also our Lord was crucified.* This is a description of perpetual opposition and persecution, which strips the true servants of God of their honors, offices, goods, or lives. Consequently, the real and sincere Church of Christ—which is his Body—lies like a dead corpse without political life or power while the <term>Outward Court</term> <note>The "Outward Court" refers to the visible, formal structures of the church, which the author argues have been taken over by corruption, while the "Inner Court" or true believers are oppressed.</note> is being trampled. It also lies dreadfully wounded and covered in blood from the cruel murders, martyrdoms, and massacres of its faithful members.

Fourthly, in **Revelation 13**, the *Two-horned Beast* is said to give life to the *Ten-horned Beast* (after it had revived into the ancient idolatrous form of *Paganism*). He does this to destroy all those who would not obey his idolatrous commands. *And he had power to give life to the Image of the Beast, so that the Image of the Beast should both speak and cause anyone who would not worship the Image of the Beast to be killed; and that no man might buy or sell, except he who had the Mark, the Name of the Beast, or the Number of his Name.* This means that as many as would not declare themselves *Roman Catholics*—and thereby adopt pagan practices within Christianity—would be famished and starved, and forbidden from living. Such is the "charity" of this tyrannical and Antichristian power toward the true members of Christ. But *blessed are the dead who die in the Lord*, as the following chapter says regarding the martyrdom of those murdered by this Papal power <note>original: "Pontifician Power"</note>.

11. Fifthly, there is also a record of Antichristian Roman cruelty in **Revelation 16** (for the Vials of wrath are poured upon the Beast, just as the Egyptian plagues were poured upon the Antichristian "Egypt"). There, the Angel of the third Vial, who turns the rivers into blood, speaks: *You are righteous, O Lord, who are, and were, and shall be, because you have judged this way. For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink; for they are worthy.*

Sixthly, just as the ruin of the *King of Babylon* is recorded in *Isaiah* <note>original: "Esay"</note>, the ruin of the *Whore of Babylon* in *St. John’s* writing is attributed to this savage <note>original: "salvage"</note> and barbarous Antichristian cruelty: the murder of the saints of God. *The voice of harpers and musicians shall be heard no more in her; no craftsman of any trade shall be found in her anymore; the light of a candle shall shine no more in her; but she is left to utter darkness and desolation. This is because the blood of prophets, saints, and all who were slain upon the Earth was found within her.* Murderers are also specifically noted in both lists of those who are excluded from the Holy City.

12. Seventhly and finally, in the description of the *Whore of Babylon*—which I have plainly shown above to signify the Church (especially the *Roman* Church) having fallen away into idolatry—there is explicit and significant mention made of this hateful branch of Antichristianism: this bloody persecution of the true members of Christ. *And the woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold, precious stones, and pearls, having a golden cup in her hand, full of abominations and the filthiness of her...*

# Foreshadowings of Antichristian Cruelty. Book II.

**Fornication:**
> *And upon her forehead was a Name written: Mystery, Babylon the Great, the mother of Harlots and abominations of the Earth. And I saw the woman drunken with the blood of the Saints and with the blood of the Martyrs of Jesus: and when I saw her, I wondered with great astonishment.* <note>The author uses "admiration" in the original sense of "wonder" or "astonishment" at a strange sight, rather than modern praise.</note>

Whoever looks upon the gorgeous pomp of the **Pope** and his ecclesiastical princes, the **Cardinals** and other great men—as well as the costly and resplendent decorations of their glistening altars and temples—can see how this **Harlot** has adorned herself with ornaments, carpets, and laces of **Egypt**, and how she has perfumed her bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon, with incense and aromatic odors. If such a person has any skill in the prophetic style of writing, he cannot deny that this foreshadowing of the state of the **Roman** Church is depicted to the life in terms of its splendor and richness. For this is how idolatry began in the world: with this **golden cup** and a costly outward appearance.

But this is not the only failing of this Church; she is also **drunk with the blood of the Saints and with the blood of the Martyrs of Jesus.** The commentary by **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a famous Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> on this part of the text is very expressive and significant:
> *He saw her with a rabid mouth, foaming and vomiting blood, as drunkards are accustomed to do.* <note>original Latin: *Vidit eam ore rabido despumante & evomente sanguinem, ut ebrii solent*</note> *John saw the rabid or enraged woman foaming at the mouth with stained froth, and vomiting blood as drunkards do wine.*

It must certainly be a wonder to all who see her that a woman so richly and gloriously dressed should have such a wild and savage nature. This astonishment must surely be redoubled when they consider how this illustrious Queen claims to be the **Universal Church of Christ** and the **Mother of Christendom**, and yet she froths at the mouth and soils her clothing by uncontrollably purging her stomach, which is over-filled with the blood of her own children. By being so wasteful with the lives of her infants, she proves herself not to be that **Universal Mother**, but a bloody and treacherous **Harlot**, just as the Holy Spirit inscribed upon her forehead: *The Mother of Harlots and of the Abominations of the Earth.*

13. Thus we have seen every part of the **concept of Antichristianism** included in our model. Just as these traits are easily found in the Church of **Rome**, they are also expressly foreshadowed in the writings of the holy Prophets as belonging to her. There is no escaping or dismissing such clear and conspicuous testimonies by any clever tricks of wit whatsoever. Her abominable crimes—categorized under the main headings of **Deception**, **Idolatry**, and **Bloodshed**—are as decisively and clearly set down in these prophecies as the events of the past are recorded in any history book. Therefore, the truth can be hidden from no one except those who either do not have the time to understand the prophetic style, or those who are blinded by prejudice and self-interest. I believe such interests are so powerful for some that they would make them hesitant and skeptical even of a mathematical proof. But I confidently declare that such clear evidence for so important a truth as we have clarified here will not be dismissed forever.

14. I am certain that the main excuse some people usually rely on will fail them. I mean those words at the very beginning of the **Book of Revelation**: *things which must shortly come to pass.* <note>original Greek: *ἃ δεῖ γενέσθαι ἐν τάχει* (ha dei genesthai en tachei)</note> From this phrase, they would argue that no events should be applied to these prophecies except those that were to happen within a short time after the prophecies were first given.

# Chapter XX. The right meaning of *the things which must shortly come to pass*. <note>original Greek: ἃ δεῖ γενέσθαι ἐν τάχει</note>

But I have, I think, sufficiently answered this doubt <note>original: "Scruple"</note> in my *Mystery of Godliness* by suggesting that such a conclusion is as unreasonable as if someone, upon hearing a report that a comedy or tragedy was to be performed in less than seven or eight minutes <note>original: "less then this half-quarter of an hour"</note>, should conclude that all its acts and scenes would not last longer than that time. In reality, the meaning is only that the comedy or tragedy will *begin* to be performed within that time. Therefore, **Cornelius à Lapide** <note>A prominent Jesuit Bible commentator (1567–1637).</note>, regarding these words—"the things which must soon happen" <note>original Latin: *Quæ oportet fieri citò*</note>—clearly and judiciously explains it this way: *This means things that will soon begin to happen, although they will not soon be finished.* <note>original Latin: *Hoc est, quæ citò incipient fieri, licet non citò finientur.*</note>

And **Alcazar** <note>Luis del Alcázar (1554–1613), a Spanish Jesuit theologian.</note> says the same of these words: *As if he were saying, "In this Revelation are contained some things which must happen soon, and others which will not be fulfilled quite so quickly."* <note>original Latin: *Quasi diceret, In hac Revelatione continentur quædam quæ citò oportet fieri, & alia quæ non adeò citò implebuntur.*</note> It is also **Grotius's** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> own note on them: *Some sooner, others later.* <note>original Latin: *Alia citiùs, alia seriùs.*</note> But because some of these sequences of visions, which reach even to the end of all things, were to begin to be fulfilled suddenly, it is said generally regarding their subject: *the things which must shortly come to pass.* <note>original Greek: ἃ δεῖ γενέσθαι ἐν τάχει</note> It is just as someone might say of an army a quarter of a mile long that "this army is at the very gates of the city," even though only those marching in the front rank have actually arrived there.

<margin>Revelation 20</margin>
Furthermore, unless the phrase "the things which must shortly come to pass" <note>original Greek: ἃ δεῖ γενέσθαι ἐν τάχει</note> signifies *that which will shortly be happening*, rather than *finished*, it is a perfect contradiction to the nature of some of the things foretold, such as the **Reign of the Saints** and the **Binding of Satan** <note>original: "Ligation of Satan"</note>. The duration of these events is predicted to be a **thousand years**. Therefore, unless a thousand years is considered a "short" space of time, the events foretold would contradict the very title of this prophetic book, if the meaning of "shortly come to pass" were what my opponents claim. From this, it is manifest that the phrase "the things which must happen" <note>original Greek: ἃ δεῖ γενέσθαι</note> does not, regarding every event, mean "which shall be finished," but "which shall be in progress" *shortly* <note>original Greek: ἐν τάχει</note>.

<margin>Chapter 2, verse 6</margin>
Thirdly, regarding the meaning of this phrase, *shortly* <note>original Greek: ἐν τάχει</note>, how "sudden" or how "short" a time must it denote? Who will define it? For the Prophet **Haggai**, when he says, *Yet a little while and I will shake the heavens and the earth, etc.*, his prediction refers to a time about five hundred years distant from the time of the prophecy. Because of this, there is no necessity to seek the completion of the **Seals** and **Trumpets** solely in the Destruction of **Jerusalem**. It is therefore to be understood comparatively as "a little time," just as **Grotius** also interprets that passage from Haggai. In this sense, I would also understand that often-repeated saying in the Book of Revelation: *Behold, I come quickly* <note>original Greek: Ἰδοὺ ἔρχομαι ταχὺ</note>. 

<margin>Revelation 6:12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17</margin>
I believe this has a special focus on the **Sixth Seal**, which is described like the **Day of Judgment**, but is actually the overthrow of the **Dragon** <note>Symbolizing pagan Roman power.</note> by **Christ**, and Christ taking the **Roman Empire** into his own hands upon the conversion of **Constantine** to the Christian religion. This happened in significantly less time than five hundred years, and was a very little time indeed in comparison to the great achievement that was accomplished by it.

Fourthly, the first **Six Seals**, the **Fight of Michael and the Dragon**, and the **Inner Court of the Temple**—all these visions (meaning their fulfillment) were finished within a shorter time than what **Haggai** calls "little."

<summary>The author argues that the biblical phrase "things which must shortly come to pass" refers to the imminent start of prophetic events rather than their rapid completion, allowing for long-term historical fulfillments. He uses the examples of an army's arrival and the thousand-year reign of saints to show that "shortly" is a relative term in prophecy.</summary>

### The right meaning of *the things which must shortly come to pass*. <note>original Greek: ἃ δεῖ γενέσθαι ἐν τάχει</note> Book II.

Fifthly, *The Outward Court of the Temple, the Whore of Babylon, the Two-horned Beast, the Ten-horned Beast, the Two Witnesses, the Virgin-Company, and the Woman in the Wilderness*—the events of all these visions are **in progress** <note>original Latin: *in fieri*</note> within less than that time which the Prophet **Haggai** calls "a little while." <note>Referencing Haggai 2:6, "Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens and the earth."</note> The Trumpets had also begun to sound within that time. But the affairs of the **Seven Churches** might have been accomplished far earlier, and they may be fulfilled over and over again; they are "flying prophecies," not as strictly fixed to a specific time and place as they seem, or as the rest of the visions are. **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch scholar who favored a more immediate, historical interpretation of Revelation.</note> has also observed this. I think this is sufficient to justify the title and subject of these prophecies: **"the things which must shortly come to pass."** <note>original Greek: ἃ δεῖ γενέσθαι ἐν τάχει</note> Nothing more than this is assumed—or rather, demonstrated—in Mr. **Mede's** <note>Joseph Mede (1586–1638), an influential English theologian whose "synchronal" method revolutionized the study of Revelation.</note> way of interpreting the **Apocalypse** <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>.

<margin>* Revelation 20.</margin>
Sixthly, my opponents are themselves forced to interpret some prophecies as events that occurred (or are to occur) more than a thousand years after the prediction. Examples include the **loosing of Satan**, the **army of Gog and Magog**, the **siege of the beloved city**, the **fire falling from heaven** upon the besiegers, the **General Judgment**, and the like. These examples contradict their own hypothesis even more, because they do not create an order or **linking** <note>original: "concatenation"</note> of visions as Mr. Mede does. Therefore, it will be harder for them to make those events fit with the phrase **"the things which must shortly come to pass."** <note>original Greek: ἃ δεῖ γενέσθai ἐν τάχει</note> 

However, in the method I support, one thing so neatly or necessarily hooks into another—the first Thunder into the seven Vials, the last Trumpet into the seven Thunders, the last Seal into the seven Trumpets, and the first six of these Trumpets into their **synchronous events** <note>original: "Synchronalls"; Mede’s theory that different visions in Revelation describe the same time periods simultaneously.</note>, just as the first six Seals do with theirs. The entire volume of visions is, in a sense, all of one piece. One thing follows another so continuously that when the first events begin to appear, the whole series may well be said to begin or to be "in the works," and to happen "quickly, quickly." Thus, Mr. Mede’s method has very little conflict <note>original: "Repugnancy"</note> with the phrase **"the things which must shortly come to pass."** <note>original Greek: ἃ δεῖ γενέσθai ἐν τάχει</note>

<margin>See Chapter 2.</margin>
And lastly, I have plainly demonstrated that the Apocalypse was not revealed to Saint John before the time of the Emperor **Domitian**. <note>Reigned 81–96 AD. The author argues that because Revelation was written after 70 AD, it cannot refer to the Fall of Jerusalem.</note> Therefore, applying the **Seals** and **Trumpets** to the destruction of Jerusalem is not only forced (as anyone can see when examining them) but also impossible, since the visions were recorded *after* that event. Those affairs cannot be among the **"things which must shortly come to pass,"** <note>original Greek: ἃ δεῖ γενέσθai ἐν τάχει</note> because they were already in the past, not the future. 

This straining of the phrase is done merely for the sake of that specific interpretation. If that interpretation were seriously maintained, it would make the Apocalypse utterly unintelligible and therefore useless to the Church. In fact, it would cause unspeakable harm by depriving us of such an illustrious proof of Divine Providence. I believe these points together are of infinitely more importance for us to hold to that common and ancient interpretation of **"the things which must shortly come to pass"** <note>original Greek: ἃ δεῖ γενέσθai ἐν τάχει</note> which I mentioned at first, rather than to this modern one. That new view has only been started to support interpretations of the Apocalypse that are not only extremely harsh and forced, but utterly impossible.

He also asserts that the visions could not refer to the fall of Jerusalem, as the book was written during the reign of Domitian, after that event had already occurred.</summary>

# CHAPTER 21.

1. The marvelous completeness of the Reformation of the Church of **England** in her **doctrines** and **practices** <note>original: Institutes</note>. 2. That she clearly condemns the **praying to saints as idolatry** <note>original: Invocation of Saints</note>. 3. **As also the adoration of the bread in the Eucharist** <note>original: Adoration of the Host</note>, where our practice of kneeling at Communion is defended. 4. Her condemnation of the **worship of images**. 5. Her conclusion that the way the **Roman Catholics** <note>original: Papists</note> worship **saints** and **images** is clearly the **same** as that of the **pagans**. 6. Her open and fair criticism regarding the decorating of their **images**, and calling them **"books for the common people"** <note>original: Lay-mens Books</note>. 7. How perfectly she has freed us from that **Egyptian** yoke <note>A biblical metaphor for spiritual slavery and bondage.</note> we lived under during the time of **Popery**. 8. **The celebration of holy days, the observation of Lent, and the use of the surplice <note>A white liturgical vestment.</note> in the sense intended by the Church of England, fully defended from any charge of superstition or anti-Christian behavior.** 9. **That the use of the surplice is not based on any political motives within the Church, but out of pure charity; along with a defense of the use of the cross in baptism.**

Having thus clearly set out the true nature or **concept** <note>original: Idea</note> of **Anti-Christianism**, and having plainly proven that the type of **Anti-Christianism** or **Antichrist** described in that concept is that very **Antichrist** which the prophecies in the Holy Scriptures prefigure or foretell, we should now proceed to a more detailed <note>original: punctual</note> application of the said concept and prophecies to the state of the Church, from the time it fell into this Anti-Christian lapse until this very day. 

But because that is a much larger <note>original: voluminous</note> project, and less pleasing to my temperament—since I take far greater pleasure in defending an injured friend than in digging into the unpleasant failures of either a stranger or a sworn enemy—I shall satisfy myself, at least for now <note>original: at this bout</note>, with that part of the application which concerns our Reformed Church of **England**. By doing so, I have no doubt I can clear her of all accusations or suspicions of being guilty of any point of true and real Anti-Christianism in any of her doctrines or practices. 

From this, it will appear how little she is affected by this frank and faithful description of it, except to give Almighty God most humble and hearty thanks. He so graciously assisted those noble heroes with the resolution and judgment to achieve such a happy and marvelous Reformation. In this Reformation, nothing is left—not one member, nor the smallest joint or part—of that odious and hateful image or **concept** of **Antichrist** which we have described. There are no frauds or falsifications of the Gospel of Christ for the benefit of a worldly church, nor the sustaining of the priesthood through a business of lies and deceptions, which would have made any honorable <note>original: ingenuous</note> man

...ashamed to be found in the Order or Profession; whereas now, if no profanity lurks in his soul, he may well consider the *Calling* an ornament to his person. And that this is not a boast, but a real truth, I shall briefly prove by running through all those branches of *Antichristianism* (whether opposing the *Privative* <note>The "privative" ends of the Gospel refer to things the Gospel aims to remove or exclude, such as sin or false worship.</note> or *Positive* ends of the *Gospel*) which I proposed in my *Idea*.

2. The first of the first kind was *Idolatry*, specifically the *Invocation of Saints and Angels*, the *Worshipping of the Host* <note>The "Host" refers to the bread used in the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>, and the *Adoration of Images*. Although the *universal practice* of the Church of **England** sufficiently clears her from such gross accusations, I think it is worthwhile, for her greater honor, to bring to light her official and declared judgment concerning these matters. This is so that all the world may notice how sound she is at the *core* in these weighty points of Religion.

<margin>Article 22.</margin> Regarding the *Invocation of Saints*, the Church openly condemns it in the Book of Articles. There, she calls it *a foolish thing* <note>original: "fond thing"; in the 17th century, "fond" meant foolish or trivial.</note>, *vainly invented, and grounded upon no warrants of Scripture, but rather repugnant to the Word of God*; so far is it from being supported by it. Furthermore, the second part of the "Homily concerning Prayer" is entirely dedicated to proving *that we are to address our prayers to none but to God himself*. That homily offers excellent arguments for that purpose, and plainly declares that Christ is our only Mediator and Advocate. The Church does the same in the Liturgy to remove any excuse for praying to saints, and concludes sharply and all at once *that invocation is a thing reserved for God; if we attribute it to the saints, it results in their reproach, nor can they well accept it from us*. This is equivalent to judging it to be *Idolatry*. For what is *Idolatry* but giving that worship to a creature which is reserved for God? Therefore, she compares it to the pagans offering sacrifice to **Paul** at **Lystra**. I have noted extensively elsewhere how receiving divine honor must result in the reproach of whatever creature receives it.

<margin>Book 1, Chapter 12, Verse 3, Section 4.</margin> I shall only urge one more point, which is very explicit and carries great weight. The argument goes as follows: *Invocation or prayer may not be made without faith in him on whom we call, for we must first believe in him before we can make our prayer to him; therefore, we must only and solely pray to God. For to say we should believe in either an angel or a saint, or in any other living creature, would be mere horrible blasphemy against God.* This is a very remarkable passage and a demonstration that the invocation of saints and angels is outright idolatry, as it plainly implies the acknowledgment of that excellence which belongs only to God. Nor can our holy Mother the Church be thought to consider it anything less than *idolatry* by calling it <margin>Book 1, Chapter 5, Section 11.</margin> *blasphemy*, since all *idolatry* is so, and is several times called so in Scripture, as I have noted in the appropriate place.

3. Now for the second point: *the worshipping of the Host*, which assumes the bread is *transubstantiated* <note>Transubstantiation is the belief that the bread and wine in the Eucharist literally become the body and blood of Christ.</note>. She is most declaredly against both the opinion <margin>Article 28.</margin> and the practice. As stated in the Book of Articles: *Transubstantiation cannot be proved by Holy Writ, but it is repugnant to the plain words of Scripture, and it overthroweth*...
