...overthrows the nature of a *Sacrament*, and has given occasion to many *superstitions*. From this, she [the Church] rightly and logically concludes that the *Sacrament is not to be carried about, lifted up, or worshipped.* For no one can worship the Host <note>The "Host" is the consecrated bread of the Eucharist.</note>, assuming it is Christ to whom Divine worship is due, without being *by the very fact* <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> an idolater, as I have proved elsewhere at greater length. And again in the same Book [of Articles], she expressly declares *that the sacrifices of Masses, in which it is commonly said that the Priest offers Christ for the living and the dead to have remission of pain or guilt, are blasphemous fables and dangerous deceits.* The truth of this is easy to understand from what we have written in our *Idea of Antichristianism* regarding idolatry and the abuse of Christ’s person and office in this monstrous error.

And in the Homily concerning the Sacrament, she expressly charges the Popish *Masses* with idolatry, attributing it to ignorance of the nature of the Lord's Supper. *What has been the cause of this gross idolatry but ignorance thereof? What has been the cause of this mummish massing <note>original: "mummish massing"; a derogatory term for the Catholic Mass, suggesting it was like a "mummery" or a silent, mechanical play-act.</note> but ignorance thereof?* And a little after: *Let us therefore so labor to understand the Lord's Supper, that we be no cause of the decay of God's worship, of no idolatry, of no dumb massing, of no hate and malice, etc.* To all this you may add what is joined at the end of the Communion in our Liturgy, namely: *That the Sacramental bread and wine remain still in their very natural substances, and therefore may not be adored (for that would be idolatry to be abhorred by all faithful Christians). And the natural Body and Blood of our Savior Christ are in Heaven, and not here; it being against the truth of Christ's natural body to be in more than one place at one time.* This Rubric <note>A "rubric" refers to the instructions or rules for conduct within the prayer book.</note> was inserted in our Liturgy with unquestionable judgment and faithfulness, and it fully achieves the purpose of its insertion. For no man, I think, can be so grossly ignorant or so openly malicious as to claim that—after this plain declaration by our Church—either himself or anyone else could become guilty of *idolatry* by that humble posture of *kneeling* at the receiving of the *Sacrament*.

<margin>Homily against the Peril of Idolatry, Part 3.</margin>
4. And lastly, regarding the *Adoration of Images*, there can be nothing more seriously protested against by any Church than this monstrous wickedness is by ours. To omit how she has criticized <note>original: "perstringed"; meaning to censure or reproach briefly.</note> them in the Book of Articles, she expressly binds the worshippers of them under a curse in her Liturgy, in the Service of Commination <note>The "Commination" is a service of Bible readings and prayers used on Ash Wednesday, specifically reciting God's curses against sinners.</note>: *Cursed is the man that makes any carved or molten image to worship it.* And in her "Homily against the Peril of Idolatry," with a passionate but unquestionable and judicious zeal, she copiously speaks against the very presence of images in churches—I mean such as are in any capacity of being worshipped. In fact, she speaks against the very making of the *image of God* or any of the *Persons of the Holy Trinity*, even of Christ himself, insofar as he is truly God, contending that *no image can be made of Christ but a lying image* (as the Scripture specifically calls images "lies"); *for Christ is God and Man. Since, therefore, no image can be made for the Godhead, which is the most excellent part, it is falsely called the image of Christ. Therefore, images of Christ are not only defects, but also lies.*

# The Church of England Vindicated: Book II.

Nor does she <note>The "she" refers to the Church of England, as personified through its official doctrines and Homilies.</note> stop here, but advances the argument—and truly quite wisely—against the images of saints. She says that their souls, which are the *most excellent part of them*, can be *represented and expressed by no images*.

But regarding the *keeping of such images in temples*, she contends and insists with a holy jealousy that it is plainly against the Second Commandment. She adds this reason: *For once they are set up, they have been, are, and always will be worshipped, and consequently become abominable idols, no different from those of the heathens.* She argues they are made of the same materials as pagan idols, and that people hold the same ideas about the saints they represent—and their roles—as the heathens did of their deities, *worshipping them also with the same rites and ceremonies*. 

To show that they hold the same opinion of their saints that the pagans had of their various gods, she compares those saints who are made guardians of kingdoms to the "tutelar gods" <note>original: *Dii Tutelares*; deities serving as guardians or patrons of a particular place or person</note>. Examples include *Belus* to the *Babylonians*, *Osiris* and *Isis* to the *Egyptians*, and *Vulcan* to the *Lemnians*. She compares the guardian saints of cities to the "presiding gods" <note>original: *Dii Præsides*; gods who watch over a specific location</note>, such as *Apollo* was to *Delphi*, *Minerva* to *Athens*, *Juno* to *Carthage*, and *Quirinus* to *Rome*. Lastly, she compares the saints honored in specific temples to *Jupiter* in the *Capitol* and *Diana* in the famous Temple of *Ephesus*.

Regarding the practice of the same saint having images in several different places, she draws a parallel between *Our Lady of Walsingham*, *Our Lady of Ipswich*, and *Our Lady of Willesden* <note>original: "Willsdon"</note> and the various forms of Venus, such as *Venus of Cyprus*, *Venus of Paphos*, and *Venus of Cnidus*. She compares sea-gods like *Neptune*, *Triton*, *Nereus*, and *Venus* to *St. Christopher*, *St. Clement*, and the *Blessed Virgin Mary*. To *Vulcan* and *Vesta*, the gods of fire, she compares *St. Agatha*. 

She then suggests that just as in ancient paganism the affairs of love, war, and diseases in men and beasts were assigned to various deities, so they are assigned to various saints in the "Popish" <note>The author uses "Popish" as a derogatory term for Roman Catholic.</note> religion. Finally, she breaks out into this passionate exclamation:

> *Where is God's Providence and due honor in the meantime? He says, "The heavens are mine, and the earth is mine, the whole world and all that is in it. I give victory, and I put to flight. Except I keep the city, the watchman stays awake in vain. You, Lord, shall save both man and beast." But we have left him neither heaven, nor earth, nor water, nor country, nor city, nor peace, nor war to rule and govern; neither men, nor beasts, nor their diseases to cure. A godly man might justly cry out with zealous indignation: "O heaven, earth, and seas, what madness and wickedness against God have people fallen into! What dishonor do the creatures do to their Creator and Maker!" Specifically, this is done by placing a religious trust in those saints they call upon for these purposes—a trust which can belong to no one else but God himself.*

5. And regarding the *way they worship these images and saints*, she asks: *What does it mean that they—following the custom of the pagan idolaters—burn incense and offer gold to images? Why do they hang up crutches, chains, ships, or wax models of legs, arms, and whole men and women before images, as if they (or the saints) had delivered them from lameness, sickness, imprisonment, or shipwreck? Is this not* WORSHIPPING IMAGES <note>original: *COLERE IMAGINES*</note>, *which is so strictly forbidden in God’s Word?*

# Chapter 21: *From All Suspicions of Antichristianism.*

And a little after, more fully and vehemently, she <note>The "she" refers to the Church of England's official Book of Homilies, specifically the "Sermon against Peril of Idolatry."</note> says: *Therefore, when we see men and women going in crowds on pilgrimages to images, kneeling before them, holding up their hands before them, setting up candles, burning incense before them, offering up gold and silver to them, and hanging up models of ships, crutches, chains, and men and women made of wax before them <note>These items are "ex-votos," offerings left at a shrine to fulfill a vow or show gratitude for a supposed miracle or healing.</note>; attributing health and safety—which are gifts from God—to the images or the saints whom they represent (as they would prefer to have it); who, I say, can doubt but that our image-maintainers, agreeing in all idolatrous opinions, outward rites, and ceremonies with the pagan idolaters, also agree with them in committing most abominable idolatry?*

<margin>Revelation 13:14</margin>
Truly, for my part, I must confess I do not at all doubt it. Therefore, from such passages as these and several others of a similar nature scattered throughout this excellent Homily of our Church concerning *Idolatry* and *Images*, I think it an easy task to prove that such a state of the Church as is described here is the very *Image of the Beast* foretold in the *Revelation*, as any man may discern from my previous *Discourse*.

But I will give myself the trouble of transcribing one or two more passages: such as the one regarding that famous act of the good King *Hezekiah* in breaking into pieces the *Brazen Serpent* (once it was abused for idolatry), even though it was set up by the special commandment of God and was so mysterious a figure of our Savior himself. *How do you think (she says) would that godly Prince, if he were now living, handle our idols set up against God's commandment directly? Regarding the *Saints' days* in our Church, they are not numerous enough for their observation to become a burden. 9. For this reason, out of a spirit of charity and tender kindness, she has humbly condescended to share certain symbols with that fallen lady of *Rome* in matters that are in themselves "indifferent" <note>original: "indifferent"; refers to *adiaphora*, or practices neither commanded nor forbidden by God, which a church may regulate for order.</note>, in order to win back Rome's deceived followers <note>original: "abused Paramours"</note> to the pure worship of God. 

This condescension, as is well known, was effective for several years, and the Catholics joined in public prayers and services with us; until that *Woman sitting on the Seven Hills* <note>A reference to the Papacy, based on the imagery of Revelation 17:9.</note>—who at every turn reveals herself to be not the mother, but the harlot who thinks nothing of having the child divided—forcibly tore away the *English Roman* Catholics from such a reasonable and Christian communion. And yet, despite all this, our Church does not cease to use this charitable courtship and sweet condescension toward them still, to win them over to a worship that is in every way as graceful as their own, but without the poison of either *superstition* or *idolatry*.

When I consider how long this has continued without the least effect upon the Catholics of this nation, I must consider anyone either dull-sighted or unjust who will not also acknowledge a third Christian virtue in our mother, the Church of *England*, added to the former ones: I mean an impregnable and invincible patience. For all this time she has not fallen <margin>Romans 10:21</margin> into that complaint of the Prophet: *All day long I have stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people*; nor into that <margin>Acts 13:46</margin> resolution of the Apostles, who, wearied by the stubbornness <note>original: "Refractariness"</note> of the *Jews*, said: *Since you judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.*

## CHAP. XXII.

*1. The direct opposition of our Church to that part of Antichristianism which would subvert the Kingly <note>original: "Regal"</note> and Prophetic roles <note>original: "Offices"</note> of Christ. 2. As also to that which strikes at his Priestly <note>original: "Sacerdotal"</note> role. 3. That she holds nothing against those other sacred titles of Christ: the Truth, Life, Light, etc. 4. A clear <note>original: "demonstrative"</note> defense <note>original: "Vindication"</note> of the government of bishops <term>Episcopacy</term> from the accusation <note>original: "Imputation"</note> of being Antichristian, based on the Book of Revelation <note>original: "Apocalyps"</note>. 5. What a source of stability that book is—if rightly understood—to the Crown and Church of England. 6. That neither the Pope's nor the Presbyterians' power is by right above the King, not even in Church-related <note>original: "Ecclesiastical"</note> causes. 7. The judgment of our Church upon this. 8. The peculiar glory of our Church, in that she is so perfectly free from all frauds and deceptions <note>original: "Impostures"</note>. 9. Her freedom from pride; 10. From Antichristian impurity; 11. And from cruelty. 12. Her Reformation is a notable <note>original: "Speciminal"</note> fulfillment of the prophecy of the resurrection of the Two Witnesses <note>A reference to Revelation 11:3–12, often interpreted by Protestants as the revival of true doctrine during the Reformation.</note>. 13. The usefulness of this defense of her for the suppressing of Catholicism <note>original: "Popery"</note> and church division <note>original: "Schism"</note>.*

1. I ask, therefore, concerning those three known roles of Christ—*Kingly, Priestly, and Prophetic* <note>These are traditionally known as the "Threefold Office" (Munus Triplex) of Christ.</note>—is not our Church very faithful and sincere in this point, and not at all guilty of such opposing and undermining of them as I have specified in my *Idea of Antichristianism*? Does our Church pretend to be *Infallible* herself, or so much as ignore or consent to the pretended *Infallibility* of others? Nay, has she not plainly declared, <margin>Article 21.</margin> *That general Councils (since they are an assembly of men, not all of whom are governed by the Spirit and Word of God) may err, and sometimes have erred, even in things pertaining to God; and that therefore things ordained by them as necessary to Salvation have neither strength nor authority, unless it may be shown <note>original: "declared"</note> that they be taken out of the Holy Scripture?* <note>This is a direct quote from the 39 Articles, the foundational doctrines of the Church of England.</note> And in the preceding Article she affirms, <margin>Article 20.</margin> *That it is not lawful for the Church to decree <note>original: "ordain"</note> anything that is contrary to God's written Word, and that she may not so explain <note>original: "expound"</note> one place of Scripture so that it contradicts <note>original: "be repugnant to"</note> another;* and finally concludes,

<margin>Article 6.</margin>
*That although the Church is a witness and a keeper of Holy Scripture <note>original: "Writ"</note>, yet as she ought not to decree anything against the same, so besides the same she ought not to enforce anything to be believed as necessary for salvation.* To this effect, she also speaks in another Article regarding the sufficiency of Holy Scriptures. *Holy Scripture (she says) contains all things necessary for salvation; so that whatever is not read therein, nor may be proven by it, is not to be required of any man that it should be believed as an article of faith, or be thought requisite or necessary for salvation.*

And again, she speaks to the same purpose in that excellent exhortation to the reading and knowledge of Holy Scripture <note>This refers to the first of the *Church of England Homilies*, published in 1547</note>: where with all earnestness she invites everyone to diligently read it, declaring, *That in Holy Scripture is fully contained what we ought to do, and what to avoid <note>original: "eschew"</note>, what to believe, and what to love, and what to look for at God's hands in the end;* and she tells us the best way to understand them in a paragraph worthy to be written in letters of gold, toward the end of the first part of the Homily. *And in reading God's Word (she says), he does not always benefit most who is quickest in flipping through the book, or in reciting it from memory <note>original: "without-book"</note>, but he who is most "turned into" it—that is, most inspired by the Holy Spirit, and most altered and changed in his heart and life into that thing which he reads; he who is daily less and less proud, less wrathful, less greedy <note>original: "covetous"</note>, and less desirous of worldly and vain pleasures; he who daily (forsaking his old sinful life) increases in virtue more and more.*

And in the second part of that Homily, she encourages her children <note>original: "Sons"</note> against those discouragements and stumbling blocks which that false and treacherous Church <note>Referring to the Roman Catholic Church</note> casts in their way, such as alleged difficulty and obscurity. She exhorts them to pray to God for assistance in reading the Scriptures, assuring them that if they are diligent and serious, God will either send some pious and knowledgeable person (as he did Philip to the Ethiopian official <note>original: "Eunuch"</note> reading the Prophets) to instruct them, or that He Himself from above will give light to our minds and teach us those things that are necessary for us, and regarding which we are ignorant. She further adds, quoting Saint Chrysostom: *That human and worldly wisdom or science is not as necessary for the understanding of Scripture as is the revelation of the Holy Spirit, who inspires the true meaning into those who search for it with humility and diligence.*

And lastly, she concludes, *That none are enemies to the reading of God's Word except those who are either so ignorant that they do not know what a wholesome thing it is; or else are so sick that they hate the most comfortable medicine that should heal them; or so ungodly that they would wish the people to still continue in blindness and ignorance of God.* How completely opposite <note>original: "diametrically opposite"</note> this spirit <note>original: "Genius"</note> of our Church is to that Antichristian spirit I have described in its opposing and undermining of the Kingly <note>original: "Regal"</note> and Prophetic roles <note>original: "Offices"</note> of Christ, is obvious for any man to see who wishes only to compare them.

This alone will also vindicate her from any accusation of the following points of "Antichristianism" against the Peace of Christ's Kingdom. And as for absolving Princes from their Oaths, what Church, unless that of *Rome*, ever pretended to such a blasphemous power?

Some who are not so well-minded may perhaps be overly inclined to imagine that the Episcopal Office and its revenues have a greater closeness <note>original: "propinquity"</note> with that *hypothesis* at the end of this Chapter than any impartial <note>original: "indifferent"</note> man can possibly judge. # The Church of England Vindicated: Book II. 472

<margin>* Luke 10:7</margin>
4. For my own part, although I do not know the exact financial values of the various Bishoprics <note>The office or rank of a bishop, or the region they oversee</note> of this nation, yet considering the size of their dioceses and the great burden of both care and expense involved in conscientiously performing their duties, I truly cannot imagine the revenue to be so large that the weight of the office does not exceed its value. We read in the Gospel that *the laborer is worthy of his hire*. Concerning the office and its dignity itself, I cannot believe that an order of the Church instituted and practiced in those ages which were "symmetral" <note>original: "Symmetral" — meaning well-proportioned or conforming to the original, pure pattern of the early church</note> can with any honesty or conscience be judged Antichristian. That the Church remained "symmetral" for about four hundred years after Christ is a demonstrable logical conclusion <note>original: "Consectary"</note> from my *Joint-Exposition*, and that exposition is so convincingly evident that no interpretation of any Scripture can be more certain.

5. Therefore, I cannot help but wonder why any true son of the Church of England should be so shy or fearful of the *Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation</note> that they dare not touch it without a pair of "mittens" made by Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch scholar whose interpretations of Revelation were often seen as too soft on the Roman Catholic Church</note> for fear it should bite them. By this, I mean they fear it unless it is unfolded—or rather, folded up—in Grotius's foolish and groundless explanations. For there is no book in the world that does more to establish the *Crown* and the *Church of England* than this holy Book of Revelation, if it is rightly and solidly understood. This is something that the wise and perceptive Prince, King *James* of blessed memory, discovered early on, and he accordingly used it against the usurpations of the Church of *Rome*. Truly, I find nothing in the Apocalypse—though the style seems mysterious and enigmatic—that is not very rational. I look upon it as the most faithful and philosophical writing ever penned. We have a taste of this in the list of evil characters who are excluded from the *Holy City*; in that list, bloody and inhumane zeal, as well as vain and deceptive superstition, are plainly criticized <note>original: "perstringed"</note>. The former is found in *phoneis* <note>original: "φονεῖς" — murderers</note>; the latter in *pharmakoi*, *deiloi*, and *pas ho poiōn kai philōn pseudos* <note>original: "φαρμακοὶ, δειλοὶ, καὶ πᾶς ὁ ποιῶν καὶ φιλῶν ψεῦδος" — sorcerers, cowards, and everyone who practices and loves a lie</note>. These refer to sorcerers, exorcists, enchanters, and writers of lying legends <note>original: "Legendists" — those who wrote fabricated stories about saints</note>, as well as fearful, intimidated spirits who are superstitiously inclined to submit to the delusions and lies of such shameless deceivers. Our faithful Redeemer of souls, who deals in good faith <note>original: "bonâ fide"</note> with mankind to rescue their abused minds from the tyranny and burden of superstition, marks these people with infamy and condemnation. The Lord *Jesus* is such a firm friend to humanity, equity, truth, and reason.

This includes authority over the Clergy as well as the Laity, and in ecclesiastical matters as well as civil ones. No Papal or Presbyterian power should be above him, just as our *English Episcopacy* <note>The system of church government by bishops</note> most justly and professedly submits to him. For why should any clergyman expect a Prince, who has received the same precious faith as themselves, to lose his power by becoming a Christian? # Chapter XXII. *From all suspicions of Antichristianism.*

...to give up so much of his natural stature that he would rank lower than the priest who baptized him. For Christianity does not take away nature or power, but employs it correctly.

Do you think any of the pagan emperors could have been brought over to the Christian faith if the *Bishop of Rome* <note>The Pope</note> had claimed headship over the empire as part of Christ’s Church? Or would they not have suspected that preaching about the "Kingdom of Heaven" was just a trick by priests to make themselves lords of the earth? Certainly not. Once a prince becomes Christian—that is, a believer and professor of the Apostolic faith contained in the Word of God in those plain and generally-accepted points of our religion—he is a person so sacred that nothing can rank above him as the head of his own dominions. For the "anointing of the Spirit" <note>referring to divine grace or inner faith</note> through which we believe for salvation is infinitely holier than any external priestly <note>original: "Sacerdotal"</note> oil. Why, then, may not such a sacred fountain be the head and influencer of the whole Church? And is Christ greater as a *priest* or as the *king* of saints? Also, who had the preeminence in the government <note>original: "Polity"</note> of the *Jews*—the kings or the high priests of *Israel*? And was not that government a type or figure <note>A prophetic symbol or foreshadowing</note> of the Church of Christ?

The plain law of Christ is indeed unchangeable <note>original: "immutable"</note>, and it ought to be so; no man on earth may set aside even a tiny part <note>original: "tittle"</note> of it. But as for authorizing interpretations, opinions, and the rites and ceremonies of religious worship, this must either be in a Christian prince’s power (and not the priest’s), or else his kingdom and its safe administration are not truly within his control. According to the eternal law of nature and reason, all these things should be in the hand of the one who is the supreme governor, and it is a contradiction of his supremacy if they are not. For he who holds the reins of men's souls rules their whole persons, and the strongest reins are those of religion. Therefore, if any power separate from the king's claims the right to order religious affairs beyond what he allows and likes, that power is effectively the king. The king himself then holds only a shaky <note>original: "precarious"</note> power, liable to be blown around and knocked off his throne by the false breath of these pretenders to the headship of the Church, as often and as violently as they please.

Therefore, while the plain and accepted law of Christ is unchangeable, anything that is doubtful or merely ritual should be interpreted, changed, or continued according to the judgment and discretion of every Christian prince. He has the most just and necessary power to adapt such things for the peace, stability, and prosperity of his kingdom. Nor do ecclesiastical powers have any inherent or essential right to attach anything to the Christian religion that is not expressly and clearly included in it according to the divine authority of the Scriptures. It is a great wrong to this religion—which is intended to be everlasting and universal—to be bound and fettered with rites or opinions that are only temporary or local <note>original: "Topical"</note>. It is equally wrong that the errors and mistakes of a "dark antiquity" <note>Referring to the early or medieval past, which the author views as less enlightened than the present Reformation era</note> should become like a law of the *Medes* and *Persians* <note>An ancient biblical idiom for a law that can never be changed or repealed</note> to more serious and...

7. Therefore, our Church has most openly and wisely declared in her *Homily on Fasting*:
> *God’s Church neither ought to be, nor can be, tied to any order made now or in the future by human authority. Instead, it may lawfully—for just causes—alter, change, or lessen those ecclesiastical decrees and orders. It may even withdraw from them entirely and break them when they lead to superstition or impiety, or when they draw people away from God rather than building them up in faith.*

<margin>Article 34.</margin> And in the *Book of Articles* <note>The Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion, the defining statements of Anglican doctrine</note>, she plainly asserts again:
> *It is not necessary that traditions and ceremonies be exactly the same in all places; for they have always been diverse and may be changed according to the differences between countries, times, and men’s manners, provided that nothing is ordained against God’s Word.*

And finally, at the close of that Article:
> *Every particular or national Church has the authority to ordain, change, and abolish ceremonies or rites of the Church that were ordained only by human authority, so that all things are done for the purpose of edification.*

If these matters—which are so flexible and subject to change—could be governed by a power distinct from and independent of the supreme power of a Christian nation, and if that power were motivated by its own private interests, what wild commotions and confusions might they cause in a Christian state? It would be like goading and spurring an ass to go one way while he sees the Angel of the Lord with a drawn sword driving him back! <note>A reference to the story of Balaam’s donkey in Numbers 22, where the animal sees a divine messenger that the rider does not.</note>

Therefore, it is most safe and just that in all matters beyond the essentials <note>original: "preter-Essentials"</note> of the Christian religion, the supreme magistrate in every Christian nation should have the power to allow or disapprove of them. No rites or opinions should become official decrees except by his authority. This ensures that the priesthood is not able (just as they ought to be so faithful to their prince as to be unwilling) to teach or decree anything against the interests of the one whose subjects they are. Nor should they act against the safety, peace, and prosperity of the *whole* state, of which they are only a part. Therefore, they should have no power to do anything independently of the prince, who is the *common father* of his entire country and whose interest is the good and welfare of all. He, therefore, must necessarily be the Head of the Church *over all causes and persons, both ecclesiastical and civil* (as our Church plainly acknowledges), so that vital influence may flow equally from him into all members of his dominions.

But this is a point that might have been more appropriately postponed until we reached the discussion of "Antichristian" opposition to the first branch of the divine life, which is *humility*—a virtue that the extreme pride of the Papal supremacy so clearly offends. However, I have already abundantly proved that there is not the slightest stain of "Antichristianism" in *episcopacy* <note>The system of church government by bishops</note> itself.

# Chapter XXII. From all suspicions of Antichristianity.

8. Regarding the Root of the Divine Life, our Church is so clearly free from these corruptions (as anyone who cares to look can see) that it is enough to mention it only briefly. However, I cannot let go of this timely opportunity to celebrate on her behalf, for she has been thoroughly reformed from that notorious, though subtle and crafty, element of Antichristianity: I mean that *self-serving policy* found in the many doctrines and practices of the Church of Rome that are so profitable for them. Our Heaven-directed Reformation has perfectly refined and cleansed us from them all. 

Reflecting on this must make our Mother, the Church of England, look very lovely and lovable to every sincere and discerning eye. Such a person cannot help but bless God for the sound judgment and faithfulness He gave to our Royal and Reverend Reformers. It must also be a great satisfaction to every honest priest or minister of our Church to know that he feeds neither himself nor the people with lies, as the Roman priesthood does. He does not put a single morsel of bread into his mouth that was stolen from the laity through fraud and deception. Instead, as he labors for the Gospel, he lives by the Gospel, and not by fictions and cunningly-devised fables.

9. It is even more apparent to anyone who considers them that our Church is cleared of those oppositions to the divine grace of *Humility* (which were specified in the ninth, tenth, and eleventh chapters). I hardly need to go through the trouble of proving it in detail. The *Pope's Supremacy* is not only argued against but sworn against, as is only just and right. And although there are specific garments <note>original: "Habits"</note> for clergymen, as I have noted above, our Church explicitly declares there is no inherent holiness in such things; they are used only for decency and to distinguish roles. This distinction between the laity and the clergy is as old as Christianity itself and has existed through all the *symmetrical ages* <note>original: "Symmetral Ages"—referring to the early centuries of the Church, which the author considers to have been pure and properly ordered</note> of the Church. Thus, it is clear that nothing remains in the structure of our English Church that, by its own nature, "Antichristianly" opposes that heavenly and Christian grace of *Humility*. However, when we look at individual people, who can prevent a layman from being as proud as a clergyman, or a presbyter from being as proud as a bishop? If we judged by personal behavior alone, everyone would be labeled "Antichristian" on those grounds.

10. It is equally evident that none of those oppositions to the celestial grace of *Purity* (noted in the twelfth chapter) are to be found in our Church. Not only that, but I think we may—without vanity, provided it is done with humble thankfulness to Almighty God, who inspired our heroic Reformers with such excellent prudence and judgment—take pride in the excellent and fitting organization of our *Universities*. There, no one is bound by vows of celibacy <note>original: "Cœlibate"</note>, nor confined to separate and solitary cells to be displayed in strange clothing with shaved heads <note>original: "circumcised crowns," referring to the tonsure</note> and gloomy or bloated faces—the way they show off strange animals through the cages at the Tower <note>A reference to the Royal Menagerie at the Tower of London, where lions and other exotic animals were kept and viewed by the public</note>. Instead, they live under freer and more manly laws and engage in noble exercises, without either the whip or the hypocrisy of superstition. They are appointed to spend their time in such things as may adorn their souls with real knowledge and virtue...

# Chapter XXII: Clearing the Church from all Suspicions of Antichristianism

Concerning the Sovereign Authority; I cannot help but declare that I do not doubt at all that the *Reformation* of our *English Church* into the condition I have briefly described was one notable *example* and *fulfillment* of the *prophecy* of the *rising of the Two Witnesses* <note>A reference to Revelation 11, where two "witnesses" of God are killed and then resurrected after three and a half days</note>. It also fulfills that *Voice from Heaven* (which is to say, the *Sovereign Power*) saying to them, *Come up here*. For every tiny detail of the *prophecy* is exactly applicable to this event, as anyone who tries will find. Furthermore, such a notable act of providence as the Protestant Reformation is not prophesied anywhere else if not in that vision. For none of the *Vials* <note>The Seven Bowls of God's wrath in Revelation 16</note> are within the *Sixth Trumpet* (where the vision of the *Witnesses* occurs), but are all within the *Seventh*, as I have already clearly proved. Nor do those other visions express the first Reformation in its chief circumstances; no vision does so except this one of the *Resurrection of the Witnesses*.

I know of nothing that should make a person hesitate to believe this, unless it is the fact that the *Witnesses* are said to be raised up after "three days and a half"—that is to say, three "Times" and a half—whereas our Reformation occurred within those Times, specifically in the last half of a "Time." But no observation is more common <note>original: "trivial"</note> than this: that a designation of time divided into parts (unless some specific detail limits it to one meaning) may signify either a space of time fully completed, or else a period ending during its last division. For example, if someone says, "*Christ rose after three days of death*" <note>original: "Post triduum mortis resurrexit Christus"</note>, no one understands that to mean Christ was dead for three entire days. Likewise, the phrase "*Some months later*" <note>original: "Aliquot post menses"</note> may just as well be rendered as "*Within some months after*." 

In the book of <margin>Chapter 38:24</margin> *Genesis*, the *Seventy* <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> expressly translate the Hebrew phrase for "about three months later" as "*as if about three months*" <note>original Greek: "ὡς τρίμηνον"</note>, whereas the genuine sense is "*within three months*" or "*when the third month was passing*" <note>original Latin: "cum tertius mensis ageretur"</note>, as the marginal notes of the scholar *Vatablus* <note>François Vatable, a 16th-century French humanist and biblical scholar</note> explain. From this, it is evident that the word "*after*" does not imply the time has fully run out, but rather that the last part of the time must be currently passing. And so it is in this prophecy: our Reformation happened in the last *Half-Time* or *Half-Day*. This doubt is easily removed; therefore, the application fits the event so well that I do not doubt this vision was a prediction of it. This should make our Reformation even more sacred to us, and it should frighten men away from either violently tearing it to pieces or more secretly and indirectly corrupting it by sneaking in old, discarded items <note>original: "ware"</note> that were disallowed and rejected by our pious and wise Reformers.

13. But this is a *supplementary point* <note>original: "Mantissa" – an addition or surplus</note> thrown in over and above our bargain. I had already finished my main task, which was to briefly prove (and, if I am not mistaken, I have done it clearly and convincingly) that the heaven-inspired wisdom and judgment of the Royal, heroic, and Reverend Reformers of our Church of *England* have purged and cleansed her from whatever doctrine or practiced profession might rightly be considered *Antichristian*. I have shown that she neither holds nor requires anything that is contrary to the truly Catholic and Apostolic Faith. This just and timely defense of her, when considered alongside

### BOOK II.

**CHAPTER I.** 1. *The positive goals <note>original: "Ends"</note> of the Gospel which the remaining limbs of Antichristianism <note>The author uses "limbs" to describe different parts of the religious system he is critiquing as being against Christ</note> oppose.* 2. *That claiming a right to the infallible interpretation of the Laws of Christ is a way of undermining his office as King.* 3. *An instance of that danger in the interpretations <note>original: "Glosses"</note> of the Pharisees.* 4. *Several passages of Scripture cited to prove the Church is infallible.* 5. *The first general answer to these claims, by asking whether the promise of infallibility is made to the whole Church, or only a part.* 6. *The second, by asking whether the promise is absolute or conditional.* 7. *A third, that the promise cannot be universal regarding every possible subject.* 8. *A specific answer to the first passage of Scripture.* 9. *An answer to the second and third.* 10. *Infallibility was a promise only to the first founders of the Christian Church.* 11. *The meaning of "The pillar and ground of truth."* <note>1 Timothy 3:15</note> 12. *A further explanation of that passage from Paul to Timothy.* 13. *That if understood as the Universal Church, it may only refer to it during the time of the Apostles.* 14. *And that the same may be said of the final citation.* 87

**CHAPTER II.** 1. *That the safe delivery of the Apostolic writings to us by the Church does not mean she is infallible.* 2. *That the clarity of Scripture in points necessary for salvation removes the need for an infallible judge.* 3. *That since Scripture does not point to any infallible judge nor any faithful keeper of traditions, it declares itself by that very fact <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> to be the only sufficient guide.* 4. *That there is not only no need for an infallible judge, but it is better that there should be none.* 5. *That the lack of infallibility does not take away the authority of the Church, as it is the duty of every person to defer to her in things that are truly debatable.* 6. *That although a visible*

# To the READER.

READER,

<image-desc>A decorative ornamental woodcut initial letter 'T' featuring scrolling foliate and floral patterns.</image-desc>
THE *occasion of the following* Apology <note>original: "Apologie." In this context, an "apology" is not an admission of guilt but a formal, reasoned defense of one's positions or writings.</note> *I have sufficiently declared in the* Apology *itself. The* reason *for its* length <note>original: "Prolixness"</note> *is based on this threefold ground: The* weightiness *of the* objections; *my* awareness <note>original: "sensibleness"</note> *of the heavy* disadvantage <note>original: "Inconvenience"</note> *I would suffer if I did not thoroughly clear myself of the* accusations <note>original: "Imputations"</note> *they carry with them; and my* ambition *to satisfy those worthy and learned persons who, out of a commendable zeal for the* Church *and for supporting the* Truth, *took the trouble to frame these objections. These considerations have made me use more than ordinary diligence to accurately answer (and, I hope, to the full satisfaction of all) every proposed* objection, *simply to* restore <note>original: "Repair"</note> *my own* reputation <note>original: "Credit"</note>—*an opportunity which was so friendly and seasonably offered to me, and for which I shall always acknowledge myself very much obliged. Furthermore, I am confident no fair-minded <note>original: "ingenuous"</note> person will think the* reputation <note>original: "Repute"</note> *of the* critics <note>original: "Proposers"</note> *is at all diminished by this necessary* recovery *of my own, even though I have fully answered the* objections *using the very* treatise <note>The "treatise" refers to his previous work, "The Grand Mystery of Godliness" (1660).</note> *from which they were raised.*

*For the* learning, talents, *and* judgment *of the* critics *are so widely recognized as eminent by all who know them, that nothing but a lack of leisure to read my entire* treatise *and compare one passage with another could have led them to misunderstand those* passages *to which they objected.*

*Therefore,* Reader, *while you read the* ten *ensuing* objections *along with my* answers *to them, you should not imagine yourself a* spectator *of a* battle *between declared* enemies, *but rather of an amicable* debate <note>original: "Concertation"</note> *between those who are real* friends, *both to one another and to* Truth *herself. For their part, they show nothing but a proper* zeal *and commendable* vigilance <note>original: "Jealousy"</note> *regarding the* doctrines *in my* Mystery of Godliness, <note>More’s "An Explanation of the Grand Mystery of Godliness" was a work of "latitudinarian" theology, attempting to provide a rational basis for Christianity while being open to various philosophical interpretations.</note> *ensuring it appears to everyone that there are no other [doctrines...]*

# THE
# APOLOGY
## OF
## Dr. HENRY MORE.

### CHAPTER I.

1. *The reason and goal for writing this apology.* 2. *The philosophical nature of this present age.* 3. *The great harmony between true philosophy and true Christianity.* 4. *Certain rules he followed while writing his treatises regarding Christianity in this rational and philosophical age. The first rule, and the reason for it.* 5. *Application of the rule to certain examples.* 6. *That the* Mundus Plebeiorum <note>original: "Mundus Plebeiorum." Latin for "the world of the common people," referring to a simplified or physical view of the universe intended for a general audience rather than scholars.</note> *seems to be the limit of the story of the Creation, and how this "Common World" itself is defined.* 7. *That the Creation of the world is a true historical or chronological epoch* <note>original: "Epocha." A fixed point in time from which a series of years is reckoned.</note> *of the entire story of the Bible.* 8. *That although all the miraculous passages in the first three chapters of* Genesis *are historically true, that does not prevent them from also having a symbolic or hieroglyphical meaning.* 9. *The opinion of several learned interpreters that all those passages are not to be understood literally, and what discretion and caution those who do understand them all literally should use regarding philosophers.* 10. *The second rule, and the reason for it.* 11. *The third rule, with the proof of it.* 12. *That his inclusion of some principles of* Cartesianism <note>The philosophy of René Descartes, which More initially admired for its mechanical explanations of the universe.</note> *in his philosophical writings,* 13. *And* Platonism <note>The philosophy of Plato and his followers, which emphasizes the reality of spiritual forms and the soul.</note> *is done in accordance with this third rule.* 14. *The fourth rule, with its reason and the author’s actions following it.* 15. *The reason for the fifth rule.* 16. *And the exquisite care the author took to practice it accordingly.*

<margin>1.</margin>
Having been informed by several sources and at various times that certain passages in my writings seem less than true and orthodox to some, I thought it my solemn duty—both to defend myself from any unfair accusations and to satisfy those who are conscientious and sincere—to maintain the usefulness of my books. Otherwise, they might lose the effectiveness they have for promoting truth and virtue. I intend to bring those places that have caused any mistake into public view, clearing them and explaining them so that there may not be left the slightest excuse for misunderstanding or taking offense at them any longer. Not only this, but I also intend to give a more general account of the unique *scope* and *design*...

# The More General Account of Chapter I.

...purpose of my treatises, both philosophical and theological, so that once it is more fully and clearly understood, any occasion for future mistake in anything may be cut off and prevented. And this, as the Law of Method requires, I will address first.

<margin>Daniel 12:4</margin>
2. Some have noted, and even complained (though I will not judge how justly), that the age we live in is a *Philosophical Age* <note>original: "Seculum Philosophicum."</note>—a searching, inquisitive, rational, and philosophical age. This is a truth so plain that it cannot be hidden. It was foreseen many ages ago by the Prophet Daniel—or rather, it was foretold to him by that glorious angel who appeared to him on the banks of the great river Hiddekel <note>The ancient name for the Tigris River.</note>: *“Many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased: this should happen at the time of the end.”* I believe it is manifest that we are even at the end of that time; I mean that this last age is in the last "half-time" of those seven that encompass the <term>latter times</term> <note>original: "ὕστεροι καιροὶ." Refers to the biblical period leading to the end of the world.</note> properly so called. Therefore, it is no wonder to me that people lately have been, and still are, so inquisitive after the truth of things.

<margin>* Verse 3</margin>
3. Therefore, so that there might be a "turning toward righteousness" as well as a "running after knowledge," and so that a real or pretended skill in philosophy might not prejudice anyone’s faith or their persuasion of the truth of the Christian religion, I set myself seriously and freely to search into the most rational grounds of all philosophical speculations. I examined those that could in any way claim to be important for either strengthening or weakening any principle of faith or the truths recorded in the Holy Scriptures. 

Now, to make my report after a most diligent and anxious investigation—one as free, I think, as any man can possibly make—I can sincerely <note>original: "ex animo."</note> avow to all the world that **there is no real clashing at all between any genuine point of Christianity and what true philosophy and right reason determine or allow.** Rather, as Aristotle somewhere speaks, **"the truth is always in harmony with itself,"** <note>original: "τῷ ἀληθεῖ πάντοτε συνᾴδει."</note> there is a perpetual peace and agreement between truth and truth, of whatever nature or kind they may be. It is only blind "superstitionists" or superficial <term>philosophasters</term> <note>A term for shallow or pretender philosophers who lack deep understanding.</note> who imagine any such <term>digladiation</term> <note>original: "digladiation." A fierce conflict or combat, literally "a fighting with swords."</note> between true philosophy and real Christianity. Indeed, I can freely profess to the world that all the philosophy to which I give even a *tentative* approval—if it were true (as it certainly is exceedingly rational)—is so far from clashing with Christian truth that, next to the Bible and its wonderfully faithful and clear prophecies, it would be the greatest strengthening of my faith in all the grand strokes of our religion that I could imagine or desire.

<margin>Luke 22:32</margin>
4. Being so fully persuaded of the firmness and soundness of our religion, and not unmindful of that saying of our Savior, *"When you have turned back, strengthen your brothers,"* <note>original: "Tu conversus confirma fratres."</note> I conceived that such a province as this was naturally assigned to my care: namely, **to present the truth of our religion in a way that would most appeal to men of a more rational and philosophical genius, since the present age abounds so much with them.** As my sincerity in this business cannot, I think, be suspected by anyone, I hope that when they understand the method or rules I follow in this design, my way of managing it will be condemned by very few. The *rules* I followed are briefly these:

# Chapter 1: The Manner and Scope of his Writings.

## How a person is to behave in this *Rational and Philosophical Age* for the purpose of winning people over to, or keeping them in, the *Christian Faith*.

### RULE I.

A person must be careful not to deny anything that the person they wish to convince holds and asserts based on clear and solid reason. And especially, they must be cautious about denying it as something contrary to the Christian faith, unless it is plainly and truly opposed to the infallible words of Holy Scripture.

4. The reason for the first part of this rule is the danger of making oneself look like a contemptible, superstitious fool <term>idiot</term> <note>original: "Idiot." In this period, "idiot" often referred to an unlearned person or a private citizen without professional knowledge, rather than its modern derogatory meaning.</note>, and thereby making oneself useless in the task one has undertaken. Their opponent would immediately interpret their religious commitment not as a result of judgment, but as a result of chance, ignorance, or the power of their upbringing.

The reason for the second part is the risk of bringing religion itself into contempt, making it seem as though it were not the command of the infallible God, but the work of fallible and mistaken men. Such men, being ignorant of the nature of things yet seeing an opportunity, might have seized the roles of lawmakers and prophets, just as Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet."</note> did. This approach might save a person from the reproach of appearing irrational if they admit to their opponent that their own religion seems irrational to them; however, in the meantime, it betrays religion to the scorn and contempt of the challenger. It makes Christianity appear no more commendable than the vilest deception that ever had the fortune to be labeled as "religion."

And lastly, the phrase is added: *Unless it be plainly and really contrary to the Infallible Oracles of Divine Scripture.* For certainly, any "reasoning" that is truly contrary to the scriptures is not true reason if it is examined to the bottom; nor are those interpretations of Scripture true if they are contrary to true reason.

5. Therefore, as a consequence of this first rule, anyone dealing with a skilled philosopher must not deny the *motion of the Earth*, as it is so logically solid and not truly contrary to Holy Scripture. For the fact that the *Earth moves annually and daily <term>diurnally</term> around the Sun* is extremely clear to natural reason, as shown by what I have written in my Letter to a Most Distinguished Man <note>original: "Epistle to V. C." V. C. stands for *Vir Clarissimus*, a title More used when writing to René Descartes.</note>, Section 7. And many have proved so well that this is not contrary to Scripture that it is enough just to mention their hard work. 

Furthermore, one cannot easily deny that the *Earth is a planet.* For that is a necessary consequence of its moving around the *Sun* just like other planets do. It also reflects light like the *Moon* and passes through the *Zodiac* <note>original: "Zodiack."</note> as other planets do. Scripture nowhere denies that the Earth is a *planet*, any more than it denies that it moves around the *Sun*. Therefore, since these and similar conclusions so strongly force themselves upon human reason and philosophical study, it would be extremely unwise and hugely damaging to the Christian religion for anyone to claim they are contrary to the Christian faith and the holy words of God. Doing so would make common and unlearned <term>idiotical</term> ideas about these things pass for the...

<summary>Henry More establishes his first rule for modern religious debate: do not reject logically sound scientific conclusions, such as the Copernican view of the Earth's motion, unless they explicitly contradict Scripture.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Henry More’s argument that Christianity should not be presented as contrary to reason or science, as doing so makes it appear as a man-made superstition like Islam.</meta>

<page-num>484</page-num>

...the indispensable articles of the Christian belief. For the disadvantage that unphilosophical positions do to a religion is conspicuous in *Islam* <note>original: "Mahometism."</note>, where stories like the *Moon* going through *Muhammad's sleeve*, the *Sun* resting in a *well*, and the *stars* hanging in chains and being as large as *mountains*, make all wise men look upon that religion as merely human—a man-made invention—and not of divine institution.

6. Therefore, as I said, it would be very damaging to the Christian faith to assert that the scientific conclusions named above are repugnant to it, unless they were truly contrary to *Scripture*. In reality, Scripture is plainly silent regarding these things. The subject of the story of the *Creation* is not the *World of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Mundus Philosophorum," referring to the universe as understood through scientific study.</note>, but the *World of the Common People* <note>original: "Mundus Plebeiorum."</note>. This is an understanding of the world that goes no further and acts in no other way than what agrees with the senses and imagination of unlearned people. Therefore, Scripture speaks of the *appearances* <note>original: "φαινόμενα" (phainomena)</note> or *impressions* <note>original: "ἐμφάσεις" (emphaseis)</note> of the universe according to those sensible *ideas* that are impressed upon the *organ* of sight. It describes the blue sky, the clouds, the sun, and the stars as being at roughly the same distance from the earth, and speaks of them as being the same size they appear to the eye. 

This is demonstrable from the text itself in Genesis 1:6, where the *firmament* or *heaven* (for they are declared to be the same) is said to be *between the upper and lower waters*, and to be made specifically to *separate them*. Therefore, both the *location* and *function* of the firmament show plainly that it reaches only to the *upper waters*—that is, the *clouds*. This is the view held by *Rupertus*, *Eugubinus*, *Pererius*, *Gregorius de Valentia*, *Augustine*, *Castellio*, *Calvin*, *Vatablus*, and *Drusius* <note>These are prominent biblical commentators and theologians from the medieval through the early modern periods.</note>. *Grotius* also seems to favor this same view. And lastly, *David the Hebrew*, surnamed *Kimhi* <note>original: "Camius." David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235) was a famous medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical scholar.</note>, stiffly contends that the proper meaning of the word *expanse* <note>original: "רקיע" (Rakiya)</note> is the *air*. Yet, within this *expanse* (which is ordinarily translated as *firmament*), the *stars*, *moon*, and *sun* are also placed (verses 14, 15, 16, 17) and described in the proportions that their visual images appear to us within this space.

Therefore, the entire scope of the world that is historically recorded in *Genesis* is limited by a *half-circle* <note>original: "Semiperiphery."</note> drawn upon the *axis* of the earth, extending at each pole somewhat above the clouds, and then rotated around. This *half-circle* thus turned will describe the *spherical space* <note>original: "Sphæricum."</note> of this *World of the Common People*. This is just as much the subject of *Moses's* history of the creation as it shall be of the final conflagration (as *Mr. Mede* <note>Joseph Mede (1586–1638), an influential English scholar known for his interpretations of biblical prophecy.</note> has judiciously defined) at the second coming of Christ on the Last Day.

7. The making or framing of the heaven and the earth is, therefore, a true historical or chronological *epoch* <note>original: "Epocha," a starting point in time.</note> of the entire story of the Bible. In contrast, the philosophical *Kabbalah* <note>original: "Cabbala." More uses this term to refer to a deeper, mystical, or philosophical interpretation of the creation story.</note> is not limited by *time*, but only explains the *nature* of the parts of God's entire creation. But here, in Genesis, the very *order of time* is noted. The *six days* might be easily distinguished by six daily rotations <note>original: "diurnal Circumvolutions"</note> of the earth, whatever their path might be, and the whole creation is a real history of things or of the *production* of the appearances of nature. As for things that seem miraculous and outside the course of nature, it is not at all contrary to reason to conceive that they were truly done by God, intended as everlasting symbols of important truths. This is consistent with several other miraculous passages of providence in the rest of the history of the Old Testament, which are standing figures or types of the greatest and most amazing...

...amazing mysteries of the Kingdom of God, such as that miraculous passage of the **Israelites** through the Red Sea, and the like.

8. So it is that the very letter of the history is true, though delivered with advantages suited to or in compliance with the **common person's understanding** <note>original: "Vulgar Apprehension"</note>. That is to say, **it is true that God formed Adam from the dust of the Earth**, "just as sculptors mold men out of clay" <note>original: "ut Plastæ fingunt homines luteos"</note>, as **Cornelius à Lapide** <note>A prominent 17th-century Jesuit biblical exegete.</note> says; "but having added a rich liquid to this dust," says **Tertullian** <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD).</note>, "[God] curdled it into clay" <note>original: "sed hunc pulverem addito opimo liquore... in argillam coagulavit"</note>. They also understand the breathing into **his nostrils** metaphorically. These metaphors are perfectly suited to the capacity of the people. Therefore, there is not the slightest conflict here between the **Historical Cabbala** and the **Philosophical Cabbala** <note>More uses the term "Cabbala" here to mean a traditional or mystical interpretation of Scripture.</note>.

It is also true that **Adam** was cast into a sleep and had one of his **ribs** made into a **woman**. The wisdom and speech of the **serpent** is also true, as **St. Ephrem**, **St. Basil**, and **Josephus** <note>Ephrem the Syrian and Basil of Caesarea were Church Fathers; Josephus was a 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> have both rationally conceived and declared. And finally, the **making of garments of skins** and the **placing of the flaming Cherubim before the gates of Paradise** are also **historically** true; though in the meantime, nothing prevents the history of all these things from being also **symbolical** and **hieroglyphical**.

9. But even if a person is personally convinced of the **historical truth** of these **symbols**, I question whether he should over-confidently assert the certainty of them in every passage to men of a more **philosophical mind**. This is especially true because very sober and well-respected writers have affirmed that some of them are **parabolical**. For instance, **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading Catholic theologian.</note> views the story of the **serpent** this way, understanding it as the **Devil** inwardly suggesting to **Eve** such reasons as might tempt her to sin. **Cyril** and **Eugubinus** also understand it as the Devil assuming such a shape. **Tertullian** understands the **flaming sword** and **Cherubim** to represent the **Torrid Zone** <note>The hot, tropical region of the Earth near the equator.</note>. And **Cajetan** again makes the story of the **rib** a parable, saying that **Adam** and **Eve** were created at the same moment in time, and that **Adam** gave names to the animals approaching him only "in an intellectual vision" <note>original: "in visione intellectuali"</note>. Therefore, it would be very unwise—since both some Christians of high standing, as well as **Philo** and other **Jewish scholars**, make several passages of these chapters **parabolical**—to insist to a **philosopher** that they are all strictly **historical**, regardless of what a man may believe in his own heart regarding this matter. But this is a tangent, perhaps not entirely necessary, though consistent enough with the natural goal of our first rule.

### RULE II.

He must, once he has admitted the conclusions of his opponent as rational, occasionally show how no point of the Christian faith is in any way weakened or harmed by them.

10. The reason for this is that otherwise, his admission of the rational grounds or conclusions of his philosophical opponent might endanger the belief in some point of the Christian faith, and harden the person he wishes to convert in his former infidelity. As a result of this rule, I must confess it may very well be that some things may occur as allowed and approved...

mentioned by me in my writings, which philosophers most easily and most generally allow, merely to take the opportunity to show that no harm or risk comes to any principle of our religion by admitting they were true. This makes me seem, in some places, to allow for the **unorganized nature** <note>original: "Unorganizedness"</note> of the **ethereal vehicle of the soul** <note>The "ethereal vehicle" refers to the subtle, celestial body that Neoplatonists believed the soul inhabits after leaving the physical body; "unorganized" here suggests it lacks a complex internal structure like organs.</note>, which I shall discuss in its proper place.

### RULE III.

That the author himself is to choose such principles or conclusions of philosophy as—having no real conflict with Scripture—are also in themselves the most undeniably defensible and demonstrable. These should be the most easily reconciled with the attributes of God and the **workings of Providence** <note>original: "Phænomena of Providence"</note>; they should also be capable of preventing or answering the greatest objections an atheist can **devise** <note>original: "excogitate"</note> against either the existence of God or the immortality of the soul and a reward in the world to come.

11. If this is not the rule that a sincere and sensible Christian should adopt regarding philosophy, it would be a matter of indifference if he did the opposite—which is so absurd at first glance that it is enough just to suggest it. To say he is not to engage with any philosophy at all—especially when he is either converting or strengthening the faith of people with a philosophical mindset—would be a wild assertion in itself. It would also be an insult to the wisdom of our ancestors, who founded universities and created laws and statutes for us to diligently study philosophy, specifically in relation to divinity itself. Therefore, this third rule seems very rational and, indeed, indispensable.

<margin>Baruch 3:24, 25.</margin>
12. In consequence of this, I think I am at least excusable for choosing some main points of **Cartesianism** <note>The philosophy of René Descartes (1596–1650).</note> and **Platonism**. For by throwing out the foolish conceit of the **Aristotelians**, who produce **substantial forms** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, these are the essential natures that make a thing what it is.</note> **from the potentiality of matter** <note>original: "ex potentia materiæ"</note>, and by admitting and declaring with **Descartes** that **matter is everywhere of one uniform nature as to the substance itself** (which I have also clearly enough proved in my *Letter to V. C., Section 6* <note>"V. C." likely stands for *Viri Clarissimi*, a title for an illustrious man/correspondent.</note>), we have the most demonstrable grounds imaginable for necessarily concluding the **existence of God**. We also conclude that the **soul is an immaterial substance that can be separated from the body**, as I have also noted in my letter to **Monsieur Clerselier** <note>Claude Clerselier was the editor and translator of many of Descartes' works.</note>. That **vastness** of the universe, which Descartes' philosophy assumes, is more consistent with the sacred attributes of God—His power and goodness—and more fitting for the Divine Majesty, whether we consider the world as the **effect** of such an all-powerful cause, or as the temple of so glorious a deity. For the ancient philosophers looked upon this universe as one majestic temple of God, of which the Temple at Jerusalem was a symbolic figure, as **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> noted in his commentary on the Book of Baruch: *O Israel, how great is the house of God! and how large is the place of his possession! Great, and has no end; high, and unmeasurable.* This is wonderfully true of the **World of the Philosophers** <note>original: "Mundus Philosophorum"</note>. Nor does this passage from Baruch conflict with the history of the Creation in Genesis, whose purpose I have...

I have noted above that this is the **World of the Common People** <note>original Latin: *Mundus Plebeiorum* — a simple, literal understanding of the cosmos</note> rather than the **World of the Philosophers** <note>original Latin: *Philosophorum* — a more complex, scientific understanding of the universe</note>, as it plainly limits the physical world to the distance of the "upper waters" or clouds.

13. In accordance with this third rule, I have also included the **pre-existence of the soul** in my writings, considering it a very rational position. I have explained its usefulness at length in my <term>Treatise</term> on the soul's immortality (Book 2, Chapter 2). Truly, I think a person may modestly assert that this is a very rational and useful opinion. I have answered <note>original: "affoiled" — cleared away or refuted</note> all the objections I could find against it, partly in the aforementioned treatise and partly in my general preface to the collection of my philosophical writings. However, all I am asserting is the logical possibility <note>original: "Rationalness"</note> of this position, not its absolute truth, as can be seen in that preface. But this does not belong to the current rule.

### RULE IV.

->Although it is not strictly necessary, it is highly desirable that the<-
->philosophical principles he chooses are not only not contradictory to<-
->Holy Scripture <note>original: "Divine Oracles"</note>, but even receive some support and<-
->approval from them. This support might be hidden within the text or<-
->history as a deeper, mystical meaning, or mentioned briefly in<-

14. The reason for this is that discovering these notable philosophical truths in Scripture does two things: it defends Religion and clears her of the insulting claim that she is ignorant of philosophy and science (as I have hinted elsewhere); and it also justifies the noble results of free reason and philosophy against the common suspicion that they are ungodly or irreligious. A specific example of this can be found in the prophet Baruch (mentioned above), which supports the idea of the **tremendous vastness of the universe**. This aligns with the principles of René Descartes and the calculations of astronomers—especially the **Copernicans** <note>Followers of Nicolaus Copernicus, who argued that the Earth revolves around the Sun</note>—who show that the entire annual orbit of the Earth is merely a tiny point compared to the immense distance between us and the stars. The structure of my entire **Philosophical Cabbala** <note>More’s work *Conjectura Cabbalistica*, which attempts to find philosophical truths in the book of Genesis</note> also follows this fourth rule and originates from it. However, the fact that I call it only a "conjecture" relates to the fifth and final rule.

<meta>This page continues Henry More’s explanation of his "Rule of Christian Prudence." He argues for a cautious approach to presenting philosophical theories—treating them as rational possibilities rather than absolute truths—to avoid upsetting the faith of the common people or the authority of the Church.</meta>

<page-num>488</page-num>
<header>The more General Account of Chapter 1.</header>

regarding the capacities of the common people <note>original: "the Vulgar"</note>, and also the more common opinions of interpreters and writers in the Church, to claim and admit these philosophical principles <note>original: "Theorems"</note> only as **rational** possibilities. As for their absolute reality and truth, we should be more wary and reserved in asserting them.

15. The reason for this rule is that **all things are to be done for spiritual growth** <note>original: "edification"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 14:26</note>. Certainly, things are done this way when they are moderated by this rule of Christian Prudence, for here everyone’s interests are served for their own good.

For those who are of a more rational and philosophical temperament are satisfied because it is granted to them that—even if we admit that all those philosophical principles that seem so undeniably reasonable to them were really true—it need not be an obstacle to believing our religion. This is because there is nothing in those principles contrary to it; indeed, Scripture itself in some places seems at least to favor them.

Then, the common people are satisfied because they are left to the easy enjoyment of their customary understandings, which are most suitable to their modest abilities. Their minds are not strained to the breaking point <note>original: "set upon the rack"</note> by examining things beyond their reach. Nor are they distressed by finding themselves disrespected or accused of holding false beliefs. The contrary views are only affirmed as things that seem rational among philosophers, but are not conscientiously and seriously urged as absolute truth.

And, lastly, the peace and authority of the Church are kept intact. These should not be broken or diminished by an overly aggressive assertion of even a more exact truth, unless we are plainly required to profess it by the clear meaning of Scripture.

In my view, considering the vast difference in people's abilities, this prudent method is essentially necessary. It ensures that no one is offended <note>original: "scandalized"</note> in their religion to the hazard of their salvation by the shipwreck of their faith. I say that since the laudable way of **oral tradition** is now out of date, it will be difficult to find anything as fit to be a substitute <note>original: "succedaneous"</note> for it as this method I have proposed.

16. In conformity to this, I wrote my *Philosophic Cabbala* <term>Philosophic Cabbala</term><note>More’s work attempting to interpret the Book of Genesis through the lens of Cartesian and Platonic philosophy</note> and the defense of it, but I nonetheless labeled it only a **conjecture**. I suspended my personal agreement or claim to its truth in the very title, as well as in the preface. I did this so the benefit might go to those who could not otherwise be satisfied, without causing any offense to everyone else. 

Indeed, to make everything certain, I have expressly suspended my agreement to anything that may seem in any way inconsistent or incompatible with the ordinary, acknowledged truths of our religion—not only in my preface to my *Cabbala*, but also in the preface to *The Immortality of the Soul*. And then again, in the *General Preface* to the *Collection* of my philosophical writings, I lay it down as a principle: **That no man's conscience is obliged to make a profession of any philosophical speculations (even if they seem to him to have mathematical certainty) against the approval of his superiors.** Regarding my *Philosophic Cabbala*, I specifically declare that I only assert the fitness and applicability of those theories, whether

This shows how perfectly my practice has followed this fifth and last rule. ## CHAPTER II.

1. *His account regarding his introduction of the idea of pre-existence in this age.* 2. *A defense of a certain passage in his Cabbala from the suspicion of anthropomorphism.* 3. *That in respect of Christ, God may in some sense be said to have a human shape.* 4. *As also regarding his frequent appearances in human shape in the Old Testament before the Incarnation.* 5. *That these appearances were usually the manifestation of the Son of God, and served as preliminary foreshadowings <term>Prolusions</term> of his Incarnation, according to the views of the Church Fathers.* 6. *That the frequency of these appearances may justify our Literal Cabbala, provided a few small additions are made to an easily understood omission <note>original: "Ellipsis"</note>.* 7. *That it is not irrational to admit that God was actually in human shape when he created Adam, and how triumphantly confident Eugubinus <note>Agostino Steuco (1497–1548), also known as Eugubinus, an Italian Old Testament scholar</note> is of this.* 8. *That if this is admitted, it matches the rest of the historical nature of the Creation and fits so well with our Literal Cabbala that it makes the meaning clear and complete without any additional explanation.*

1. **A**nd indeed, to give the world its due, I do not encounter any significant objections in the many rumors I have heard against anything in the collection of my philosophical writings, except for the **pre-existence of the soul** and a charge of **anthropomorphism** <note>original: "Anthropomorphitism"; the belief that God has a physical body or human form</note> regarding my *Literal Cabbala*. But as for the first, I answer that I acted according to the reasonableness of my third rule. In such a time of excessive liberty and atheistical boasting about philosophy, I could not in good conscience hide such a **theory** <note>original: "Hypothesis"</note>, which I believed to be of uniquely great use against those who deny the existence of God, his Providence, and of
