...and a life to come, based upon rational and philosophical arguments. This covers the reasonableness and usefulness of the opinion. But as for my formal agreement to it as true, I have already declared in my *General Preface* that I have suspended my judgment on this point. I declare again that I completely agree with the judgment of our Church in this matter, and I believe it is every man’s duty to do the same in cases such as this.

2. Now, concerning that charge of **Anthropomorphism** <term>original: "Anthropomorphitism"; the attribution of human characteristics or form to God</term>, it arises from my *Literal Cabbala*, chapter 1, verse 26: *Come, let us now make Man; and I will make him after the same image and shape that I bear myself, etc.* and verse 27: *So God created Man in his own shape and figure, with an upright stature, with legs, arms, hands, with a face and mouth to speak and command, as God himself has.* This, I confess, if considered alone, might justly give anyone reason to think the writer is an **Anthropomorphite** <term>one who believes God has a human body</term>. 

But if the reader looks at the *Defense* of his *Literal Cabbala* regarding this 27th verse, one would think it impossible for him to either imagine or report such a thing about the author. For in that *Defense*, he writes the following: *It was the opinion of the Anthropomorphites that God had all the parts of a man, and that we are, in this sense, made according to his Image. This opinion is in itself vain and ridiculous if not rightly understood (and I shall explain the right understanding of it shortly). Yet, the opinion of those who imagine God to be a finite being seems little better to me—those who take care to place him far from the stench of this terrestrial globe so that he may sit "pure in a pure place"* <note>original: καθαρὸς ἐν καθαρῷ χώρῳ</note> *and so confine him to the Heavens, as Aristotle seems to do, if he is indeed the author of the book "On the Universe"* <note>original: "De Mundo"</note>. *For it is a contradiction to the very Idea of God for Him to be finite, and consequently for Him to have a physical figure and parts.* Therefore, it is evident that I am so far from Anthropomorphism that I judge it an impossibility for God to have any physical figure at all.

3. But in what sense God may be said to have a **human shape** cannot be unknown to us who call ourselves Christians and acknowledge Christ to be the **God-man** <note>original: Θεάνθρωπος, or "Theanthropos"</note>. For in this way, the very human shape is His shape; and His shape is our shape (for He has made it *His* by taking it upon Himself). Thus, we were created according to that very shape which God designed to take for Himself in the Incarnation of the Eternal Word. Consequently, this literal text may be seen as a "typical prophecy" <note>A "type" or symbolic prefiguration of a future event</note> and an early hint of the Incarnation of Christ.

4. Furthermore, a person cannot for any valid reason deny that the history itself is true; God did appear in **human shape** when He created and organized the adornments of this Earth. This aligns with what I suggested above regarding the entire narrative in these first three chapters of *Genesis*—namely, that it is **historical**. The Scriptures expressly suggest that God has appeared several times in human shape. For example, in Genesis 32:24: *And Jacob was left alone, and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day.* Jacob declares of this man (v. 30) that he was God: *And Jacob called the name of the place Peniel; For I have seen God face to face, and my life is spared.* The fact that He is called a *Man*, is said to wrestle, was seen by *Jacob face to face*, and that they spoke with one another, demonstrates plainly that it was a human shape.

...shape that God took. And the ancient Fathers—*Theodoret, Justin, Tertullian, Hilary, Ambrose, Cyril* and others—understand it as the Son of God, the Word that was to be made Flesh.

And again, in *Exodus* 33, God is said there to speak with *Moses* face to face, and also to have hands and a back. He who also appeared to *Gideon* in *Judges* 6 is called *Jehovah*, yet Gideon perceived him to be a man. He is said to have a staff in his hand, with which he touched the meat and unleavened cakes that were presented, and so caused a fire to arise out of the rock to consume the sacrifice. And in Chapter 13, where *Manoah* says to his wife, *“We shall surely die, because we have seen God,”* yet he is repeatedly taken by *Manoah* and his wife to be a mere man in the earlier parts of the story. From this it is plain he was God in human shape.

5. And *Molinæus* <note>original: "Molinæus"; Pierre Du Moulin (1568–1658), a prominent Huguenot theologian</note> in his work *Vates* interprets one of the three men whom *Abraham* greeted at his tent door in *Genesis* 18—and with whom *Abraham* particularly had so much discussion regarding the destruction of *Sodom* in the latter part of the chapter—to be *Christ*. He also identifies Christ as the one who conducted the children of *Israel* through the desert. "For God," says he, "even under the Old Testament ruled the Church through Christ, who indeed was the one whom the Israelites tempted in the desert, as the Apostle testifies in 1 Corinthians 10:9." <note>original: "Deus enim (faith he) etiam sub V. Testamento per Christum regebat Ecclesiam, qui quidem is fuit quem Israelitæ tentaverunt in deserto, teste Apostolo, 1 Cor. 10. 9."</note> "And these appearances were a kind of prelude and beginning of the future manifestation of Christ through the Incarnation." <note>original: "Erántque hæ Apparitiones futuræ manifestationis Christi per Incarnationem quædam quasi Anteludia & Primordia."</note> "This was the opinion of Ambrose, in his book *On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 8, where he maintains that Melchizedek was Christ himself, and denies that those things said about him could apply to a mortal and sinful man." <note>original: "Hæc fuit sententia Ambrosii, lib. De iis qui initiantur Mysteriis, cap. 8. ubi Melchisedecum vult esse ipsum Christum, & pernegat ea quæ de eo dicuntur posse convenire homini mortali & peccatori."</note> 

For this opinion, *Du Moulin* has produced so many and such solid arguments in Book 4, Chapter 14, and has so cleverly weakened all the reasons of the opposing party, that it is hard for one to refrain from including this appearance of *Melchizedek* to *Abraham* (blessing him after his battle with the four kings) among other instances of God manifesting himself to mankind in human shape. To which I will only add one more example noted by *Calvin* regarding *Daniel* chapter 7, verse 13. There, upon the phrase, *“Behold, one like the Son of Man,”* <note>original: "Ecce quasi Filius hominis"</note> he says that *Irenaeus* understands this appearance to be of *Christ*, and as a prelude to his Incarnation. And quoting *Tertullian*: "Here the Son of God performed a prelude to his humanity." <note>original: "Hic prælusit Filius Dei Humanitati suæ."</note> And again in Chapter 8, verse 15, regarding these words, *“Behold, there stood before me as it were the appearance of a man,”* <note>original: "Ecce stetit coram me quasi species viri"</note> he says: "It is probable that this passage also should be understood as referring to Christ, who is now called 'as it were a man,' just as before. For he had not yet put on our flesh so that the name of 'Man' could properly belong to him, etc." <note>original: "Probabile est etiam hunc locum de Christo intelligi, qui nunc vocatur quasi vir, quemadmodum antea. Nondum enim induerat carnem nostram, ut propriè competeret nomen Hominis in ipsum, &c."</note> Some also interpret chapter 10, verse 16, as referring to *Christ*: *“Behold, one like the similitude of the sons of men touched my lips.”* But it is plain enough already that God, even under the Old Testament, frequently appeared to men in human shape, which served as so many symbolic preludes <note>original: "Prolusions"</note> to the real Incarnation of the Son of God.

6. Therefore, since *Christ* under the Old Law had so thoroughly adopted this shape for himself in his outward appearances by using it frequently, and since he was also destined to appear in it and live upon earth in it in the ages to come, is it such a harsh thing to allow the *literal* sense of the text to be such as I have suggested in my *Cabbala* <note>More's philosophical commentary on the book of Genesis</note>? And is it so wrong to understand that *Image* of God, in which *Adam* was to be made, as an external figure—just like the one God himself so often appears in when he wishes to visibly converse with men? What hurt is there in this, unless it be that it obliges men to greater humanity, mercifulness, and tenderness of respect even toward the very *bodies* of men? This is what *Moses* seems plainly to hint at in *Genesis 9:6*:

> *Whoever sheds man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: For in the Image of God made he Man.*

But killing properly concerns the body, and not the *soul*. Therefore, this argument seems most naturally to concern that external and perishable part, and to warn us against treating rudely—much less rashly destroying—that fabric which, in some sense, is fitly called the *image of God*. He frequently appeared in that shape in his interactions with men, according to the sense of ancient *expositors* <term>original: "Expositors"; biblical commentators or interpreters</term>. Therefore, my *Cabbalistical Paraphrase* <note>More refers here to his own work, *Conjectura Cabbalistica*, where he interprets the Book of Genesis</note> may be understood this way where it is said, [<insert>*I will make him after the same Image and Shape I bear myself,* and *presently after, with a face and mouth to speak and command, as God himself has,*</insert>] namely, at such times as he thinks fit to converse with mortals in a visible shape: *I will make Man of that shape which I myself will use when I appear in any perceptible figure.* This is one sound and unexceptionable sense of the paraphrase, if we assume an *ellipsis* <term>a gap or omission in text</term> and provide a supplement like this.

7. But because it is so easily acknowledged that God so frequently takes on the human figure (as has been noted above), there is no harshness or conflict with reason to admit that even at the time he pronounced those words, *Let us make Man after our own Image*, he was then actually in that very shape. This opinion *Eugubinus* <note>original: "Eugubinus"; Agostino Steuco (1497–1548), an Italian humanist and theologian who argued for a "perennial philosophy" connecting all religions</note> in his *Cosmopoeia* not only asserts but triumphs in: "Therefore, the Son and Word of God approached the creation of humanity in a human form, image, and habit, bearing a most beautiful, divine, and pleasant form, surpassing the beauty of all human forms. <note>original: "Accessit ergò Filius ac Verbum Dei ad creationem humanam in forma, imagine habitúque humano, gerens speciosissimám Divinissimámque formam & jucundissimam, omnium humanarum formarum pulchritudinem superantem."</note> Upon seeing and gazing at this, it must be believed that the forefather of our race [Adam] was mad with love, and almost died for the Creator, who was more beautiful than all women. <note>original: "Quam videntem & intuentem generis nostri principem censendum est amore insanisse, Creatórémque omnibus fœminis speciosissimum penè deperiîsse."</note> The most merciful and most beautiful one, taking on this appearance and divine beauty—which he was after many ages to assume even unto flesh and bone—created Man, bestowing upon him this great appearance, he himself the first Archetype <term>the original model or pattern</term>, himself most beautiful, the Creator of a most beautiful offspring. <note>original: "Hanc speciem Divinámque pulchritudinem Clementissimus Formosissimúsque assumens, quam erat post multa tempora usque ad carnem & ossa assumpturus, creabat Hominem, largiens ei speciem hanc tantam, ipse primus Archetypus, speciosissimus ipse, speciosissima prolis Creator."</note> How great or of what kind do you believe the beauty of that first man was? What honor in his face? What graces resided there? Two Gods were immediately seen, one like the other as far as ability allowed: one Creator, the other created. But that one was the true God and incomparably more beautiful; this one a small and made God, yet similar to that great one. <note>original: "Quantàm qualémve credas fuisse primi Hominis illius venustatem? quantum in ore decus? quas gratias insedisse? And a little after, he asserts that Christ conferred with *Abraham* and appeared to *Moses* in the bush in such a shape as this—that is, truly human, but divinely beautiful. And after these many overflowing streams of eloquence, he at last binds all up again with this very strict reasoning: "It was not a sin for God to have then assumed that shape, which was afterwards ours..." <note>original: "Non erat nefas Deum illam, quæ postea nostra fuit, tunc assumpsisse"</note>

"...that he assumed a likeness; for if it had been wrong <note>original: *nefas*</note>, he never would have assumed it." As if it were a prejudice to the belief in the Incarnation of Christ to be slow in admitting that he had already assumed human shape when he said, *Let us make Man after our own Image.*

8. And if this is admitted even once, it will correspond very well with the *historical truth* of the whole narrative (for as I have indicated above, I mean it is *historically true*). There cannot be the least harshness in our *Cabbalistical Paraphrase* <note>Henry More’s own work, *Conjectura Cabbalistica*, which provides a mystical interpretation of Genesis</note>, even if we suppose no *ellipsis* <term>an intentional omission of words</term> nor make any *supplement*, but read it exactly as we find it: *Go to, let us make Man; and I will make him after the same Image and Shape that I bear myself, with an upright stature, with legs, hands, arms, and a mouth to speak and command, as I myself have.* For it is evident that while God appears in human shape, he possesses all of these. ### CHAP. III.

1. *Ten more objections sent from a capable source, and therefore to be answered more carefully. The proposal of the first objection, concerning the nature of Christ's body after his Resurrection and Ascension.* 2. *That he does not assert that the heavenly body lacks organs <note>original: "Unorganizedness"</note>, but only mentions the idea in accordance with his second rule.* 3. *That he explicitly asserts that the heavenly body is organized, but refrains from claiming it consists of earthly flesh and bones, in observation of his first rule.* 4. *His search into the nature of a glorified body according to Scripture, and what grounds there are for it having an angelic property.* 5. *That good angels have bodies, and that they are of a bright <note>original: "Lucid"</note> nature.* 6. *Proofs of the brightness and angelic nature of our Savior’s body after the Resurrection, his appearances being so perfectly like theirs.* 7. *That the glorified body is a spiritual body, and what is meant by a "natural body"* <note>original: σῶμα ψυχικὸν (sōma psychikon)</note>*, and what by a "spiritual body"* <note>original: σῶμα πνευματικὸν (sōma pneumatikon)</note>*, and that this latter implies a consistency that is more fiery and bright.* 8. *That the glorified body is a heavenly or celestial body, not in a moral sense but in a physical sense, along with the danger and unreasonableness of the opposite opinion.* 9. *That the heavenliness of the glorified body again signifies its brightness and splendor.* 10. *That the brightness of these bodies is also testified to by the ancient Fathers.* 11. *That it is clear from these premises that calling our Savior’s body "organized light" is a justifiable expression.* 12. *As is the saying that he adapted <note>original: "assimilated"</note> his body to the regions he passed through during his Ascension, if rightly understood.* *15. And secondly, even if it did, provided that they be acknowledged as celestial and spiritual flesh and bones—as they must be in a celestial and spiritual body—it does not conflict with <note>original: "breaks no squares with"</note> his understanding. 16. That "spiritual flesh" seems to be what St. Paul is referring to in his account <note>original: "enarration"</note> of the Mystery of the Resurrection.*

BUT the objections I have answered so far have come to my knowledge only through frequently repeated rumors and verbal discussions. Those that follow I am required to address, not only for the reasons mentioned before, but also because they were sent to me by a capable person, organized into the specific numbers, order, and words in which I shall present them here. They are ten in number, and all are taken from my *Mystery of Godliness*. Because the purpose of that treatise—and the title itself—is of greater weight and consequence than most of my others, I consider myself obligated to satisfy these objections more carefully and to clear myself and my book from any appearance of danger or error of which we might be suspected. The first of these objections is stated in these words:

->Objection I.<-

> *Book 5, Chapter 3, Section 1. He says, "It cannot be imagined otherwise than that Christ's body adapted itself <note>original: "assimilated it self"</note> to the regions through which it passed during his Ascension, and finally became perfectly celestial and ethereal, organized light, not flesh and bones." (Chapter 4, Section 1).*

2. Regarding what I wrote in the third chapter of this fifth book concerning the *homogeneity* <term>uniformity of substance</term> and *unorganizedness* <term>lacking complex internal organs like a terrestrial body</term> of the *heavenly body*, I wish to be understood as not asserting it as a fact, but only admitting it as a possibility. This is because it is the more general opinion <note>original: "conceit"</note> of philosophers that only *terrestrial bodies* are organized. I included this point merely for this purpose: to show that even if their confident belief were true, it would not hinder the capacity for life's functions, such as *senses*, *understanding*, and the like. Therefore, the soul may enjoy itself outside of its *terrestrial body*, even according to this hypothesis. In this, I have followed my second proposed rule.

3. But in the very first section of the following chapter, I adopt the opinion that I find most rational and most acceptable to all orthodox Christians: namely, *that this glorified body is organized*. But whether I am right to call it *organized light* will be clearer after we have examined the nature of a *glorified body*. Nor do I know where the "sting" of this objection lies, unless it is in the end of it, which would suggest that I deny that Christ’s body, which he now has in heaven, consists of flesh and bones.

But if the objector means *terrestrial* flesh and bones, is it a mistake to deny it? Especially for me, as I describe myself as a "fisher for philosophers," wanting to draw them to or keep them in the Christian faith? For how harsh would it seem to those who follow the *Ptolemaic hypothesis* <note>The ancient view that the Earth is the center of the universe, surrounded by solid crystalline spheres</note> that a body of earthly flesh and bones should bore its way through spheres harder than crystal for many tens of thousands of miles, until it finally ascends above all the heavens to sit at the right hand of God? And for those who are *Copernicans* <note>Followers of Copernicus, who believed the Earth orbits the Sun</note> or *Cartesians* <note>Followers of René Descartes</note>, who believe the *heavens* are all made of a fluid, subtle substance,

# Chapter 3: On Christ’s Body after His Ascension

How inconsistent <note>original: "incongruous"</note> it must necessarily seem to them also that a heavy *terrestrial* <note>earthly</note> body of flesh and bones should inhabit and live in such a subtle and piercing element, since the *air* at the top of some mountains is already too thin for our *lungs*. Furthermore, the purer *heavens* are so subtle that they would quickly take apart and consume to atoms any such *terrestrial* consistency of flesh and blood as is spoken of here—to say nothing of the inconsistency of such an earthy and heavy body having no suitable support <note>original: *ereisma* (Greek for a foothold or foundation)</note> to walk upon.

Therefore, since the Scripture asserts no such thing regarding the *glorified body of Christ* (but calls him "the *Lord from heaven, heavenly*"), nor do any of the Three Creeds, I thought it appropriate, according to my first rule, not to needlessly deny anything rationally solid in my *opponent's* <note>original: "antagonist"</note> view, but to grant that the body of Christ in heaven is not *terrestrial* flesh and bones, but of a more refined nature. For the Apostle says <margin>1 Corinthians 15:50</margin> expressly, *“That flesh and blood cannot inherit the Kingdom of God.”*

4. But this is a point of such great importance that it must not be passed over so briefly without a closer search into the true nature of a *glorified body*, according to the clear and natural indications of the Holy Scripture. From this, it will become clear whether or not I have correctly asserted that the *glorified body of Christ is organized light*.

According to the testimony of Scripture, we shall find that a *glorified body*—or that body with which those who attain that blessed Resurrection (the most precious hope of all true Christians) shall be rewarded—may be honored with these three titles: *angelical, spiritual, and celestial*.

It is an *angelical body* because the *sons of the resurrection* are said to be equal to angels <note>original: *isangeloi*</note>; that is, in every actual respect that contributes to any real perfection or happiness, they are equal to *angels*. For Christ argues this way <margin>Luke 20:36</margin>: *“They cannot die, for they are equal to the angels”* <note>original: *isangeloi gar eisi*</note>. This would hardly be an illustration, much less a proof and convincing inference <note>original: "illation"</note>, unless it is understood in the sense I suggested above. For it would be a weak <note>original: "languid"</note> kind of reasoning and provide little satisfaction to conclude the *sons of the resurrection* are immortal simply because they are immortal just as the *angels* are immortal. That looks like proving the same thing by the same thing <note>original: *idem per idem*</note>.

And yet this would be all there is to it, if they were equal to the *angels* only in that one respect. Nor would they be properly said to be equal to them, especially in such general terms, if they only matched them in this one particular. Just as something could not be said to be of equal length <note>original: *isomekes*</note> or equal height <note>original: *isoupses*</note> to another if it only had a third part of its length or height. 

But taking "equal to angels" <note>original: *isangelos*</note> in the broad sense it naturally implies—that the *sons of the resurrection* are absolutely equal to the *angels* in all such actual respects as I mentioned above—then this *immortality* will necessarily be included as part of the whole sum. Nor can the condition of their *bodies* be left out regarding their nature and glory; rather, a *son of the resurrection* and an *angel* must be exactly the same in every such regard. Indeed, our Savior seems plainly to assert as much in those words that follow: "and they are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection" <note>original: *kai huioi eisi tou Theou, tes anastaseos huioi ontes*</note>. Where "sons of God" <note>original: *huioi tou Theou*</note> clearly looks like an explanation <note>original: *exegesis*</note> of "equal to angels" <note>original: *isangeloi*</note>, and shows that those who are once the *sons of the resurrection* clearly become *angels* thereby.

<summary>More argues that Christ's glorified body is not made of earthly flesh and blood, which could not survive the subtle environment of heaven, but is instead "organized light." He supports this by equating the "Sons of the Resurrection" with angels, suggesting their bodies share the same immortal and spiritual nature.</summary>

# His Answer regarding Lucidity, Chapter 3

...thereby. For what are the sons of God <note>original: υἱοὶ Θεοῦ / בני אלהים (*uioi Theou* / *benei Elohim*)</note>, that is to say, *Angels*? For they were *Sons of God* in a moral or spiritual sense before the Resurrection.

<margin>* Book 3, chapter 19.</margin>
5. Therefore, it will help <note>original: "conduce"</note> somewhat toward a better understanding of the nature of a glorified body if we search the Scriptures to see what the nature of *angelic bodies* is. It is said in *Psalm* 104: *Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flaming fire.* Upon this text, Hugo Grotius <note>A prominent 17th-century Dutch legal scholar and theologian.</note> comments freely and (truly, I think) not unskillfully in this manner: *“That angels have bodies, though very subtle ones, was the opinion not only of the schools of Pythagoras and Plato, but also of the ancient Jews and ancient Christians. Aristotle is the inventor of ‘intelligences’ separated from all matter, whom many follow too excessively* <note>original: περισσῶς (*perissōs*)</note> *in theological matters.”* <note>original Latin: *Esse Angelis corpora, sed subtilissima, non Pythagorae tantùm & Platonis Schola sensit, sed & Judaei veteres & veteres Christiani. Intelligentiarum ab omni materia secretarum faber est Aristoteles, quem nimis περισσῶς in rebus Theologicis multi sequuntur.*</note> That the Church Fathers were of this opinion, Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, a 16th-century occult philosopher.</note> has also noted in his *Occult Philosophy*; and particularly Methodius <note>A 3rd-century Christian bishop and martyr.</note> (as cited in the works of Photius) describes the nature of an angelic body in this way: that it is *a compound consisting of pure air and pure fire* <note>original: τὸ ἐκ καθαροῦ ἀέρος καὶ καθαροῦ πυρὸς συνιστάμενον σύγκριμα</note>, and that every such *composition* is *of the same substance as the angelic beings* <note>original: τοῖς ἀγγελικοῖς ὁμοούσιον</note>. Furthermore, the author of the Letter to the *Hebrews* confirms this again in Chapter 1, verse 7, showing that the passage in the *Psalms* cited above must be understood as referring to *angels* properly so called.

That they have *bodies*, therefore, I think there is little question to be made. Observations in Scripture will make it just as plain what the nature of those bodies is with which the best sort of them are clothed. For there are many instances showing how *fiery* <note>original: "igneous"</note> and *luminous* <note>original: "lucid"</note> they are. But we shall content ourselves with one or two. Truly, that of *Exodus* 3:2—which *Saint Stephen* repeats in *Acts* 7:30—regarding the Angel of the Lord appearing to Moses in a *flame of fire* in a bush, *in a flame of fire* <note>original: ἐν φλογὶ πυρός</note> (which corresponds well to the passage in *Hebrews* taken from the *Psalms*: *and his ministers a flame of fire* <note>original: καὶ τοὺς λειτουργοὺς αὐτοῦ πυρὸς φλόγα</note>), is very suitable to that interpretation by Grotius upon that Psalm. It implies that the bodies of the more glorious angels are *fiery* and *luminous*; that is to say, they are of such a fiery nature that they have more in common with the kindness of *light* than with the fierceness and greediness of what we ordinarily call *fire*. This accords well with the circumstances of that apparition: that the bush was not consumed by it.

Another remarkable example of the *lucidity* <note>brightness or light-giving quality</note> of the bodies of *angels* is found in *Acts* 12. While *Peter* was sleeping between two soldiers in the prison, bound in chains, *the Angel of the Lord is said to come upon him, and a light to shine in the prison, etc.*

I will only add one instance more, which is *Daniel* 10:5, where the angel that instructed *Daniel* is described this way:
> *Then I lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, a certain man clothed in linen, whose loins were girded with fine gold of Uphaz: His body was also like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as lamps of fire, and his arms and his feet like in color to polished brass, and the voice of his words as the voice of a multitude.*
This appearance of this angelic shape is certainly *fiery* and *luminous* enough, and so *glorious* that it overcame the Prophet and made him fall into a swoon or trance. These few hints shall suffice as an indication of what kind of body an angel has, and from this, it is manifest that they are very *luminous* and *glorious*.

<summary>The author argues that angels possess subtle, luminous bodies composed of "pure air and fire," citing both classical philosophers and biblical accounts like the burning bush and Daniel's visions to prove their physical yet glorious nature.</summary>

### Chapter 3: Of Christ’s Body after his Ascension

6. Therefore, based on this assumption that our bodies become *angelic* at the last day, whoever is endowed with the kind of body reserved for the *children of the resurrection* will be—if he chooses to show himself—this *radiant* <note>original: "lucid"</note> and *glorious*. To prove this, I need no more examples than that of our Savior Christ's body. For all our bodies at the resurrection are to be made like his *glorious body*, <margin>* Philippians 3:21.</margin> as the *Apostle has expressly declared. 

How *radiant* and *angelic* his body was after his ascension into heaven (which is the main point in question) may appear from *Revelation 1:13*, where *one like the Son of Man is said to be clothed with a garment down to his feet, and wrapped around the chest with a golden sash <note>original: "girt about the paps with a golden girdle"</note>. His head and his hair were white like wool, as white as snow; and his eyes like a flame of fire; and his feet like fine brass, as if they were burning in a furnace; and his voice like the sound of many waters. A sharp two-edged sword came out of his mouth, and his countenance was like the sun shining in its strength.* 

This body, I think, is sufficiently *radiant*, and not only *angelic* in a general sense, but expressly and almost exactly conforming to that of the angel who appeared to *Daniel*, as anyone who chooses to compare them may observe. And yet, this is Christ in a physical and human shape, in the same body he carried out of the grave with him at his resurrection, as he testifies of himself in verse 18: *I am he who lives, and was dead; and behold, I am alive forevermore; Amen.* What could be clearer? But he also adds, *And I have the keys of hell and of death*; that is, I can also deliver others from the state of mortality and crown them with immortal life. This is done by *changing their lowly bodies <note>original: "vile bodies"</note> and fashioning them like his glorious body, according to the power by which he is able even to subdue all things to himself*, as the Apostle says in *Philippians 3:21*.

A similar appearance of our Savior also seems to occur in *Revelation 10*, where an angel is said to be *clothed with a cloud, with a rainbow on his head, his face like the sun, and his feet like pillars of fire.* This body of Christ is certainly sufficiently *fiery* <note>original: "igneous"</note> and *radiant*.

I will only add his appearing to *Saul* <note>The Apostle Paul, prior to his conversion.</note> from the heavens as he was going to *Damascus* in *Acts 9*. The Apostle says that *suddenly there shone around him a light from heaven, and he fell to the earth and heard a voice saying to him, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" And he said, "Who are you, Lord?" and he said, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting."* Can anything be more explicit? 

Paul recounts <note>original: "rehearses"</note> this marvelous occurrence two more times in the *Acts* of the Apostles, in *Chapter 22:6* and again in *26:13*. In the first of these passages, it says that *those who were with him saw the light and were afraid*, which shows that it was not an internal vision but an external and real presence of Christ. In the latter, speaking to King *Agrippa*, he says: *At midday, O King, I saw on the road a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those who journeyed with me.* This again confirms not only the reality, but the exceeding great splendor of the physical presence of Christ. This is also consistent with the passage in *Revelation*: *And his countenance was like the sun shining in its strength.*

<summary>The author argues that the resurrected human body will be radiant and "angelic," using the post-ascension descriptions of Jesus Christ in Revelation and the Book of Acts as primary evidence. He emphasizes that Christ's glorious, light-filled appearance was a physical reality rather than a mere internal vision.</summary>

### His Answer concerning the Radiance <note>original: "Lucidity"</note> Chapter 3

6. From all of this, I hope it is clear enough that, as our Savior has said that the *sons of the resurrection* become *by that very fact* <note>original Latin: *ipso facto*</note> like angels in condition—both in the brightness and composition of their bodies as well as their immortality—so experience perfectly matches this theory. The body of our Savior after his resurrection matches exactly in light and glory the most magnificent appearances of angels in either the Old or New Testament. This alone, one would think, should be enough to assure us of the *radiance* <note>original: "Lucidity" or "Luminosity"</note> of Christ's body, as well as all of our *resurrection bodies*, as I may call them, which are to be made like his glorious body.

7. But there are two attributes of this body still remaining, the right understanding of which may further contribute to the assurance of this truth. The first is the *spirituality of this body*: *1 Corinthians 15:44*. "It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body; *there is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body*." For so it is written, "*The first man Adam was made a living soul, the last Adam a life-giving spirit*."

Now it is clear from verses 36 and 38 that the subject of the Apostle’s discourse here is the *body* of those who attain a happy resurrection. He is not speaking of the principle that lives in the body—the soul or spirit of a man (for that is the same in both states)—but of the body itself. From this clear and obvious point, I think it is most reasonable to understand that the *resurrection body* is called *spiritual* not because it is moved by a spirit (for the soul is a spirit that moves the natural body), but because the body itself has become *spiritual*. 

I must admit that *Calvin* <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the influential French theologian of the Reformation.</note> seems to reject this idea, but merely out of his lack of knowledge in philosophy. For he criticizes those *who claim the substance of the future body undergoes a change* <note>original Latin: *qui substantiam corporis futuræ sit ejus immutatio*</note>. Calvin seems to be afraid of the idea that the body is "spiritual," fearing it implies a *substantial change* or, as the academic thinkers <note>original: "the Schools"</note> say, a *specific* <note>original: "Specifical"</note> one. This would certainly contradict the idea of our Savior having the same *identical* <note>original: "Numerical"</note> body in which he suffered. But according to true philosophy, there is no *specific* change in even the most opposite forms <note>original: "modifications"</note> of matter imaginable, but only an *accidental* one—as *Descartes' philosophy* suggests, and as I believe I have abundantly proved in my letter to *V.C.* <note>Likely a reference to one of the author's correspondents; V.C. is often an abbreviation for *Vir Clarissimus*, meaning "most distinguished man."</note>. Therefore, there is no problem in admitting that the *resurrection body* is a *spiritual body*—that is to say, that its structure is made of more subtle parts than those that make up earthly bodies.

<margin>Genesis 2:7.</margin>Therefore, I believe that the most genuine meaning of these words—*There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body* <note>original Greek: *Έςι σῶμα ψυχικὸν, ϗ ἔςι σῶμα πνευματικὸν*</note>—is this: that there is such a heavy, lumpish body until God breathed into that earthly statue the breath of life, *and man became a living soul* <note>original Greek: *ϗ ἐγένετο εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν*</note>. From this, it takes the name *natural* <note>original Greek: *ψυχικὸν*, literally "soulish"</note>, following the story of *Adam*. It means nothing more than this: a body such as *Adam* had—namely, one that is in itself dead, inactive, dull, and lifeless as a statue, as it shows itself to be again once the soul has left it. And this is what the Apostle clearly points to in the following words: *For so it is written, the first man Adam became a living soul* <note>original Greek: *Ἐγένετο ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος Ἀδὰμ εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν*</note>.

<summary>The author argues that the resurrected body is "spiritual" not just because it contains a soul, but because its physical matter becomes more subtle and radiant, modeled after the transfigured body of Christ. He defends this view against Calvin's theological objections by using Cartesian philosophy to explain how matter can change its properties without losing its identity.</summary>

# Chapter 3: Of Christ’s Body after His Ascension

...living <note>original Greek: *zōousan*</note>. Because of this, as I said, the Apostle calls this *Adam-like body* <note>original: "Adamical Body"</note> a "natural body" <note>original Greek: *sōma psychikon*</note>, rather than a "physical" one, even though we usually translate it as "physical" as if that were the word in the original Greek. But the meaning is this: that part of Adam's person which was visible and corporeal was alive and active only because of that breath of life <note>original Greek: *pnoē zōēs*</note> which God breathed into him. This "breath" is the soul, along with its immediate vital tools for operating the body—that more subtle bond <note>original Latin: *vinculum*</note> that unites them both together. 

However, the "last Adam" (Christ), and all who are made to match him and his glorious condition, become—even in their external and bodily personality—life-giving spirits <note>original Greek: *pneumata zōopoiounta*</note>. They possess spiritual bodies <note>original Greek: *sōmata pneumatika*</note>, which are not inherently dull or statue-like. Instead, they have a nature that contains its own *activity* and contributes wonderfully to the soul's most lively, divine, and expanded operations. With respect for the opinions of others, I believe this to be the true meaning of the Apostle's words in 1 Corinthians 15:45.

How fiery <note>original: "Igneous"</note> and radiant <note>original: "Lucid"</note> such a body must be, according to reason and philosophy, I will not argue at length here. I will only mention what the excellent Hippocrates <note>A famous ancient Greek physician</note> says about the more noble operations of the mind: that they are performed by virtue of a certain pure and light-like substance in the human body. He calls it a pure and light-like abundance <note>original Greek: *katharēn kai phōtoeidē periousian*</note>, as you may see in my *Treatise of the Immortality of the Soul*, Book 2, Chapter 8. What I have written there, and in my *Mystery of Godliness* (Book 6, Chapter 6, Section 3), will sufficiently prove whatever else might have been relevant to add here.

8. The last attribute of the *Resurrection Body* is that it is *Heavenly* or *Celestial*, as it says in the same chapter: *The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven* <note>original Greek: *ho Kyrios ex ouranou*</note>. "Here, 'from heaven,'" says Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a prominent 17th-century Dutch scholar and theologian</note>, "is used in the Hebrew manner to mean 'heavenly' or 'celestial,' implying he already possesses a celestial body." *As is the earthy, such are they that are earthy; and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly: And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.* 

And then it follows: Now this I say, brethren <note>original Greek: *Touto de phēmi, adelphoi*</note> (which mainly concerns those who will be found alive at the Last Day), that *flesh and blood cannot inherit the Kingdom of God.* Therefore, immediately after, he must inform them that although *we shall not all die, yet we shall all be changed*, and so on. It is therefore true for all people who shall enter into eternal life that they shall have *heavenly* or *celestial bodies*. This is the most simple and rational explanation of these verses. It does not mean they will only have "heavenly" bodies in a *moral* sense or a *spiritual* meaning—suggesting bodies in which they are simply "heavenly-minded." Such errors and weak <note>original: "dilute"</note> interpretations are very dangerous; they invite people to turn the chief article of our faith into a useless and hollow Familist <note>The "Family of Love" or Familists were a radical religious group that often interpreted literal biblical events as purely internal or allegorical experiences</note> fantasy. Instead, it means they shall have a heavenly body in the same sense that Adam had an earthy one: he was not called "earthy" because he was *earthly-minded*, but because his body was made of an *earthly substance*.

Therefore, our bodies at the Resurrection will be *really* and *physically* heavenly, not only *morally*. We shall be such in our bodily [constitution]...

<summary>The author argues that the resurrection body is "spiritual" and "heavenly" in a physical sense, possessing a light-like substance rather than being merely a metaphor for a moral state of mind.</summary>

### His Answer Concerning Radiance — Chapter 3

8. ...constitution, just as our Celestial Lord is in his; we shall bear his image of heavenly glory and brightness, not only in a *moral* but also in a *natural* sense. For there can be no other easy and natural meaning of the text but this: since the subject being discussed is the body itself at the Resurrection, and it is compared with *Adam's earthy* body in a *physical*, not *mystical* meaning. Nor can I imagine how interpreters could be pulled so forcefully away from such an obvious and true sense, were it not for certain false preconceptions in philosophy that had corrupted their minds and perverted their judgments. Specifically, they held to the *hypothesis* of *Ptolemy* <note>An ancient astronomer who believed the Earth was the center of the universe</note> and *Aristotle*, who claimed the substance of the heavens was of a hard, crystalline nature. For the soul to act in such a "heavenly body" as that would have been a ridiculous fiction indeed. Besides, *Aristotle* defines heavenly bodies as a "fifth element" <note>original Greek: *pempton stoicheion*</note> or "fifth essence" <note>original Greek: *pemptēn ousian*; also known as the quintessence</note>—a body *specifically* distinct from the rest of the elements. Sounder *philosophy* does not do this, but rather considers all *matter* to be of one kind. Therefore, that body which is now truly *earthy* may, if God wills, become in a moment as *perfectly* and *physically heavenly*, and yet remain the same *numerically identical* body <note>term: "Numerical Body" refers to the exact same individual entity, rather than just a similar copy</note>.

9. I say then, that the Apostle does not speak according to the gross mistakes of *Aristotle* or *Ptolemy*, but according to that more ancient and true philosophy which has the reputation of being a "God-given philosophy" <note>original Greek: *philosophia theoparadotos*</note>; and Divine Truth will be found everywhere consistent with itself. By an *Heavenly Body*, I would therefore understand an *Angelical Body*, for angels certainly have bodies suitable to the region in which they live and inhabit. I have suggested above that the heavens are *fluid*, as they most certainly are according to the most ancient and divine philosophy. This is even suggested by the roots of the Hebrew word for "heavens": *shamaim* <note>original Hebrew: שמים</note> is derived from *esh* <note>original Hebrew: אש, meaning fire</note> and *maim* <note>original Hebrew: מים, meaning water</note>, as if it were a kind of fiery, bright *liquidness*, or *liquid radiance*. The Greek word *ether* <note>original Greek: αἰθήρ</note> reflects this same idea. From this, it is again clear that our *resurrection bodies* will be well-supplied with the seeds and principles of *light* and *splendor*. They will be more beautiful and full of luster and glory than the heavenly matter itself—just as that part of the earth which becomes a human body is more precious and beautiful than the earth was before it was shaped into a frame fit for the functions of life. So, whether we consider the *angelic nature*, *spirituality*, or *heavenliness* of the body at the Resurrection, there is every reason to conclude that it will be of a *bright* and *radiant* nature.

<margin>Matthew 17:2</margin>
10. This is not only agreeable to reason and Scripture, but also to the sayings of the Church Fathers themselves, such as *St. Jerome*, *St. Macarius*, *St. Ephrem*, and *St. Augustine*, as you may see in *Vossius* in his *Theses on the Glorious Body* <note>original Latin: *Theses De Corpore glorioso*</note>. The first of these asserts that Christ will return to judgment in the same glory he took on when he was transfigured upon the mountain before his Apostles. As you know, *his face shone like the sun, and his garments were white as the light*. But at his return to raise the dead, he will transform our bodies into the likeness of his own most glorious body—which, in his Transfiguration, was (and will then be again) as bright as the sun. *Macarius* describes the splendor of glorified bodies by comparing them to the radiance of *Moses's* face when he had talked with God on the mountain;

# Chapter III. Of Christ’s Body after His Ascension.

10. ...which was such that the people could not behold it because of its excessive brightness. This he makes a type and resemblance of how in the resurrection of the righteous, the bodies of the worthy will be glorified <note>original Greek: Πῶς ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει τῶν δικαίων δοξασθήσονται τὰ σώματα τῶν ἀξίων</note>. And in another Homily, he says: "The dwelling place from heaven, not made by hands, is clothed with the glory of divine light, as they have become children of light" <note>original Greek: Τὸ οἰκητήριον δὲ τὸ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ τὸ ἀχειροποίητον περιβέβληται δόξαν φωτὸς θεϊκοῦ, ὡς τέκνα φωτὸς γενόμενοι</note>. And in another: "There is neither male nor female there, for all are transformed into a divine nature" <note>original Greek: Οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκεῖ ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ, εἰς θεϊκὴν γὰρ φύσιν πάντες μεταβάλλονται</note>. All these passages sound very grand regarding the glorious condition of the Resurrection. But nothing is more express for our purpose than that of Saint Ephrem in his *Discourse of the Resurrection*: "The bodies of the righteous," he says, "shall shine seven times more than the rays of the sun" <note>original Latin: *Justorum corpora septuplum supra Solis fulgebunt radios*</note>. Here is light and brightness sufficient. But certainly, none of the bodies of the saints shall outshine the body of Christ himself. Saint Austin <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo</note> says this glory was in his body ever since the hour of his Resurrection: "The brightness in Christ's body when he rose again must be believed to have been hidden from the eyes of the disciples rather than absent; for a human and weak sight could not have borne it" <note>original Latin: *Claritas in Christi corpore cùm resurrexit, ab oculis Discipulorum potiùs abscondita fuisse, quàm defuisse, credenda est, non enim eam ferret humanus atque infirmus aspectus*</note>.

11. How angelical, how spiritual, how heavenly or celestial, and how refulgently bright and glorious the bodies of the blessed are at the Resurrection, I have sufficiently described—and more particularly the body of our Savior, which shone around Saint Paul and Saint John like the sun in its full strength. Therefore, now at length to make a more close and precise application of what has been said to solve the objection: What harshness is there in calling that body *light*—that is to say, a *lucid* or *luminous body*—which for brightness exceeds the sun itself, according to the testimony of Holy Writ? Or what incongruity is there in saying it is *organized* <note>term: "organized" here means possessing the physical structure of a living body</note>, since it is so according to the common consent of the whole Church and the meaning of the Scriptures? What error or heterodoxy is there in avowing it perfectly *celestial* and *ethereal*—that is, *entirely heavenly*—in such a sense as Adam’s body was *entirely earthy*? This is according to what is written: *The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven* <note>original Greek: ὁ Κύριος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ</note>, *that is, the Lord Jesus, the Heavenly man from heaven*. And who should be entirely heavenly, if not he? And what business does Earth have either to descend from heaven or ascend there? Or what body more radiant and shining than the sun in its greatest brightness can be *vitally organized* unless it is of an *heavenly nature indeed*? For were that light or brightness the splendor of a sublunary <note>term: "sublunary" refers to the earthly realm below the moon</note> fire, it would consume the subject to cinders or ashes, and its combustibility would also declare the subject to be earthy or terrestrial. But since none of these things are true, we have every reason in the world to conclude the body of our Savior is *entirely celestial*.

12. But it may be the error lies in saying that the *body of Christ adapted itself to the regions it passed through in his Ascension*. But is this any more unreasonable than that Christ accommodated his body to his terrestrial interaction with men before his Ascension? That body, which would be of itself (since it was a glorified body) of such a radiant luster, nevertheless held to those more humble laws of an ordinary earthy dwelling, as Saint Austin himself observed above. For otherwise, he could not have conversed with his disciples, nor could Thomas have been satisfied in that dense and tangible way he desired. Therefore, though there was a powerful principle of a more exalted and overflowing glory and brightness in the body of Christ...

# His Answer touching the Lucidity Chap. III.

After his Resurrection, he restrained this glory to the humble conditions of an *earthly body* for its immediate purposes at that time. However, the *heavenly* radiance it eventually attained is abundantly proven by his appearance to St. Paul from heaven on the road to *Damascus*.

Therefore, what problem is there in admitting that he gradually released this hidden glory and adapted his body to the regions he passed through during his *Ascension*? This is most important regarding the *agility* and *lightness* of his body. He did not change his *human shape*, since I explicitly acknowledge it when I call his body *organized light*. But the earthly <note>original: "terrestrial"</note> qualities of his body were changed; it is unlikely that it remained as heavy in those thinner atmospheric regions as it was when it walked upon this solid earth. I believe his *upward* motion was not forced <note>original: "violent" in the Aristotelian sense of motion against an object's nature</note> but *spontaneous*; it was not beyond the nature of a *glorified body* but natural to it. If these points are carefully considered, I trust they will remove any apparent harshness from my phrasing. I never intended to suggest that his body dissolved into mere *air*. Instead, though it was structured and organized, it kept its exact shape and features while all the burdens of its earthly state were overcome and removed.

13. So far, I believe everything is clear and sound. However, as I noted at first, the main force of this objection likely lies at its end. The offense is not so much taken at my calling Christ's body *organized light*, but at my denial that it consists of *flesh* and *bones*. But before I give any answer, I will recite the words from the passage in Book 5, Chapter 4, Section 1:

> *For there is no problem in acknowledging the glorified body of Christ to be in human shape, and that this organized light will sit as steadily on a heavenly <note>original: "ethereal"</note> throne as a body of flesh and bones on a throne of wood or ivory.*

In defense of this passage, I first answer using the words of St. Paul: *flesh and blood cannot inherit the Kingdom of God*. I believe the same logic applies to *flesh* and *bones*. But here you will make a distinction, following Calvin, and say the Apostle refers to *flesh* and *blood* in their current state: "But understand flesh and blood in the condition they are in now" <note>original Latin: *Cæterùm carnem & sanguinem intellige quâ nunc conditione sunt*</note>. This suggests a distinction between *natural* and *glorified* flesh and blood. It is just as legitimate for me to use this distinction as it is for others. Therefore, I answer that when I contrast a *body of flesh and bones* with our Savior's *radiant body*, I mean *natural flesh and bones*, not *glorified* ones. Consequently, I do not deny that there is *glorified flesh and bones* in the illustrious body of Christ.

Furthermore, I ask in the second place: by which Creed accepted by the Universal Church are we required to believe that the glorified body of Christ consists of flesh, blood, and bones? This seems, at first glance, contradictory to the Apostle’s explicit words, as well as unsuitable to the nature of the *heavens*. Modern philosophers conclude the heavens are entirely *fluid*; if they were not, the inconsistency would seem even more severe to them, as I noted earlier. On this point, the Objector is silent. I cannot imagine where the focus of this opposition will land, unless it rests upon the fourth Article of our *English Church* <note>The Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England, the defining statements of Anglican doctrine</note>, which...

# Chapter III: *On Christ's Body after His Ascension.*

...yet he has prudently declined it, as being of doubtful interpretation. The words of the Article <note>Article IV of the Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England, which outlines the official doctrine on the Resurrection</note> are these:

> *Christ did truly rise again from death, and took again His body with flesh, bones, and all things appertaining to the perfection of man's nature, wherewith He ascended into heaven, and there sits until He return to judge all men at the last day.*

14. For this Article to be used to infer or affirm that the glorified body of Christ has flesh, blood, and bones, it must imply that Christ, from His first ascension into heaven until the last day, does sit there with a body of flesh and bones. But this is only one interpretation of the Article. For it may only mean that Christ did indeed—as is most certain—take up His body again with flesh and bones, as appears in that experience of Thomas <note>referring to the Apostle Thomas being invited to touch Jesus’s wounds in John 20:27</note>, and that He ascended with it into heaven. But the Article does not say that He *sits* there with it—that is, with a body of flesh and bones—until He returns to judge all men at the last day. And if it does not say this, it does not contradict the idea that the body of Christ, which shone so radiantly around St. Paul when he went to Damascus, had neither flesh nor bones in the proper sense. Therefore, the meaning of the Article, not being determined by any higher authority, leaves us free on this point. Nor do I think that the authors of the Article—observing how cautious and considerate they were in that restriction of ["*all things that appertain to the perfection of man's nature*"]—ever intended that the belief in flesh and bones in the now-glorified body of Christ should be an essential part of this Article. Nor does Mr. Rogers <note>Thomas Rogers (c. 1553–1616), author of an influential and widely read commentary on the Thirty-Nine Articles</note> include it among the propositions which he lays out as being comprised within the same.

15. But suppose the intent of the Article was to include this also: *that the glorified body of Christ not only had in its ascension, but still has, and ever will have until He returns to judgment, a body of flesh and bones;* provided they be *celestial and spiritual flesh and bones* (as it is without controversy a *spiritual* and *celestial body*), that would cause no disagreement <note>original: "break no squares"</note> with my own views and conceptions. For I do, in the very text of my treatise, acknowledge this glorified body of Christ to be organized light. That is to say, though at a distance Christ is surrounded with gleams and rays of inaccessible light and glory—which envelop His body just as an atmosphere of emitted <note>original: "perspired"</note> vapors is rightly conceived to surround the body of every man, especially when he is a little warmer than ordinary—yet if any mortal could get within this so radiant photosphere <note>original: "Photosphere"; here used to mean a sphere of light</note> (as I may call it), or orb of glory and brightness, and approach near enough to see the frame and features of such a divine body, the symmetry of His face would be so exquisite, and the color <note>original: "tincture"</note> of His complexion so transcending all the comparisons of the poets' rubies and roses, and the ravishing look of His eyes so far surpassing the most pure and benign light of the fairest stars, that no heart could escape being struck into a faint <note>original: "swoun"</note> at the sight of such overcoming beauty and majesty, nor the soul of the beholder from being carried quite away in an ecstatic fit of love, joy, and transporting admiration. And therefore, as I acknowledge the outward features to be thus perfect and distinct <note>original: "articulate"</note> in this glorious body, would it be so hard a thing to allow the <term>formative power</term> <note>original: "Plastick power"; in 17th-century philosophy, the "plastic power" was the subconscious force within a soul or nature that gives shape and structure to matter</note> to do its <meta>office</meta>

There is a natural flesh, and there is a spiritual flesh.* <note>original: Σπείρεται σὰρξ ψυχική, ἐγείρεται σὰρξ πνευματική. Ἔστι σὰρξ ψυχική, & ἔστι σὰρξ πνευματική.</note> 

Therefore, it is no wonder that our Liturgy, in the administration of Baptism, asks the godfather, *"Do you believe in the resurrection of the flesh, and the everlasting life after death?"* For my part, I must confess, I suspect that *celestial* and *spiritual flesh* is more truly "flesh" (according to a well-known aphorism of *Hermetic Philosophy* <note>A tradition of esoteric philosophy based on writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note>) than this which we wear in this life. And as I acknowledged before that it has complexion, color, and admirable features, so I do not doubt that it is just as substantial and solid to the touch in its <term>tonic motions</term> <note>original: "Tonick motions"; a philosophical concept referring to the internal tension or vibrational energy that gives matter its form and solidity</note> as our flesh is when gripping, tugging, wrestling, or during any such exercise of our strength. My views concerning the *nature of a glorified body* are, in every respect, beyond reproach. Therefore, having sufficiently cleared this up, we will now proceed to the second objection.

# Chapter IV. *His Answer regarding the Sameness of the Body, etc.*

...his own words, with the recital of the passage upon which it is grounded. 8. His *Answer* to the *Objection*. 9. *Grotius's* *exposition* <note>original: "Gloss"</note> upon that passage in *Job*, *I know that my Redeemer lives, etc.* <note>original: "Scio quòd Redemptor meus vivit, &c."</note> and *how fittingly that text is used in our funeral service.* 10. *The summary of his account of the four chapters mentioned above, regarding the Sameness of the Body at the Resurrection.*

1. THE second Objection concerns the Identity or *Sameness*, so to speak, of our *Bodies* at the *Resurrection*, as if I denied that we then had the same Bodies, and consequently denied the Resurrection itself. Because this charge is so great and the point is of such huge importance, before I either set down or begin to answer the objection more specifically in the exact words in which it is framed, I shall give an account of the whole purpose and management of this theory in the four chapters where I discuss it in my *Mystery of Godliness*. This is to provide fuller assurance that I have delivered nothing unorthodox <note>original: "Heterodox"</note> or repugnant to the Christian Faith in that entire discourse.

2. I say, therefore, that it is evident to anyone who will carefully read the above-mentioned chapters that their aim and purpose is only this: namely, to defend the Article of the *Resurrection* in its essential, useful, and indispensable sense—which is, *that we shall at the last day be revived into a visible and physical personality, in which we shall feel ourselves to be the very same people, and truly possess the very same bodies (and appear to others to have them), just as much as we ever felt ourselves to have the same body or appeared to others to have it in this life.* This, without any controversy, is the most plain, obvious, and necessary substance of this Article, and the only sense that is clearly included in any of the Creeds of the Church or any of their Articles. This, therefore, is the task that I undertake to prove against the attacks of the Atheist; this is the solid and indispensable truth that I defend in these chapters against all his insults and objections. In the meantime, I do not deny that it is the same *numerical body* <term>Numerical Body: The philosophical idea that the resurrection body consists of the exact same physical atoms as the original body.</term> that rises again in the Resurrection, according to the most precise notions of the Scholastic philosophers <note>original: "School-men"</note>.

3. To give, therefore, a brief account of each chapter as it relates to our present purpose: In the first chapter, the Atheist attacks this Article when it is framed with the difficulties that attend the notion of the *same numerical body* in the most disadvantageous sense used by the Scholastic philosophers (*for with those who hold that the Soul gives the Body its individual identity <note>original: "individuates"</note>, there is no difficulty at all*), and with the claim that every body rises out of the grave. You may read their objections in Sections 4, 5, and 6. The state of the question that they take advantage of is described in Section 1. But I decline to answer based on that framing of the question, as I am only concerned with proving the Article of the *Resurrection* in the sense I have defined above—which is the only essential and useful sense of the Article, and beyond which neither Scripture nor any of the Creeds assert anything. In doing this, I have followed my first rule.

# His Answer concerning the Sameness [of the Body], Chapter IV.

...objections of the Atheist in the previous chapter are not solid arguments, but mere quibbles <note>original: "Cavils"</note> against the essential and vital meaning of this Article [of Faith]. The specific details that Scholastic theologians <note>the "Schools" refers to medieval university scholars</note> or other divines have attached to it do not necessarily belong to its true nature. I demonstrate this in the first three sections of this chapter.

But in the fourth section, the Atheist launches a new attack based on the meaning of the word *Resurrection* [Latin: *Resurrectio*], as if it implied the rising again of the exact same *physical body* <note>original: "Numerical Body"</note> in the strictest Scholastic sense. To this I answer, first: *That the Latin word "Resurgere" [to rise again] does not necessarily imply any such thing. For example, if a city or a temple is razed to the ground—even from its very foundations—it is truly said to be "rebuilt." It is both considered and called the same temple or city again, even if not a single stone from the former structure were used, provided it is rebuilt on the same ground according to the exact same floor plan <note>original: "Ichnography"</note>.* That floor plan serves as a permanent mark of its identity, showing it is built upon the same lines as before. Similarly, even if the *same physical matter* <note>original: "Same Numerical Matter"</note> were not gathered together to form the same body at the Resurrection, the unchanging personality resides in the soul. Therefore, this body—which is united with the soul and built, as it were, upon that stable and unchanging foundation—becomes by that very fact <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> the same body as before. This is just as the temple or city is called "the same" when rebuilt on the same plot of ground and following the same lines as the original. 

This is consistent with the bold assertion of the learned knight *Sir Kenelm Digby*, who, I well remember, somewhere in his writings speaks to this effect: *That once the soul is stripped of her present body, if she were afterwards given a body made out of one of the most distant rocks in Africa or America, this body—upon its vital union with the soul—would be the same physical body she had before.* This also agrees with the views of several significant philosophers and Scholastic theologians—*Averroes, Avicenna, Durandus*, and others—who argue that *individuality comes from the form [the soul] alone, and that the matter and the individual person are given their identity by it.* To this, *Aristotle* plainly gives his support in his book *On the Soul* <note>original: "De Anima"</note>, <margin>Book 2, chapter 1.</margin> where he says: "We say that substance is one kind of being. One part of this is matter, which in itself is not a specific thing; another part is the shape and form, by which it is then called a specific thing; and the third part is the combination of these two." <note>original: "Λέγομεν δὴ ἕν τι γένος τῶν ὄντων τὴν οὐσίαν, ταύτης δὲ τὸ μὲν ὡς ὕλην ὃ καθ’ αὑτὸ μὲν οὐκ ἔστι τόδε τι, ἕτερον δὲ μορφὴν καὶ εἶδος, καθ’ ἣν ἤδη λέγεται τόδε τι, καὶ τρίτον τὸ ἐκ τούτων."</note>

But then, secondly, I further answer the current objection by noting that "Resurrection" [Latin: *Resurrectio*] must be interpreted according to the broad meaning of the original terms it translates—namely, the Greek words *anastasis* and *egersis* and the Hebrew word *tchiah*. In themselves, these words mean only "giving life" <note>original: "Vivification"</note> or "rising into life" <note>original: "Erection into life"</note>. However, because they are used to describe those who have, in some sense, ceased to be alive, they signify "restoration to life" <note>original: "Revivification"</note> in that context. Therefore, the Atheist’s objection based on the word "Resurrection" is utterly defeated. Thus I have fulfilled my duty <note>original: "managed my Province"</note> against him in this second chapter and shown that he cannot prove any falsehood in either the Scriptures or our Creeds.

5. Additionally, in the third and fourth chapters, the Atheist launches new attacks against this very important Article of Faith. In the former, he argues that there is no Resurrection of the Body because it is unnecessary, given that the soul enjoys such free and happy activity without it. In the latter, he argues that human nature is not capable of possessing a body as excellent and exalted as the *heavenly* body.

<summary>The author argues that the "sameness" of the resurrected body depends on the soul's enduring identity and a "floor plan" of personality, rather than the reuse of the exact same physical atoms. He cites philosophers like Aristotle and Sir Kenelm Digby to support the idea that the soul gives the body its individual identity.</summary>

### 5.
Whether the body is judged to be as it is, or whether it is thought to be beyond the power of Christ to reward us with such stupendous bodies—to both of these points I have fully and sufficiently answered in these two latter chapters. I do not need to dwell on these objections, as they do not concern the present point at hand: namely, the *sameness of the body*. However, I thought it appropriate to mention them all to show my thorough plan of defending this grand Article of our Faith in such a substantial and useful sense as the Scripture and the Creeds require us to believe, standing against all the quibbles <note>original: "Cavils"</note> and objections of those who pretend to be *Rationalists*. This is why I have so carefully managed this task according to the instructions of my first rule, as I have already mentioned.

### 6.
But I will now also show that I have not neglected the direction of my fifth and last rule. I will show how cautious I have been to avoid varying from or contradicting that more detailed and precise opinion of the Scholastic theologians <note>original: "the Schools"; referring to the established academic traditions of the medieval and early modern universities</note> on this point—that is to say, the *physical identity <note>original: "Numerical Identity"; the idea that the resurrected body consists of the exact same atoms as the original</note> of the body*, even in their strictest sense of the term. 

This will appear from several passages. For instance, in the first of these four chapters, in the first section, the Scholastic state of the Resurrection is described: namely, that *we shall have the same physical bodies in which we lived here on Earth, and that these very bodies shall rise out of the grave.* To this I immediately added: *This doctrine the Atheist very dearly hugs as a pledge in his bold imagination <note>original: "conceit"</note> of the falseness and vanity of all the other Articles of Religion.* By inserting the phrase "in his bold imagination," it is clear that I am so far from denying the doctrine of the Scholastics that I am actually scolding the atheist for doing so.

Again, in Section 7, where I speak of this more precise position of the Scholastics, I write: *These and such like are the arguments of those who would overthrow religion based on this advantage, as they judge it; they aim at something that seems to suggest a kind of incongruity and incredibility in the matter, but it will not result in a total impossibility.* You can see what those arguments against the Scholastic position are in the fourth, fifth, and sixth sections above. Here again, I am so far from rejecting or condemning the opinion of the Scholastics as being completely indefensible that I suggest the "advantage" the opponents think they have is not as great or overwhelming in itself as it is in their own estimation and imagination. For I say, "*based on this advantage, as they judge it.*" 

Besides this, I suggest that all the force of their arguments against this position is merely a "tendency"—and a "seeming" one at that—toward persuading someone of a kind of inconsistency or lack of credibility. I flatly deny that it will at all amount to a real *impossibility* of the thing. And whatever is at all possible with God is easy for Him, because He is infinitely all-powerful <note>original: "Omnipotent"</note>.

And again, in the very last clause of this chapter, I express a special care to keep the Scholastic concept untouched and whole in these words: [*But what I answer, I would be understood to direct to the Atheist and Infidel, permitting those who already believe the substance (which I have rightly stated above) to imagine the details <note>original: "vary their phancies with what circumstances"</note> however they please. But for those others, I must hold them to tough meat <note>A metaphor for rigorous, difficult-to-swallow logical arguments</note>, and keep my skirts as short as I can <note>An idiom meaning to leave no loose ends or vulnerable points for an opponent to seize upon</note>, so that they do not trip me up.*] In this, I most accurately and carefully conform myself to the purpose and meaning of my...

# His Answer touching the Sameness Chapter IV.

### 6.
My first and last rule is this: *I assert nothing more to the "Gentleman Atheist" or "Philosopher Infidel" regarding the Resurrection* than what is defined by the Scripture and the accepted Creeds of our Church, *which I declare to have no contradiction at all with the most precise reason*. 

But for those who take any pleasure or find any ease and satisfaction of mind in the conclusions or terminology of the Scholastic theologians <note>original: "School-Divines"; scholars who used logic and philosophy to explain Christian dogma</note> regarding this point, they are left free to enjoy their own understandings. They may, if they please, either imagine it necessary that all *bodies should rise out of the ground*, the earth being cast aside (as that opinion is stated in Section 1), or else conceive only that God will, by his omnipotence, gather all the particles of our *bodies*—whether flying in the air or floating in the water—and frame them together on the surface of the earth *without first moving them into any hollow places in the ground*. Concerning such things, they may vary their fancies as they please, provided they do cordially believe the above-mentioned substance of the Article. *This is the only thing I have been concerned with in this dispute; however, I have nowhere denied the Scholastic notion of the identity of the body at the Resurrection.*

This is enough to clear me from all suspicion of heterodoxy <note>original: "Heterodoxness"; holding opinions at odds with established religious doctrine</note> regarding the Resurrection. It would be superfluous to further allege how expressly I declare (Chapter 7, Section 2) that *I do not deny the possibility of the same physical body <note>original: "Numerical Body"; the idea that the resurrected body is made of the exact same atoms as the one that died</note>, not even in the most strict (though unnecessary) meaning of the Scholastic schools*. 

But for me to insist upon such *strictness*—that is, to fight for it with the very people for whom I most intended my writings—would be to go against those useful rules that I had maturely and deliberately proposed to myself. My design was the *winning over of those in this, my more Rational and Philosophical Age, to a sincere and heartfelt embracing of the Christian faith*—at least as many as currently *stand apart from it*—and to keep those within the faith who have already embraced it. This may serve as a more general vindication of my position on this point.

### 7. 
I will now set down the particular objection in its formal wording.

As for 1 Corinthians 15, that chapter is so far from asserting this truth that it plainly says it is *not* the same body. Just as God gives to the blades of wheat grains quite distinct from the seed that was sown, so at the Resurrection he will give the soul a body quite different from that which..."
