# Chapter IV. Of the Body at the Resurrection.

...which was *buried* is as different as a *spiritual* body is from a *natural* body, or an *heavenly* one from an *earthly* one.

8. Therefore, I now briefly and specifically answer this objection: First, it is not a requirement of faith to believe that every body said to rise at the Last Day must rise out of a grave, since not all bodies were buried. But that is only an external circumstance; I assume the main weight of the objection concerns the *same body*. 

Secondly, therefore, I say that I do not claim it cannot be proved from Scripture that the *same body* shall rise again, but rather that it is the same *numerical body* <note>original: "Numerical Body"; a philosophical term meaning the exact same physical matter or atoms</note>. I acknowledge that it would indeed undermine the Resurrection if the body said to rise were not, in a very proper sense, the "same." And I believe it is properly the same if it is acknowledged to be as much the same with the body that was buried as that body was with itself during this earthly life. I freely acknowledge it to be so, though I decline to assert that it is the same *numerical body* in the ordinary sense of *numerical* used by the more rigid sort of Scholastic theologians <note>original: "School-Divines"; medieval and early modern scholars who used strict logic to define church doctrine</note>. My claim, therefore, is only this: that it cannot be proved from Scripture that the mystery of the *Resurrection* requires the revival of the exact same *numerical body* according to the strictest meaning of the Scholastics.

I believe I have safely asserted this without the least harm to the substance of this article of the Christian faith. I have already clearly declared myself in the previous *section concerning the identity* of people at the Resurrection: the same individuals who die and are buried shall truly appear in their own persons on the Day of Judgment, just as if the bodies that were interred were immediately reanimated by their souls again and started out of their graves. To give an example, they shall be as truly the same people as *Lazarus* was when he rose *body* and *soul* out of the grave after he had lain there for four days. I think *Lazarus* was sufficiently the same in both *soul* and *body*. Therefore, it is evident that I do allow and profess that there is the same body at the Resurrection, because I claim it is as much the "same" (whatever that *sameness* consists of) as the body is to itself in this life. I also acknowledge that this *sameness* of the body aligns with the intent of the three approved Creeds and Scripture, as the *Resurrection* implies as much in both. I hope this is a sufficient answer to this second objection.

9. Therefore, I might now move to the third objection, were it not for the need to clear up a doubt regarding that text from *Job*, which I mentioned modern interpreters are now wise enough not to understand as referring to the *Resurrection* at all. In saying this, I must confess I was thinking of *Hugo Grotius's* commentary <note>original: "Gloss"</note> on the text, "I know that my Redeemer lives, etc.," which is as follows: 

"The Jews never referred these words and those that follow to the Resurrection, even though they scrutinize everything that could possibly be interpreted that way. Quite a few Christians have used them to prove the faith of the Resurrection; but to do so, they were forced in their translations to deviate significantly from the Hebrew, as noted by Mercerus and others. The Hebrew reads: 'I know that my Redeemer lives, and that he shall stand at last in the field. Even if they (namely, diseases) should consume not only my skin but also *this* (namely, the fat which is under the skin)...'" <note>original: "Hæc verba & quæ sequuntur Judæi nunquam ad Resurrectionem retulere, cùm tamen omnia rimentur quæ aliquam in speciem eò trahi possunt. Hebræa sic sonant: Scio ego Redemptorem meum vivere, & illum postremò staturum in campo. Etiamsi non pellem tantùm meam sed & Hoc (nempe arvinam quæ sub pelle est) consumerent (morbi scilicet,)"</note>

"...yet in my flesh I shall see God <note>original: "in carne tamen mea Deum videbo"</note> (that is, I shall experience His favor) <note>original: "id est, propitium experiar"</note>. See *Job* 42, where *Job* is also said to see *God with his eyes.* These events and expressions, which serve as a type <term>Type: a biblical person, event, or symbol believed to foreshadow something in the future, especially in the life of Christ or the afterlife</term> and likeness of the Resurrection, are appropriately applied by our Church to the Resurrection in the Funeral Service <note>original: "Office of the Burial of the Dead"</note>. For the Scripture itself abounds with such typical allusions in matters that are so undeniably true to all good Christians as the Resurrection of the body. Therefore, it does not detract from the excellence of our Liturgy <term>Liturgy: the set forms of public worship in the Church</term> to imitate that appropriate and useful liberty of language. The words are exceedingly fitting and significant, and those passages of *Job's* history are an accurate foreshadowing of that happy reward given by our Redeemer at the Resurrection on the Last Day.

10. To conclude, therefore: the summary of my account concerning what I have written about the Resurrection in the chapters mentioned above is this: I have asserted and defended against the atheist or unbeliever the full substance of that article of the *Resurrection*, as far as it is expressed in either Scripture or the three *Creeds* <note>The Apostles', Nicene, and Athanasian Creeds</note>. In the meantime, I have not denied those more technical details that the Schoolmen <term>Schoolmen: medieval and early modern academic theologians (Scholastics) known for highly technical and logical arguments</term> argue for—particularly the idea of the same *numerical body* <note>original: "Numerical Body"; the belief that the resurrected body must consist of the exact same physical atoms as the original body</note>. Rather, I most clearly affirm that the *same body* will arise, according to Scripture and the aforementioned Creeds. I maintain that we shall be as really and *sensibly* <note>meaning "perceptibly" or "feelingly"</note> the same persons to ourselves, and as *conspicuously* the same to others—in both body and soul—as we were in this life. Therefore, I have fully addressed the current objection. 

I am confident that no honorable person will think it appropriate that the overly precise <note>original: "curious"</note> decisions of the Schoolmen—who were immeasurably fussy <note>original: "nice"</note> in their conclusions, beyond what Scripture warrants or solid philosophy supports—should be accepted as Articles of Faith. To do so would be a great disadvantage to the Christian religion, especially in this philosophical age, where there is such diligent search and great success in discovering truth. For certainly, there must be a wide difference of judgment regarding the correct idea of the *sameness* of the body between those who view the human body as stable and permanent as the solid banks of a river, and those who view it as being almost as fluid as the river itself. There is just as great a difference regarding the necessity of this stability between those who believe the body itself is capable of feeling and perception, and those who consider the body as incapable of feeling as the very clothes we wear.

But however that may be, it was necessary for my purpose—as one who claims to the philosopher that my religion is rational—not to make myself look like a fool to someone whom I expect to follow reason strictly. I will not needlessly swallow down things that I find neither faith nor reason require of me. And what is this but a precise observation of my first rule? But I must confess that both faith and reason require me to believe that we shall have the *same body* at the Resurrection, whatever this *sameness* consists of. And for my own

If anyone has anything more substantial to say for Episcopacy than this, let him speak. And lastly, at the close of Section 22, I do expressly declare, *That there is no more effective way imaginable to make the people believe in good earnest that religion is worth looking after, than to find themselves looked after so carefully and affectionately* in reference to religion *by persons of such honorable rank and quality.* All of these passages are perfectly contradictory to the charge this third objection lays against me.

<header>Chap. V. His Answer touching Episcopacy.</header>

*...in my judgment, cannot but be very useful, as it carries with it both a detection and rebuke of the corruption <note>original: "degeneracy"</note> of the present age, and a warmth and encouragement to hasten those good times, by striving to correct our lives according to this pattern we have of them.*

<margin>1 Corinthians 1:12</margin>
2. Now let anyone judge whether I call *Episcopacy* a *faction* or not, or whether I propose all these ways of division as false and illegitimate. Since those systems so clearly contradict one another—such as *Calvinism* and *Arminianism*, or *Episcopacy*, *Presbytery*, and *Independency*—some of them must be true. Just as either *Calvinism* or *Arminianism* must be *true* in the points where they contradict each other, so too, among those forms of government, some of them must be *right*. For it is intolerably wrong for the Church to be left without any government. Therefore, not all the things named there are condemned or rebuked—nor is any of them properly condemned simply by being mentioned in that way—though some of them may be deserving of condemnation in themselves. Even if they had all been good in their various kinds, men might still fail to behave well, or with proper moderation and manner, in their personal feelings and biased support for them. But it does not follow at all that because something good is followed in a factious way, the thing itself loses its goodness—much less that it becomes the "faction" itself. It is no different than when the Apostle says, *While one says, I am of Paul, and another, I am of Apollos, are you not carnal?* <note>original: "1 Cor. 1. 12."</note> No one would understand him to be accusing *Apollos* or himself of being carnal <term>carnal: worldly or motivated by human passions rather than the Spirit</term>, but only those who created factions under the pretense of following them with great zeal.

3. And therefore, I say that men may pursue good things (among which I have already stated *Episcopacy* belongs) just as they may follow good men, even the Apostles themselves, in a factious manner. This is all that can be drawn from this paragraph concerning *Episcopacy*: not that it is a faction, but that it can be managed in a factious and biased way. That is, it can be valued excessively and out of proportion (as this paragraph suggests), as if the entire *Millennial Happiness* <term>Millennial Happiness: the thousand-year period of peace and Christ's reign mentioned in the Book of Revelation</term> consisted only in *Episcopacy*. To put it another way: people may become so obsessed with one good thing that they become indifferent to the success of everything else, and settle entirely on that one point. Even if that one thing were *Episcopacy* itself, such an attitude would still be a factious and biased affection. It would fall short of the goal of the Gospel, which aims equally at nurturing all things that are essentially and indispensably Christian, such as those I have listed in this paragraph in my description of the happy ages to come.

4. Therefore, I believe it is perfectly clear that I am far from charging *Episcopacy* itself with being a faction, or with anything else that sounds negative. On the contrary, in this very preface, I have argued for it as the best kind of church government and have provided reasons for it. To state my own judgment even more fully: it is not only much more preferable than *Presbytery* in itself, but it is also better suited to support the interests of *Protestantism*. When I speak of this, I mean only the *main and principal object*, not every single thing that Church Discipline might reach. The conclusion of this paragraph plainly implies this in these words: *For these are such as deserve to be held up with all possible care and strictness*. This is as much as to say that the severity of Discipline is to be exercised, if anywhere, more especially in these core areas. *Other things are to be so gently recommended that conscientious men may not be distressed by them*—that is to say, the same severity should not be used in matters that are not of such an essential nature, especially toward those who are conscientious and of the character I shall describe more fully when I answer the eighth Objection.

But in the meantime, I think it is already quite plain that I do not claim that Church Discipline should include *only* the generally acknowledged Articles of the Christian Faith and the plain, essential duties of life. Rather, I am saying that this is the *principal object* of it, as I declared in the previous paragraph: *That the main end of Church Government and Discipline is the supporting and promoting of the Christian life, etc.* This does not exclude, but rather implies, other things of a secondary nature that contribute to the greater beauty and completeness of the Christian system <note>original: "Oeconomy"—referring to the organized administration or "household" of the Church</note>. These may be introduced as needed as a *subordinate goal and a secondary focus*. Therefore, I do not destroy Church Authority regarding matters of indifference <term>things indifferent</term>; instead, I establish it or leave it intact.

8. No one could question this if they simply compared one part of my Preface with another. They are too far removed from the reputation and merit of either being or starting a church that is purely Apostolic.*

# Chapter V. Authority in things indifferent.

...exercising their discipline on behalf of such truths and rites as are plainly and admittedly Apostolic, while being more flexible and easy regarding additional circumstances, and completely cutting off all useless and complicated opinions. *I finally add: this one simple and noble rule of government, if faithfully kept, is the most effective means imaginable for making the world good, and for both the unity and growth of the Church. It is infinitely superior to all those many clever tricks and petty schemes of the most professional politicians in the Church of Rome; provided we are not crude and messy, but respectful and dignified in our public worship.* This statement cannot be proven true unless we assume the Church has the power to appoint and determine the modes and circumstances of public worship. Since these modes may vary and yet all be decent, it is therefore <term>indifferent</term> <note>In theology, "indifferent things" (or adiaphora) are practices or ceremonies neither commanded nor forbidden by God, and thus left to the discretion of leaders.</note> which one is chosen. It is certainly left to Authority to make that choice, and others ought to submit to it. *Let all things be done decently and in order.* So it is abundantly clear that it never entered my mind to take away the right of commanding "indifferent things" from public authority. And thus, I think I have fully satisfied this fourth objection. Let us now move to the fifth.

->**Objection V.**<-

*He calls Christ’s Divine Nature that "passive, contemptible Divinity" which resided in him. (Book 5, Chapter 1, Section 5)*

9. To resolve <note>original: "assoiling"</note> this objection, which appears so shocking at first glance, we need only to look at those two sections where I mention the *passivity* of that Divinity residing in Christ. For it will immediately appear what I mean by this *passive Divinity*. I do not mean the *Eternal Word* <note>original: "Logos"—the Second Person of the Trinity</note> with which he is <term>Hypostatically united</term> <note>The "Hypostatic union" is the theological term for the union of Christ's divine and human natures in one person.</note>, but the <term>Divine nature</term> <note>original: θεία φύσις (theia physis)</note> (that Divine nature which, in some sense, all Christians partake in) which was communicated to the human nature of Christ in a measure far beyond his fellow humans. It is this Divinity, therefore, that I say is passive—I mean the *God-like Humanity* of Christ, who was also a <term>partaker of the Divine nature</term> <note>original: κοινωνὸς τῆς θείας φύσεως (koinonos tes theias physeos)</note> in that more moral and spiritual sense common to him and us, only he was anointed with the "oil of joy" more eminently than his fellows. This is that Divinity which I say is properly *passive*, and which seems so contemptible to worldly men, as will soon appear from the two sections where I speak of it.

<margin>*Book 4, Chapter 12, Section 3.</margin>

> The first of them is this: *And indeed, how could it ever enter the mind of a purely worldly person to think of an humble, passive, soul-softening, self-denying, and self-surrendering Divinity residing in any person? Or if it did, how could they think there was any great value in that spirit, more than in the spirit which seems to the world more impressive and noble? But certainly this is more precious in the eyes of God than all other things in the world; and whatever injury is done to this, it is like the touching of the apple of His own eye. Can it enter the mind of any man to think that I understand this humble, passive, soul-softening, self-denying, and self-surrendering Divinity to be the Second Person of the Trinity, the Eternal and Immaterial Word?* 

But I am comparing here the character of Christ with that of *Apollonius* <note>Apollonius of Tyana was a 1st-century Greek philosopher often compared to Jesus by early critics of Christianity.</note>, who claimed a kind of Divinity, and whose biographer *Philostratus* tried to portray him accordingly.

# His Answer touching the Passivity Chap. V.

10. But this pretension of Divinity among the greatest philosophers of the Heathen is more crude and unrestrained—more like that of *Lucifer*, who said, *I will be like the Most High* <note>original: "Similis ero Altissimo"</note>—than like the example of the humble Son of God. For their partaking, forsooth, of the *Divine Nature* is to ascend into the secure throne of perfect *apathy* <term>apathy</term> <note>In this context, apathy refers to the Stoic ideal of "apatheia," a state of being unmoved by emotions or external suffering.</note> and *immateriality*. "The goal," says Plotinus, "is not to be without sin, but to be a god" <note>original: "Τὸ τέλος οὐκ ἔξω ἁμαρτίας εἶναι, ἀλλὰ θεὸς εἶναι"</note>; the meaning of which is that the goal of their highest level of virtue (which they call "Paradigmatic" or model-like) is not to be without sin, but to be without passion—and indeed, without all compassion. They wish to be moved by nothing, but to securely enjoy themselves and to become invulnerable to any events of this mortal life. This is the peak of Divinity which they strive for. In contrast to this, I have described that most lovely and lovable Divine spirit living in our Savior; it is far from this *Lucifer-like pride*, but is an humble, *passive*, *soul-melting*, *self-afflicting*, and *self-resigning Divinity*. Therefore, it is the kind of Divinity that Philostratus <note>Philostratus (c. 170–247 AD) was a Greek writer who wrote a famous biography of Apollonius of Tyana, a pagan philosopher intended to rival Jesus.</note> could not even dream of when he tried to portray his great model *Apollonius*.

11. And it is plain that in the section the *Objector* cites, there is no other meaning than this. For the whole section reads as follows:

> *But he whom they numbered among the transgressors, and took to be the most vile of men—because he was not recommended by anything that the animal life* <term>animal life</term> <note>The "animal life" refers to a focus on worldly status, physical beauty, and social power rather than spiritual values.</note> *likes and applauds (such as noble birth, the power of popular eloquence, honor, wealth, authority, high education, beauty, courtesy, pleasant conversation, and the like)—he is, I say, despite this general contempt from men, very highly prized by him who is the infallible Judge. His ways are not as our ways, nor his thoughts as our thoughts. But so that he might align our understanding with his own, he raised Jesus Christ from the dead, bringing that passive, contemptible Divinity that lived in him into a deserved victory and triumph. He rebuked the blind world for its ignorance of that Life which is most dear and precious to himself, making him alive whom they maliciously killed, and preparing a way for universal homage for him who was universally scorned and became the off-scouring of all things* <note>original: "περίψημα πάντων," meaning the lowliest scrapings or refuse.</note>, *even though his Spirit, Life, and Nature were of more worth than all things of the world combined.*

Certainly, it must seem very marvelous to others as well as myself that anyone could miss my meaning in this section and pretend that I call the *Divine Nature in Christ* (understanding by that the Eternal *Logos* <term>Logos</term> <note>The "Logos" is the Greek term for the "Word," referring to the eternal, divine second person of the Trinity.</note>) a *passive, contemptible Divinity*. For I do not speak of the *Divine Logos* here, much less say it is *passive*. Nor do I call the Divine Nature in Christ "contemptible" in the other sense; instead, I condemn others for viewing it as such. I declare how highly prized it is by 그 Judge who alone is infallible (whose ways are not as our ways, nor his thoughts as our thoughts), despite the general contempt it receives from men. And again, when I say, *That he raised Jesus Christ from the dead, bringing that passive, contemptible Divinity that lodged in him into a deserved victory and triumph, rebuking the blind world for its ignorance of that Life that is most dear and precious to himself*, it is plain I speak of the *God-like Humanity of Christ* <note>original: "Deiform Humanity of Christ"</note> (if I may so speak), which was *passive* and capable of death itself. But I am so far from calling it contemptible that I accuse the...

### CHAP. VI.

1. *A few remarks concerning the person of Nestorius from Spondanus.* 2. *A full description of his heresy from Justellus's collection of Church Canons.* 3. *A citation from Justinian's Decree to the people of Constantinople.* 4. *That the heresy of Nestorius was that he did not hold any physical or real union (such as exists between body and soul) between Christ's human nature and the* Word <note>original: "Logos"</note>, *but that they were really separated from one another—proved from several passages of the previous citation.* 5. *The same further demonstrated by two more citations from the Council of Ephesus, as recorded in Photius's letter to Michael, Prince of Bulgaria.* 6. *Another to the same purpose from a brief collection of councils titled* "Anonymous" <note>original: "Ἀδέſποτον"; meaning a work without a known author.</note>. 7. *Another from the Synodicon.* 8. *Several passages produced from Book 1 of his "Mystery of Godliness" that are diametrically opposite to the above-mentioned characteristics of Nestorianism.* 9. *Other passages of a similar nature produced from the fifth and tenth books.* 10. *The specific objection proposed, together with other secondary claims from hearsay.* 11. *That the academic schools are mistaken in their definition of* Individual Substance <term>Suppositum</term> <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a "suppositum" is an individual, complete substance that exists on its own.</note>. 12. *The true definition of it, from which also the true concept of* Personhood <term>Hypostasis</term>, *Subsistence, and Person is to be understood.* 13. *His answer to the specific objection proposed above.* 14. *His answer to the secondary claims.* 15. *That in those very passages where they would raise their charge of Nestorianism, he has not deviated from the meaning and language of creeds and councils, specifically the Council of Chalcedon.* 16. *And of the Athanasian Creed.*

# Chapter VI. His Answer concerning Nestorianism.

...then by a certain relation or appropriation to the Eternal Word, rather than by a real union. I say, all these passages plainly imply that the heresy of **Nestorius** was that he conceived the **Word** and **Jesus** as being really disjoined. Therefore, his was the same heresy as that of **Diodorus**, Bishop of **Tarsus**, "who felt that there was one Son apart who was born of the Holy Virgin, and another true Son of God the Father." <note>original: "Qui alterum esse sensit Filium seorsum qui de Sancta Virgine natus est, alterum verum Filium Dei Patris."</note>

5. This will further appear from the Council of **Ephesus**, as we find it in **Photius's** Epistle to **Michael**, Prince of **Bulgaria**. In this letter, having described the union of the human and divine nature in Christ—"One Christ, one Son, the same above from the Father without a mother, and below from a mother without a father; the same in another, in person, in one hypostasis" <term>hypostasis: the underlying substance or personhood; in theology, the union of Christ's two natures in one being</term> <note>original: "Εἷς Χριϛὸς, εἷς υἱὸς, ὁ αὐτὸς ἄνω ἐκ Πατρὸς ἀμήτωρ, ϗ κάτω ἐκ μητρὸς ἀπάτωρ, ὁ αὐτὸς δὲ ἐν ἄλλῳ, ἐν προσώπῳ, μίᾳ ὑποϛάσει"</note>—he immediately adds:

> "This our one Lord Jesus," he says, "that thrice-wretched fellow" (meaning Nestorius) "being not afraid to cut asunder and to divide into two persons <term>hypostases</term>, made one a mere man in his own proper person, apart, without the Word (whom we all believe to have assumed him), and the other, God apart by himself, without this assumption of the human nature." <note>original: "Τοῦτον δὴ τὸν ἕνα Κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριϛὸν εἰς δύο τέμνειν ϗ διαιρεῖν ὑποϛάσεις ὁ τρισάθλιος ἐκεῖνος οὐ πεφρικὼς, τὸν μὲν ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον ϗ χωρὶς προσλαβόντος Λόγου κατ’ ἰδίαν ὑπόϛασιν ἐπλάττετο, τὸν δ’ ὡς ἀνὰ μέρος ϗ γυμνὸν τῆς προσλήψεως."</note>

And a little after, corresponding to our former citation, it is added:

> "Moreover, he being wholly perverted in his reason would not allow the most holy Virgin—the Mother of Christ according to the flesh, who most properly and truly brought forth God the Word incarnate—to be called the Mother of God <note>original: "Deipara"</note>. But just as he stripped the Son of his Godhead, so he deprived the one who gave him birth of the title 'Mother of God'." <note>original: "Ἀλλὰ γὰρ τὸν λογισμὸν ὅλως διαϛραφεὶς, οὐδὲ τὴν αὐτοῦ κατὰ σάρκα μητέρα, τὴν παναγίαν παρθένον, τὴν κυρίως ϗ ἀληθῶς τὸν Θεὸν Λόγον σεσαρκωμένον τεκοῦσαν, οὐδὲ ταύτην καλεῖν Θεοτόκον ἠνείχετο. Ἀλλὰ ὥσπερ τὸν υἱὸν ἀπεϛέρει τῆς Θεότητος, οὕτως ἠλλοτρίω ϗ τὴν γεννησαμένην τῆς Θεοτόκου κλήσεως."</note>

6. Again, regarding the same Council of **Ephesus**, in a brief collection of the six ecumenical councils by an anonymous author (titled *Anonymous* <note>original: "Ἀδέσποτον" (Adespoton)</note>):

> "The third holy and Ecumenical Council was held at Ephesus against the ungodly man-worshiper Nestorius, who was indeed Patriarch of Constantinople, but one who divided and cut the Lord Christ completely apart. For he said he was a mere man, and not God incarnate; therefore, he would not call the Holy Virgin the Mother of God, but only the Mother of Christ." <note>original: "Ἡ δὲ τρίτη ἁγία ϗ οἰκουμενικὴ Σύνοδος γέγονεν ἐν Ἐφέσῳ κατὰ Νεστορίου τοῦ ἀνθρωπολάτρου ϗ ἀσεβοῦς, Πατριάρχου μὲν γενομένου Κωνϛαντινουπόλεως, τὸν Χριϛὸν δὲ διαιροῦντος ϗ κατατέμνοντος. ψιλὸν γὰρ ἄνθρωπον ἔφη ἔλεγε, ϗ οὐ Θεὸν σεσαρκωμένον, ὅθεν οὐδὲ Θεοτόκον, Ἀλλὰ Χριϛοτόκον τὴν ἁγίαν παρθένον ὠνόμαζε."</note>

7. I will only add one passage more, and that is out of the *Synodicon*, Number 81:

> "To Sisinius succeeded in the See of Constantinople that crack-brained priest of Antioch, Nestorius, who wounded the word of truth by refusing to call the most holy Virgin the 'Mother of God' and by being unable to bear glorifying the union of the Savior of all, Christ, according to his person <term>hypostasis</term>." <note>original: "Νεϛόριος ἐξ Ἀντιοχείας ὁ φρενοβλαβὴς πρεσβύτερος διαδέχεται τὸν Σισίνιον, ὃς τῆς ἀληθείας τὸν λόγον παρέτρωσε, Θεοτόκον λέγειν τὴν παναγίαν παρθένον μὴ προσέμενος, ϗ τὴν καθ' ὑπόϛασιν ἕνωσιν τοῦ Σωτῆρος τῶν ὅλων Χριϛοῦ δοξάζειν οὐκ ἀνεχόμενος."</note>

### Chapter VI: His Answer Concerning Nestorianism.

4. ...then by a certain relation or association with the Eternal *Word*, rather than by a real union; I say, all these passages plainly imply that the heresy of **Nestorius** was that he conceived the *Word* and *Jesus* to be truly disjointed. This will further appear from the records of the Council of **Ephesus**, as we find in the letter from **Photius** <note>Photius I (c. 810–893), Patriarch of Constantinople</note> to **Michael**, Prince of **Bulgaria**. In this letter, having described the union of the human and divine nature in Christ as, "One Christ, one son, the same above from the Father without a mother, and below from a mother without a father; the same and not another, in one person, one subsistence <term>hypostasis — the fundamental reality or 'personhood' of Christ</term>," <note>original Greek: Εἷς Χριστὸς, εἷς υἱὸς, ὁ αὐτὸς ἄνω ἐκ Πατρὸς ἀμήτωρ, καὶ κάτω ἐκ μητρὸς ἀπάτωρ, ὁ αὐτὸς δὲ οὐκ ἄλλος, ἐν προσώπῳ, μία ὑπόστασις</note> he immediately adds: 

"This our one Lord Jesus (he says), that thrice-wretched fellow [meaning Nestorius], not fearing to cut apart and divide into two subsistences <term>hypostases</term>, fashioned one as a mere man in his own subsistence <term>hypostasis</term>, apart, without the Word (whom we all believe assumed him), and the other as God separately and alone without this assumption of the human nature." <note>original Greek: Τοῦτον δὴ τὸν ἕνα Κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν εἰς δύο τέμνειν καὶ διαιρεῖν ὑποστάσεις ὁ τρισάθλιος ἐκεῖνος οὐ πεφρικὼς, ὃ μὲν ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον καὶ χωρὶς προσλαβόντος Λόγου κατ᾿ ἰδίαν ὑπόστασιν ἐπλάττε, τὸν δὲ Θεὸν ἀνὰ μέρος καὶ γυμνὸν τῷ προσλήμματι.</note> 

And a little later, corresponding to our previous citation, he adds: 

"Moreover, being wholly perverted in his reasoning, he would not even bear to call the most holy Virgin—the Mother of Christ according to the flesh, who most properly and truly gave birth to the incarnate God the Word—the Mother of God <note>original: *Deipara* or *Theotokos*</note>. But just as he deprived the Son of his Godhead, so he also alienated the one who gave him birth from the title of the Mother of God." <note>original Greek: ᾿Αλλὰ γὰρ τοὺς λογισμοὺς ὅλως διαστραφεὶς... τῆς Θεοτόκου κλήσεως.</note>

6. Again, concerning the same Council of **Ephesus**, in a brief collection of the six ecumenical councils by an anonymous author (titled *Adespoton* <note>meaning "without a master" or anonymous</note>): 

"The third holy and ecumenical Council was held at **Ephesus** against the ungodly man-worshipper <note>original: *anthropolatrou*</note> **Nestorius**, who was indeed the Patriarch of **Constantinople**, but one who divided and cut the Lord Christ completely apart. Χριστοτόκον τὴν ἁγίαν παρθένον ὠνόμαζε.</note>

7. I will only add one more passage, and that is from the *Synodicon*, Number 81: 

"**Nestorius** of **Antioch**, that brain-damaged priest, succeeded **Sisinius** in the See of **Constantinople**. He disregarded the word of truth by refusing to call the most holy Virgin the Mother of God <note>original: *Theotokos*</note>, and by being unable to tolerate the belief in the subsistence-based <term>hypostatic</term> union of Christ, the Savior of all." <note>original Greek: Νεστόριος ἐξ Ἀντιοχείας ὁ φρενοβλαβὴς πρεσβύτερος... ἕνωσιν τοῦ Σωτῆρος τῶν ὅλων Χριστοῦ δοξάζειν οὐκ ἀνεχόμενος.</note>

"He certainly felt that there was one Son separately who was born of the seed of David and the holy Virgin, and another who was properly the Son of God the Father." <note>original Latin: "Sensisse utique alterum esse Filium seorsum qui de femine David & sanctâ Virgine natus est, & alterum propriè Filium Dei Patris."</note> Because of this, he also denied the Blessed Virgin was the *Mother of God* <term>The Greek term is "Theotokos," meaning God-bearer</term> <note>original Latin: Deipara</note>. Having heard myself accused (by frequently repeated rumors) of the Nestorian heresy—even as recently as since I began writing this answer—I think it is my duty to be more accurate in describing it. 3. From Book I of the Code, Title I, in **Justinian's** official edict <note>original: Rescript</note> to the people of **Constantinople**:

### Chapter VI: His Answer Concerning Nestorianism.

*Nestorius, who distorted the word of Truth, not allowing the Holy Virgin to be called the Mother of God, nor agreeing to that orthodox opinion of the personal union <term>The original term is "hypostatical union," referring to the union of Christ's divine and human natures in one individual person.</term> of Christ the Savior of the World.*

7. Out of all this, it is exceedingly plain that the heresy of **Nestorius** consists of this: that he divided and cut completely apart the *Humanity* and *Divinity* of *Christ* into two separate substances <term>The original term is "hypostases," used here to mean distinct individual existences.</term>, making *Christ* a mere man. By doing so, he denied the Incarnation of the Word, the Godhead of *Christ*, and the honor that belonged to the Blessed Virgin for bringing him forth—whom we all rightly call the only-begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man, as the Athanasian Creed has precisely declared.

8. Now I will show how perfectly opposite not only my judgment, but that very treatise out of which some would slander me with **Nestorianism**, is to these marks of it which I have produced. This may appear not only from my asserting and arguing everywhere in that treatise for the *Divinity* of *Christ* (so that he might be a proper object of the Divine worship we give him), but also from several particular passages. For example, in Book 1, Chapter 5, Section 1: *That Christ is not a mere man <note>original Greek: ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος (psilos anthropos)</note>, or a mere creature, but a Divine person <note>original: Hypostasis</note>, or truly, really and physically (not allegorically and morally) joined with that Person which is called the Word <note>original: Logos</note>. If men would not bring their own stubborn preconceptions, but listen to the easy and natural tone of the text, the beginning of Saint John’s Gospel would put this out of all controversy.* 

And again, in Section 4: *Therefore Christ ought not to be a mere man, but God; that is, he ought to be really and physically united to the Deity, with God being present not just by assistance <term>In this context, "assistance" refers to God helping a person from the outside, rather than being one with them.</term> but by indwelling life <term>The original term is "information," a philosophical term meaning to give form or life to something, like a soul animating a body.</term>; so that just as body and soul are one man, so God and man may be one Christ.* 

And in Section 5: *Therefore, the denying of either the Divinity of Christ or the Trinity seems a subversion of the Christian religion. And not only that, but also that fanatical piece of arrogance in some enthusiasts, who would make their union with God the same as that of Christ’s.* 

And lastly, in Section 6: *For is not 그 Spirit that created and framed all things able to reform us to the most blameless level of humility, self-denial, dependency upon God, love of our neighbor, obedience to magistrates, faith, temperance, and holiness, without being any more personally <note>original: Hypostatically</note> united with us than with the earth, sea, sun, moon, and stars, and the natural parts of the creation? Therefore we conclude that to assert that the union of any true Christian with God is the same as Christ’s union is a bold, useless, and groundless opinion, and inconsistent with and destructive to the Christian religion.*

9. Can anything be more directly opposite to **Nestorianism** than these passages, or any proofs more compelling to clear anyone from such a charge? So it is unnecessary to produce any more places for my justification. And yet I cannot help glancing at what I have noted for the greater confirmation of the Trinity of the Godhead and the *Divinity* of *Christ* in Book 5, Chapter 17, Section 2. There, I used the authority of the *Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, which is more uniquely manifest to us to be of Divine inspiration than any other book, except perhaps *Daniel*, or at least in a higher measure than it or

#### Chapter VI: His Answer regarding Nestorianism.

9. I will close all with what I have set down in Book 10, Chapter 6, Section 1, where I declare that one plain expression of **Athanasius**—[*As body and soul is one man, so God and man is one Christ*]—is better than all the intricate definitions of things in the Scholastic schools, which reach no greater personal union <term>original: hypostatical union; the union of divine and human natures in one person</term> than that of the body and soul. I added immediately after: *Whereas I dare say, if it were searched to the bottom, the union between the divinity and humanity of Christ is more "one" and more exact than that of soul and body, which they call hypostatical.* Is this *to cut asunder and divide our one Lord Jesus Christ*? <note>original Greek: κατατέμνειν καὶ διαιρεῖν τὸν ἕνα Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν</note> Is this to cut asunder and divide our one Lord **Jesus Christ** into two individual persons <note>original: hypostases</note>, and not rather to allow him, if it were necessary, a more close personal union than there is between body and soul?

10. Thus fully have I cleared myself from all general accusations of **Nestorianism** <note>Nestorianism: The heresy that claimed Christ was two separate persons, one human and one divine, rather than one person with two natures.</note>. I thought it appropriate to do this more thoroughly because of the frequency with which the charge has been repeated, and because of the late and fresh arrival of it to my astonished ears. I will now set down and answer the specific objection.

### Objection VI.

*He introduces a human person in Christ, Book 6, Chapter 15, Section 1, page 258, and afterwards, without any hesitation, calls it so ten times in that chapter, and several times afterwards.*

I will also add what was hinted to me at second-hand from Book 9, Chapter 2, Section 6, where I declare, *How the humanity of Christ and the Eternal Word may be personally <note>original: hypostatically</note> united without any contradiction to human reason—as long as that reason is not corrupted with the nonsense of the Scholastic schools—and both their individual existences <note>original: hypostases</note> remain still entire.* And afterward, in the same section, I bring in *Christ as made up (if one may so speak) of the second person <note>original: Hypostasis</note> of the Trinity and of that human person that lived in Jerusalem*. Speaking of two persons in Christ in this way—even though I expressly declare them *personally* united again and again in this chapter—seemed to cause some worry of heresy to some. But it is strange that either these passages in this chapter, or those mentioned in the objection, should ever move anyone to imagine me in the least bit guilty of **Nestorianism**, especially if they had ever noticed those other passages of my book that are so perfectly and expressly contrary to it.

11. But I will show how utterly blameless these passages also are, after I have briefly settled the true notion of *Person* <note>original Latin: Persona</note> and *Hypostasis*. I cannot do this without first considering the true and allowable notion of a *subject* <note>original Latin: Suppositum; in Scholastic philosophy, an individual substance that exists in itself.</note>. For I must confess I believe the Scholastic schools are mistaken in their ordinary definition of it, when they define it as *a singular substance existing by itself completely and incommunicably* <note>original Latin: Substantia singularis per se exsistens completè & incomunicabiliter</note>. For even if it is true that there are innumerable examples of such "subjects" that exist completely by themselves, it will be hard to prove that there are any that do so "incommunicably." That is to say, it is hard to prove their nature is such that God cannot create some substantial form or other which he may adapt to this present subject, so that this and the added *actualization* <note>original Greek: ’Εντελέχεια (entelecheia); the realization of a potentiality, here referring to a soul-like form.</note> may make *a single being in itself* <note>original Latin: Ens unum per se</note>, and so grow together into one single subject. To deny this would be a reproach to the Divine Omnipotence.

### His Answer concerning Nestorianism. Chapter VI.

**Nestorius**, who perverted the word of Truth, did not allow the **Holy Virgin** to be called the *Mother of God*, nor did he yield to the orthodox opinion of the **hypostatic union** <term>hypostatic union: the theological doctrine that in Christ, a human nature and a divine nature are perfectly united in one single person (hypostasis)</term> of Christ, the Savior of the world.

From all of this, it is exceedingly plain that the heresy of **Nestorius** consists in this: that he divided and cut completely apart the **humanity** and **divinity** of Christ into two separate persons <note>original: hypostases</note>, making Christ a mere man, and so denying the Incarnation of the Word, the Godhead of Christ, and the honor that belonged to the Blessed Virgin for bringing forth him whom we all rightly style the only-begotten Son of God—perfect God and perfect man, as the **Creed of Athanasius** <note>The Athanasian Creed is a Christian statement of belief focusing on Trinitarian doctrine and Christology, emphasizing that Christ is both fully God and fully man.</note> has precisely declared.

8. Now I will show how perfectly opposite not only my judgment is, but also that very treatise from which some would slander <note>original: asperse</note> me with **Nestorianism**. This may appear not only from my asserting and contending everywhere in that treatise for the **divinity of Christ**, so that he might be a proper object of the divine worship we give him, but also from several particular passages. As in Book 1, Chapter 5, Section 1: *That Christ is not a mere man <note>original Greek: ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος (psilos anthropos)</note>, or a mere creature, but a divine person <note>original: hypostasis</note>, truly, really, and physically (not allegorically or morally) joined with that divine person who is called the Word <note>original: Logos</note>. If men would not bring their own stubborn preconceptions but listen to the easy and natural air of the text, the beginning of Saint John’s Gospel would put this beyond all controversy.*

And again, in Section 4: *Therefore Christ ought not to be a mere man, but God; that is, he ought to be really and physically united to the Deity, with the Deity being present not by assistance only, but by internal union <note>original: information; in this context, it refers to the soul "informing" or giving life and form to the body</note>. Just as the body and soul are one man, so God and man may be one Christ.*

And Section 5: *Therefore, the denying of either the divinity of Christ or the Trinity seems to be a subversion of the Christian religion.* And not only so, but I also condemn that fanatical display of pride in some enthusiasts who would make their own union with God the same as Christ’s union.

And lastly, Section 6: *For is not that Spirit that created and framed all things able to reform us to the most blameless level of humility, self-denial, dependency upon God, love of our neighbor, obedience to magistrates, faith, temperance, and holiness, without being any more personally <note>original: hypostatically</note> united with us than with the earth, sea, sun, moon, stars, and the natural parts of the creation? Therefore we conclude that to assert that the union of any true Christian with God is the same as Christ's union is a bold, useless, and groundless opinion, inconsistent with and destructive to the Christian religion.*

9. Can anything be more diametrically opposite to **Nestorianism** than these passages? Or can there be any proofs more significant to clear anyone from such a charge? It is therefore unnecessary to produce any more places for my justification. # Chapter 6: His Answer regarding Nestorianism.

...any other. But I will close all with what I have set down in Book 10, Chapter 6, Section 1, where I declare that that one plain expression of **Athanasius**—[*As Body and Soul is one Man, so God and Man is one Christ*]—is better than all the intricate definitions of things in the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the Scholastic theologians of the Middle Ages whose complex logical definitions dominated university learning.</note>, which reach no greater <term>hypostatic union</term> <note>original: Hypostatical Union; the theological doctrine that in Christ, a human nature and a divine nature are perfectly united in one single person.</note> than that of the body and soul. I added immediately after that: *Since I dare say, if it were searched to the bottom, the union between the Divinity and Humanity of Christ is more unified and more precise than that of soul and body, which they call hypostatic.* Is this to cut asunder and divide our one Lord Jesus Christ? <note>original Greek: κατατέμνειν & διαιρεῖν τὸν ἕνα Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν</note> Is this to divide our one Lord **Jesus Christ** into two <term>hypostases</term> <note>original: Hypostases; the plural of hypostasis, meaning an individual person or substance.</note>, and not rather to allow him, if it were necessary, a more close <term>hypostatic</term> union than there is between body and soul?

10. Thus fully have I cleared myself from all general accusations of <term>Nestorianism</term> <note>The heresy that Christ existed as two separate persons—one human and one divine—rather than one person with two natures.</note>. I thought it appropriate to do this more industriously because of the repetition of these rumors, and because of the recent and startling way it has reached my ears. I will now set down and answer the specific objection.

->**Objection 6**<-

> *He introduces a human person of Christ in Book 6, Chapter 15, Section 1, page 258, and afterwards, without any softening of the term, calls it so ten times in that chapter, and several times afterwards.*

I will also add what was hinted to me at second-hand from *Book 9, Chapter 2, Section 6*, where I declare: *How the Humanity of Christ and the Eternal Word may be hypostatically united without any contradiction to human reason, when it is unspoiled by the trivialities of the Schools, and how both their individual realities may still remain entire.* And afterward, in the same section, I describe *Christ as made up (if one may so speak) of the second person of the Trinity and of that human person that lived in Jerusalem.* For speaking of two *Persons* in this way in *Christ*—even though I expressly declare them <term>hypostatically</term> united again and again in this chapter—seemed to cause some worry about unorthodoxy in some people. But it is strange that either these passages in this chapter, or those mentioned in the objection, should ever lead anyone to imagine me in the least bit guilty of **Nestorianism**, if they had ever noted those other passages of my book that are so perfectly and expressly contrary to it.

11. But I will show how utterly blameless these passages also are, after I have briefly settled the true notion of <term>person</term> <note>original: Persona</note> and <term>hypostasis</term>; which I cannot do without first taking into consideration what is the true and allowable notion of a <term>suppositum</term> <note>A technical term in logic and theology for an individual substance that exists by itself.</note>. For I must confess I believe the Scholastic theologians are mistaken in their usual definition of it, when they define it as: *A singular substance existing by itself completely and incommunicably.* <note>original Latin: Substantia singularis per se existens completè & incommunicabiliter</note> For even if it were true that there are innumerable examples of such individual subjects that exist completely by themselves, yet it will be hard to prove that there are any that do so *incommunicably*. That is to say, it is hard to prove that their nature is such that God cannot create some substantial form or other which he may adapt to this present individual subject, so that this and the additional actualizing principle <note>original Greek: Ἐντελέχεια (Entelecheia)</note> may make a being that is one in itself <note>original Latin: Ens unum per se</note>, and so be merged into one individual substance <note>original: Suppositum</note>. To deny this would be a reproach to the **Divine Omnipotence**.

<header>His Answer regarding Nestorianism. Chapter 6.</header>

12. Therefore, it would be much safer to define a <term>suppositum</term> <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a *suppositum* is a complete, individual substance that exists on its own and is the subject of its own actions.</note> as a singular or individual substance that exists completely by itself, but not "incommunicably." By this, I mean it does not yet actually act as a <term>potential principle</term> <note>A "potential principle" refers to a component that has the capacity to combine with something else to form a single, unified being.</note> to create a <term>single entity in itself</term> <note>original Latin: *Ens unum per se*</note>, as the <term>metaphysicians</term> <note>Philosophers who study the fundamental nature of reality and being.</note> say. This is the only reliable definition of a *suppositum* I can find. I only need to add that <term>hypostasis</term> in its concrete sense is the same as *suppositum*; in the abstract sense, it means "subsistence" <note>original Latin: *Subsistentia*</note>. Furthermore, even in the language of the <term>Schools</term> <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional university theologians and their formal logical systems.</note>, the word <term>to subsist</term> <note>original Latin: *subsistere*</note> is sometimes used for an individual substance even if it exists dependently on another *suppositum*, as is the case with the human nature of Christ. Noting this in passing will prove useful later. Finally, as for a **person** <note>original Latin: *Persona*</note>, it is nothing more than a <term>rational individual substance</term> <note>original Latin: *Suppositum rationale*</note> and adds no new confusion regarding whether it can be shared or not.

13. With these things established, I will briefly answer the objection. First, I do not introduce a "human person" of Christ frankly and without qualification. When I first used the term, I asked for permission modestly and cautiously, saying: *"Now that the human person of Christ (as I may call it) is not to be set aside, etc."* I inserted those words because I was convinced in my own judgment that if something that could otherwise be its own individual substance <note>original: *Suppositum*</note> combines as a "potential principle" with some other person <note>original: *Hypostasis*</note> to form one single person, it then loses the proper nature and definition of an individual person. At that point, it is not *actually* a person on its own, but only *potentially* one. It is only in that sense that it can be called a person <note>original: *Hypostasis*</note>, and the same logic applies to the term "human person."

Secondly, it was necessary for me to use this less precise term because of the people I am arguing against—namely, the **Familists** <note>The "Family of Love," a radical mystical sect that believed members could achieve a divine state and become "one" with Christ in a literal, non-symbolic way.</note>. If I had only said "the human nature of Christ," they would have quickly dissolved that expression into a mystical meaning. They would have claimed that the particular human nature of everyone in their sect was the "human nature of Christ" with which the *Eternal Word* is united. They boast of being **"Godded with God"** and **"Christed with Christ."** Therefore, I could not argue against them directly and leave them no room for escape without using this specific expression.

Thirdly, it does not bring in **Nestorianism** at all. Even though I name the "human person" of Christ alone, I am no more <term>cutting asunder and dividing him into two persons</term> <note>original Greek: κατατέμνειν κὴ διαιρεῖν εἰς δύο ὑποστάσεις</note> than someone who names the "human nature" of Christ alone is <term>cutting asunder and dividing him into two natures</term> <note>original Greek: κατατέμνειν κὴ διαιρεῖν εἰς δύο φύσεις</note>. If those were cut apart, it would certainly destroy the <term>hypostatic union</term> <note>The doctrine that Christ is one person with two distinct natures, human and divine.</note> as well.

14. Fourthly, regarding the objections from Book 9 based on the phrase, *"both their persons remaining still entire,"* and the phrase in the same section, *"of Christ consisting of the second Person of the Trinity and that visible person who lived in Jerusalem"*: it is clear that I am saying the two <term>hypostases</term> <note>individual persons or substances</note> are hypostatically united. This is the exact opposite of **Nestorianism**, which divided them and denied the hypostatic union, as you saw above. And although I say that the persons remain entire, the fact that I so explicitly state they are "hypostatically united"...

# Chapter 6: His Answer regarding Nestorianism

14. This union shows plainly that the two natures do not remain entirely separate, but are united *without confusion*; this is a concept that the Orthodox Faith is as careful to maintain as any other. Furthermore, I declare, according to my own understanding of these things, that although I name two *<term>hypostases</term>* <note>In this context, a "hypostasis" refers to a distinct, individual existence or "personhood."</note> in Christ, I understand the human *hypostasis* to be called that only in an improper sense, based on the definition I previously gave for a *<term>suppositum</term>* <note>A philosophical term for an individual substance that exists on its own.</note>.

15. And lastly, I add to all this that I have not departed from the very language and meaning of the Church Councils and the *Athanasian Creed* by venturing to say that the *human person* of *Jesus* concurs with the *Divine hypostasis* to form *one Christ*. For it is well known and noted that the Greek Church calls the *three <term>hypostases</term>* by the names *properties* <note>original Greek: *ἰδιότητας* (idiotetas)</note>—and I believe at this very day *characteristics* <note>original Greek: *ἰδιώματα* (idiomata)</note>—as well as *persons* <note>original Greek: *πρόσωπα* (prosopa)</note> and *hypostases*. Budé, in his *Commentaries*, says: "Hypostasis, in the Divine Trinity, is the same thing as *property* and *person*." <note>original Latin/Greek: *Ὑπόστασις, in Trinitate Divina, idem est quod ἰδιότης & quod πρόσωπον.*</note> Gregory Nazianzen, in his sermon *On the Epiphany*, writes: "When I speak of God, you are illuminated by one light and by three. Three according to the *properties*—or *hypostases* if anyone prefers to call them that, or *persons*—but one according to the logic of the *essence*, or divinity." <note>original Greek: *Θεοῦ δ' ὅταν εἴπω, ἑνὶ φωτὶ περιαστράφθητε καὶ τρισί...*</note> Again, Photius quotes from the fifth oration of Eulogius: "The Divine is essentially one, admitting no plurality. Therefore, even if we name *hypostases*, or *persons*, or *properties*, wanting to interpret as far as possible what the mind has grasped, we do not divide the 'One,' nor partition the Unity, nor tear apart the Oneness." <note>original Greek: *Ἐν κυρίως ἓν τὸ θεῖον...*</note> And a little later it is again clear from the same author that the Greek theologians acknowledged "the one nature of God existing in three properties." <note>original Greek: *τὴν μίαν Θεοῦ φύσιν ἐν τρισὶν ὑπάρχειν ἰδιότησιν.*</note> But it is already sufficiently clear that "property" and "hypostasis" are used interchangeably to mean the same thing.

Now, this being admitted, it is manifest that the Council of *Chalcedon* allows for a coming together of the two hypostases, *human* and *divine*, to form that *one person* who is called Christ. This matches what you heard above from the Council of *Ephesus*: "One Christ, one Son, one person, one hypostasis." <note>original Greek: *Εἷς Χριστός, εἷς υἱός, ἓν πρόσωπον, μία ὑπόστασις.*</note> But the actual words of the Council of *Chalcedon* are these: 

> We confess one and the same Jesus Christ—Son, Lord, Only-begotten—acknowledged to be in two natures without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation. The difference of the two natures is not removed by the union, but rather the *property* <note>original Greek: *idiotes*</note> (meaning the hypostasis or proper existence) of each nature is preserved and concurs into one person and one hypostasis, not as if divided or partitioned into two persons. <note>original Greek: *Ἕνα καὶ τὸν αὐτὸν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν υἱόν, μονογενῆ...*</note>

My expressions are very consistent with this in my ninth book, chapter 2. My words imply a *hypostatic union* without confusion—a growing together into one hypostasis, not the destruction of anything that comes together to form this one person, Christ. To the extent that his human nature is *potentially* and *improperly* still an hypostasis, it may be called such according to the <term>Schools</term> <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional university theologians and their formal logical systems.</note>, as I noted above; but it is never to be properly and actually such on its own.

16. Then, in defining what is meant by *perfect man*, it adds: *subsisting of a rational soul and human flesh, not merely consisting of them* <note>original Greek: ἐκ ψυχῆς λογικῆς καὶ ἀνθρωπίνης σαρκὸς ὑφιστάμενος, not συνιστάμενος (*ek psychēs logikēs kai anthrōpinēs sarkos hyphistamenos*, not *synistamenos*)</note>. And can there be "the thing subsisting" <note>original Greek: τὸ ὑφιστάμενον (*to hyphistamenon*)</note> without a *hypostasis*? Can there be the *concrete* reality without the *abstract* quality? Can there be blackness without something black, or hardness without something hard? Or, if *hypostasis* signifies something concrete, then it and "the thing subsisting" are one and the same. But I must confess that according to the language of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to medieval and early modern scholastic philosophers and theologians.</note>, as well as my own judgment,
<margin>to subsist <note>original Greek: ὑφίστασθαι (*hyphistasthai*)</note></margin>
is used here in a less precise sense. However, since it is used, and I understand *hypostasis* in no other sense than the Creed does when I apply it to the human nature of *Christ*, I think I am entirely blameless for doing so. And thus the whole accusation of *Nestorianism* <note>A heresy suggesting that Christ was two separate persons—one divine and one human—rather than one person with two natures.</note> has vanished into a mere *dispute over words* <note>original Greek: λογομαχία (*logomachia*)</note> or something even less significant.

# Chapter VII. His Answer regarding God's conveying, etc.

...asserted <note>The OCR "serted" completes the word "asserted" from the previous page.</note> nothing regarding a false persuasion in religion being the command of God beyond the meaning of this aphorism. 18. A summary recital of all the restrictions of the assertion, by which its harmlessness is fully demonstrated. 19. The seventh objection proposed, and clearly and satisfactorily answered.

1. We should proceed now to the seventh objection raised from the tenth chapter of the tenth book, concerning God's conveying a false persuasion into a person even in matters of religion. This is a point worth searching into carefully and stating correctly. Therefore, I must confess I had already done this according to my best judgment (being moved by various reports and some personal discussions against several passages of that chapter) before I received this paper of objections. To do it more satisfactorily, I drafted an accurate account of all those passages that I noticed seemed paradoxical <note>original: "Paradoxical"; seemingly absurd or self-contradictory</note> to others. Once I have presented this to better clarify and free sections 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 from any present misunderstanding or future mistakes, I will then propose this seventh objection *in its exact terms* <note>original Latin: *in terminis*</note> and apply a full and particular answer to it. The account concerning things that may give offense in those sections follows here, arranged into certain aphorisms contained in the said sections.

### Aphorism I.

> *That nothing but the conviction of conscience in a soul that is sincere can properly be the official announcement <term>promulgation</term> <note>original: "Promulgation"; the formal act of announcing or making a law known</note> of any law, will, or command of God to that soul.*

2. The reason for this principle is that someone who is sincere is willing and ready to know and do anything that is the mind of God for them to do. They use their best efforts to know and do it, and the sense of their conscience (which is, as it were, the *ear of the soul*) is inclined and attentive to receive the voice or command of God from whatever direction it sounds, or whatever he shall command: *Speak, Lord, your servant hears you.* <note>A reference to 1 Samuel 3:9</note>

In contrast, one who is not sincere—who is false to the light they currently have and knowingly and intentionally sins against their own conscience—may justly be compared to someone who stops their ears and will not hear the law of their Prince. Since it was nevertheless in their power to hear it, this law is justly deemed to have been announced to them. When the occasion requires, they are to be prosecuted just as if they had actually heard the Prince’s proclamation, and they incur the same penalties as those offenders who did hear it. Therefore, it is unique to the sincere and unfeignedly conscientious that no law or command of God is considered announced to them unless their consciences are convinced. Just as one cannot naturally conceive that any speech or voice reached a man's ear if, though listening and waiting, he could not hear the slightest whisper of it. This principle seems so clear to me that no one should doubt it. The second is this:

### Aphorism II.

*That where there is no law made public <note>original: "promulgated"</note>, it is no sin or transgression to act or profess the opposite.*

These are the words of the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in Romans 4:15</note>, *That where there is no law, there is no transgression.* This is not only true of the Law of Moses, of which he speaks, but it is universally true. This is because *sin* can be nothing else but the *transgression of a law*, and nothing can be a law without being officially announced <note>original: "Promulgation"</note>.

### Aphorism III.

*That a full and firm conviction of conscience in a soul that is sincere is the public announcement <note>original: "Promulgation"</note> of a law or command from God to that soul.*

The reason is that the sense of conscience is the very "ear" of the soul. It cannot receive a command from God in any other way than by being fully and firmly convinced that this or that is His command. This conviction is, so to speak, the King’s Great Seal <note>The official seal used to authorize state documents</note> by which the soul is authorized to act.

### Aphorism IV.

*That nothing which has any real depravity <note>original: "turpitude"</note> or immorality in it can justly be claimed to be the voice or command of God. Likewise, what is truly and admittedly moral cannot be claimed to be anything other than His command, whether to the sincere or the insincere.*

For the light and law of nature—and of eternal and immutable morality—cries out so loudly in the soul of the sincere person that they would never admit such foul impulses, much less see them as coming from God. Nor would they be ignorant of what is so plainly moral, as this aphorism implies. As for the insincere person, since he stops his ears against that more holy and evident law, his false delusions and stubbornness <note>original: "obduracity"</note> in wickedness are most justly blamed on himself.

3. Thus far we have been bold enough to proceed with these established principles <note>original: "dogmatically"</note>. We come now to a point which we will discuss as a question before we venture to conclude. It is this: *Whether a full and firm conviction of conscience in a sincere person—regarding a religion into which some false things are incorporated (but without any moral depravity, and of such a nature that no moral sincerity could discover their falsehood)—can be rightly said to be the command of God to that soul, whether for trial or punishment.* 

I hope the state of this question will appear to any impartial judge to be set at a very safe level. There is nothing in it that implies any sinful action in the person who is thus persuaded or convinced. Therefore, there is not the least suggestion or implication that God is the author of sin. For where there is no law, there is no transgression, as was concluded above. Nor do I know how God can be rightly said to be the author of sin in any case; not only because it is contrary to Divine Goodness and Righteousness <note>original: "Rectitude"</note>, but also to the very nature of sin itself for it to be irresistibly forced upon someone, since all actual sin is voluntary.

4. Indeed, God has laid inevitable paths of mischief and calamity within the structure of His Providence,

->For to the wicked,<-
->The divinity sends countless pains on sea and land,<-
<note>original Greek: Τοῖς γὰρ ἀλιτροῖς / Εἰν ἁλὶ καὶ γαίᾳ μυρία πήματα δαίμων</note>

which fearless and reckless men will certainly incur, and so fall into a very

<header>Chapter VII. Persuasion into the mind of his Creature.</header>

...forlorn condition of the soul, and through the habit of sinning lose all sense of conscience and the difference between good and evil. Such people are given up to a "reprobate sense," committing all wickedness with an uncurbed greediness because they have no inner principle to restrain them. But they bring this deplorable condition upon themselves by entangling themselves in the unavoidable sequences of Divine *Nemesis* <note>original: "Nemesis"; here meaning divine retribution or the natural consequences of moral law</note>, which is interwoven into the very nature and essence of the soul herself and the things she has to do with. God, I say, is the author of the necessary and inevitable consequences and chains of events, but we ourselves are the cause of our being ensnared <note>original: "illaqueated"</note> by them.

5. Regarding those who have become "Ethiopians" in wickedness <note>A reference to the proverb "Can the Ethiopian change his skin?" (Jeremiah 13:23), used here to describe those whose sinful nature has become fixed and unchangeable</note>, God is not the author of the darkness of their sins. Furthermore, their state is not properly defined as a state of sinfulness so much as a state of mere brutishness; "For vice is innate in beasts" <note>original: "Κακία γὰρ σύμφυτος τοῖς θηρίοις", as Trismegistus speaks</note>. And just as virtue is a perfection below God, as Aristotle says, so is this state a condition below the nature of man. Aristotle therefore calls it *brutality* or *beast-likeness* <note>original: "θηριωδία" or "θηριότης"</note>; conversely, those men who are more than morally good, he (along with the Lacedemonians) styles "divine men" <note>original: "σεῖος ἄνδρας" (a Spartan dialect form of "theios andras")</note>. 

So, if God were in any sense the cause of such a condition, according to Aristotle’s opinion, He would be the author of a disastrous transformation <note>original: "calamitous Metamorphosis"</note> rather than of anything that can properly be called vice or sin. Though it is a state far worse than sin, it is removed from our present consideration, where we assume nothing to be either immoral or brutish. Therefore, when I have examined this question to the bottom, I hope I shall arrive at a solution that will prove beyond objection.

6. The question, I believe, will necessarily lead us to these three particular inquiries:
*   First, whether it is compatible with the nature of God to convey a false persuasion into the mind of His creature.
*   Second, whether it is compatible with Him to convey such a false persuasion that might oblige the person to act or profess according to this persuasion religiously and conscientiously. (This will come very close to the seventh objection to be proposed.)
*   Third and last, whether this false conviction or persuasion may rightly be called the "command of God" to the person thus persuaded.

The most obvious and yet the weightiest arguments against the first point—and consequently against all the points in this question as I have stated it—are these two:
1.  That it is repugnant to God’s *veracity* <note>Truthfulness</note>.
2.  That it would destroy our belief in God in all things if we once admit that He would convey a false persuasion to us in anything.

But so that we may be better able to answer these difficulties with the fullest satisfaction, we shall first endeavor to find out what the Holy Scripture likely determines regarding this point, according to the mind of the more learned commentators.

Romans 11:32: "For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all. Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!" <note>original: "Συνέκλεισε γὰρ Θεὸς τοὺς πάντας εἰς ἀπείθειαν, ἵνα τοὺς πάντας ἐλεήσῃ. Ὢ βάθος πλούτου καὶ σοφίας καὶ γνώσεως Θεοῦ."</note> Upon this text, Vatablus <note>François Vatable, a 16th-century French humanist and scholar</note> says: "He allowed them to be under the dominion and power of unbelief; he makes us resist grace for a time, so that, finally covered in shame, we may thirst for his mercy" <note>original: "Sub imperio & potestate incredulitatis sivit esse, facit ut ad tempus repugnemus gratiæ, ut rubore tandem perfusi sitiamus ejus misericordiam."</note>. The Apostle here treats the Jews' lack of belief <note>original: "incredulity"</note> regarding Jesus being the Messiah.

# His Answer regarding God's conveying a false persuasion, Chapter VII.

Again, *John 12:39: Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said, "He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts, so that they should not see with their eyes nor understand with their hearts, and be converted, and I should heal them."* Calvin says: "It was impossible for them to escape this punishment, since God had once decreed to cast them into a reprobate sense <note>original: "reprobum sensum"; a mind rejected by God and unable to judge rightly</note>, and to turn the light of his word into darkness for them." <note>original: "Hanc poenam ipsis impossibile fuit effugere, cum semel Deo statutum esset ipsos in reprobum sensum conjicere, & verbi sui lucem illis vertere in tenebras."</note> But Clarius speaks more moderately: "This means they could not believe because of a blinded mind and an obstinate soul, and that God permitted this through their own vice and fault." <note>original: "Significat non potuisse illos credere ob excaecatam mentem & obstinatum animum, idque Deum suo ipsorum vitio & culpâ permisisse."</note>

It is not entirely irrelevant to add the example of God assisting *Elisha* in defeating the army of the King of *Assyria*, when they tried to besiege him in *Dothan* (2 Kings 6:18): *And when they came down to him, Elisha prayed to the Lord and said, "Smite this people, I pray you, with blindness." And he struck them with blindness according to the word of Elisha. And Elisha said to them, "This is not the way, neither is this the city: follow me, and I will bring you to the man whom you seek." But he led them to Samaria.* On this passage, Grotius notes: "Deception against an enemy was considered lawful at that time." <note>original: "Dolus in hostem licitus habebatur illo tempore."</note>

7. But there is a more excellent <note>original: "eximious"</note> instance in 1 Kings 22 regarding *Ahab's* going up to *Ramoth-Gilead* (verse 19): *And Micaiah said, "Hear therefore the word of the Lord. I saw the Lord sitting on his Throne, and all the host of Heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left. And the Lord said, 'Who shall persuade Ahab that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-Gilead?' And one said in this manner, and another said in that. And there came forth a Spirit and stood before the Lord, and said, 'I will persuade him.' And the Lord said to him, 'How?' And he said, 'I will go forth, and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' And he said, 'You shall persuade him, and prevail also: go forth and do so.'"* This is a very notable example of what is declared more generally by the Prophet *Ezekiel* (Chapter 14:9): *And if the prophet be deceived when he has spoken a thing, I the Lord have deceived that prophet.* Castellio translates this as: "I, the Lord, have deceived that prophet" <note>original: "Illum ego vatem Jova decepi"</note>, adding this gloss: "I have breathed upon him with a false spirit. God gives a bad prophet to a bad counselor." <note>original: "Falso spiritu afflavi. Malo consultori malum vatem dat Deus."</note>

8. But *Cornelius à Lapide* <note>a prominent Flemish Jesuit exegete (1567–1637)</note> speaks more extensively and precisely on this passage, where he proposes this question: "Why is the permission of deception in God called an 'Action'—namely, 'Deception'?" <note>original: "Cur permissio deceptionis in Deo vocatur Actio, putà Deceptio?"</note> To which he answers: 

"Because this permission in God is certain and effective, and it surely produces the effect. For God, because he penetrates and thoroughly sees both the weakness and inclination of the human will, and the cunning, power, and wickedness of the devil's will, foreknows that such a man, here and now, in such circumstances, will certainly and infallibly be deceived by the Demon if he himself permits the Demon to do it and loosens the reins to let him be tempted and deceived. Having this foreknowledge, God says and decrees, 'I permit the Demon to tempt and deceive such a person'; from which it certainly follows that the person is tempted and deceived. Just as a hunter who releases a hunting dog in front of a hare is said to set the dog upon the hare (because the dog naturally and certainly attacks the hare if it is released), so also God, by permitting the Demon a certain deception—which the Demon could not do without God's permission—is considered to deceive through him. For what one does through another, he is seen to do by himself. Therefore, God permits evil in one way, and man in another: man permits it negatively, but God permits it positively." <note>original: "Quia haec permissio in Deo est certa & efficax... Aliter ergò permittit mala Deus, aliter homo; homo negativé, Deus positivé."</note>
