# Chapter VII. Persuasion into the mind of his Creature.

To all of this he further adds that this deception is also rightly called an action of God, because it is a punishment from him; and so he concludes: "When, therefore, a person is certainly deceived by this permission and punishment from God, he is said to be deceived by God. In this way, God mocks the mockers" <note>original: "Cùm ergò ex hac Dei permissione & punitione certò decipitur homo, à Deo decipi dicitur. Sic Deus deludit illusores"</note> (Proverbs 3:34). And upon Psalm 18:26 (Psalm 17 in the Vulgate), "With the devious you will show yourself devious," <note>original: "Cum perverso pervertêris"</note> he explains it this way: "You will act not candidly or kindly, but (so to speak) crookedly, maliciously, and perversely—that is, you will act craftily, severely, and with hostility. Thus he proceeded against the stubborn Pharaoh, enticing and drowning him deceitfully in the Red Sea." <note>original: "Non candidè, non benignè, sed (ut ità dicam) pravè, malignè & perversè, id est, vafrè, severè & hostiliter ages. Sic incessit contra contumacem Pharaonem, alliciendo & mergendo eum dolosè in mari rubro."</note> This commentary is more than sufficient regarding these passages from Micaiah and Ezekiel.

9. And these last words of Cornelius regarding Pharaoh's overthrow are very suitable to that of Joshua 11:20: *For it was of the Lord to harden their hearts, that they should come against Israel in battle, that he might destroy them utterly, and that they might have no favor, but that he might destroy them, as the Lord commanded Moses.* This is consistent with the proverbial aphorism <margin>See chapter 5, verses 2, 3.</margin> "Those whom Jupiter wishes to destroy in his anger, he first drives mad." <note>original: "Quos iratus perdere vult Jupiter, eosdem priùs dementat." This is a classical proverb suggesting that divine punishment often begins with the loss of one's reason.</note> This seems to have been Pharaoh's case all along. For he was so intoxicated with a false persuasion that his gods and his magicians would be able to hold out against the God of the Hebrews and his servants Moses and Aaron, that because of this presumption—in which he was hardened, just as the Canaanites were to fight against Israel—he would not let Israel go; God having given him up to this delusion. And this, with submission to better judgments, I conceive to be that hardening of Pharaoh's heart so often mentioned in the Story.

It is worth noting that while this hardening is mentioned sixteen times, Pharaoh is said to harden *his own heart* only three times (and in the Septuagint <note>The Septuagint is the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> only twice). It is also remarkable that while Exodus 9:34 says that *Pharaoh hardened his heart*, immediately in the very first verse of the following chapter God says of that very time and hardening, *For I have hardened his heart.* So, one does not exclude the other, as there was a natural tendency and willingness in Pharaoh’s own heart to be thus sealed and hardened.

Three times it is said that Pharaoh hardened his own heart, four times that Pharaoh's heart was hardened, but no less than nine times that the *Lord* hardened his heart. The Lord himself declares plainly and openly that he would do this so that he might show his power and multiply his signs and wonders, so that their fame might fill the world and be recorded for all future generations, as you may see in Chapter 10:1–2, Chapter 9:16, and Chapter 7:3–4.

10. Here Cornelius again explains it much in the same sense as he does that passage from Ezekiel: "God is said to have hardened Pharaoh permissively. Note here: God permits sins in a different and far more powerful way than a man (for example, a Prince) permits them. For God holds the wills of all men in his hand, so that he can bend them in whatever direction he chooses; but the will of man cannot go out into any work, whether good or bad, without God's nod, unless God loosens the reins of his permission for it—indeed, he even positively concurs and cooperates with the person to produce this act and work. Just as he who holds a lion tied by a rope, if he loosens and releases it, and the freed lion kills someone, the one holding the lion is said to have killed that man—not by himself, but through the lion he released; so also God, allowing the will..." <note>original: "Deus dicitur indurâsse Pharaonem permissive. Ubi nota, Aliter & longè potentiùs permittit peccata Deus quàm homo, v.g. Princeps, eadem permittit. Deus enim omnium hominum voluntates in sua habet manu, ut eas quaquaverfum flectere possit; voluntas verò hominis sine Dei nutu in nullum omnino opus sive bonum sive malum exire potest, nisi Deus illi permissionis suae laxet habenas, imò cum illa positivè concurrat, & coöperetur ad actum & opus hoc producendum. Sicut ergò is qui leonem fune constrictum tenet, si eum laxet & dimittat, leóque solutus aliquem occîdat, dicitur tenens leonem hominem illum occidisse, non per se, sed per leonem quem dimisit; ità & Deus finens vo-"</note>

# Chapter VII. His Answer regarding God's conveying a false persuasion into the mind of His creature.

10. "...because he wills to sin and to harden himself in sins, God Himself is said to harden him, especially because by His <term>concurrence</term><note>Theological term for God's cooperation or underlying support for all actions in the universe.</note> He joins in this act of hardening." <note>original: "voluntatem peccare & in peccatis se obdurare, dicitur ipse eandem obdurare, præsertim quia suo concursu ad hunc actum obdurationis concurrat."</note> He also adds another consideration according to which God may be said to harden Pharaoh's heart, namely, "by withdrawing from him His grace which would soften his heart; just as the Sun hardens clay, not by positively producing hardness, but by drawing out the moisture that was tempering and softening the clay." <note>original: "subtrahendo illi gratiam suam quæ cor ejus molliret; sicut Sol indurat lutum, non positivè efficiendo duritiem, sed exfugendo humorem qui temperabat & molliebat lutum."</note> Or, as one who lets a young kitten fall out of his hand from off a bridge into the river is not so properly said, in a positive sense, to drown the kitten as one who flings it from there into the water: for the one exerts a force on the kitten, while the other only ceases to hold it.

11. The result of all these citations and considerations, in brief, is this: That whenever God is said expressly to harden the heart of Pharaoh, to blind the *Jews*, or deceive the Prophets, it is to be understood as the *permission* of these things—but a permission so powerful and effectual that it may justly be said to imply a certain and unfailing outcome. This means God does not properly act positively Himself, but permits His creatures to act in such a way that the effect attributed to God will necessarily and unavoidably follow. This being acknowledged in immoral and sinful actions as well as in simple ignorance and mistake, it is more than enough for my present purpose. That purpose was only to conclude, in a more general way, that God may, and sometimes does, convey a false persuasion into the mind of a person certainly and effectually, though permissively. This was the first inquiry contained in the main question.

12. Now, as for the objections against this conclusion—namely, that it is supposedly inconsistent with God's truthfulness and destructive to our trust and belief in Him—I hope we shall not find it hard to <term>assoil</term><note>original: "assoil" — meaning to resolve, clear, or discharge an objection.</note> them. Regarding the first objection, I answer that just as God sometimes exercises His severity and sometimes His mercy (which are two opposite modes of divine justice), it causes no inconsistency at all with either attribute, because they are applied to different occasions and subjects. Similarly, for God to make use sometimes of His veracity and sometimes of that "policy" which His practical wisdom (by which He acts in managing the affairs of the world) thinks convenient, and which does not clash with either His justice or goodness, is not at all harsh or inconsistent, provided it is applied to distinct occasions and objects. For indeed, when the occasion and object change, the exercise of this or that specific virtue must also change, or else it will hardly prove to be a virtue at all. 

For example, if *severity* were used against someone who was a fit object of *mercy*, if any judge acted in this way, the action would lose the title of "severity" and take on the appearance of "cruelty." Likewise, if *veracity* (truthfulness) were used in a case that required proper policy conformable to justice and goodness, it would lose the name of "veracity" and deserve the title of "impolicy" or "unwisely handled." 

As an illustration: if a person was thoroughly assured that someone, along with his companions, came to his house with a murderous intention to kill an innocent person—perhaps his rightful Prince who had escaped from the murderers—and that he could not secure the Prince from those barbarous pursuers in any way except by some device to make them believe he had left the house; if instead of this necessary artifice he should, in plain terms, tell the murderers the Prince was there, would this be the virtue of veracity, or not rather...

<summary>This page argues that God "hardens" hearts not by active evil, but by withdrawing grace or permitting natural consequences, similar to how the sun hardens clay by removing moisture. The author also suggests that God's absolute truthfulness must be balanced by His wisdom and justice in specific contexts, much like how a person might rightly deceive a murderer to save an innocent life.</summary>

# Chapter VII. Persuasion into the mind of His Creature.

...rather, at best, an instance of most dangerous and mischievous folly? For it seems a strange virtue that is devoid of all goodness, and that must necessarily be the handmaid of the grossest injustice, of murder, and even of the most wretched <term>parricide</term><note>The killing of a parent or close relative; here used to signify a heinous betrayal of one's primary allegiances.</note>. Therefore, in cases such as this, it does not conflict with the virtue of veracity to avoid speaking the truth, since veracity has no proper purpose here, and thus would result in no proper moral action. Nor can he remain silent (let us suppose) without endangering his own life and betraying the life of his prince.

Therefore, if he speaks what is not true, he is "speaking a falsehood" rather than "lying" <note>original: *Mendacium dicere* than *mentiri*</note>. This is the best distinction I know to protect the reputations of several Church Fathers and <term>expositors</term><note>Scholars who interpret and explain scripture.</note> who—referencing the example of the *Hebrew* midwives, whom God rewarded for the clever story they told the infant-murdering *Pharaoh*—have concluded that it is lawful to lie in some cases, as *Cornelius* mentions in this passage. These scholars included *Rupert*, *Cassian*, *Bede*, *Clement*, and *Origen*. He also adds *Chrysostom* and *Jerome*. It is safest to understand their views in this sense: for we must not commit any moral evil so that good may result, and "lying," properly defined, implies some immorality and impurity.

However, simply speaking what is false contains no inherent immorality. Otherwise, no one could engage in a debate or state a false <term>axiom</term><note>A starting proposition or premise in an argument.</note>. If a stated axiom—one that matches neither the mind of the speaker nor the reality it describes—is not morally evil, then that disconnect between the spoken falsehood, the mind, and the facts carries no moral guilt. What moral evil can there be, then, when it is spoken for a good end and in very appropriate circumstances? For what is inappropriate in some respects is very appropriate for certain subjects. Just as pain is very unpleasant to the senses, it is very appropriate that a stubborn <term>refractory</term><note>Stubbornly resistant to authority or control.</note> sinner should be afflicted by it.

Therefore, just as it is said of *Unity* (which is one of the Divine Attributes), "There is no good in unity, unless that unity exists in what is good" <note>original: *Nihil boni est in Unitate, nisi Unitas sit in bono*</note>; so I say of *Veracity*: "There is no good in truth-telling, unless that truth-telling serves a good end" <note>original: *Nihil boni est in Veracitate, nisi Veracitas sit in bonum*</note>. Goodness is the measure of all moral perfection in humans, just as it is certainly the most supreme attribute in God and the measure of everything we might call His "moral attributes" by way of analogy. Nothing can be rightly called an act of His severity, mercy, governance, truthfulness, or the like, unless it shares in His goodness and does not involve more evil than good. In whatever situations that might happen, the goodness of God would not fail to use a form of His justice or wisdom that is the opposite of whatever would cause such a bad outcome. These things, if properly considered, are more than enough to prove that God’s conveying a false persuasion into the mind of His creature by "certain and effective permission" <note>original: *permissione certâ & efficaci*</note> may not conflict at all with the Divine Veracity.

13. This is certainly true regarding God. However, concerning the human examples I have discussed here, I will not assert them any further (except for that major instance) than I already have in my book, *The Mystery of Godliness*, in this same chapter, section 6, with these words: *For if introducing a false persuasion in itself be not simply evil, how can it be evil when used...*

# Chapter VII. His Answer Concerning God’s Conveying a False Persuasion into the Mind of His Creature.

...for a good end, and by an unerring *Wisdom*, and from an infinite *Goodness*? If we were invested with such powers, no one could dispute that we might also take the liberty to do so as well. And yet *Clement of Alexandria* (*Stromata*, Book 7) says concerning the "good Christian" he describes: "Whatever he has in his mind, he also carries on his tongue toward those who are worthy to hear," etc. <note>original Greek: Πᾶν ἄρα ὃ, τι περ ἂν ἐν νῷ, τοῦτο καὶ ἐπὶ γλώττης φέρει πρὸς τοὺς ἐπαΐειν ἀξίους</note>. And shortly after: "For he both thinks and speaks the truth at the same time; except perhaps as part of a treatment, just as a doctor might lie or tell a falsehood to those who are sick for the sake of their recovery" <note>original Greek: Ἀληθῆ τε γὰρ φρονεῖ ἅμα καὶ ἀληθεύει· πλὴν εἰ μήποτε ἐν θεραπείας μέρει, καθάπερ ἰατρὸς πρὸς νοσοῦντας ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ τῶν καμνόντων ψεύσεται ἢ ψεῦδος ἐρεῖ</note>, "will lie or tell a falsehood" <note>original Latin: *mentietur aut mendacium dicet*</note>. It is as if he hinted at the very distinction I noted above. But this is more than was necessary.

14. As for the second objection—that this supposition might be destructive to our faith and trust in God, and that if this were once admitted, we could never know when He spoke the truth or was being earnest with us (that is, whether the religion we currently believe in is true)—the answer is not far to seek. I say, therefore, that although a false religion might be commanded by God, it is no hindrance to finding the true one. For though it may be His command, it does not come with the same circumstances as His <term>absolute and enunciative command</term><note>An "absolute command" refers to God's ultimate, unchanging truth, while "enunciative" refers to truths He declares clearly and directly.</note>.

Such certainties include the supreme holiness and inimitable miracles of the true Prophet, express voices from Heaven giving testimony to Him, His rising from the dead, and His visible ascending into those mansions of glory. Finally, there is the perfect agreement of the whole religion with the most exact Reason, having nothing in it repugnant to it, and being attested to by illustrious prophecies, many of which occurred at great distances from the events they predicted. No <term>permissive command</term><note>A situation where God "permits" or allows a false belief to persist as a trial or punishment, rather than declaring it as absolute truth.</note> of God can be accompanied by such advantages.

Therefore, by purifying our minds, perfecting holiness in the fear of God, and using free and unprejudiced Reason, a person shall (with God’s assistance) be fully able to distinguish the *Permissive* command of God from His *Absolute* or *Enunciative* command. They will know at last that the former was for trial or punishment, but that now they are truly under His most perfect and absolute command. So easy and natural, so close and friendly a union is there between *Truth* and the *Soul* when they once meet. Falsehood may indeed be somewhat familiarized to a person through use and custom, but when Truth meets with a purged and prepared soul, it is like the greeting of two old, intimate acquaintances; their embraces are very close, hearty, and sincere.

This supposition, therefore, is no prejudice at all to Christianity, but rather its mighty advantage. For if mankind were persuaded that, for all they know, their current religion might only be a permissive command imposed upon them for punishment or trial, it would engage them not to immerse themselves so much in the world. Instead, it would lead them to live holily, to meditate seriously on divine matters, to pray fervently, and to seek diligently what the true religion actually is. This would undoubtedly confirm the Christian more strongly in his religion—since Truth gains a greater empire over the minds of men the more it is tested—and it would be the quickest way to turn all people who seriously used this principle toward Christianity. Thus, I have fully cleared the first particular inquiry comprised in

# Chapter VII. Persuasion into the mind of His Creature.

...in the main question from the chief objections made against it.

15. The second [question] was whether it is compatible with the nature of God to convey a false persuasion in practical matters—those which religiously and conscientiously oblige the person so persuaded to act or to refrain from acting accordingly. The decision on this, I believe, is not difficult if we consider the case of King Ahab, who was deceived by God’s effective permission of that lying spirit who offered his service in that matter. <note>In 1 Kings 22, God allows a "lying spirit" to deceive Ahab's prophets to lead him into battle.</note> For his belief in that guaranteed success, which he thought was promised to him from God, was clearly of such a nature as to oblige his conscience to fight the Lord’s battles against the uncircumcised.

Furthermore, the example of God conveying the persuasion to Abraham that He wanted him to sacrifice his son is beyond all exception. For it is clear that Abraham was so persuaded, both by his actions in the history and by what is said of him in **Hebrews 11:17**:

> *By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac; he who had received the promises was ready to offer up his only son... reasoning that God was able to raise him up even from the dead, from which he also received him back in a figurative sense.*

If he had not been persuaded that he was indeed meant to sacrifice him, it would have been no trial of his faith. But God never intended for him to sacrifice his son; therefore, this persuasion He conveyed to him was false, yet it absolutely obliged his conscience to act, in order to provide proof of his wonderful faith in God.

To these I will only add the words of the Son of Sirach <note>original: *Siracides*; refers to the author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus/Sirach in the Apocrypha.</note> in **Chapter 4**, concerning the method that Divine Wisdom is said to use in her dealings with men, in **verse 17**:

> *For at first she will walk with him by crooked ways, and bring fear and dread upon him, and torment him with her discipline, until she may trust his soul and test him by her laws. Then she will return to him by the straight way and comfort him, and show him her secrets.*

By these "crooked ways," and this "fear and dread and tormenting discipline," I believe we may well understand the unnecessary <term>scrupulosities: excessive worry about sin or moral behavior</term> of conscience that arise from current ignorance, from which the person is not yet ready to be freed. These are unnecessary, I say, in themselves, but useful for the person's current condition to test his obedience and make him capable of the sight and enjoyment of those treasures of secrets which the Lord has laid up for those who seek Him in sincerity and truth. These secrets are the proper and <term>connatural: belonging to a person or thing from birth; innate</term> perfection and happiness of the soul, while other things are more foreign and accidental. As our Savior Christ says, "If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own?" <note>original Greek: Εἰ ἐν τῷ ἀλλοτρίῳ πιστοὶ οὐκ ἐγένεσθε, τὸ ὑμέτερον τίς ὑμῖν δώσει;</note> <note>Luke 16:12</note>. But I had already made it plain enough that it is not incompatible with the nature of God to convey such a false persuasion into the mind of man, which by its own nature necessarily obliges him to act conscientiously upon it.

16. And so we have finished the first two inquiries. The third is whether such an *effective*, though *permissive*, false persuasion from God—which obliges the conscience to act or to refrain from acting in a certain way—may rightly be called the command of God. I think it is evident that it should rightly be called so. For what can be called the command of a prince, if not a certain and effective communication from him—regarding something to be done, professed, or omitted—to the <term>cognoscence: knowledge or awareness</term> of his subject, under circumstances where it is morally impossible for the subject...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether God can be said to "command" a person to believe something false for the sake of trial or punishment, specifically through the concept of a "Permissive Command."</meta>

...to doubt it, should it not be called the Prince’s command?

16. But you will object that though it is a *certain* and *effective* transmission and communication of a thing that obliges the conscience to act, it is only *permissive*, and therefore not a true command. Here, I am very willing to reach a compromise with my opponent and define it simply as a *Permissive Command*. This is not as grammatically incorrect as it might seem at first glance, but it makes very good and justifiable sense, which will be easily shown by this obvious illustration. 

Suppose a mighty Prince should knowingly and intentionally, through silent consent, allow the Keeper of his Broad Seal <term>The Great Seal used by a monarch to authorize official documents.</term> to sign a commission or command to certain parties in a province of his Empire to act in a specific way—but not contrary to any of his laws already published in that province. Because of this, the people cannot have the slightest doubt concerning the legitimacy of the document. I ask: do these parties who receive this Broad Seal not receive a command from their Prince? And I ask further: is it anything more than a *Permissive Command*? I do not mean *permissive* in contradistinction to *mandatory* (for that would indeed make little sense), but rather an obliging instruction from their Prince that comes to them only through his silent consent and permission. 

This is what I understand to be a *Permissive Command*; it is one that will protect the parties from all blame or harm from the Prince’s displeasure, since they have his Broad Seal to authorize their actions. No one else has any authority to violently hinder their proceedings until they receive a certain and infallible instruction from the Prince himself—not just *permissive*, but *spoken* and *positive*—telling them to do so. However, there has never been, and I think there never will be, any such positive command given by God to persecute those who, in the hope of eternal life, sincerely and conscientiously worship and serve him, even if they have some errors they have found it morally impossible to recognize. This has been our *supposition* <note>original: "Supposition" — a premise or starting assumption for an argument.</note> throughout this entire chapter.

17. Therefore, having correctly stated and clarified the three details of the question proposed, we shall now be so bold as to conclude with this fifth aphorism.

### Aphorism V.

> *A full and firm conviction of conscience in a sincere soul—regarding a religion that includes some false elements, but no moral wickedness, and of such a nature that no amount of moral sincerity could discover their falsehood—is rightly called the Permissive Command of God to that soul, intended for either punishment or trial.*

This assertion, I hope, will appear both true and modest to all impartial judges. I add that this is the most I have asserted in this chapter, as anyone who reads it candidly and fairly may observe. For when I speak of God fixing the sincere and conscientious in a specific persuasion for a time through the inevitable paths of Providence, and how God is truly said to command a person when He conveys a practical persuasion to them (by whatever act of *Providence* it may be) so that there is no room left to doubt it is His command, and so on: it is obvious from the very way I speak,

### Chapter 7: Persuasion in the Mind of His Creature

I want to clarify that I do not understand this persuasion or command of God in any false religion (not even in the specific types of falsehoods we are discussing here) in a **positive** sense, but only a **permissive** one. I do not mean that in such a case God, as it were, rises from his seat to act or speak. Instead, he simply lets the natural course of things go on and does not stop the flow of secondary causes <note>Secondary causes: Natural events, human choices, or environmental factors that lead to an outcome without God performing a direct miracle.</note>. Such a persuasion is conveyed from God into the mind of a person by a **certain and effective permission** <note>original: *permissione certâ & efficaci*</note>.

This is the most that ever entered my mind while using these terms in this chapter regarding God conveying a false persuasion into the mind of his creature. Namely, that he does not do it by a positive and particular exercise of his power upon that creature, but only by an effective permission of secondary causes. This is actually less than what many interpreters seem to allow without hesitation. I was perhaps less cautious in my phrasing because I used a style parallel to the language of the Bible, which says of God, "*I harden*" and "*I deceive,*" and similar phrases, even though these are only to be understood **permissively**. Furthermore, I could not imagine anyone would be so uncharitable as to misinterpret me as strangely as I believe those have done who took offense at this chapter. For when I speak of the **trains of providence** and of the **intervention of providence**, it was very easy for them to understand that I meant nothing more than the **series** or **connections** of secondary causes. We imply as much in common speech (such as when we say it was a "good providence" that I met someone in a specific place, while others say "good luck," "bad luck," and the like). Additionally, learned writers themselves often use the terms **providence** <term>original: πρόνοια (pronoia)</term>, **fate** <term>original: εἰμαρμένη (heimarmene)</term>, and **chance** <term>original: τύχη (tyche)</term> interchangeably.

18. Therefore, to conclude, let us briefly summarize all the restrictions and limitations of this suspected assertion (which are already implied in the way it was handled) and see if it does not prove itself to be an innocent, modest, and harmless claim, even to the most rigid and severe judges. For:

**First**, as I have indicated in this chapter, this religion (which, despite having something false or erroneous in it, I claim to be the command of God) is so perfect that it professes the one and only true God, a life to come, and a blessed immortality for those who serve him in sincerity and truth.

**Secondly**, that which is supposed to be false or erroneous in this religion excludes any moral turpitude <term>moral turpitude: wicked, immoral, or shameful behavior.</term> and has nothing to do with what is properly considered sin.

**Thirdly**, this command is not a **positive** but a **permissive** command, even though this **permission** is **certain and effective**, as commentators say when they admit such a permission even in things that are immoral and wicked. That is not the case here, as shown in the second restriction, and therefore it makes our assertion exceedingly safe and beyond reproach.

**Fourthly**, this command to practice or profess such a religion is said to be for either the punishment of past faults or for further trial. The injunction and command may rightly be understood to apply to the part of the religion that is undeniably true, rather than the part that is erroneous. It is as if the command of a master to his servant should

...follows the form of a specific rule: *I want you to wait on me at such a meeting, even if your clothes are old or out of style.* The main weight of the command rests upon that undeniable duty—*serving his master*—which the master will not excuse, even though his servant is not dressed in the best fashion. In fact, it may even be the master’s pleasure that he should not be yet. But the servant has a full warrant to serve, and no man ought to hinder him from serving in the clothes he has. The same can be said of the **state of mind** of a religious person <note>original: "Religionist"</note> which is not yet free from error and ignorance, but is joined with **blameless sincerity** <note>original: "irreprehensible sincerity"</note>. Such a person is to serve God even in that less-refined or less-perfect state, because his Master has commanded him to do so; therefore, no man may rightfully hinder him.

Fifthly, and lastly: I do not claim that any person who is not sincere has received this command. Rather, the lack of the proper "garb" <note>In this analogy, the "garb" or "habit" refers to the person's beliefs or state of mind.</note> is his own fault, and he is therefore subject to all proper correction and punishment from those in authority.

Thus, our assertion is entirely harmless and inoffensive toward both God and man. By misunderstanding our meaning, some would create such a stir and drama about it as if it were nothing less than blasphemy; yet, when rightly understood, it is such a plain truth that even the greatest skeptic could not doubt it.

19. And so, I think I have fully addressed all the suspicious guesses or bad reports regarding those passages of the Tenth Chapter of my Tenth Book which seemed most paradoxical. I now believe myself well-prepared for a sufficient answer to the Seventh Objection **literally** <note>original: "in terminis," meaning "in its own terms" or "exactly as written"</note>, which is this:

### Objection VII.

> *He says that God may, and does, infuse into men false persuasions in matters of religion, using Islam <note>original: "Turcism"</note> and Judaism as examples, which contradict the Christian faith. (Book 10, chapter 10, pages 517, 518).*

This objection is presented sharply and seems, I confess, to stand in a very dangerous position. But in a specific answer to it, I say first: that nowhere in those pages, nor anywhere else, do I affirm that God **infuses** a false persuasion into men. That Scholastic word "**infusion**" <note>In traditional theology, "infusion" refers to God directly "pouring" a quality or grace into the soul through a supernatural act.</note> sounds quite contrary to my meaning, as if He "infused" falsehood in the same way He is said to infuse graces—by a **special** and **active** operation upon the mind. Instead, I have already fully declared that I understand everything I have said concerning God's conveying a false persuasion into a person in a **permissive** way, not an **active** one.

Secondly, it should be considered (as I noted in the previous section) that these persuasions which God is said to "convey" to any man in matters of religion are supposed by me to be free of all **moral wickedness** <note>original: "Turpitude"</note>. Furthermore, the conveyance is only permissive, which theologians allow even in the foulest acts of wickedness. So, we are safe from any harmful implications.

And lastly, although I do not hesitate to use **Islam** and **Judaism** as examples—even in those things where they contradict the Christian belief—yet...

Once again, I reply that this only applies to matters that involve no moral wickedness <note>original: "Turpitude"</note>. I assume an invincible ignorance <note>Invincible ignorance is a theological term for a lack of knowledge that a person cannot overcome by reasonable effort, meaning they are not morally responsible for it.</note> in those who are so persuaded, and that God’s role in conveying this persuasion is not active <note>original: "positive"</note>, but only permissive. As I noted before, theologians <note>original: "Divines"</note> do not hesitate to admit this permissive role even in actions that are truly and heinously immoral and sinful. 

However, in this case, I am assuming invincible ignorance—that the Jewish or Muslim person <note>In the 17th century, "Turk" was the standard term for Muslims.</note> has lived without any opportunity to be correctly instructed in the Christian religion, but is sincerely minded toward the truth wherever they may find it. This is clearly my assumption throughout this entire chapter and beyond, which plainly implies that the errors they hold do not properly have the nature of sin. Therefore, this seventh objection, though it seems dangerous at first glance, is easily, safely, and sufficiently answered by what I have already established. All that can be proven of this charge is only this: *that God permissively allows some defect in a person, which yet has neither any moral wickedness in it nor the nature of sin.* For the Scholastic philosophers include a "voluntary act" <note>original: *Actus voluntarius*</note> in the definition of sin, and have also determined that "invincible ignorance makes an act involuntary" <note>original: *Quod ignorantia invincibilis parit involuntarium*</note>. Thus, the edge of this objection is perfectly dulled, and its danger fully avoided.

## His Answer concerning Liberty in Religion. Chapter 8.

The ignorant disorder of the sectarians <term>Sectaries: a term used here for members of radical religious groups outside the established church</term> is criticized <note>original: "taxed"</note> for not obeying the commands of their superiors in matters that are truly debatable or indifferent.
16. To claim that political rights are forfeited in other cases is a dangerous undermining of the security of all Protestant princes, and serves no interest but that of the wicked Pope of Rome.

1. The eighth objection concerns *liberty of conscience*. I must admit that this right is a very direct consequence <note>original: "Consectary"</note> of the fifth aphorism in the previous chapter. Despite this, it has no worse consequence than preventing the persecution of sincere, though mistaken, men in matters of religion—people whose errors involve no moral depravity <note>original: "Turpitude"</note> and who are themselves of a peaceful and non-persecuting nature.

But if such a man as this is not allowed to keep what is his own because the Spirit of God has not yet fully enlightened him to reach a complete and perfect knowledge of the truth, it would introduce a principle with far worse consequences than protecting innocent men from religious persecution. Specifically, it would mean that *dominion is founded in grace* <term>Dominion being founded in Grace: the radical idea that only those in a state of God’s grace (the "elect") have the right to own property or hold political power</term>. This is one of the most ridiculous—and I wish it were only that—indeed, one of the most harmful principles ever adopted by the sectarians. It is a view that exposes not only the fortunes of private citizens, but even those of monarchs and princes, to the grasping tyranny of the Pope and the blind fury of any group of arrogant fanatics who, claiming to be the only "saints," will scramble to seize all power for themselves. 

This is that wild opinion of *Wycliffe* <note>John Wycliffe (c. 1320s–1384), an English theologian and reformer</note>, for which the more moderate Protestants rightly criticize him, but which the Papists <note>A derogatory term for Roman Catholics</note> wrongly condemn him for. In reality, it is the very same principle the Pope uses in all his savage and barbarous treatment of those he chooses to call heretics—from the greatest prince to the lowest peasant. It is clear, therefore, that our claim excludes a principle of the most dangerous consequence imaginable to princes and monarchs as well as the common people; however, I do not see any negative consequences arising from my own position.

2. Furthermore, does not the primary interest of Christianity lie in this right to *liberty of conscience*? And am I not speaking of it here? I am not referring to minor disagreements among the Reformed Churches themselves. If this principle were once accepted worldwide, would it not keep the *Turks* <note>In the 17th century, "Turk" was the standard term for Muslims or the Ottoman Empire</note> from persecuting any sincere *Catholic* <note>original: "Papist"</note>, and the *Catholics* from persecuting any sincere *Protestant*? Would it not make *Protestants* very careful and gentle, avoiding the harsh treatment of their own sincere and conscientious members over differences in opinion or ceremony? In my view, this would be the safest and most appropriate character <note>original: "Complexion"</note> for the Church of Christ that any good Christian could hope for.

3. And truly, for my own part, I cannot hide my judgment on this matter; I must openly declare that a Christian who is as sincere as I have described—someone blameless in their behavior, heart-felt in their belief in all the essentials of Christianity, and filled with the fear and awe of the

### Chapter 8: His Answer Regarding Liberty in Religion.

...before God <note>original: "Divine Majesty"</note> that he cannot help but keep a good conscience in all things, as if in the sight of God. He is sincerely loyal and faithful to his Prince, and ready and desiring to comply with his spiritual governors in anything his conscience will permit. His conscience is so sound that it feels obliged to comply with them in all things it recognizes as indifferent <term>Indifferent: matters of religious practice that are not essential to salvation or explicitly commanded by scripture, and thus subject to church authority</term> and not against the Word of God. He would do this rather than have his right to an exemption become an excuse for others to abuse this liberty of conscience—specifically those who would be irresponsible <note>original: "wanton"</note> or false to the Church. 

I say, to persecute such a man as this, even if he is mistaken or entangled in some non-essential <note>original: "preter-essential"</note> opinions and scruples—which his obvious sincerity demonstrates to the world are not within his power to avoid—I say, for anyone to crudely harm such a man, or to offend one of these "little ones," would be the same as touching the apple of God’s eye and being harmful to Christ himself, who is so protective of them. I am so confident in the clarity of this case that I dare appeal even to the most hard-hearted person to judge it. And yet, this is the sum of my entire plea for liberty of conscience in this and the two following chapters, at least regarding any differences between Protestants in any nation. You can see that the *Protestant* I plead for is of such a faithful and moderate character, and of such sound judgment, that even though it affects him personally, he still thinks it fitting that the whims of men should be restrained by financial fines to avoid the abuse of an overly-indulged *liberty*. He believes this so that men are not too eager to break the *order* of the Church to follow their own fantasies, or the fantasies of more cunning and confident deceivers. I think no man who wishes well for the peace and prosperity of the Protestant Church will complain about such a law.

4. But the aim of my entire argument is more properly directed toward resolving cases involving nations with several different religions. Therefore, those who wrongly interpret my handling of this controversy are being very unfair. This argument actually supports a significant interest of the Christian religion in general, rather than harming the interest of any particular Church—unless it is the *Roman* Church. That Church is so exceedingly corrupt, yet so allegedly infallible, that I must confess nothing can be as terrifying to her as this right of *liberty of conscience*, even in the blameless circumstances I just described.

But it need not be so for any *Protestant* Church. This Hero brandishes a sharp sword from his mouth, and his name and title are proclaimed before him, for he is explicitly called *The Word of God*. <margin>Revelation 19</margin> But this is an unexpected departure from our topic; let us return to the point at hand.

I say then that for all Protestant Churches, whose religion is based on the *Bible*, it is no great loss or *impropriety* <note>original: "Indecorum"</note> for them to offer a well-limited indulgence (as I described above) to their weak but sincere followers <note>original: "Nurslings"</note>. It is no different than the head of a household allowing—or even providing—separate accommodations for those family members whose health or constitutions make them less fit to dine at the common table. This does not diminish his authority; rather, it is a more discreet and commendable exercise of it.

Where everything is merely dead painting or carving, everything can be arranged according to the whims <note>original: "curiosity of the fancy"</note> of the artist. Similarly, idle and sterile virgins might, with less danger, force their bodies into the extreme slenderness that suits their own foolish imaginations. But every true *Church of Christ* where a *spirit of life* exists (and she must never forget that this is her true condition) is like a pregnant woman. Therefore, she must above all things take care not to be too tightly laced, for fear of causing dreadful miscarriages. These principles are so fair and, in a sense, so necessary, that they cannot be hidden from anyone to whom the life of God has been revealed.

5. *But you will say this is only speaking in general terms; I will therefore state the current objection in the formal words of the opponent.*

## Objection 8

He says that *Liberty of religion is the common and natural right of all nations and persons*. (Book 10, chapter 11, page 521). And the *sovereign power of God sets the sincere believer <note>original: "Religionist"</note> free from external force and power*. (Ibid., page 520). By the "sincere believer," he means everyone who truly believes that God exists and that he rewards those who seek him. However, he argues that more is required of such a sincere believer than what is found among the Turks <note>In this period, "Turks" was often used as a general term for Muslims</note>. He claims this view overthrows all laws for church government and discipline.

### Chapter VIII. His Answer regarding Liberty in Religion.

...common and natural right of all nations and persons. <margin>Hugo Grotius, *On the Law of War and Peace*, Book 2, Chapter 20.</margin>
And truly, the ancient Christians and Church Fathers spoke more openly regarding this subject, and without such caution and restriction. *Grotius* gives several examples in his *On the Law of War and Peace* <note>original: "De Jure Belli & Pacis"</note>. He cites one of the canons of the Council of *Toledo*: "The Holy Synod commands that from now on, no one shall use force; for God has mercy on whom He wills, and whom He wills, He hardens" <note>original: "Præcipit Sancta Synodus nemini deinceps vim inferre; Cui enim vult Deus miseretur, & quem vult indurat"</note>. Also *Tertullian* says: "The New Law does not avenge itself with a punishing sword" <note>original: "Lex nova non se vindicat ultore gladio"</note>. He also cites the Constitutions of *Clement*, *Athanasius*, and *Chrysostom* for the same purpose—authors who explicitly exclude force and compulsion in bringing men over to Christianity.

Also remarkable is what Bishop *Jewel* notes from *Chrysostom* in his 19th Homily on *Saint Matthew*: "Does a sheep ever pursue a wolf? No, but the wolf pursues the sheep. For so Cain persecuted Abel, not Abel Cain; so Ishmael persecuted Isaac, not Isaac Ishmael; so the Jews persecuted Christ, not Christ the Jews; heretics persecuted Christians, not Christians heretics. Therefore, by their fruits you shall know them" <note>original: "Nunquid ovis lupum persequitur aliquando? Non, sed lupus ovem. Sic enim Cain persecuted est Abel, non Abel Cain: sic Ismael persecutus est Isaac, non Isaac Ismael: sic Judæi Christum, non Christus Judæos; Hæretici Christianos, non Christiani Hæreticos. Ergò ex fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos"</note>. By this, he plainly implies that persecution for the sake of conscience <note>original: "Conscience sake"</note> is a very un-Christian or anti-Christian symptom. And he speaks sharply again in the same Homily: "Whoever you see rejoicing in the blood of persecution is a wolf" <note>original: "Quem videris in sanguine persecutionis gaudentem, Lupus est"</note>. He that is a persecutor is no sheep of Christ, but a wolf. And lastly (for it would be an endless task to pursue this common topic), there is that pointed suggestion from the Apostle: *He who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit.* There is such a great antipathy between the carnal and the truly born-again <note>original: "Regenerate"</note> Christian. This should make any man afraid to feel any persecuting impulses arise in his breast, as these are indications of a nature like that of *Cain*, *Ishmael*, or a wolf, and a certain sign that he is none of Christ's sheep.

Therefore, I must admit I do not see what is so hateful or monstrous about my assertion. It is a conclusion drawn from arguments that I honestly do not know how to avoid, nor, I think, does anyone else. They are contained in this tenth chapter of the tenth book. For my own part, I had no motive to write as I did except for the mere love of truth and a serious desire to promote the interests of Christianity.

7. Secondly, as for that addition from page 520, it is not a new accusation but contains reasons for the previous assertion: namely, that considering the sincerity of the religious person—in which he is so faithfully and genuinely bound to the sovereign power of God—he should not be dealt with harshly by any inferior power. This assumes he possesses the integrity and sincerity that I have referred to throughout this subject, which I described more explicitly in the proof of my first aphorism in the previous chapter, as well as in the third section of this one. And truly, I think if anyone reads those descriptions of the sincere religious person I am pleading for attentively, they will not hesitate to declare that such a person would surely be acquitted before the strictest judges—even a *Minos* or *Rhadamanthus* <note>In Greek mythology, Minos and Rhadamanthus were legendary judges of the underworld known for their absolute inflexibility and justice.</note>—because the person is so innocent...

We may as well expect that the diameter of a circle should be proportional to its circumference, or the diagonal of a square to its side, as expect that one thing or one truth should serve all purposes and all occasions. Indeed, though it were in our power to create truth as we please, and to set that stamp and title upon whatever proposition would serve our purpose best, yet we would find that it would not serve all emergencies, nor fit all occasions, nor be exempt from all exceptions.

As for example, because this position [**That liberty of religion is the natural and common right of all nations and persons**] does not please some, take the opposite to it: [**That no nation or person can claim liberty of religion as their right**]. Will not this position prove just as **incommensurable** to human affairs and be burdened with just as great inconveniences?

For if no nation or person has any right to profess any religion except what is in all points true, then every nation (since they are persuaded of the truth of their own religion, otherwise they would not belong to it) will presume they have the right to persecute any other nation that differs in religion from them. <header>Chapter VIII. *His Answer touching Liberty in Religion.*</header>

...different religion as false. This would set the whole world at odds; it would incite the **Muslims** <note>original: "Turk"</note> against the **Christians**, and cause dissenting **Christians** to fight one another. It would bring the **Pope** back to rule over **Protestant** kings and princes, and arm the **sectarian** mobs—who fancy themselves **inspired** <note>original: "Inspiradoes"; a term for those claiming direct, private divine revelation</note>—against the orderly, reformed churches.

Furthermore, if no private individual has the right to religious liberty, then he is bound to the religion of his prince and nation, whatever it may be. (For if he is allowed to judge for himself, his right is preserved.) But sober and godly men usually view this as a great insult to religion. It reeks too much of outright **atheism**, as if all religions were the same and were merely various methods for governing the people.

And lastly, taking away this right to religious liberty and exposing dissenters to persecution is a doctrine with very biased and harmful consequences. From this, all atheists and profane people will profit immensely, as there is no obstacle to prevent them from enjoying all the pleasures of this life. However, the painful and unbearable burden—not only of losing their fortunes but of suffering cruel persecution—will fall only upon those who are conscientious and have the fear of God before their eyes. These are significant disadvantages of the position opposed to ours (besides whatever other arguments are produced in my treatise, which I need not repeat here), if any negative consequences can steer a man away from a popular opinion and reveal its falsehood.

II. To answer more directly and satisfactorily: I say that the right to religious liberty, as I have defined it, has no negative consequences at all. It does not overthrow any proper laws for church government and discipline. It can only oppose the interests of a church that *ought* to be opposed—namely, the Church of **Rome**. But for those churches that are reformed according to the pattern of the earliest and most **Apostolic** times, they need not fear that our assertion will overthrow the laws of their church government. Rather, it will enlarge their jurisdiction—by which I mean it will help others to accept or imitate similar laws. For what hinders men from coming over to the truth except those **Babylonian** <note>original: "Babylonish"; in this context, a Protestant rhetorical term for the perceived corruption or tyranny of the Roman Catholic Church</note> chains of barbaric and anti-Christian persecution? The fear of this persecution acts as the fetters that hold them in that **Egyptian** bondage and captivity <note>A biblical metaphor for slavery or spiritual oppression</note>.

Again, when there was no external force or coercion to make men Christians—as was the case for several hundred years—were there no laws for church government and discipline during all that time? Therefore, religious liberty does not take away or overthrow all laws for church government and discipline; instead, it prevents men from making any unacceptable and scandalous ones. This was one reason that kept the Church from that anti-Christian decline during the entire time before the Empire officially converted to Christianity. But external force imprints truth and falsehood, superstition and religion alike upon the **cowed** <note>original: "daw'd"; dazed, intimidated, or overawed</note> spirits of men.

# His Answer touching Liberty in Religion. Chap. VIII.

Thirdly, in my answer to the fourth objection, I have plainly shown that I allow the Church the power to order and appoint **matters of indifference** <term>original: "things indifferent"; religious practices or ceremonies not explicitly commanded or forbidden by Scripture, which the Church may regulate for the sake of order</term>. Therefore, I cannot be thought to intend the overthrow of all laws for Church government by this assertion. For my judgment is that *schism* is such a heinous and perilous sin that no institution of the Church—provided she stays within the bounds of matters of indifference (which the Church of **Rome** does not)—should excuse a person from joining in public worship with the national Church in which they live, or from conforming to her orders.

Fourthly, I plainly declare (as I hinted at first) that this right to religious liberty is forfeitable. I particularly express how it may be lost: namely, *by mixing with it such principles as are contrary to good manners and civil rights, or are repugnant to that very principle of liberty of which we speak.* This forfeiture is so broad and, in a way, so universal, that in the very chapters on this subject, I acknowledge the theory I plead for is very difficult to put into practice. So, there is room enough—and perhaps too much—left in the world for the exercise of ecclesiastical jurisdiction.

Fifthly, the person for whom I plead an exemption from any harsh treatment is one I imagine to be exceptionally simple and sincere-hearted—a true **Nathanael** <note>A reference to John 1:47, where Jesus describes Nathanael as a man "in whom there is no guile" or deceit.</note> in whom there is no guile. I have drawn his character once already, and I will bring him into view again, though in a more condensed draft. 

His conduct is beyond reproach; he holds an unshaken belief in all the essentials of the Christian religion; his conscience is sacred to him, and he does all things as if in the sight and presence of God. He maintains unbreakable loyalty and faithfulness to his Prince and complies with his Church to the utmost that his conscience will permit—that is, in all matters of indifference. His conscience is so well-regulated that he thinks it his duty to do so. Lastly, he has such a deep appreciation for order and unity in the Church, and is so wary of having the common interest of **Reformed Christianity** weakened and shattered by needless and mischievous schisms, that even if he himself were to be punished—being unable, due to some invincible scrupulosity, to submit to every order of his Church—he would very willingly undergo any tolerable **fines** <term>original: "mulcts"</term> rather than allow his own immunity to give an occasion for the either the restless or the malicious to abuse the claim of liberty of conscience to ruin and undermine the peace and safety of the **Reformed Religion**. 

This is the character of the **Sincere Religionist**, for whom I seem so concerned that he may receive fair treatment in all parts of the world. If others knew his worth, I think they would sooner reward him than harm him. They would set a great price upon him as a rare jewel, for there are so very few such spirits to be found in a whole province, or even a whole kingdom—perhaps not as many in number as the seven gates of **Thebes** or the seven mouths of the River **Nile**.

And lastly, so that there may be no escape for hypocrites and those who pretend to be sincere only to create schisms or abandon the Church, I set up this barrier in the twelfth chapter: namely, *a solemn oath, including a profound call for divine vengeance upon soul and body, asserting that nothing moves them to depart from the Church but a pure conviction of conscience; and that they have no secular design at all in their change, no worldly gain...*

13. This *knowledge of the Lord*, which protects the world from injury and wrong, is certainly not any *argumentative hair-splitting* <term>original: "Disputative Subtilty"</term> or meticulous decision regarding the *mystery of His nature* <term>original: "Essence"</term>. Rather, it is the actual *participation in the Divine Nature through a manifestation of life and spiritual awareness* <term>original: "Dispensation of Life and Sense"</term>. For there can be a real separation from the life of God even where there are many meticulous disputes <term>original: "Altercations"</term> concerning His nature and His more incomprehensible attributes, as well as great study of and claims to the deepest speculations about His unknowable characteristics. But the knowledge of God that brings this happiness to mankind, as mentioned in the Prophets, is not *academic theory* <term>original: "Scholastick Theory"</term>, but a *living and felt experience* <term>original: "Vital and Sensible enjoyment"</term>. *God is love, and he who lives in love lives in God, and God in him.* <note>1 John 4:16</note> And again, *He who does not love does not know God, for God is love.* <note>1 John 4:8</note>

Therefore, it is this knowledge of God—which is a *manifestation of life and awareness*—from which those truly happy times of the **Messiah** <note>original: "Messias"</note> are described in **Isaiah**. This is that true anointing <term>original: "Unction"</term> of the Spirit, that precious ointment poured upon **Aaron’s** head, running down to the very edges of his garments <note>A reference to Psalm 133:2, where the anointing of the High Priest Aaron symbolizes unity and divine blessing.</note>. When this outpouring overflows the earth, as the waters cover the sea, all wickedness, cruelty, and harmful behavior will certainly be drowned in such a holy and sacred flood.

# Chapter VIII. His Answer regarding Liberty in Religion.

...Christ’s immediate representative <note>original: "Vicegerent"</note>, and obedient to our spiritual fathers. We should be obedient not only in doing and professing those things that are clearly of an absolute rightness and truth, but also in reaching a compromise with them for the sake of peace in matters that are truly debatable. We must comply with them for the sake of unity and good order in all things of an indifferent nature <term>things of an "indifferent nature" (adiaphora) are ceremonies or practices not specifically commanded or forbidden by the Bible</term>, *not pleasing ourselves, but every one pleasing his neighbor for his good to edification*, as the Apostle speaks. This is the most wholesome, the most strengthening, and the most robust constitution of the Church of Christ that can be desired—one that will most certainly wear out all the assaults of her enraged enemies.

15. For it is plain and evident that we are in a state of war with the Church of **Rome**, who are more cunning in their military discipline than is to be wished. The clergy and all the religious orders of that Church are one perpetual and actually formed army of that **King of Pride** <note>A polemical reference to the Pope.</note>, and all his emissary priests and **Jesuits** are so many scouts of this great Universal <note>original: "Oecumenical"</note> Commander of **Rome**. And shall the true Church of Christ, in the mean time, keep no better order than a herd of oxen, which are seen every now and then to turn against one another and gore each other with their horns? 

We are to consider ourselves as one military body, as a beautiful army with displayed colors. We must keep rank and file, moving slower or faster at the discretion and word of our commanders. Therefore, whatever readiness of mind there may be, or whatever ease and skill in doing things that make a commendable show in themselves, the exercise of those gifts must be regulated according to the laws that concern the whole body. If the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets even as individual men, they ought much more to be subject to the commands of their superiors and to the interest of the whole Church, so that all things may be done with unity and order. 

But some men find themselves filled with a greater fervency and zeal for **formalities**, or believe they have more popular gifts for **prayer** and **exhortation**. For these men to burst out and run ahead in their careers without waiting for the direction of their superiors would be as if a sudden whim <note>original: "the Toy"</note> should seize the best-mounted troopers to set off galloping madly just because they find their horses run so freely. Such behavior would turn the orderly march of the army into a confused horse race and throw the ranks into a retreat <note>original: "rout"</note> even without an assault or pursuit from any enemy.

Therefore, everyone ought to have a disciplined and subdued spirit. We must be prudent and deeply aware of the common interest of the whole of **Reformed Christianity**. Every person should regulate his actions according to that law, rather than acting according to the promptings of his own private **natural inclination** <note>original: "Genius"</note> to please himself for personal profit or popularity. He should be governed by his superiors in matters of an indifferent nature and keep "rank and file" in his march. He must not break order, even if the path is not a smooth "carpet-way," but requires him to sometimes tread in the wet and other times upon sharp stones. To be so delicate as to refuse to go against one’s own private opinion in indifferent matters is not so much a matter of staying true to **conscience** as it is indulging one’s mere **temperament** <term>original: "Complexion"; referring to one's physical and emotional disposition</term>. It is to lose the opportunity of subduing one's lower nature and of strengthening those faculties of the soul that are more purely rational and intellectual. # Chapter IX. His Answer regarding the Lack of Conviction of Conscience, etc.

8. I have, I hope, by this time abundantly satisfied this ninth objection; we come now to the tenth and last.

->Objection X.<-

*He says that the Laws of God are like words in an unknown tongue until the Conscience is convinced (Book 10, Chapter 10, as I recall). From this, it necessarily follows that it is no sin to act against these Laws if a person believes it to be lawful. Thus, those who thought they were doing God a good service by killing the Apostles were not sinners for doing so.*

This seems to be a very sharp and stinging objection, purposefully saved for the final place so that the entire "Decalogue" <note>original: "Decalogue"; usually referring to the Ten Commandments, here used to mean a set of ten objections</note> of objections may end like a well-crafted epigram, where the greatest wit and life are found in the final conclusion. But no objection can do any real damage to solid truth. Although I must confess that this objection is very stoutly and sharply launched, like a dart thrown from a strong and agile arm, my security lies in the fact that it has missed the mark. It does not reach the actual heart of the question. 

For in the book and chapter cited, the words upon which this objection is raised are these: *namely, that the immediate dictate of Conscience in a soul that is sincere is the Command of God; but that before his voice is heard there, his will is not promulgated to that person. For nothing but the conviction of Conscience that this or that is the will of God is properly the promulgation <term>The formal proclamation or making known of a law</term> of his will to every particular soul; otherwise, it is only like the recital of the Law in a language the people do not understand, and therefore it can take no hold upon them.* 

To this, also add my marginal note: *This is how it is for those who are sincere; but in those who are not, it is like the stopping of the ears against the reading of the Law in a known language.* 

It is plain here that the most essential part of the question has been omitted by leaving out the phrase [*in those who are sincere*]. Therefore, the objection—though very strong—cannot touch or harm any of our positions through those fearsome consequences. This is because of how I have stated the question in this tenth chapter, both regarding the *person* and also regarding the *subject matter* of the *Command*.

9. For I assume the person is *Sincere*, and what I mean by *Sincerity* I have fully explained under my first Aphorism <term>A concise statement of a principle or truth</term>, and there is no need to repeat it here. As for the *matter* of the Command, I assume it to be things that are not discoverable by the "light of Nature" <note>Moral truths that should be obvious to any rational human being without special revelation</note>, such as the belief in historical events that happened many ages ago, and the religious precepts and ceremonies that depend upon them. 

But I have expressly declared in my fourth Aphorism (taken from this tenth chapter) *that nothing that has any real wickedness <note>original: "turpitude"</note> or immorality in it can justly be claimed to be the voice or Command of God to either the sincere or the insincere.* From all of this, we are well-equipped to answer this last objection.

I say, therefore, that such Laws of God as are merely *Positive* <term>Laws based on specific divine decrees rather than universal morality, such as specific rituals or historical requirements</term>, or those that depend upon history and miraculous revelation, are like words in an unknown tongue to someone who is *truly sincere* until their conscience is convinced. This is what I say, and this is all I have said in that tenth chapter, and no ill consequences can follow from it. For while I will not argue that the *insincere* might be guilty of breaking even those *positive laws* (because who knows—if they had kept a good conscience, God might have...

<meta>This page continues the author's response to the tenth objection, which argued that if laws aren't binding until the conscience is convinced, then people could commit crimes like murder in God's name without sinning. The author is refuting this by distinguishing between specific religious decrees (Positive Laws) and universal morality (Moral Law).</meta>

### His Answer regarding the Lack of Conviction of Conscience, Chapter IX.

...impart those truths to him as well?) yet for the *sincere* person, who has done and continues to do everything they can to understand and perform the will of God in all things, I say, if he is not yet convinced, it may well be looked upon as a secret mystery <note>original: "Arcanum"</note> of Providence that he is not. I believe he is justly excused from any obligation to those laws, or any guilt for breaking them, because they have not been announced to him, even though he has tried with all attention and desire to hear their voice in his conscience. This is according to our second maxim <note>original: "Aphorism"</note>: *That where there is no law announced, it is no sin or transgression to act or profess the contrary.* Otherwise, the Heathens might be judged as violators of the ceremonial Law of Moses, even those who never had any opportunity to know it; whereas the Apostle says, <margin>Romans 2:12</margin> *that as many as have sinned without the Law shall also perish without the Law*. As Clarius <note>Isidore Clarius, a 16th-century Italian theologian</note> notes on this text, this means, "They will not perish because they violated the written Law, but because of that Law which was engraved upon their souls" <note>original: "Non peribunt propterea quòd scriptam Legem violaverint, sed illam quæ animis illorum insculpta fuit"</note>.

To this you may add that "invincible ignorance" <term>ignorance that a person cannot overcome through reasonable effort</term> makes an act involuntary. According to the schools of theology, sin is a *voluntary act* <note>original: "Actus voluntarius"</note>, as I observed above. Therefore, there is no problem in admitting that the transgression or failure to observe these types of laws by one who is "invincibly ignorant" and unconvinced of them (as we suppose a truly sincere person to be) does not have the proper nature of sin in that person, though it might in someone who is insincere. This failure to receive the truth, or this lack of conviction, may be a trial, a punishment, or a fatal defect, but it does not properly have the nature of sin, because it is entirely and perfectly involuntary and absolutely out of the person's power to change. For the nature of sincerity is to do all we can, and no one can do more than that. Therefore, I will easily admit that it is no sin to act against—that is, to break or not observe—such "Positive Laws" <term>specific commands or rituals decreed by God, rather than universal moral principles</term> of God, as long as a person remains unconvinced in the circumstances I have described, firmly believing that it is lawful for him not to observe them and being fully persuaded they do not apply to him.

10. Nor will that horrible consequence follow, which was added to the end of the objection: *That then those who thought they were doing God a good service in killing the Apostles were no sinners for doing so.* For this is directly against my fourth maxim: *That nothing that has any real filthiness or immorality in it can justly be claimed to be the voice or command of God; nor can that which is really and admittedly moral be claimed not to be His command, for either the sincere or the insincere.* I have also given the reason for this: because the light and Law of Nature, and of eternal and immutable morality, cries louder in the soul of the *sincere* person than to allow him to accept such foul impulses, much less to view them as coming from God. Nor could a sincere person be ignorant of any essential morality as if it were not God's command. As for the *insincere* person, since he stops his ears against that more holy and evident Law, his false delusions or stubbornness in wickedness are most justly blamed on himself.

Or, if you prefer, it can be put more briefly: this objection is completely off-track and misses the point of the question. Our debate does not concern the eternal Moral Law of God, but only "Positive Laws" (specific decrees). <header>Chapter 9: In what cases it takes away Sin.</header>

...those who profess one God and a life to come. To kill such people under the pretense of heresy against the Jewish religion was, I believe, a most hideous murder, especially since they were such simple and sincere people. This goes against that Royal Law of God written in *capital letters* upon our souls: *Do not do to another what you would not have done to yourself* <note>original: "Quod tibi fieri non vis, alteri ne feceris"</note>. Therefore, their belief that they were doing God a good service could not excuse them from the crime, nor make it anything other than sin for them. For it is not the *firmness* of our *conviction* or *lack of conviction* that will guarantee an act is not sinful, but rather the perfect sincerity of the person. This applies only if their *conviction* regarding what is false, or their *lack of conviction* regarding what is true, arises from no fault of their own, but is "invincible ignorance" <term>ignorance that cannot be overcome by reasonable effort</term>—and only in such matters that even the most refined moral character cannot reach the knowledge of.

This is the true state of the question, from which the killing of the Apostles can find no excuse. For it is impossible that someone with such a sincere heart and morally upright mind as I assume in this debate should be invincibly ignorant of the fact that killing such holy and harmless men as the Apostles would be murder, or something extremely similar to it. For those who are *insincere* and immoral, sin always lies at their own door. And this, I hope, will fully satisfy this last objection.

# Chapter 10: A Summary of All His Answers.

I have clearly shown that, in my view, a "convinced conscience" will not excuse any act that contains any moral wickedness <note>original: "Turpitude"</note>.

And while in the ninth objection I am accused of attacking all Church government and leaders, including our own, I have made it evident that I have not spoken against any Church government at all—unless it is in my Preface. In that section, I briefly conclude that the Presbyterian system is not "by Divine Right" <note>original: *Jure Divino*</note>, which is still not an attack on that form of government. As for the spiritual leaders themselves, I have attacked none, though I have freely criticized the notorious failures of some. Regarding our own leaders, I have made it clear that I could not have been talking about them, because they were not then in existence, but were *politically* dead when I wrote that treatise <note>The author refers to the period during the English Civil War and Interregnum when the Church of England's hierarchy of bishops was suppressed</note>. In the preface to my *Synopsis*, I argue that God has miraculously raised them up again as the true successors of His witnesses from the *First Reformation* here in *England*. 

Lest some call this *flattery*—just as others have mistaken my words elsewhere for *attacking* and *railing*—I cannot miss this chance to declare how far I am from intending any flattery. Rather, I believe this to be a solid truth that should not be hidden. If those whom it most concerns believe this, it may give them a greater obligation to persist and move forward in the path and footsteps of their revered predecessors, who were such wise and zealous rejecters of the Church of *Rome*. If there are any who would dampen their zeal in this matter, I will declare to all the world that they are worse enemies to the *English Episcopacy* <term>the system of government by bishops in the Church of England</term> than the fanatics <note>original: "Phanaticks"; a term often used for radical religious dissenters</note> themselves. Therefore, it is not out of *flattery*, but out of true *faithfulness*, that I have spoken so grandly in that preface regarding the miraculous restoration of our Gracious Sovereign and the Church.

Again, while in the eighth objection I am charged with pleading for a "Liberty of Conscience" that would overthrow all Church government and discipline, I have shown that I am far from supporting such a liberty. In fact, I have restrained and bounded it with such limitations that those who would abuse that claimed right will think I have taken all liberty away from them.

Moreover, in the seventh objection, I am charged with holding that God can and does put false beliefs into men's minds regarding religion. I have clearly shown that I do not claim He "infuses" such beliefs, but only that He may be said to convey them *permissively* (by allowing the course of external causes to continue without His special intervention). This is no more than what most theologians admit regarding even the greatest sins.

Regarding the sixth objection, which suggests a hint of *Nestorianism* <term>a heresy claiming Christ had two separate personhoods, one human and one divine, rather than two natures in one person</term>, I have demonstrated from the records of the ancient Councils that I have directly and specifically refuted *Nestorianism* in my own treatise. In those passages where they try to find suspicion of that heresy, I have actually spoken in agreement with the ancient, accepted Confessions of Faith.

And as for the fifth objection, where I am said to call Christ’s Divine...
